Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season and will be the largest storm system to make landfall in the region since Hurricane Helene in September 2024. Hurricane Isaias’s forecasted path toward the Gulf Coast has already impacted crude oil and natural gas production in the region. The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. The U.S. Gulf Coast is home to a large portion of the U.S. refining fleet, and the impacts from Hurricane Isaias could affect refinery operations . events.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
events.summary: Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal in New Mexico. The penalty comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data. A New Mexico district court judge said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences." Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal." "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." Meta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reaction Tesla earnings loom after Musk calls SpaceX merger a 'good idea' Intel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind schedule Investors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act.

events.title: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for misleading Facebook users
events.summary: A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties Wednesday after a jury found in September that the social media giant misled users about their data privacy. Why it matters: The penalties come nearly a decade after the Cambridge Analytica scandal first broke and signal that Big Tech can face significant financial consequences for misleading users about their privacy. Driving the news: Judge Francis Mathew determined the penalty amount Wednesday, handing New Mexico a win as the only state to take its claims to trial after 48 others settled. Mathew concluded New Mexico was entitled to $219.5 billion based on the state's maximum $5,000 penalty multiplied by 43,899,720 violations. He reduced that to $25 billion. Meta did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. The company has previously said it expects to appeal the decision. Catch up quick: In September, a New Mexico jury said Meta had committed 43 million "willful violations" of the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act. Mathew found that Facebook's privacy controls failed to give users meaningful control over their data and that third-party app developers could access their information through the platform's systems. Mathew found Mark Zuckerberg knew users didn't understand how data privacy works, and exploited that, noting that the CEO had once written that users "probably don't understand their current privacy settings or care about who sees their updates." Zuckerberg also wrote that the company should give users "a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don't encourage it." Zoom out: The suit followed reporting that revealed data firm Cambridge Analytica had harvested data from more than 50 million Facebook users to craft political ads during the 2016 election. After the scandal, Facebook promised more transparency, but the court found Meta failed to consistently inform users when their data was misused. events.title: GM's OnStar gets an AI makeover — but humans will still answer when airbags deploy
events.summary: GM executives confirmed to Business Insider that humans are still staffing OnStar call centers to handle emergencies. General Motors GM says it's keeping humans in its OnStar call centers to help with emergencies. It comes as OnStar is getting a fresh makeover, complete with AI. "The stakes are too high," an exec told BI about the human-in-the-loop. GM is giving OnStar an AI overhaul. The automaker says it is not coming for the person who answers when your airbags deploy. On Wednesday, during the company's tech conference, GM Forward, Ed Nightingale, GM's vice president of digital products, told Business Insider that the automaker would continue to use human OnStar staffers on emergency calls to contact first responders. "That's something that isn't changing," Nightingale said. "We feel that, when it comes to a crash or a problem being solved, they want to make sure that there's a human in the loop. The stakes are too high." The company declined to comment on how long those call-center humans will be a part of its OnStar plans. Humans-in-the-loop are a notable constraint on GM's AI ambitions. Other AI-enabled companies, such as SpaceX, have recently highlighted how few customer calls are routed to humans. It also comes as the company gives OnStar — its 30-year-old in-car emergency service — a much bigger job. GM showed off OnStar AI on Wednesday. It's a new voice assistant designed to understand a vehicle and the driver using it. The automaker said it can answer questions about vehicle alerts, control some functions, plan routes around bad weather, and offer more context-aware suggestions, including from information through a driver's digital calendar. The assistant subscription will arrive first on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq via an over-the-air update in the coming months, GM said. Other vehicles will follow. GM also plans to unify its brand-specific mobile apps under the OnStar AI name next summer. Onstage, Sterling Anderson, GM's chief product officer, said the company was turning the 30-year-old service into "an intelligent platform." The shift is part of a large bet from GM. GM is focusing heavily on its tech capabilities. On recent earnings calls, CEO Mary Barra has highlighted GM's subscription products . Anderson previously told Business Insider about how AI has allowed the company to cut product development time in half , starting with the GMC Hummer EV, which only took 20 months of development. Industry-average product development is typically around 5 years. On Wednesday, the company also highlighted the development of its hands-off, eyes-off self-driving features, set to make their debut in the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. GM still has to persuade drivers that the new tools are valuable enough to use — and, in some cases, pay for. Nightingale said subscriptions only retain customers when drivers can see the benefit. events.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
events.summary: Meta has been hit with numerous legal fines this year Published 21 October 2026, 19:01 BST Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices. A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data. "The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices". Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful. The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety. New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal. That firm utilized data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time. New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too. Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added. Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been. They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said Wednesday. "Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable." The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional. Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter. He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021. Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order. While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine. It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices. New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children. The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children". California and several other states had collectively sued Meta over similar issues related to a lack of child safety features on Meta's platforms and resulting harms to children. Meta and the states reached a mutual settlement deal, which did not include a fine or any admission of wrongdoing, to end that case only a few days into what was expected to be a multi-week trial. events.title: BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds
events.summary: BlackRock's Rick Rieder is bullish on this area of the credit market for the first time in a "long time." The CIO of global fixed income lays out his fourth-quarter fixed-income outlook in an exclusive interview. Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview. Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration. "Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook , released Wednesday. That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance." While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus. The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC) , which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit. Best opportunities include hyperscalers Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3. That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet , Amazon , Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG. "They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it." Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July , that stood at 8.5%. That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised. "Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield." Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names. "There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be." The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out. Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle , which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits. Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve , which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool . The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said. "They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure." Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added. Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

events.title: GM is betting compute and AI will help it compete with Chinese automakers
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When GM announced its new fourth-generation EV platform on Wednesday, what the automaker didn’t share was almost as notable as what it did. The new EV platform, part of a series of technology-focused announced during its annual GM Forward event in New York, didn’t talk about suspension geometries, dash-to-axle ratios, and torsional rigidity, all nerdy automotive terms that translate to how people will experience a car. Is it supple or sporty? Does it have a refined stance? When it hits a pothole, does it feel like a bank vault or a paper plate? Instead, GM’s announcement centered on novel battery chemistries, revamped electric motors, and an entirely new central computing platform and electrical architecture that will connect every system in the car, including acceleration and power, steering, braking, and active safety features as well as software. Lots and lots of software. “We think vehicles can become a more capable and helpful part of everyday life if we make them spaces that understand context, reduce friction, and give people back moments that would otherwise be consumed by the demands of the road,” Sterling Anderson, executive vice president, global product, and chief product officer at GM, told TechCrunch in a recent interview. That sure doesn’t sound like a traditional automaker’s pitch. Then again, since the arrival of Tesla, Rivian, and Chinese automakers, the industry hasn’t been the same. Ride and handling still matter, but they’re table stakes. What sets vehicles apart today is largely defined by software. Anderson has talked about this future GM before. Last year, the company announced plans to overhaul the electrical and computational guts of its future vehicles in a bid to deliver faster software, more capable automated driving features, and a custom, conversational AI assistant. This year, GM is providing more details and dates. This technological overhaul is set to debut in 2028 with the Cadillac Escalade IQ. The company will also rollout an autonomous highway driving feature in 2028 that will allow drivers to have their hands and eyes off the road and without the need to be ready to take over. The software race includes hardware European and U.S. automakers have spent years chasing the prospect of software-defined vehicles, but have often fallen short. Volkswagen Group had so much trouble with its own in-house effort, including its troubled Cariad unit, that it struck a $5.8 billion joint venture deal with relative newcomer Rivian. GM has been on its own capitally intensive software adventure. The company has bet heavily on software in recent years. It ditched the popular smartphone projection technology Apple CarPlay for nearly all of its EVs, and instead turned to a Google-based infotainment system, which is actually quite capable even if it doesn’t yet live up to the standards set by Tesla and Rivian. It’s poured billions into software and autonomous vehicle technology development too. GM’s capitalized software amortization expense in 2025 was $866 million, which gives a sense of how much it is spending even as it spreads out the cost over years. Like many legacy automakers, GM has come to the conclusion that the old approach to electronics, which scattered computer chips throughout the vehicle, was holding it back. For fourth-generation EVs, GM will centralize much of those functions on a Central Compute Unit (CCU) that’s 40-times more powerful than its existing systems. Eliminating smaller chips on the edges will help trim wiring by 30%, saving weight and simplifying assembly. GM notes that this new CCU will work on fossil fuel models, too, though it will debut in the Cadillac Escalade IQ, a vehicle that is shaping up to be the automaker’s technological flagship. The CCU will handle the usual propulsion and chassis controls, but also perception and active safety. That should help pave the way for more advanced autonomy features, which GM also announced on Wednesday. Such a move was perhaps inevitable. Pressure on automakers has been building on all sides. Domestically, Tesla has been pushing the boundaries of autonomy, in part because it developed a true software-defined vehicle. Automakers like GM are also feeling pressure from Chinese manufacturers, which have shortened development cycles to two to three years, down from the usual four to five years. GM intends to match that cadence. Alongside announcements about battery chemistries and autonomy, GM outlined how enterprise AI tools have sped up vehicle development across every sector as it pushes to slash its traditional four-to-five-year development timeline in half. GM gave a brief glimpse of its revamped development strategy.

events.title: Musk's SpaceX stock gift is 'tip of the iceberg' for Trump Accounts, Altimeter's Gerstner says
events.summary: In an X post on Monday, Elon Musk said that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year. Brad Gerstner, founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, said on Wednesday that the gift would go to Trump Accounts in an exclusive interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "Elon is the tip of the iceberg," said Gerstner. Elon Musk said earlier this week that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year, and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner said Wednesday that the stock donations would come via Trump Accounts . If it happens, that donation of $10.5 billion worth of shares is just the beginning, according to Gerstner, the founder of Invest America and an architect of Trump Accounts, the new tax-deferred investing accounts for children. "Elon is the tip of the iceberg," Gerstner told CNBC's "Squawk Box" in an exclusive interview on Wednesday. "This is the most giving country on the planet," he said. "I told the president, I think I can raise $100 billion over the course of the next 12 months to sponsor all of the kids in America." In addition to Musk, Gerstner said he had also talked to "every major tech CEO and founder." A $100 billion fundraising target would represent about one-sixth of all U.S. charitable giving. Americans donated $592.5 billion in 2024, according to the latest data from the National Philanthropic Trust . Gerstner has committed about $35 million to help seed the investment accounts for kids in his home state of Indiana. CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approach Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations Thousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher payments Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September, which allow Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a change from previous guidelines that only allowed diversified, low-cost index funds . "The Treasury targeted this carve-out at mega-donors and large philanthropic foundations, such as the Dells, who made a multibillion-dollar charitable pledge," said Adam Bergman, founder of IRA Financial and a tax attorney based in Miami. "It allows them to donate large blocks of publicly traded stock without triggering substantial capital-gains taxes." The move to permit stock donations could pave the way for more large-scale gifts, and a number of other philanthropists are poised to participate, Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano also told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Oct. 8. "They range from small to mega," he said. "We do have mega donors in the nine-digit range, you know, bunches of them." In the broader world of charitable giving, Treasury's temporary regulations also give donors unusual influence over children's investments , according to lawyers and philanthropic experts who spoke with CNBC. "As @TrumpAccounts continues to grow we look forward to more philanthropists joining the movement and helping children across America jumpstart their financial future," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in an X post Monday . The latest Trump Account comments come weeks after the Treasury Department auto-enrolled more than 60 million children . Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts , are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number. Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also claim a one-time $ 1,000 pilot program contribution from the Treasury. Gerstner also said Wednesday that there is a push to expand access to the accounts to all U.S. citizens under age 40. "Why not pull forward 20 years of IRAs? We can create all of those today," he said. "So if Elon says then, I want to give to everyone under 40, or OpenAI says I want to give to everyone under 40, there's a vehicle, there's a vessel that they can start compounding in ... those are the types of things we are working on." In addition to more than 70 million children under 18 in the U.S., about 90 million U.S. citizens are between 18 and 40 years of age, according to CNBC's analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data. However, expanding Trump Accounts to Americans under age 40 would require a legislative change from Congress. In an X post on Tuesday , Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, called the proposed expansion a "game-changer," and said he would "lead the bill in the Senate to make it happen." Gerstner told CNBC on Wednesday that expanding the Trump Account age limit is "wildly popular" among congressional Democrats and Republicans. events.title: GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
events.summary: General Motors is hoping to reduce the time it takes to develop vehicles, targeting a roughly two-year cycle as it expands its use of artificial intelligence, simulation and vehicle software. GM says it is using artificial intelligence, simulation and more concurrent engineering to shorten development and reduce physical testing. The automaker is also expanding in-vehicle AI and plans to introduce eyes-off highway driving beginning with the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market. The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half. GM also reconfirmed that by 2028 , it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models. "All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan. The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers. "Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation. Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster developed with SpaceX, fueling merger speculation Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity How lower fuel economy targets could boost pickups and V-8 engines Stellantis CEO urges incentives for carmakers who build in Europe as Chinese rivals gain ground GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal. The event comes as Chinese automakers are growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage. GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities . Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses. He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad. "There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise." GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines. The company said those coming vehicles – regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems. That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features. The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs. GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact. GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling back billions of dollars in investments in EVs , it remains committed to producing them. "We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them." GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development. The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed.

The tail of the Cambridge Analytica data scandal is long — and it keeps costing Meta gargantuan sums of money. On Wednesday, a judge ordered the social media giant to initiate its biggest payout yet: $25 billion to the state of New Mexico for the tech giant’s role in deceiving resident users over its data privacy practices, The New York Times reports . The huge sum follows a two-week trial in which a New Mexico jury deliberated over the company’s alleged wrongdoing. The jury found that the company behind Facebook and Instagram had committed 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws, each of which carried a $5,000 penalty, the outlet notes. Part of the case revolved around the company’s handling of a third-party app linked to the Cambridge Analytica data breach, The Wall Street Journal reports . Other parts involved its data privacy policies and its efforts to mitigate misinformation on its platform. Cambridge Analytica was an outgrowth of a British defense contractor , SLC Group, that specialized in influence operations and other political work. The company notably worked with the Trump campaign during the 2016 presidential election. It was also involved in a number of controversial initiatives . “We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years,” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez told journalists at a press conference, commenting on the case’s resolution. Meta has said that it will appeal the decision. “This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” said C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s Chief Legal Officer, in a statement shared with TechCrunch via email. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge,” he added. events.title: 'Musk' director Alex Gibney isn't afraid to make powerful enemies
events.summary: Director Alex Gibney's Elon Musk documentary, "Musk," is in theaters now. Jabin Botsford/Getty Images From Scientology to disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes, documentarian Alex Gibney has never met a subject too big or too controversial to tackle. Then came Elon Musk. When Gibney was approached with the idea to do a documentary on the Tesla and SpaceX CEO in 2022, his plan was straightforward: Tell the story of how Musk used his businesses to become one of the most powerful figures in the world. But when he was ready to deliver a two-hour feature film on Musk two years later, his production company issued him a directive a filmmaker rarely hears: Make it longer. It was 2024, and the breadth of Musk's influence had expanded into the political sphere. With Gibney's subject helping President Donald Trump campaign for a second term, then later spearheading the second Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency , Gibney's story had expanded. His documentary would need to, too. Elon Musk. Finn Gomez/Getty Images The result is "Musk," an incisive, nearly four-hour documentary that chronicles the personal, professional, and political life of the richest man in the world. From his controversial acquisition of Twitter, which he renamed X; to his relationships with the mothers of his children; to the accidents tied to Tesla's self-driving feature, Gibney's film is a comprehensive look at the scope of Musk's power and influence in the 21st century. Gibney even found a clever workaround for featuring Musk in the doc after he declined to be interviewed. Playing on Musk's belief that we are all living in a simulation , the director used AI to craft an avatar of Musk, who speaks in quotes amalgamated from his past interviews. Business Insider's " Director's Chair " series features career-spanning interviews with the people helming Hollywood's biggest movies and TV series. Read more stories here . Of course, a man as powerful and outspoken as Musk has already voiced his displeasure with someone else controlling his narrative. After the movie's world premiere at the Venice Film Festival in September, Musk threatened to sue Gibney's production company for defamation. Musk has also bashed the movie on X , stating: "Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don't even know me (but still have an axe to grind). He has ZERO integrity. Horrible human." Hearing from angry subjects is nothing new for Gibney, who was the subject of the Church of Scientiology's full-page newspaper ads decrying his work over 10 years ago tied to the premiere of his documentary "Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief." "With Elon Musk — and he's not unique in this, but he specializes in it — he begins tweeting horrible things about people and the next thing you know, this army of followers and bots starts to gin up the rage matrix," Gibney told Business Insider. Not that he's rattled yet. With decades of documentaries speaking truth to power under his belt, Gibney has developed thick skin and some top-secret harassment survival strategies. "Let's just say I've taken some precautions," he said. For the latest interview in Business Insider's Director's Chair series, Gibney talks about creating an AI Musk, being followed by Scientologists, and his nerve-racking experience in a self-driving Tesla. On creating an AI Musk avatar and making the movie longer Business Insider: You thought you had finished this movie in 2024. Was it daunting to go back down the Elon Musk rabbit hole when HBO asked you to? Alex Gibney: Yeah, it was daunting. We had to renegotiate the budget and all sorts of other stuff. But I got why HBO wanted that. And when Musk hitched his wagon to Trump, it was clear: This is big. I started out making a film about 21st century power, which in this case involved economic power but also tech power. Now, add to that political power, and suddenly it's a really big story. Was AI Musk in the original movie?  The idea of it was. We had put in a placeholder for it, but we were also anticipating that maybe we might get an interview with him at some point. It was kind of an epiphany to do it this way. It came out of past experience: What's the workaround for somebody who won't or can't talk to you? In "Client 9" and "Zero Days," we came up with workarounds that fit those stories. The key here was to find a workaround that would fit this story. That's how we ultimately came up with the idea of the avatar. Did it unlock anything in you regarding using AI tools in your work in the future? I think it will depend on the project. AI has become a kind of suitcase term for everything from Siri to AGI. In this instance, this was a human effort using AI tools, which revolved mostly around sync; in other words, making the lips and the body sort of move with the voice. But there was also designing the room, what he was going to wear, the gamer chair. The further we pushed it and the more interested we got in AI with the company we used, Makemake A.I., this idea of memes and looking at his own image, that's where we came up with certain scenes where you see the back of his head and he's watching himself. Those were things that we improvised on. Tesla CEO Elon Musk attending the start of the production at Tesla's "Gigafactory" on March 22, 2022 in Berlin. PATRICK PLEUL/POOL/AFP/Getty Images On the qualities Musk and Elizabeth Holmes share and Tesla's image I couldn't help but think about your Elizabeth Holmes doc, "The Inventor," when watching "Musk." The "fake it 'til you make it" ethos that's baked into Silicon Valley, has that been fascinating to observe? Both Holmes and Musk are founders who are amazing salespeople hoping that what they bet on takes off.  I think there is a similarity with Elizabeth Holmes. What was rattling around in my head through this was confidence. Musk, like Holmes, was able, through force of confidence, to convince people of things that they knew not to be true. That became a superpower. The big difference between Tesla and SpaceX and Elizabeth Holmes is that those are real products. The Tesla S is a great car. These reusable rockets are extraordinary, and we show the magnificence of that in the film. Not to take anything away from him or those companies, but there's also the bullshit factor. The idea of going to Mars and the promises. And you can see how they repeat themselves and get bigger and bigger. Oh, yeah, full self-driving! I'm sorry, Tesla's self-driving option is still a level two system, and over 60 people have died . ( Editor's note: Tesla has maintained that its Autopilot feature requires constant driver attention, and that its vehicles issue prompts warning the driver to stay alert and hold the steering wheel.) events.title: While Amazon blocks AI agents, Walmart rolls out the welcome mat
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers. The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely . Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others. Now, it’s expanding on those efforts with more technology to prepare for a world where AI agents become mainstream, said Walmart President and CEO John Furner, speaking at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco on Wednesday. The technology will support agentic shopping from both Walmart and the company’s discount warehouse, Sam’s Club. It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user. What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent. The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer, and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do. With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set. The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified, and you can cap their spending. The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary. Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent. Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . SpaceX plans to split compute between its internal uses and outside customers. The company could rent out its compute "several times over if we said yes to everyone," Musk said. SpaceX's AI rivals are clamoring to rent computing power from the artificial intelligence and rocket company, CEO Elon Musk said. "We are also, frankly, hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and by dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute," Musk said during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call Tuesday. Musk said SpaceX could rent out the company's compute "several times over if we said yes to everyone." SpaceX, however, is reserving a chunk of that capacity for its own AI ambitions, including scaling its AI chatbot Grok and Cursor , the coding startup it recently acquired. Musk said SpaceX is seeking to devote roughly half of its compute to internal uses and rent out the other half to third parties. That balance could change month to month, he said. "It's going to be dynamic," said Musk. "And obviously, our approach is to rent at the — effectively the spot market rate as opposed to sign these long-term deals." The company expects the value of compute to increase as AI models improve and ultimately generate "more useful intelligence per watt," said Musk. "And the value of that compute is proportionate to the useful intelligence per watt," Musk said, adding that rental rates for older Nvidia H100 chips have climbed from when they were new. "I think that's likely to continue," said Musk. "I think we're going to face a shortage of super intelligence compute. And that shortage is going to remain for a long time." Musk likened the situation to Monty Python's famed cheese shop sketch, in which a customer repeatedly asks for different cheeses only to find that none are available. "We've actually tried to offload some of our inference compute to other cloud providers so that we can use more compute for training," the CEO said. "And we get the cheese shop sketch." events.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty over the Cambridge Analytica case
events.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. ROBERTO SCHMIDT / AFP via Getty Images A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion over how it handled its users' data. It could be the largest penalty against Meta in history. Meta recently agreed to an $18 billion settlement over the impact of its tech on kids. A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for misleading users about how it handled their data and for failing to prevent misinformation on Facebook. The ruling could be the largest penalty in Meta's history. Last month, Meta settled a child-safety lawsuit  brought by a group of US states for $18 billion. The New Mexico case focused on Meta's handling of user records that Cambridge Analytica used for campaign purposes during the 2016 election. New Mexico alleged that Facebook misrepresented the extent of users' control over their data on the app. "Facebook's wrongdoing—over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public—goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis J. Mathew wrote in the ruling. "It relates to the way in which Facebook induces people onto the platform and ultimately keeps them there." In a statement, Meta's chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, said the penalty "makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico." "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney said. "We are confident we will prevail on appeal." A jury ruled against Meta last month, finding the company committed nearly 50 million violations of a New Mexico law prohibiting deceptive trade practices. Each violation carries a penalty of up to $5,000. Some Meta executives, including CEO Mark Zuckerberg, were deposed in the case. New Mexico first sued the company in 2021, and the case went to trial last month. In internal Meta communications presented at the trial, Zuckerberg appeared to obfuscate methods for users to hide their data. "Give them a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don't encourage it," Zuckerberg wrote in one internal message. Meta's next move remains unclear. The company didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. This is a breaking news story. It will be updated. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Meta plans nonvoting shares, eyeing more stock sales to fund its AI dreams
events.summary: Meta plans to introduce new non-voting stock, people familiar with the matter said, which suggests it’s likely to lean heavily on new share sales to fund its AI buildout. The plan, which could be announced as soon as Wednesday when Meta reports quarterly earnings, will allow the company to issue new stock — for acquisitions, to lure top AI talent, and to pay for chips — without diluting Mark Zuckerberg’s control. Alphabet made a similar move in 2014, executing a 2-for-1 stock split that introduced non-voting shares alongside super-voting shares, which allowed the combined control of co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin to remain at just over 50%. That made it easier for the company to issue $85 billion of new stock earlier this year to pay for AI investments; half of the new shares carry no voting rights . A Meta spokesperson declined to comment. Big tech companies have historically been able to balance out the new stock they issue by buying back shares in the market. But they have paused stock repurchases as the cost of their AI investments mount, and now find themselves as net issuers of shares, which risks diluting insiders’ stakes.

events.title: The internet is having a very bad cybersecurity day
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The internet is having a bad day, from a cybersecurity perspective. Government websites around the world went offline , Reuters reported, after AI discovered critical security vulnerabilities that impacted the programming language PHP . The issues were severe enough that the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) advised organizations using PHP on their systems to either immediately update or take their systems offline until they could. But the PHP update wasn’t the only headache cybersecurity folks were facing on Wednesday. Node.js , the open-source JavaScript runtime environment, also dropped a security surprise of its own when it shared that four high-severity vulnerabilities were just patched in its latest release. One allowed remote code execution, and two others would have permitted a TLS validation bypass, potentially allowing attackers to bypass checks intended to verify a server’s identity. In addition, LiteLLM, a popular open source proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, was compromised by an attacker who injected malicious code, the company shared in a post on X on Wednesday afternoon. The malicious artifacts were published to PyPI (Python Package Index), Docker Hub , and GHCR (GitHub Container Registry), the post noted. The malicious code was said to include an information stealer that targeted cloud credentials, passwords, and AI service credentials, in addition to a remote access trojan that could allow hackers to execute commands on compromised systems. LiteLLM said it has now removed the malicious releases and images and advised anyone who installed them to follow the remediation guidance it provided. And wait, there’s more! An Indian certificate authority, eMudhra, had its private keys compromised , potentially allowing attackers to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. Security pros have called this a massive cleanup job and one that’s “bigger than Heartbleed .” (The latter is a reference to the critical security vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptographic software library). These issues come on the heels of other security breaches and hacks, including the breach of the cloud-native database-as-a-service, TiDB Cloud, which the company announced on Monday. Other hackers have been exploiting four patched Plex Media Server flaws, collectively called Plex2Shell. And last week, cybersecurity company BeyondTrust warned customers to patch a critical zero-day in its Remote Support product, which had been exploited since August. Though the issues were unrelated to each other, their back-to-back arrival highlights the challenges cybersecurity teams now face. This is particularly important as AI could make it easier for attackers to exploit vulnerabilities once discovered. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Will an AI-cloned free tool spell the end of expensive software?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts An AI-cloned free tool is being dubbed 'the end of software' Some developers want to use AI tools to break the power of big tech and "take back the internet". ( Getty: Malte Mueller ) It's being called "the end of software" and the dawn of a new era of AI-powered piracy. New AI tools are disrupting the tech industry itself, making it relatively easy and quick to clone an existing piece of software and replicate its features. Earlier this month, a small team of developers used AI tools to create near-identical, free versions of two commonly used products: Microsoft Office, think programs like Word and Excel, and Adobe Creative, which includes Photoshop. A licence to use Adobe's Creative Suite costs more than $1,000 per year, but the cloned version is free. ( Supplied: Artcraft ) Around the same time, a different tool called Reverse Engineer Anything that helps developers use AI to deconstruct and replicate features in other pieces of software shot to the top of trending projects on software repository GitHub. For some, this new generation of tools will disrupt software in the same way MP3 file-sharing networks in the late 1990s changed how we listened to music and watched movies, replacing CDs and DVDs with streaming. But whether this will give more power to users or further concentrate power in the hands of AI companies remains to be seen. 'Set the clock back' to the 1990s internet Brandon Thomas is one of the developers who recently announced they had used AI tools to copy the Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative suites. A 15-year veteran of the US tech industry, he sees himself fighting a "war" for the future of the internet. In the 1990s, "everything [online] was nerdy, hackable, and weird," he told the ABC. "Everything in this era could be inspected, copied, shared with friends, remixed. It was amazing." But over time, the internet became more standardised and bland. Spaces for innovation and personalisation, like Geocities or Myspace, were replaced by closed ecosystems that tightly controlled user access. This is "enshittification", a term coined by writer Cory Doctorow in 2022 to describe the perceived decline of online spaces. Social media platforms like Facebook initially attracted users with clean, chronological feeds and personal connections, then pivoted to intrusive ads and sponsored content. Search engines became crowded with sponsored ads and affiliate-marketing spam, pushing out organic search results. Software makers shifted to subscription-only models with automated billing and predatory cancellation fees, in some cases worth 50 per cent of the annual contract. The cloned version of Adobe Photoshop, Photocraft, has similar features and layout. ( Supplied: ArtCraft ) For some, AI is part of the problem, as "slop" content floods online spaces. But for Mr Thomas, AI is the solution. "AI flips the tide of this war in a way legislation never did," he said. "We can build anything, even triple-A video games and operating systems. "This is the most excited I've felt for the future in a long time. "I think we have a great opportunity to take back the internet from the monopolistic platforms that became rent-seekers and behaved badly to us as users and customers." How AI is making software easier to copy Think of a piece of software like a cake from a bakery. To copy the recipe, you could break into the bakery and steal the list of ingredients (the source code), for which you would be quickly prosecuted. Or you could reverse engineer the cake by tearing it apart, tasting it, and studying it under a microscope. This is known as "decompiling". You can then bake the cake based on what you learned. Each time you bake the cake, you tweak the recipe so the result more closely matches your description. Marek Kowalkiewicz, an expert on the digital economy at Queensland University of Technology, said AI dramatically sped up this process. "[AI-powered reverse engineering] is not very different from having a bunch of human software developers doing the same thing, but it's way faster and cheaper," Professor Kowalkiewicz told the ABC. Experts say AI's dominance of the US market brings risks all of its own. Reverse Engineer Anything, the viral tool on GitHub, dramatically streamlines the reverse-engineering process by allowing a user without coding skills to replicate features from other software at no cost. The mood is giddy and chaotic in reverse-engineering forums where users share their projects.

events.title: Investors eye proxy fight at Mattel
events.summary: A big Mattel shareholder is preparing to mount a proxy fight at the toymaker and push the company toward a sale, according to people familiar with the matter. Southeastern Asset Management has been considering whether to nominate new directors at Mattel as part of a proxy fight, the people said. The activist has been pushing the company for months to sell itself, following double-digit sales declines in Fisher-Price and other key segments, as well as profit-margin pressures. The issues became more acute after Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz left to join Skydance: Mattel shares, which are down 15% so far this year, dropped by 5% on the news of his replacement, former Condé Nast CEO Roger Lynch. The stock rebounded following a Wall Street Journal report that the company had drawn takeover interest by Authentic Brands Group. Southeastern’s plans could change, the people cautioned, and no decision has been made. It’s unlikely the activist could secure full control of Mattel’s board, but a proxy fight would serve as a referendum on the direction of the company. Under Mattel’s bylaws, an investor can only nominate two directors, except in specific circumstances. Separately, Ariel Investments, another big Mattel shareholder, has told other investors that it believes a change needs to happen at Mattel, according to another person familiar with the matter. In a recent CNBC appearance, Ariel founder John Rogers said the company should sell itself, an unusual posture for a famously management-friendly investor. Mattel said in a statement that it engages with all shareholders but declined to comment further. Ariel and Southeastern didn’t respond to requests for comment.

Iran’s authorities present the decades-old nuclear programme as a sovereign right and an achievement gained despite strikes, sabotage and assassinations. Rezaei described it as “national wealth” on Tuesday. Iran has also used low-enriched uranium for civilian purposes like manufacturing radiopharmaceuticals and for power generation at the Bushehr plant in cooperation with Russia. The authorities argue that surrendering the nuclear programme under military pressure would amount to capitulation, if it did not guarantee that Iran would not be left exposed to more attacks. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly emphasised since the start of the war that he wanted to dismantle the Iranian nuclear programme. US Vice President JD Vance, however, suggested earlier this month that a “meaningful” reduction in the level of enrichment capacity may satisfy US demands. Before Israeli and US attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities in June 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated that Tehran possessed 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60 percent. A nuclear bomb would need enrichment of more than 90 percent. The attacks, followed by further US-Israeli strikes on nuclear sites in 2026, severely damaged Iran’s nuclear infrastructure. With the IAEA unable to inspect key facilities, the current size, condition and whereabouts of much of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile remain unverified. Tehran has refused access to the IAEA to inspect its nuclear facilities since the war started, accusing the agency of advancing Western interests through adopting resolutions and referring the nuclear file to the United Nations Security Council . Iranian authorities maintain they are not pursuing a bomb. But senior Iranian officials, like Rezaei, have publicly questioned the validity of being a party to the international nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty if Iran’s nuclear facilities and other infrastructure continue to be attacked. Still, Iranian officials have hosted numerous foreign diplomats this week. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was in Tehran on Monday after attending a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries a day earlier. There were also indications of visits to Tehran by other Arab officials. US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is also reported to have met Israeli security officials earlier this week. These meetings did not appear to have decreased the prospects of renewed war. But speaking at a conference for Iranian exporters in Tehran on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi cautioned that the country faces threats of more attacks and expansive economic sanctions . “The reality is that the country is truly in war conditions and the war continues. We have not reached peace conditions and are away from it, so all decisions must be made within war conditions,” he said. Parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told Munir that Iran had “nothing new” to tell Washington and expected realisation of conditions offered in New York last month to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. Mediators did not publicly divulge details of their proposals to Tehran this week, but were told the US needed to build trust by accepting Iran’s conditions. These include returning to the June memorandum of understanding and recognising an Iran-Oman deal over temporary transit in the Strait of Hormuz .

events.title: 25 items you may be recycling by mistake, and why you shouldn't be
events.summary: Recycling standards vary widely across the US, which can make it confusing to know what your city will pick up and what you need to drop off yourself. Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post Recycling standards vary across the US, with municipalities often setting their own unique rules. Recycling the wrong material or including wet or dirty items can contaminate the waste stream. Some items may need to be dropped off at specific locations rather than collected. Many of us have been guilty of "wish-cycling" — that is, tossing every piece of paper, plastic, metal, or glass in the blue bin, assuming it's probably recyclable. Unfortunately, recycling is more complicated than that. "There are literally thousands of recycling standards across the country," Rajesh Buch, a professor at Arizona State University, where he teaches a course on sustainable business, told Business Insider. That's in part because recycling systems that sort through piles of discarded items can cost tens of millions of dollars. "In most communities," he said, "they don't have the resources to have these fully loaded, full-capacity systems." The disposal of household batteries, for example, is a common source of confusion. While the EPA  recommends  that single-use household batteries be sent to specialized battery recyclers, it also says that "in most communities, alkaline and zinc carbon batteries can be safely put in your household trash." For residents of New York City, however, the Department of Sanitation's guidelines declare this is illegal and dangerous, citing risk of fire and explosion. New York City residents are required to dispose of their batteries at waste drop-off sites or at stores that accept them. Conflicting standards can be confusing, but dumping every container or scrap can contaminate the waste stream, Buch said. Earth911 has a recycling locator that can help you find where to dispose of certain recyclables, or you can pay a company like TerraCycle to do the work for you. That said, there are some items that almost always need to go in the garbage or a special recycling facility. Here is a list of 25 of them. 1. Aerosol cans Some locations accept aerosol cans for recycling, but you'll want to make sure they're empty. Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Aerosol cans are metal with plastic caps , which should be recycled separately. Some recyclers accept the cans, but others don't. You'll want to make sure they're empty if you can recycle them, especially if the cans contained chemicals. "Some of these are dangerous to put in the blue bin," Buch said. 2. Batteries Energizer batteries are on display at a Wal-Mart store in Chicago. John Gress/Reuters Some cities, like Seattle and New York, have barred people from throwing batteries in the trash because they can cause chemical leaks and fires. Batteries usually can't be recycled curbside, either. Instead, a battery recycling facility needs to take them, Buch said. If you want to recycle them, you can find retail locations willing to take batteries on the site Call2Recycle . 3. Chip bags and other snack wrappers Mateusz Slodkowski/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Chip bags, granola bar wrappers, and other snack packages are often multi-layered materials, Buch said. "You've got foil on the outside," he said. "You've got a plastic coating on the inside, and that's not recyclable." The machines aren't able to separate the layers, he said. Some brands' packaging is recyclable through How2Recycle, though you'll have to drop it off at a participating grocery store or retailer. 4. Coffee mugs and other ceramics Reuse or donate old mugs if you can because ceramics are difficult to recycle. Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images There isn't good technology to recycle ceramics, Buch said. They can even damage equipment. The same is true for heat-resistant glass used to make items like baking dishes. Unwanted ceramics can usually be discarded in the household trash. 5. Coffee pods 50 billion coffee pods get made yearly Gado/Getty Images Over the years, coffee companies have made their pods more environmentally friendly by switching to a different type of recyclable plastic. But you still can't just toss them in your recycling right out of the machine. "The foil is recyclable," Buch said. "The plastic is recyclable." But you have to remove the foil top from the plastic cup. As with all other recycling, it should be clean and dry. Even when properly separated, though, the pods can be what Buch calls a "nuisance item." They're so small that they often fall through slots or holes in sorting machines instead of getting recycled. "Anything that's 2 inches or smaller is going to fall out of the sorting system," Buch said. There are still ways to recycle some pods, though. Nescafé accepts pods you return to them, for example. 6. Diapers Tim Boyle/Getty Images Disposable diapers are difficult to recycle "even if you didn't have all the poop inside," Buch said. They contain a variety of materials, like plastic and cellulose. Some recycling companies like TerraCycle might take them, but municipal facilities most likely won't. Some companies abroad, like Germany's BASF, are making advancements in chemically recycling diapers using the process of gasification, Plastics News  reported . 7. E-waste A worker dismantles old computers and electronics at E-Parisara, an electronic waste recycling factory. Uriel Sinai/Getty Images Cellphones, printers, and computers contain plastic, metal, and a mix of other materials that make them poorly suited for standard recycling systems. Many cities have separate facilities where you can drop off e-waste, or you might be able to schedule a special pickup. For example, if you have a coffee maker that's gone kaput, a retailer like Staples might recycle it and other small appliances for free. 8. Inflatable pools and toys Children in Los Angeles swim in an inflatable pool. Jae C. Hong/AP In 2018, the US generated 35.7 million tons of plastic waste and only recycled about 9% of it, according to the EPA's most recent estimates . Because there are so many different kinds of plastics, it can be difficult to know what you can and cannot throw in your blue bin. Many plastic containers have a little symbol: recycling arrows with a number in the center. This is what's known as a resin identification code . Most recycling facilities accept empty, clean, dry number 1 or 2 plastic. Some locations accept numbers 1 through 7, while others won't take numbers 3, 6, or 7. It's best to check before you chuck your plastic in the bin. PVC, which is number 3, is used to make inflatable pool toys, faux leather, and other goods, and is very difficult to recycle . 9.
