events.title: AI tools discovered the PHP vulnerability that could take down 70% of the Internet. Now the race is on to patch it before AI-powered hackers attack
events.summary: Increasingly powerful AI tools are at the center of a new war between those who want to use them to supercharge cyberattacks, and the defenders who are harnessing the same tools to fend them off. Today, the defenders are hoping they got a leg up in identifying a critical issue that stands to take down 70% of the internet if left unaddressed. While the software flaws have now been found and patches issued, the question remains whether enough of the internet will deploy the patches in time, before hackers start exploiting the vulnerability to attack websites and steal vital data. Most web pages run using an open-source programming language called PHP. That language is maintained by the PHP Foundation. Today, the foundation disclosed two “critical” software vulnerabilities and issued an emergency patch, urging websites to implement it immediately or take down their websites until they are able to. The vulnerabilities are named CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively called “php2shell.”   As reports broke overnight of the vulnerabilities ahead of the patch’s official release, some opportunistic attackers tried to exploit it. Cloudflare, a global cybersecurity company that helps secure millions of websites, according to its website, began seeing “early attacks,” according to its CTO Dane Knecht. While instances of successful breaches are still limited and unfolding, one startup owner reported that the PHP bug is “real bad” and says everyone should be “afraid” after hackers allegedly stole their source code, exposed cookie data, and leaked legal documents. Multiple governments have decided to take websites offline as a safety precaution, including some agencies in the Netherlands and Finland, Reuters reported . The Federal Bureau of Investigation’s (FBI) Cyber Division and the National Security Agency (NSA) both issued statements urging potentially affected organizations to update their services, as did the Prime Minister of Japan, the European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT), and several other national agencies. “The impact of the PHP vulnerabilities is massive, [and] can expose a large number of websites to immediate attacks if not patched in time,” Gang Wang, Associate Professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois’ Grainger Engineering, told Fortune . The bugs allow bad actors to remotely execute code on flawed, not-yet-patched PHP systems. Attackers can use that as an “entry point into the network hosting that machine, and from there potentially carry out attacks that cause significant damage,” Wang’s colleague David Nicol, Director of the Information Trust Institute at the University of Illinois’ Grainger College of Engineering told Fortune . Among the most well-known sites that run on PHP is WordPress, which powers roughly 40% of all websites, according to Reuters. But PHP is ubiquitous across the web, having started as a small project back in 1994 and grown up with the modern internet. For example, Facebook launched in 2004 as a PHP website, although in 2020 the company embarked on a major effort to update to different software. Other popular sites using PHP include Microsoft.com, Wikipedia.org, Archive.org (now temporarily offline ), Theguardian.com, and Baidu.com, according to w3techs. An initial analysis by the cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks identified 22.6 million potentially vulnerable instances. OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman said PHP was his “first programming language,” in a post about the vulnerability discovery. OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, as well as other AI tools, played a key role in finding the vulnerabilities. “Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said in a blog post . “It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.” The backstory: Three parties discovered different elements of the bug Multiple security organizations independently found the issue around the same time, in August. All of them used AI to help find the vulnerabilities. They then banded together in a coordinated effort with the PHP Foundation to develop fixes and coordinate the disclosure of the vulnerabilities and rollout of the patch, OpenAI said.  Technically, the first to discover part of the issue was the California-based AI red-teaming firm Calif. OpenAI had invited Calif to join its Patch the Planet initiative, an effort to proactively find and patch security vulnerabilities in digital infrastructure. Calif decided to investigate PHP because it “stood out as a high-impact target,” the company says . It reached out to Volker Dusch at the PHP Foundation, and then “got to work hacking PHP.”  The Calif team was “not expecting to find anything critical” since PHP has been highly scrutinized by the cybersecurity community for years. In fact, the bug they eventually found had “been present in PHP for 14 years,” OpenAI’s Brockman pointed out in his post. “A limited version of it had been discovered in 2024 and wasn’t considered significant at the time.” But now that AI models can run attack sequences autonomously, almost no vulnerability is too difficult to exploit. “Php2shell shows how AI can help uncover buried flaws and turn complex exploit chains into practical attacks, increasing the potential risk,” TJ Sayers, Senior Director of Threat Intelligence at the Center for Internet Security told Fortune . On Aug.1, Calif found the first issue using GPT-5.6 Sol. It then informed OpenAI, which looked into the issue on its own and found additional elements of the bug. This made the discovery more comprehensive, but almost made clear that the flaw was more serious than Calif had originally realized, an OpenAI spokesperson told Fortune. Then, OpenAI began chatting with the PHP Foundation about the issue. Through those conversations, OpenAI learned that Wiz, a Google-owned cybersecurity company, was also talking to them about the issue. Researchers at Wiz had independently found the vulnerabilities in August. They decided to investigate PHP in the first place because it’s “the backbone of the internet,” a Wiz spokesperson tells Fortune , acknowledging that the parallel initiative may seem like a “coincidence,” but the Wiz team’s charter is to investigate high-impact digital infrastructure, and PHP was top of mind. The Wiz team identified the first issue on Aug. 19, using a combination of Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, and Wiz Atlas. “With 70% of the Internet affected, the impact of php2shell cannot be overstated,” Wiz said in a blog post announcing its findings. “It marks an AI inflection point. events.title: Thousands march for school funding in Greece
events.summary: Public sector workers and teachers joined student protesters, amid growing youth-led demonstrations across Europe. Milan’s youth follow France in violent cost-of-living protests Thousands of students and teachers ‌have rallied across cities in Greece, demanding more funding for ⁠education, including better facilities and smaller ⁠class sizes. The demonstrations echo a wave of youth-led protests across Europe this month, including in France and Albania, where anger over rising costs and alleged corruption has led to clashes with police and major property damage . list 1 of 3 Cost of living protests hit Belgium, Italy, Portugal and France list 2 of 3 How will Europe deal with youth-led protests? list 3 of 3 Portugal cost-of-living protesters pour back into camps cleared by police Greek police said about 10,000 demonstrators, including school and university students, rallied peacefully in central Athens and the capital’s suburbs on Wednesday. “From Greece to France, we want public, free education,” protesters chanted as they gathered outside Parliament, where students staged an overnight sit-in nearby before the rally. Others joined the protests in Thessaloniki, Patras, Larissa and other cities ⁠across Greece in solidarity with growing demonstrations in France and elsewhere in Europe, where rallies demanding educational resources have morphed into angry demonstrations over soaring living costs. In Greece, the protests add pressure to ⁠Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and his centre-right government as the country prepares to hold elections in mid-2027 amid a weakening economy. Greece struggled with a serious debt crisis from 2009 to 2018, during which the government agreed to spending cuts in exchange for three European Union and International Monetary Fund bailouts worth about 290 billion euros ($326bn). But the measures have impacted Greek workers , who are among the poorest in Europe and struggle with stagnant wages, high rents and rising energy costs. The average monthly salary of 1,500 euros ($1,685) sits at 2009 levels, with many young Greeks having been priced out of housing in ⁠cities by skyrocketing rents. “Surviving here is very difficult; the ⁠rent is really high, the houses are really small. Our parents can’t make ends meet to pay for our rent, the electricity, for our life here,” university student Georgia Foukidou, 21, who joined the protest in Athens, told the Reuters news agency. The protests on Wednesday included strikes by primary and secondary school teachers protesting low pay and staff shortages, while substitute teachers demanded permanent positions and reduced class sizes. Public sector workers and other unions also joined the demonstrations. Education Minister Sofia Zacharaki said prior to the protests that she was listening to student demands, noting that the government was spending more than 733 million euros ($823m) on new student residences and facilities upgrades. Mitsotakis’ government has also pledged about one billion euros ($1.12bn) in state subsidies and other benefits to offset increased energy costs for households and businesses due to the Iran war and inflation.

events.title: New Mexico AG lawsuit accuses Epstein's attorney and accountant of facilitating sex trafficking
events.summary: New Mexico's attorney general sued Jeffrey Epstein's long-time personal lawyer and accountant for allegedly facilitating Epstein's sex trafficking operation. The suit alleges that the attorney, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, helped finance and conceal Epstein's sex trafficking, which included the abuse of girls and young women at his Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County, New Mexico. New Mexico 's attorney general on Wednesday filed a federal lawsuit accusing Jeffrey Epstein 's long-time personal lawyer and accountant of facilitating Epstein's sex trafficking operation. The civil suit alleges that the attorney, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, helped finance and conceal Epstein's sex trafficking, which included the abuse of girls and young women at his Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County, New Mexico. Indyke and Kahn are beneficiaries of Epstein's 1953 Trust, co-executors of Epstein's estate, and administrators of the revocable trust, whose name comes from the year of the convicted sex offender's birth. New Mexico's suit asks a judge to block Indyke and Kahn from receiving payments from the estate as the case proceeds in U.S. District Court in New Mexico. The suit alleges the two men participated in a sex trafficking venture in violation of the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act; and that they violated New Mexico's Racketeering Act by engaging in kidnapping, criminal solicitation, and conspiracy. Attorney General Raul Torrez's office said that Epstein's estate is currently valued at more than $107 million, and the suit says Indyke and Kahn are eligible for bequests of $50 million and $25 million, subject to the availability of funds. "Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible," Torrez said in a statement, which was released as he appeared at a press conference flanked by two survivors of abuse by Epstein, Anouska De Georgiou and Julia Molchanova. Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working "The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico," Torrez said. "Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences." The suit comes a month after The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York had opened an investigation into Indyke and Kahn. De Georgiou said at the press conference that her abuse by Epstein and his accomplice, Ghislaine Maxwell, "did not happen in isolation." "It could not have continued for as long as it did without people facilitating it, looking the other way, or choosing to do nothing to stop it," De Georgiou said. "Accountability cannot end with Epstein and Maxwell. It must extend to those who knowingly made their abuse possible, especially those who stand to profit from it. That includes anyone who knowingly helped make Epstein appear legitimate to conceal his abuse of women and girls." Daniel Weiner, an attorney for Epstein's estate, in a statement to CNBC, said, "Both Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn reject as categorically false the allegations that they knowingly facilitated or assisted Mr. Epstein in his sexual abuse or trafficking of women, or that they were aware of Mr. Epstein's actions while they provided legal or accounting services to him." "They are confident that they will prevail on the claims asserted against them," Weiner said. "Neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General's investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit," Weiner said. "Messrs. Indyke and Kahn have given multiple depositions in civil lawsuits and have testified at length before the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Government Reform," the attorney said. "Had the New Mexico Attorney General wanted to learn the actual facts of their professional services for Epstein, the Attorney General or his staff could have reached out to schedule interviews. Messrs. Indyke and Kahn have cooperated with any and all investigations when asked to do so." The lawsuit alleges that Indyke and Kahn personally profited from their relationship to Epstein, who killed himself in a federal jail in New York in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on child sex trafficking charges.

events.title: SpaceX offers employees 20% extra pay to help bring its Memphis supercomputers online
events.summary: Elon Musk has previously said he was living in an Airstream trailer on the Memphis site. Bloomberg/Getty Images SpaceX is offering employees a 20% pay bump to volunteer to help build its data centers in Memphis. The company is looking for "leaders" who can "remove blockers", according to emails seen by BI. Elon Musk said on Tuesday he often spends "four days a week" in Memphis working on SpaceX's data center buildout. SpaceX is offering employees a pay bump to temporarily move to Memphis and help build its data centers. Elon Musk's rocket company is giving employees a 20% pay increase if they volunteer to spend six weeks assisting its critical supercomputer buildout , according to an email seen by Business Insider. "We now need leaders — current and emerging — to guide teams and remove blockers as we bring more supercomputers online," read the email, which was sent in early October to all SpaceX employees. It specified that volunteers did not need to be managers already, adding that construction experience is a plus and that "drive matters most." Employees who put themselves forward should expect to spend six weeks on-site in Memphis, Tennessee, or Southaven, Mississippi, where SpaceX is currently expanding its huge Colossus 1 and 2 data centers to meet surging demand for its compute business. Volunteers "must be in good performance standing," with more than one year of tenure preferred, the email said. Employees who volunteer will receive a 20% premium on their base salary or on their hourly rate of pay for the period of their assignment, and be eligible for "bonuses tied to program success." SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. The email described the reallocation of employees from other parts of SpaceX to assist the company's data center buildout as a "surge," a tactic employed by the company to divert employees and resources to mission-critical projects. In 2022, CNBC reported that SpaceX offered employees pay bumps of between 10%-25% to temporarily relocate to Texas as it attempted to launch its Starship megarocket . The company has been offering "surging" employees a 20% premium on their salary to move to Memphis since at least August, according to another email seen by Business Insider that called for "SpaceX experts and aces" to work for the next three months on the data center buildout. The email said the program is intended to end on December 31, 2026, but could be extended. SpaceX will cover travel expenses and logistics, both emails said. SpaceX's compute cash cow The supercomputers in Tennessee and Mississippi, which were originally built by xAI before the startup was folded into SpaceX in February, have become a critical part of the company's business. In SpaceX's earnings on Tuesday night, the rocket giant said AI revenue that includes leasing out its compute to other companies — including Anthropic and Google — had soared to more than $7 billion, nearly half SpaceX's entire quarterly revenue. On the analyst call, CEO Elon Musk said that SpaceX was being "hounded relentlessly" by companies looking to rent out its compute, adding that they could have rented it out several times over. SpaceX has been shifting executives in addition to rank-and-file employees to oversee its aggressive expansion. Business Insider previously reported that the company had placed a former Starship executive in charge of building out its compute capacity in Memphis. Musk told investors on Tuesday he was also spending most of his time in the city as he looked to push SpaceX toward a target of bringing an extra 10 gigawatts of compute online by the end of 2027. "I've been spending, personally, a lot of my time in Memphis, often four days a week," the SpaceX CEO said. He previously said he was living in an Airstream trailer on the site. events.title: With new ideas and human-directed AI, researchers solve a 31-year-old math mystery
events.summary: Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture By Xinzhi Zhang , Senior Researcher Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. Foundry Labs bridges the distance between Microsoft breakthroughs and the builders, scientists, and curious minds who can put them to work. The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent.

events.title: Actors, writers condemn UK anti-terror law targeting Sally Rooney
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? In an open letter on the cover of the New Statesman, dozens of leading figures term the UK law banning Palestine Action a ‘repressive absurdity’. Dozens of leading writers, actors and activists have condemned the UK law used to proscribe Palestine Action as a “repressive absurdity” in an open letter backing Irish novelist Sally Rooney, whose books have been withdrawn from sale in the United Kingdom. The letter comes after Rooney said her books had been pulled from sale in the UK due to her public support for Palestine Action, a group the British government designated as a “terrorist organisation”. list 1 of 3 UK PM adviser’s wife expresses ‘support’ for Palestine Action list 2 of 3 Sally Rooney’s books pulled from UK over Palestine Action support list 3 of 3 UK police rule out probe into Palestine Action post by PM adviser’s wife Signatories include actors Paul Mescal – who played in an adaptation of her book Normal People, Susan Sarandon and Tilda Swinton; broadcaster Gary Lineker; and writers Arundhati Roy, Naomi Klein, JM Coetzee, Zadie Smith and William Dalrymple. Filmmaker Jonathan Glazer, philosopher Slavoj Zizek, musician Kate Nash and the Irish hip-hop group Kneecap have also signed the letter. “Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist. Her books must be available to the public,” the letter reads. “Their withdrawal from sale, on the basis of ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation, is an affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country.” The letter appears on the cover of this week’s New Statesman magazine, two weeks before the Supreme Court is set to hear a case on the ban. “We categorically reject censorship – whether direct or indirect – and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity,” the letter concludes. Rooney’s publisher, Faber & Faber, said on Wednesday that the withdrawal stemmed from “circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work” and to continue sales would be an “unconscionable situation for a publisher”. Rooney has said that further publication of her work could constitute a “serious criminal offence”. She said she had made “every effort to be honest” with the public about her beliefs and intentions, adding that she was “wholly prepared to accept the consequences”. E-books of Rooney’s work have also been removed from sale in the UK, although some physical copies remain available in bookshops. She has authored four best-selling novels, selling more than six million books globally.

events.title: New Mexico took on Meta alone and won a $25 billion judgment over Facebook’s privacy violations
events.summary: A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy and content moderation policies on Facebook. Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount, which state Attorney General Raúl Torrez described as “one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history.” Torrez said the verdict should be a warning for tech companies and that New Mexico would continue to hold them accountable. “This judgement should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” Torrez said at a news conference. Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws go state education spending. “We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years,” said Torrez, who acknowledged that the money would be tied up if Meta appeals as expected. Representatives for Meta, which previously said it plans to appeal the September verdict, didn’t immediately respond to a message seeking comment about the amount. The Menlo Park, California-based company was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings Wednesday afternoon and its shares were trading 2% higher following the penalty announcement. New Mexico goes it alone Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws when a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, harvested Facebook user data to generate targeted political ads for the 2016 election. Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case, but New Mexico chose to take the social media company to court on its own. Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum that affected its stock price. Lawyers for Meta argued for paying no more than $3.4 billion. An award 10 times that or even more would violate due process, was unconstitutional and would not hold up under appeal, they said. Meta argued the state failed to prove misleading statements about privacy and that content moderation actually harmed New Mexicans. Interest on the penalty would accrue during an appeal, but the number of violations Meta is charged with could be reduced. Meta attorney Matt Nicholson argued in court that a sum as high as $40 billion would be “shocking to the conscience” while an attorney for New Mexico, Randi McGinn, urged standing up to “tech titans who think they are bulletproof and can do whatever they want.” Company argues that the state failed to prove harm The state’s case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads. The now-defunct firm’s clients included the 2016 campaign for President Donald Trump. Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state’s entire population, not just Facebook users, were deceived by the company’s public statements about privacy on the platform. Facebook’s lawyers argued that the state failed to prove whether people were actually harmed by these deceiving statements. “The jury didn’t make findings that any New Mexican heard or saw these statements, or was harmed by them,” said Nicholson during a hearing Oct. 1. New Mexico prosecutors also argued that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate on the platform. Defense attorneys vehemently denied the allegations, saying the company’s content moderation policies are robust and freedom of speech has to be considered. Jury finds more than 43 million violations of state law New Mexico was the only state to pursue a trial around the Cambridge Analytica scandal after 48 other states signed a settlement for $18 billion in August. Besides New Mexico, Florida was the only other state that did not sign the settlement, which included an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach. During the trial, jurors assessed whether Facebook misled users about privacy and content moderation 34 separate times. State prosecutors, though, argued Facebook’s statements deceived the entire population of New Mexico and extended beyond social media users. In the end, jurors agreed with this premise and found Facebook liable for 2.1 million violations on certain counts, bringing the total number of violations to over 43 million. Facebook’s attorneys have argued in subsequent court filings that the state’s consumer protection laws don’t apply to people in New Mexico who weren’t using the platform at the time. Torrez told reporters following the verdict that all money awarded will go into a fund for the state’s education system. The state is also seeking an injunction to stop similar practices. Meta questions evidence and tally of violations In appealing the jury’s verdict, Meta might reduce the number of violations and therefore the total financial penalty. Lawyers for the company said it was unprecedented for the state to count the number of violations based on how many individuals may have heard or seen the misleading statements from the company, arguing there was no evidence these statements ever harmed anyone. During closing arguments, lawyers for Facebook said the state’s evidence was outdated and that despite having five years to gather material, New Mexico found only one other instance of a data breach. In one of the few wins for the defense, jurors found the state didn’t prove that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic. The state said the company favored certain accounts and allowed for violent or inaccurate content to proliferate. Attorney Randi McGinn said in her closing argument for the state that Facebook profited off harmful content, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg denied during his video deposition. Zuckerberg said the company has to carefully balance freedom of speech with content moderation. Attorneys for Facebook said the company has adapted its policies since the state’s lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it removes 99% of content that violates standards. ___ Schuettler reported from Phoenix. Schuettler is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Collectors sent rare Pokémon and sports cards to get graded. Then thieves stole nearly $1 million worth of them from the FedEx truck taking them home
events.summary: Collectors send their cards to authenticators for one reason: to find out what they’re worth, and usually to make them worth more. A card that comes back graded from an authenticator often comes sealed in plastic with a high grade can sell for many times what it did raw. This month, a batch of them got the news they’d been waiting for. Their grades were in, some of them perfect 10s, and the cards were on their way home via delivery. But suddenly, the tracking stopped updating. On Oct. 13, thieves broke into a FedEx truck outside Professional Sports Authenticator’s (PSA) office in Santa Ana, Calif., and drove off with nearly $1 million in Pokémon and sports cards. The collectors who owned them had spent months and thousands of dollars in fees proving what the cards were worth—all for thieves to take two pallets of the cards and make off with the rare collectors’ items. “The Santa Ana Police Department is actively investigating a theft that occurred on October 13, 2026, at 1610 E. St. Andrew Place,” the department said in a statement to Fortune . An officer responded to PSA, and police said about two pallets of cards were stolen from the truck and a third was disturbed. “The estimated value of the stolen cards at the time of the incident was $963,000. However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined,” the department said, referring to PSA’s insurance payout, which is capped at what each collector guessed before PSA graded the cards. An increasing asset No arrests have been made, and the cards have not been recovered. And for the thieves, the timing was good. Pokémon cards have risen 3,261% in value over 20 years, more than any other card category. Demand once ran so hot the Pokémon Company doubled its print run to cool speculation . One of the collectors hit is a YouTuber with 148,000 subscribers who posts as SKY-B Cards. His channel usually shows his hands opening packs of cards. On Oct. 19, he showed his face and walked viewers through what he’d lost. The video has more than 72,000 views. “These were 104 cards that I’ve accumulated over two years,” he said. “There are many irreplaceable cards in here that I will never see again.” He said he handed them to PSA at its booth at the National Card Show in late July, which is about as careful as a collector can be. Grading finished in October, 20 days ahead of schedule, and PSA shipped the cards back on Oct. 13 with next-day delivery. By Friday, they still hadn’t arrived, and the tracking had stopped updating. He called PSA, which told him not to worry and to fill out a lost-item form. The next day, PSA emailed to say a FedEx vehicle carrying its orders had been burglarized “after leaving our PSA facility in Southern California.” The company said it had deactivated the certificates on the stolen cards and warned selling platforms to watch for them. It also said it would pay him “based on fair market value up to the maximum insured value you selected for each card.” The YouTuber said he selected that value in July, before anyone had graded anything. Every card in his order was insured at up to $1,500, and the whole order at up to $156,000, and added he paid more than $8,000 in grading fees. When PSA grades a card and decides it’s worth more than its declared value, it usually charges the customer extra. SKY-B said PSA’s estimates put several of his cards above $1,500, including a Tyrese Maxey valued just under $2,000. “Our customer service team has contacted affected customers directly and is arranging compensation based on fair market value,” a PSA spokesperson told Fortune . “We understand the impact this has on collectors involved, many of whom see these cards as far more than a financial asset.” A PSA spokesman told NBC Los Angeles the company would also return grading fees, which SKY-B didn’t mention. His order included several one-of-one cards, printed in a single copy and serial-numbered to prove it, along with a Barry Sanders autograph numbered three of five and a LeBron James card that was cut wrong at the factory. Collectors often pay more for that kind of mistake. He also had a question for whoever took them: “If you’re watching and you’re the guy that stole these cards, what are you going to do with them, man?” PSA’s email said the company would review its procedures and look at “enhancements or education for shipping partners.” “The security of our customers’ shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation,” FedEx said in a statement to Fortune . “Further questions should be referred to local investigators.” “Anyone with information regarding this incident is encouraged to contact the SAPD,” police said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Netflix has dipped its toe into theatrical. Is it ready to jump in?
events.summary: Netflix overhauled its content and theatrical leadership ahead of its third-quarter earnings report. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos has said the streamer needs new avenues for growth and to improve execution around its content strategy. Yet Netflix's theatrical strategy is in flux, with only a few wide releases and resistance to the big-budget operations of the traditional movie studios. Netflix is making itself clear: It's a streaming-first business. During the company's third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday, co-CEO Ted Sarandos reiterated the streaming giant's long-held stance that its content, which it spent $20 billion on last year, is meant for its subscribers and, therefore, should be delivered to customers on its streaming platform as quickly as possible. Yet, the company is set to have 30 theatrical releases in 2027, on par with what it brought to cinemas in 2026. And while not all of these features are expected to have wide releases or long runs in theaters, Netflix is testing the waters with projects like Greta Gerwig's "Narnia: The Magician's Nephew," which will have a wide release and a 49-day exclusive theatrical window when it hits cinemas in February. The company seems poised to carve a new path forward as it grapples with viewership stagnation and a stock slump of roughly 30% since January. How its theatrical ambitions fit into a streaming-first strategy remains a question mark. "Theatrical releases are a net positive for reach and streaming demand," Alicia Reese, analyst at Wedbush, wrote in a note Wednesday. "Netflix's more amenable attitude toward exclusive theatrical windows will not only facilitate better relationships with talent, but also add a new revenue stream and build interest in its streaming service. This follows the pattern we have seen with the major studios' streaming platforms over the past several years: theatrical releases don't cannibalize the streaming window, as Netflix fears." Ahead of its Tuesday earnings report, Netflix restructured its C-suite, bringing in former Disney executive Peter Rice to take over as the company's chief content officer , ousting 10-year veteran Bela Bajaria . Netflix also dismissed Dan Lin, the company's head of film, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal changes. That came just days after it laid off roughly 1,000 employees including Lin's right hand Doug Belgrad as well as Sheroum Kim , the director of independent film, according to various media reports. It's unclear who Netflix will tap to take over Lin's position. The company aims to restore quality to the brand and utilize Rice's expertise in talent relations to lure big names in an increasingly competitive market. Still, Netflix executives seemed to downplay the change in leadership during the company's earnings call. "Our business and our business flywheel are working," Sarandos told investors during the company's earnings call. "There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S. ... It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like." Sarandos said the streamer had "some really solid doubles and triples this year," but suggested the company needs more "home runs." In an emblematic moment during Tuesday's call, Sarandos highlighted a deal with Disney , struck in October , to bring the Ice Age films and others to the streaming service, and gave a nod to that company's CEO, Josh D'Amaro. "We already are seeing some of those benefits from the Ice Age movies. All five of them hit our top 10. That's really exciting," the Netflix co-CEO said. "And by the way, yes, Netflix just plugged a Disney movie on our earnings call. You're welcome, Josh." In a bid to capture consumer attention and broaden its subscriber funnel, Netflix has spent years diversifying its offerings to include video games, live sports and quick-turn documentaries on buzzy cultural moments. But more recently, it's lacked some of the water-cooler-type hits like "Stranger Things," "Bridgerton" and "Squid Game" that previously boosted subscriptions and viewership numbers. "We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," Netflix said in its shareholder letter Tuesday. "Engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy." And yet with Netflix stating plainly that it needs new avenues for growth — and against the backdrop of a foiled deal to buy the Warner Bros. film studio — investors and onlookers are once again looking at the theatrical business. "I think there's a place for the theatrical for Netflix," Matthew Condon, equity research analyst at Citizens, told CNBC. "Especially, as the competition for time and attention just continues to increase." "If they really want to build stickier fan bases around some of their [intellectual property], I think theatrical could be a good avenue for them to do that," Condon said.

events.title: Nvidia marketing executive Laura Fay, who reported to CEO Jensen Huang, has retired after a decade
events.summary: Nvidia. JOSH EDELSON / AFP via Getty Images Nvidia vice president Laura Fay has retired after a decade at the company. Fay grew Nvidia's enterprise marketing team from roughly 60 to 600 employees. Nvidia brought in Google Cloud's Alison Wagonfeld as its first chief marketing officer this year. Laura Fay, a longtime Nvidia marketing executive who reported to CEO Jensen Huang, retired in July after roughly a decade at the AI chip giant. Fay formerly served as Nvidia's vice president of global enterprise marketing, overseeing campaigns, events, analyst relations, and partner marketing. She said her team grew from roughly 60 to 600 people by the time she left. Fay was among 36 employees on an internal list obtained by Business Insider last year of company leaders reporting directly to Huang . Prior to joining Nvidia, she spent 22 years at Cisco, concluding her tenure there as VP of global marketing. Fay said Huang recruited her to build Nvidia's enterprise marketing organization as the company looked to expand beyond gaming. "I want to change the world, and I want you to change it with me," she recalled him telling her on their first call. Fay said she began considering retirement around her 10th anniversary in January, though a call from Huang congratulating her and expressing hope that she'd stick around for another decade persuaded her to stay a little longer. Nvidia declined to comment. Fay's retirement came as Nvidia also brought in new marketing leadership. In February, the company hired Google Cloud executive Alison Wagonfeld as its first chief marketing officer. The Wall Street Journal reported at the time that Wagonfeld would oversee all marketing and communications teams and assume responsibilities previously divided among several leaders. Those changes follow another longtime marketing departure. Greg Estes , Nvidia's former vice president of corporate marketing and developer programs, retired in 2025 after roughly 15 years at the company. Several other longtime Nvidians have retired this year, including sales chief Jay Puri, chief accounting officer Donald Robertson, and VP of hardware engineering Robert Huang. Some retirees told Business Insider that Nvidia's exponential stock run helped precipitate their decisions. Nvidia's communications organization has also undergone a shake-up as scrutiny around the company has intensified, with roughly 15 employees departing since 2025 amid a reorganization under new leadership. events.title: Offshore wind farms can enhance maritime security, report says
events.summary: Offshore wind farms can enhance maritime security through greater co-operation and surveillance technology, a new analysis says. The report from the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington said that although offshore wind infrastructure has become more prevalent in recent decades, too little progress has been made in looking at how it could benefit national security. “By planning for dual-use capability from the outset, the United States can turn energy infrastructure into a force multiplier for national security, one that strengthens surveillance and warning in an increasingly contested maritime environment,” the CSIS report said. The analysis pointed out that in recent years, maritime and subsea infrastructure have become increasingly important – and also vulnerable to attack. “Subsea cables, which carry roughly 95 per cent of the world’s internet traffic, are particularly vulnerable to disruption,” the report said. In May, undersea internet and data cables were damaged in the Red Sea, causing connectivity problems for users in the Middle East, India and Pakistan. The cables were eventually repaired and most experts said that they had probably been severed by accident, but the incident still put subsea cable vulnerability in the spotlight. CSIS's report indicated that the proliferation of aerial drones, autonomous naval tools and unmanned underwater vehicles were also putting maritime security and subsea infrastructure in a more vulnerable position. It added that, concerningly, drone threats no longer come from state actors, but also from gangs and drug traffickers. The report concluded that if private offshore wind farm developers and governments could reach a consensus on how to best equip turbines with surveillance, sensors and data tracking tools, the end result could be “enhanced maritime domain awareness”. It highlighted the addition of surveillance systems to wind farms in and around Norway, Belgium, Poland and the UK. During a round-table discussion on Wednesday, Allegra Dawes, an energy security fellow at CSIS, said greater co-operation in enhancing offshore wind farms for maritime security could create a “force multiplier” effect, particularly for the US. “I think it gives guidance on the technologies that can actually create a stronger national security environment and also a stronger infrastructure backbone for energy,” she explained. Doug Wolfe, chief technology officer for Mighty Waves Energy, added that artificial intelligence could also be used along with the surveillance-enhanced wind turbines to bolster security on several levels. AI, he said, could help automate a lot of different maritime security workflows, while also helping to better understand what's happening under the sea. “It could very quickly characterise and detect whales, different types of whales and frequencies and all of those kinds of things,” he said.

events.title: ‘Give us a raise or let us save money’: California state workers go on strike over pay, healthcare, and Gavin Newsom’s return-to-work mandate
events.summary: California state workers began a one-day strike Wednesday, urging Gov. Gavin Newsom’s administration to agree to a new contract that increases workers’ pay, ensures affordable healthcare access and allows more flexibility for remote work. SEIU Local 1000, the largest union for California government workers which represents more than 100,000 employees, including auditors, nurses and counselors, hit the picket lines in cities across the state for the first time since the union’s founding in 2004. Members overwhelmingly voted to authorize the strike earlier this month, accusing the state of failing to bargain in good faith after their contract expired in June. “We are going on strike because we know the Newsom administration can and must do better,” Anica Walls, the union’s president, said in a statement. “They must return to the table and bargain in good faith toward a contract that allows state workers to afford groceries, childcare, rent and other necessities.” The strike follows an order by Newsom requiring state workers to return to the office four days a week by July 1. Newsom, who’s preparing to leave office in January and eyeing a 2028 presidential run, argued that the mandate would improve workplace collaboration and innovation, which will help government better serve the public. He vetoed a bill backed by the union last month that would have required state agencies to provide a written justification for requiring workers to report to the office. The California Department of Human Resources said it was coordinating with the union and with state departments, which have contingency plans in case government operations are disrupted by the strike. “The department remains focused on achieving a fair and responsible agreement and continues to be available at the bargaining table,” it said in a statement. The union argues that remote work saves the state money it would otherwise spend on office space and improves people’s work-life balance. The union is also pushing for the state to raise workers’ salaries by 20% over the next three years and increase the state contribution toward employees’ healthcare costs. State workers are fighting for a better future, said Josh Guile, who works for the secretary of state’s office and leads a labor council within the union. “Today we’re out here to say enough is enough,” Guile said at a rally in Sacramento. “We deserve a fair contract.” Jessica Brooks, an innovation analyst at the state’s Department of Health Care Services, said she was picketing because the state refused to bargain in good faith. The state should give workers a raise in part to help them afford costs associated with reporting to the office most of the week, she said. “It’s got to be one or the other: Give us a raise or let us save money, both personally and with the state by working from home,” she said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Flaw in PHP computer language leads to shutdown of websites around world
events.summary: Precautionary takedowns come as experts say bad actors could exploit vulnerability in language used by 70% of sites Websites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web. Belgian, Dutch, Finnish, French and German sites were among those that governments took down temporarily as they scrambled to patch the critical weakness in PHP, a language used by almost 70% of websites . The vulnerability in the programming language, which became public on Tuesday, sparked warnings from national security agencies in Washington and London. It means millions of websites will need to be fixed. One internet infrastructure expert said Russian state actors or organised criminals could exploit the flaw to carry out cyber-attacks. Wordpress, one of the most common website systems, uses PHP, as does Wikipedia, the messaging software Slack and – at least historically – much of Facebook. The Wikimedia Foundation said it had taken down several systems on Wednesday as a precautionary measure until they could be patched. The organisation behind the language issued a patch on Wednesday after researchers testing cyberdefences discovered the flaw. The US National Security Agency told all organisations using PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately. It said the vulnerability could “provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database”. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for “backdoors installed by an attacker”. Prof Alan Woodward, a cybersecurity expert at Surrey University, said: “It was very surprising and troubling because of the extent to which PHP was used around the world. PHP issued a patch very quickly. The big thing is for everyone using it to get that in to make sure their systems are safe. “The troubling part is there is going to be a long tail of websites who may not be maintained as well and they are going to remain vulnerable, which means we may see weeks and months of ongoing attacks. For the big juicy targets, I hope to goodness they are being patched quickly.” A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Woodward said there was a window of opportunity for bad actors. “There is this race and some people unfortunately don’t even know they are in the race.” OpenAI said it led a coalition of researchers that discovered the flaw and claimed “frontier AI” had been key. The researcher who found the weakness, however, said they did not use models that were not available to the general public. In the UK, websites belonging to Edinburgh, Bristol and Oxford councils were taken offline. In France, local government websites including that of the Paris police prefecture went offline on Wednesday, as did in the Netherlands the national digital identity service, the website of the house of representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity centre. Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert, said: “There’s going to be a lot of automatic exploitation of this.” The bug might allow cryptocurrency miners to exploit vulnerable servers at other people’s expense, he said. He also said large crime organisations and Russian state actors could use the vulnerable sites as a launching pad from which to conduct distributed denial of service (DDoS) and other cyber-attacks. The issue highlighted the poor state of internet infrastructure, Woźniak said, something that was being brought to light by advancing AI models but that had been a long-developing problem. The underlying vulnerabilities the researcher found were decades old. “This is an environmental problem in an industry where there’s an incentive to move fast and make changes,” he said. “There’s an incentive to deploy a thing and then never update it and not think about maintenance.”

events.title: Amazon abandons $427 million GW campus data center plan and pledges land donations worth $65 million instead
events.summary: Amazon is reversing its plan to expand its data center footprint in Virginia—forgoing its $427 million plan to build data centers on George Washington University’s Virginia campus it had signed an application for in February. The company will donate roughly 25 acres of the property to Loudoun County for community facilities instead. The agreement, dubbed “Project Potomac Promise” by Loudoun County Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall, calls for Amazon to withdraw its data center site plan, abandon legal action to pursue development on the property, and work with the county to rezone the remaining land for mixed-use development—with housing as the predominant use. Amazon will also contribute $5 million to the county’s affordable housing efforts through the Loudoun County Affordable Housing Trust Fund. “My goal was to disallow data centers or infrastructure that could support data centers on this property,” Randall said in a press conference alongside Amazon Web Services data center delivery vice president Joshua Weissman. “Through our collaborative, respectful conversations, Amazon has agreed to forego its proposed application for data centers, and of note, forego any legal action to realize data center development on this site.” Weissman told Fortune in a statement “Loudoun will be a focus for Amazon’s Built Together commitment we announced a few weeks ago, which includes tuition assistance for community colleges and local project funding.” Amazon has a long history in Virginia’s “data center alley ,” where the highest concentration of data centers in the world is located. The company launched its Northern Virginia cloud region in 2006, and according to Weissman, invested more than $63 billion with more than 3,400 Amazon employees in Loudoun County itself since 2011. Amazon had announced in 2023 it intended to invest an additional $35 billion in data center campuses across the state by 2040.  Loudoun County also reported there were approximately 233 existing data center buildings , representing about 56.5 million square feet of space in the county. Data centers generated approximately $1.2 billion in real and personal property tax revenue in fiscal 2026, or 39% of the county’s overall budget. A land donation worth $65 million Under the agreement, Amazon is dedicating approximately 25 acres along Route 7 to Loudon County, with a stated fair market value of about $65 million. The land is intended to accommodate a community arts center and an indoor sports and recreation facility. Randall said the county would organize public meetings to solicit residents’ input on the redevelopment. She said she expects the rezoning process to take about a year—even under a “fast-track” schedule. “What we’ll probably do is focus first on the indoor sports arena,” she said, “and focus more on the community arts center first as the rezoning process is going through.” How Amazon’s plan unraveled In February, GW president Ellen Granberg announced the university had sold the campus, but did not initially identify the buyer or disclose the purchase price. The university said the transaction would help support its “long-term financial health.” A significant portion of the proceeds were marked for an endowment supporting the university. In March, the university’s student newspaper, The GW Hatchet identified Amazon Data Services as the buyer, who purchased it for $427 million. “It just came as a sudden announcement one day that they had sold the property, and that they couldn’t disclose the buyer because there was some kind of a confidentiality agreement,” former GW professor Ellen Scully-Russ previously told Fortune . “But of course, a student newspaper did their due diligence, and by the end of the day, they knew who it was, and they knew the price, and they communicated that to the community.” In late July, Amazon filed a site plan for a proposed data center development. Named “Bridgefield Tech Center,” the proposal called for four two-story data center buildings totaling more than 800,000 square feet. However, in April, Algonkian district supervisor Juli Briskman called for county staff to examine the potential effects of the proposed development. Briskman said the purchase price of $427 million—roughly four times the assessed property’s value—and the property’s zoning status made it reasonable to expect Amazon to pursue data center construction. But by July, Briskman challenged the prospect of adding another large data center. “Replacing the George Washington University campus with four massive data center buildings would be a profound loss for our community,” Briskman said in a press release . “The site offers a generational opportunity for education, research, housing, and other forms of economic development that could directly benefit Loudoun residents. I strongly oppose this proposal and will fight it every step of the way.” Amazon eventually decided to pursue a deal with Loudoun County and abandon its data center investment. “There was not a moment where it was decided that this was a bad idea,” Weissman said. “We just heard from the community. We partnered with Loudoun, and we just decided this was just the right thing to do.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Celebrating the educators shaping the future of learning
events.summary: Meet the educators shaping the future of learning Teachers and schools hold a special place in students’ lives. They help students discover what excites them, believe in their potential, and imagine who they might become. Through a deeply human partnership among educators, students, and families, education builds knowledge, confidence, and dreams for the future. Today, we celebrate those who have earned advanced recognition within our Microsoft Elevate for Educators community this year: over 54,000 Expert and Fellow educators, more than 1,100 Showcase schools, and 20 inaugural Beacon schools and systems . Together, they join a community of more than 100,000 educators who learn from one another, build their skills, and open new possibilities for every learner to thrive. As teaching and learning evolve, teachers and school leaders are defining what responsible innovation means for education. Microsoft is committed to supporting their expertise and judgment, so technology strengthens students’ curiosity without replacing their thinking. Supporting educators means giving them opportunities to learn, too. Microsoft’s latest AI in Education report finds that 88% of educators surveyed have used AI for school purposes, yet 53% have not received training from their institution. And 66% want training monthly or quarterly. Educators are asking for ongoing professional learning and clear guidance to put it into practice. In partnership with leading education organizations worldwide, Microsoft Elevate for Educators provides a global peer community, professional learning, practical resources, and a pathway that recognizes educators and schools as they progress. It reflects Microsoft’s investment in the people and institutions that help students excel, building skills and widening opportunity for every learner. So many of us can name a teacher who helped us see ourselves differently, or a school that gave us a sense of possibility. Behind those moments are people doing extraordinarily demanding work. Microsoft Elevate for Educators is our way of saying: you matter, your work matters, and you deserve a place where others understand the challenges, have creative solutions, and can help you be your best. Celebrating educators leading the way As educators progress through Microsoft Elevate for Educators, they build skills, strengthen classroom practices, and put Microsoft for Education tools to work. Experts advance classroom innovation, while Fellows build on that experience to mentor peers and lead change beyond their own classrooms. We celebrate the 2026–2027 Microsoft Elevate Expert Educators and 2026–2028 Educator Fellows for their commitment to learning and supporting one another. Schools at the frontier of technology implementation Schools can also progress through Microsoft Elevate for Educators and earn recognition for strengthening teaching and learning. Microsoft Elevate Showcase Schools demonstrate excellence in technology integration, exploring new ways to use digital tools to support educators and enrich learning experiences. This year, we welcomed our first-ever Microsoft Elevate Beacon Schools and Systems . This new designation recognizes leadership at scale through strategic technology planning that brings tools, people, and practices together to extend innovation across entire school systems. Together, Showcase and Beacon Schools are at the frontier of technology use in education, showing how emerging tools can expand what is possible for learners. By sharing what works and what doesn’t, they can help other schools turn innovation into practice. Spotlight: A culture of confidence in Australia What happens when educator learning and innovation becomes a whole school effort? At Canterbury College, a K12 school in Queensland, Australia, Microsoft Elevate educators share their learning through collaboration and teacher meetups. Teachers use Microsoft Copilot to personalize resources and help students explore independently. The biggest change that we see is that there is confidence in doing something new. And in a school, that’s everything. With leadership supporting teachers to learn and share, their growing confidence is strengthening teaching across the school. Feeling inspired? Your journey can start today. Educators can begin as Explorers and schools can join as Pathfinders at any time of the year. From day one, you’ll build skills, connect with peers, put new ideas into practice, and develop a portfolio toward advanced recognition. The next application window for Expert Educator and Showcase School recognition opens in November . We celebrate the educators, schools, and school systems whose ideas and generosity inspire others and bring new possibilities to classrooms worldwide. events.title: Why social media has become an election issue in Brazil’s presidential race
events.summary: Critics have accused the tech giant Meta of censoring the political campaign of President Lula and favouring Bolsonaro. In the race to be Brazil’s next president, the final two candidates are appealing to voters not only at rallies but online as well. On Sunday, incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will face right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in the final round of the election. list 1 of 3 Meta, Facebook to drop fact-checkers: What does this mean for social media? list 2 of 3 Bolsonaro’s election fraud claims spark ‘unprecedented crisis’ list 3 of 3 Brazil leaders condemn ‘terrorist acts’, vow to defend democracy The race is expected to be tight. But in its final days, questions have festered over whether the digital arena has been a level playing field for the two candidates. The social media giant Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, has faced accusations before Brazil’s top election authority, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), that it suppressed Lula’s content and favoured material promoting Bolsonaro. Meta’s products rank among the most popular social media platforms in Brazil, and political ad spending on its sites has grown at a breakneck pace. An analysis from the Brazilian news outlet G1 found that Meta received at least 288m Brazilian reais ($57m) in direct campaign spending in 2026, double what it received during the 2022 presidential race. That increase marks a shift in how Brazil runs elections. More than 76 percent of Brazilian voters now get their news online, said Andre K Rodarte, a researcher at the Digital Democracy Centre at the University of Southern Denmark. With social media eclipsing traditional advertising, Rodarte explained that a growing class of politicians is using provocative, viral messaging to connect with voters. He pointed to the success of online influencers like right-wing personality Nikolas Ferreira and left-wing activist Erika Hilton, who each were reelected this year to Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies with record numbers of votes. “You are seeing people transitioning from information-producer roles to politics, and they are just getting more and more power, more and more votes,” Rodarte told Al Jazeera. “If this is the media landscape they are dealing with, it’s unlikely they will adopt a different campaign style, or different style of politics.” But critics warn that this shift to online campaigning has put political hopefuls at the mercy of Big Tech corporations and their biases. In Brazil, the reliance on online campaigning first took off in 2018, with the election of President Jair Bolsonaro, according to Leticia Cesarino, an anthropologist at the Federal University of Santa Catarina who studies far-right politics online. Jair, a far-right leader, is the father of this year’s presidential frontrunner, Flavio Bolsonaro. When Jair first ran for president eight years ago, his platform promised tough-on-crime tactics and a return to traditional Christian family values, which he spread through bite-sized social media posts. At his 2019 inauguration , supporters chanted “Facebook!” and “WhatsApp!” in unison to show their support for his online presence. “Since then, the left and pro-democracy actors have slowly come to recognise the importance of such media for elections and learned how to deploy it strategically,” Cesarino told Al Jazeera. “They still lag significantly behind the far right when it comes to digital communication, though, especially since the kind of logic that underlies the attention economy is structurally beneficial to the kind of alarmistic, simplistic, affect-laden far-right discourse.” But during his presidential term, Jair used his social media platforms to cast doubt on the accuracy of Brazil’s election system. After losing the 2022 election, Jair continued to spread false claims that the vote had been rigged. His supporters ultimately stormed three buildings – Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace – in the capital, Brasilia, on January 8, 2023, after Lula was sworn in. In the aftermath, the TSE ruled that Jair had abused his position to undermine the election and prohibited him from holding public office for eight years. He is currently serving a separate 27-year sentence for plotting a coup. He is also barred from using social media. The scandal “really shocked a lot of policymakers and political elites to act”, said Vicky Wyatt, a campaign director at Eko, a coalition advocating for more accountability from tech companies. Although Brazil had already passed some data privacy and data protection laws, leaders added a slew of new regulations after Jair’s presidency. Brazilian law now bans depictions of electoral candidates generated by artificial intelligence (AI), and it also requires any political ads using AI to carry a disclaimer. Content that advocates violence, hate speech or gender-based discrimination is also considered illegal.

events.title: Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect
events.summary: IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect . He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028. Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors , received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes. Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals. Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces. Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs. At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November. Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management. Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents. Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD ’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM , engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon . An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011. He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee . Schindler is an IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu honorary life member and a MTTS honorary life member.
