events.title: GM simulated 300,000 EV battery designs—using 34,000 years of computer time—before building a single cell. Now comes the physical part
events.summary: General Motors says it simulated more than 300,000 designs for its next EV battery before building a single physical cell. The run took 300 million CPU hours, or one computer running around the clock for 34,000 years, by GM’s math. GM pitched the number Wednesday at its GM Forward event as proof it can halve the traditional four-to-five-year vehicle development process, to about two years. With the battery, the team went from first pack concept to formal program approval in one month. Nearly every announcement ran on the same logic. GM’s self-driving software logs more than 3 billion simulated miles a day, against about 1 million real-world miles a month. Factory teams rehearse assembly in digital models. Fortune reported Tuesday on the culture change gripping the top American auto-seller: engineers rewarded for missed stretch targets and a battery chief who says, “I want to see red.” Sterling Anderson, the former Tesla Autopilot chief GM hired as chief product officer in 2025, recently told Fortune it’s “effectively the third phase in the evolution of product development for humanity,” built on “probabilistic, large data-requiring methods.” This is what he meant. That said, the battery won’t reach volume production until 2028. A battery built on a long shot The cells use lithium manganese-rich chemistry, or LMR, which GM says offers 33% more energy density than lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, the cheap chemistry China dominates, at comparable cost. They use roughly 30% to 40% nickel, battery engineer Andy Oury told Fortune , versus about 85% in today’s high-nickel cells. GM plans to build them with LG Energy Solution at their Ultium Cells joint venture in Spring Hill, Tenn. “We’re not licensing this from China,” Kurt Kelty, GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability, told Fortune . By his own account, most of the industry considers LMR a long shot, and GM made the call with perhaps 60% to 70% of the data. LMR has historically struggled with short cycle life and voltage decay, but GM believes it has solved that. Proof will come from GM’s $900 million Battery Cell complex in Warren, Mich., due to be fully operational later this year and ramping toward a couple thousand cells a day. The cone course On Fortune ‘s recent visit to Warren, Jason Fischer, a 28-year GM veteran who leads the AI push in engineering, demonstrated a digital car sliding off a cone course until engineers tuned it in simulation, work he said would take months with a real car. GM holds weekly “tall pole” reviews of whatever is slowing each job. “I’m convinced that we’re going to be able to do things just as fast as China,” Fischer said. At GM Forward, the company said its fourth-generation EV platform should deliver about 20% more range per kilowatt-hour. It is expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter, with a 20% more compact pack and drive units with 40% fewer parts. In factories, GM’s PlantBrAIn platform has moved battery packs through assembly 30% faster, and Gen 4 vehicles will check their own wiring on the line. The platform will also carry an updated version of Super Cruise. The brain goes into the Silverado GM’s new central computer, with 40 times today’s processing power and 30% less wiring, debuts in 2028 on the Cadillac Escalade IQ, then spreads to GM’s highest-volume gas SUVs and trucks, three-row crossovers and Gen 4 EVs. It enables the other headline: autonomous highway driving, announced last year for the Escalade IQ, is coming to gas-powered full-size SUVs and light-duty pickups. Pre-production vehicles are testing on closed courses. The driving software trains largely through self-play, with versions of itself playing the merging car and the surrounding traffic. Much of the method came from Cruise, the robotaxi unit GM absorbed in 2024. Rashed Haq, GM’s vice president of autonomous vehicles, told Fortune that GM kept “a lot of the methodologies” for the next-generation Super Cruise. Current Super Cruise customers have logged more than 1.2 billion hands-free miles. The real-world miles come from hundreds of GM data-collection vehicles and from retail customers who have opted in to share data. GM says it has optimized its training enough that an improvement spotted in the software can reach the road within a single day. An OnStar AI assistant arrives on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq via over-the-air update in the coming months. Anderson told Fortune a four-person team once had a voice prototype running in a Lyriq about 30 days after he asked for one. Starting in 2027, a single OnStar app will replace OnStar Guardian and the separate Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet and GMC apps, adding cameras that automatically record incidents; GM says it can’t access the recordings. GM Fleet, about 20% of annual sales, gets its own AI assistant, and OnStar Fleet has more than 2.4 million subscribers, which GM says is twice its nearest competitor. None of this is cheap. GM says it is investing more than $16 billion in U.S. R&D and manufacturing this year, after about $7.6 billion in EV-related charges last year. events.title: GM is giving OnStar an AI makeover
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. General Motors is adding a personal AI assistant to OnStar as part of a broader makeover of the subscription-based connected car service that the U.S. automaker launched 30 years ago. The OnStar AI Assistant will debut in the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV in the coming months, with more GM vehicles to follow, the company said Wednesday at its GM Forward event in New York, where it made a series of other technology announcements covering software, automated driving, EVs, and its electrical architecture. The company said it will launch a new OnStar mobile app in 2027 that will complement and sync up with its in-car software. The new OnStar mobile app will replace the current OnStar Guardian app that launched in 2020 as well as vehicle brand apps for Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC. This tech-centric reboot is unlike other attempts to modernize OnStar and it notably puts agentic AI at the center. The company has updated the safety and roadside assistance service numerous times in its history, especially in the past five years as it tried to stay apace of emerging and tech-forward competitors like Tesla. In 2021, the company expanded its OnStar Guardian app, which offered crash detection, emergency assistance and location sharing, to anyone with a compatible phone, even if they didn’t own a GM vehicle. A year later, GM started using Google Cloud’s conversational AI Dialogflow to recognize specific spoken requests and expanded in 2023 to give drivers responses to common queries like routing and navigation assistance — all part of GM’s plan to build a $25 billion subscription business by 2030 . GM continued to focus on generative AI, but relied on Google to provide the experience. The company said last year that Google Gemini would roll out in vehicles in 2026. The OnStar AI Assistant is an in-house effort and one aimed at giving the driver and passengers an interactive and custom experience — and become even more embedded in their daily lives. “OnStar is now transitioning to be a connected intelligence platform, not just the call center that it’s historically been known as, but a mechanism for interpreting, understanding, and providing predictive, proactive support to its owners,” GM’s VP of global product and chief product officer Sterling Anderson told TechCrunch in an interview ahead of the GM Forward event. For instance, cameras on the vehicle will be connected to the software to offer live views as well as crash and safety recordings. Users can set up the connected cameras to turn on automatically if the vehicle senses an impending event — for instance an aggressive horn honk — then capture the event and upload it to the OnStar app. Users will be able to use voice to control certain functions on the vehicle, including climate, and ask questions about any specific vehicle feature. The launch coincides with efforts throughout the auto industry to stay apace of Chinese automakers with technology that is central to the vehicle — and no longer a slapped on gimmick or feature. But that has required GM to change its approach to software development, adopt AI tools, and even design a new electrical and centralized compute vehicle architecture. The announcement also comes after GM has been criticized and even fined for sharing data with third parties. Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission finalized an order that bans General Motors and its OnStar telematics service from sharing certain consumer data with consumer reporting agencies. The finalized order also requires the automaker to be more transparent with its consumers and obtain their explicit consent on certain data collection. GM said Wednesday that customers will have the ability to decide what data is shared, and that the recordings have time limits and are encrypted. GM said it and OnStar cannot access Connected Camera recordings. A GM spokesperson later shared that third-party sharing a “feature-specific and consent-based, with information shared only as needed to provide requested functionality.” Customers can manage permissions and withdraw consent, however those who choose not to share certain data may have limited access to related features, while other OnStar services would continue, according to GM. events.title: Vodafone says 24 million scam calls came via one little-known company
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Vodafone's owner accuses rival Aussie Broadband of being behind millions of scam calls to customers TPG's Vanessa Hicks has called on the regulator to do more to stop scam calls at their origin. ( ABC News: Chris Taylor ) Vodafone analysed millions of scam calls on its network during a one-year period, finding 98 per cent came from internet phone company Symbio. Symbio is owned by Aussie Broadband who says stopping the scammers is very difficult. Aussie Broadband has committed to working with Vodafone's owner TPG to reduce the volume of scam calls while Australia's Scams Prevention Framework is due to be introduced next year. Vodafone's owner has accused its rival, Aussie Broadband, of being involved as a carrier in almost all of the scam calls made to its customers in a one-year period. It analysed millions of scam calls on the Vodafone network between July 2025 and July 2026 and found 98 per cent of the calls — more than 24 million — came via little-known internet phone company Symbio. Symbio is owned by Aussie Broadband. "Every time we see this type of scam campaign we give the evidence and the data to Aussie Broadband for them to investigate and block the bad actors," Vanessa Hicks, executive at Vodafone's parent company TPG Telecom, said. "We want more urgent action to stop this activity closer to the source and stop these calls reaching Australians." Vodafone collected data on scam calls on its network and found the vast majority originated with Symbio. ( ABC News ) Symbio sells Australian phone numbers in bulk to companies, allowing them to make calls via the internet. Aussie Broadband CEO Brian Maher said Symbio had about 500 customers on-selling those numbers. Each of those customers may on-sell numbers to thousands of other users. He said that because Symbio had no oversight of who its customers were selling phone numbers to, stopping the scammers was very difficult. "Where we find a persistent bad actor, then we will disconnect them," Mr Maher said. He said the company used detection software and a team of more than 20 people to reduce scam calls. "We've got plans to invest further into the future, and we'll continue to do that," Mr Maher said, but declined to say how many additional staff would be hired. "It is unfortunate that they've called us out publicly, but we accept that they're frustrated and we want to work with them to solve the problem," he said. Perth-based Ian Odlum posted on Instagram last month about a strange call he received. "I just received a call from someone saying they were from the Australian Federal Police," he said in the post. Mr Odlum said the scammers emailed him to "verify" they were from the AFP, then told him they had seized an individual and their laptop, which contained his personal information. The caller told him he needed to come to Narrogin Police Station, around 200 kilometres from Perth. "It was a very calm, very kind person explaining that they weren't going to ask for my information, but that they needed to speak to me and it was very important," he said. Mr Odlum refused to travel to Narrogin, and the caller hung up. "I don't know exactly what he would have gotten out of this, but it's really scary how real this scam feels," he said. Vodafone's fraud team investigated and found police stations in Western Australia, Queensland, South Australia and the AFP had all been impersonated by calls from Symbio's network. "What we've seen in this particular scam is over 2,400 calls, and this was just in a one-week period in September," Ms Hicks said. The regulator, the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA), said checks made on that particular scam showed regulation was working, saying "the traffic was identified, notifications were passed upstream and blocking occurred". "The apparent sources were multiple overseas telcos, and the ACMA did not identify non-compliance by an Australian telco," the regulator said in a statement. Mr Maher said Aussie Broadband had made "significant progress" over the past month in reducing the number of scams. "We're working as hard as we can, but we need many more pieces of information to be shared with us to solve the problem, and we're working hard to do that," he said. "We are the largest wholesaler in the market, and therefore we would have a higher proportion of scam calls." Symbio warned by the regulator over scam activity The regulator warned Symbio in 2024 after finding the company did not properly investigate scam calls and failed to share information quickly with other telcos.

events.title: Bushfires cost Australia $6b a year as El Niño summer looms, report finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Supercharged fire seasons cost Australia $6b annually as El Niño summer looms Bushfires could cost Australia almost $182 billion over the next three decades. ( ABC News ) New modelling reveals fire seasons are now 21 per cent longer, with 5.6 million homes at risk. The damage bill is $6 billion a year, with a single major bushfire event costing almost $30b. Large parts of Australia are bracing for a hotter and drier summer due to El Niño. As Australians prepare for a summer influenced by what is likely to become the strongest El Niño on record, a new report reveals billions of dollars are being spent tackling bushfire seasons supercharged by climate change. The modelling, commissioned by Emergency Leaders for Climate Action (ELCA), found the country's fire seasons have lengthened by 21 per cent since 1979 due to warming global temperatures. The longer seasons are costing the Australian economy $6 billion each year, with a majority being spent on harm to health and wellbeing, ahead of damaged businesses and lost homes. ELCA's Greg Mullins, a former Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner, said the high costs come as climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, squeezes fire seasons closer together. "The fire seasons are longer, they're overlapping between states and we're getting catastrophic fire weather," he said. "Previous studies only looked at insured costs, which were far less, but costs across the economy are huge; in 30 years that's $180 billion." Black Summer highlights cost of extreme fires The ELCA report found half of Australian households are exposed to bushfire risk, at 5.6 million, while major events, such as the Black Summer fires, cost almost $30 billion. The 2019/20 bushfires tore through about 45 per cent of the Snowy Valleys Council (SVC) local government area (LGA), killing one person and destroying almost 200 homes. There were almost 9,000 livestock fatalities within the LGA and 400,000 hectares of land burnt. Nearly half of the Snowy Valleys region was burnt during the Black Summer bushfires. ( Supplied: James Hayes ) The local council spent more than $50 million on direct recovery, which included road repairs and managing damaged and fallen trees. SVC's manager of technical services, Glen McGrath, said the region was still recovering from the event more than six years later. "You look at the softwood industry, they had a very large impact and it takes 20-plus years for softwood or pine tree to grow and be harvested and processed through the local industry processes, so they won't be coming back online until 2040 or thereabouts," he said. "There's still a number of houses that weren't rebuilt after the fire, so there's widespread impacts and recovery efforts still." Research has found the Black Summer bushfires cost Australia's tourism industry almost $3b , while the Insurance Council has found the event accounts for about $2b of the $2.58b in bushfire claims since 2019. Preparation key ahead of high-risk summers While no two events are the same, El Niño often brings hotter and drier conditions to southern and eastern parts of Australia. Despite 2026 shaping up to become Australia's wettest El Niño year on record , drier than average conditions are starting to persist across parts of the country's east. "In the last three months since El Niño has been active, we've seen drier-than-average conditions along much of the eastern seaboard," senior climatologist at the Bureau of Meteorology Felicity Gamble said. "Extending from central Queensland through to south-east Queensland, down the New South Wales eastern seaboard and across southern Victoria and Tasmania." Greg Mullins says the burning of coal, oil and gas is supercharging bushfire seasons. ( ABC News: David Sciasci ) There are concerns that unusually hot temperatures, combined with an increase in baseline warming due to climate change, could increase the risk of "flash droughts" this summer. "When we get heatwaves, vegetation gives up its moisture very quickly … so things can very quickly turn into drought-like conditions and that drives fires," Mr Mullins said. The ELCA report found better preparation can prevent millions of dollars in bushfire damage. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) Given the typical "lag effect" seen during an El Niño, there is speculation next year could become the hottest on record globally, leading to a particularly bad fire season in 2027/28. But the ELCA report also found that better protecting infrastructure and homes could avoid $600m in bushfire losses and protect more than 5,600 jobs each year.

The U.S. National Security Agency’s sent out an alarming warning on Wednesday that two critical holes had been found in PHP, with patches already issued by the PHP Foundation . PHP is a server-side programming language so widely used for web applications that it powers roughly 70% of the websites on the internet; by some accounts, that’s more than 33 million sites . It is also used by popular content management systems like WordPress. The NSA warned that these holes are so severe that if a website can’t be patched immediately, it should be pulled off the web until it can be. The holes allow attackers to infiltrate the server’s file system or a database that may be used by the web app. Interestingly, these holes have been tucked away in all versions of PHP since version 5, which was released in 2004. Websites not running relatively current versions of PHP will have some updating work to do, as PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported. The recommendation is to update the web server to the current version of PHP, which is 8.5.12. So how did two such ubiquitous, decades-old flaws that affect nearly every website on the internet suddenly come to light? AI, naturally, particularly via OpenAI and Google’s Wiz. Security testing company Calif was engaged in OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative to find flaws in open-source source software. Using GPT‑5.6 Sol, it found one of the flaws, OpenAI disclosed in a blog post . Separately, the Wiz team also used AI, namely its Wiz Atlas security AI agent, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to find multiple vulnerabilities in PHP. Both OpenAI and Wiz followed responsible security research practices and worked with PHP on patches before publicly disclosing the flaws. Then they all worked together to flesh out what they found, and test the patches, drawing in a host of others to help. Wiz thanked Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Imperva, Microsoft, and Vercel. (While WordPress sites use PHP, WordPress has issued a statement saying that the flaw isn’t WordPress specific, and sites running its CMS must patch their servers and work with their web-hosting companies to ensure their sites are protected.) OpenAI says that these flaws were found by researchers before hackers discovered them. So there were no reports of exploits in the wild. This is also in part because, before AI, these flaws were too hard for hackers to exploit. “With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts,” Wiz warned in its blog about the flaws. In other words, this is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented because of AI, but is also a high risk only because of AI. Now that the issue has been disclosed, hackers are fully in the know. The race is on for the internet to patch tens millions of websites before hackers can attack the unpatched ones. Hence the NSA’s guidance that if you can’t patch your PHP website right away, you’re better off pulling it offline until you can. events.title: Trump-aligned super PACs pour millions into once-safe GOP House seats
events.summary: Trump-aligned super political action committees are spending millions in districts Republicans won comfortably in 2024, including Ohio’s 10th, Michigan’s 4th and North Carolina’s 11th, a sign the GOP is being forced to defend a broader House map. Trump’s main super PAC, MAGA Inc., reports spending $300.5 million through Oct. 14 and still held $164.3 million in cash three weeks out from Election Day, new filings show. The spending comes as Republicans defend an expanding House battlefield and Trump’s approval rating sits at 36% in a new New York Times/Siena poll. President Donald Trump has made good on his claim of putting more than $300 million of his political war chest into the 2026 midterm election . New campaign finance filings released Tuesday night show millions flowing into House districts that were barely competitive two years ago, underscoring how far the GOP's problems have spread in the final weeks of the campaign. MAGA Inc. , Trump's main super political action committee, reported $300.5 million in disbursements through Oct. 14, with a quarter of that election cycle total — $75.5 million — being spent in the first two weeks of October, according to new Federal Election Commission filings. It still held $164.3 million in cash, and Trump said Tuesday his political operation would spend more than $400 million by Election Day. Much of the money is moving through two new Trump-aligned groups. MAGA Inc. has sent $200 million to No Going Back PAC and $25 million to Safety & Affordability PAC , which have already reported more than $209 million in independent expenditures between them, according to FEC filings. The spending is also likely to ease months of Republican anxiety that Trump would sit on his massive war chest rather than deploy it in the midterms. GOP operatives had worried as recently as September that MAGA Inc.'s cash would remain largely on the sidelines. Safety & Affordability has spent $3.76 million in Arizona's 1st District, $1.84 million in Maine's 2nd, $1.60 million in Wisconsin's 3rd, $1.48 million in North Carolina's 1st and $1.40 million in Ohio's 10th. It has also put more than $1 million each into Pennsylvania's 8th, Ohio's 9th and Michigan's 7th, according to a CNBC analysis of the PAC's filing . Several are established battlegrounds. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates Wisconsin's 3rd, North Carolina's 1st, Pennsylvania's 8th, Ohio's 9th and Michigan's 7th among its 21 "Toss Up" races. Other places Trump is donating show Republicans being forced onto less familiar terrain. In Ohio's 10th District, Safety & Affordability PAC has spent about $1.4 million defending Republican Rep. Mike Turner, who won by 18 points in 2024. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee now lists the seat among a new tier of possible 2026 pickups , while the National Republican Congressional Committee only began spending there this month, according to AdImpact. No Going Back has also spent roughly $5 million each in Republican-held Michigan's 4th and North Carolina's 11th, while putting another $14.4 million combined into Democratic-held Florida's 14th and 25th, according to a CNBC analysis the PAC's FEC filing . At the same time, other Republican groups are beginning to triage. The Congressional Leadership Fund, House Speaker Mike Johnson' s super PAC, stopped spending on advertising in Iowa's 1st, New Jersey's 7th, Michigan's 8th and Ohio's 1st districts, the Associated Press reported last week. Trump-aligned groups, meanwhile, have spent about $1.4 million across those four races, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. Republicans still hold the advertising edge in 25 of the 42 House races rated "Toss Up" or "Lean" Republican or Democrat by the Cook Report, according to AdImpact . But the political environment continues to move toward Democrats. Of the 21 House races Cook rates as "Toss Ups," 16 are Republican-held and five are held by Democrats. Trump's PACs have also spent big in the Senate, according to the new filings. No Going Back has spent nearly $30 million in Michigan , $27.8 million in Ohio , $11.8 million in New Hampshire and $9.9 million in North Carolina , according a CNBC analysis of the new FEC filings . Those four races alone account for roughly $79 million. Trump's own standing may help explain the pressure. A New York Times/Siena College poll released Wednesday put his approval rating at 36%, with 59% disapproving. Voters in the poll disapproved of his handling of the cost of living by 69% to 29% and gas prices by 73% to 24%. Democrats led by 10 points when voters were presented with the House candidates actually running in their districts. Trump's allies are also trying to solve a turnout problem: getting voters who backed him in presidential elections to show up when he is not on the ballot. MAGA Inc., in its latest filing , reported a $16.2 million Oct. 8 disbursement labeled " voting education .

events.title: A major security flaw found using an OpenAI model is causing internet chaos
events.summary: A PHP vulnerability found by cybersecurity researchers using GPT-5.6 Sol could affect as many as 70% of websites. MASTER/Getty Images The internet is ablaze after cybersecurity researchers using AI found a bug in the PHP programming language. Greg Brockman said bad actors could use the exploit to steal private user data. The FBI and NSA have advised people to either take down websites or update their software. OpenAI said that 70% of the world's websites could be in peril after cybersecurity researchers using its AI models found exploits in a popular programming language. The National Security Administration's cyber division advised all web providers that use PHP, a widely used open-source language, to take their systems offline or update their software after OpenAI said one of its models found two "critical" flaws in the language's infrastructure. Greg Brockman , the president of OpenAI, said in an X post that hackers could exploit the vulnerability to steal private user data or modify websites. "We consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory," OpenAI said in a blog post. While OpenAI said the vulnerabilities appear to have been identified before any attackers discovered them, the public disclosure set off a race for companies and governments to update their websites and apply fixes before hackers could exploit the bugs. "We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up," Dane Knecht, Cloudflare's chief technology officer, said in a post on X. Numerous websites, including those belonging to governments and the media, went offline on Wednesday to address the issue. PHP is a popular programming language that often handles the behind-the-scenes work powering websites that require user logins and online orders. The critical flaw was first identified by Calif, a cybersecurity research company using GPT-5.6 Sol . Wiz, another cybersecurity company, independently uncovered the issues, OpenAI said. The companies are part of an OpenAI-led initiative called "Patch the Planet," which aims to make the world's digital infrastructure more secure. OpenAI has also warned that as cybersecurity researchers continue to probe software vulnerabilities using its ever-advancing frontier models, more security failures will emerge. An engineer at Microsoft pointed out that the PHP vulnerability was discovered with an older model. "I don't think the world is prepared for the sheer number of vulnerabilities newer models will uncover," the engineer, Nicolas Bustamante, said on X. The public disclosure on Wednesday by OpenAI and others of the existence of the exploits triggered urgent messages from leaders worldwide, including the Japanese Prime Minister. "We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," said Sanae Takaichi. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Israeli military conducts massive "power projection" operation near Iran's border
events.summary: Dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets conducted a sortie on Monday, flying as far as the Iranian border, according to Israeli and U.S. officials. Why it matters: The operation, more than 800 miles away from Israel, took place a week before the Israeli elections and on the same day Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Israel's Ovda Air Base. The sortie wasn't connected to Hegseth's visit. While some Israeli and U.S. officials said the sortie wasn't unusual and that it was meant to deter Iran, it could have led to a miscalculation, triggering an Iranian response and reigniting the war. Behind the scenes: The exercise involved dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft, the sources said. It followed a flight path consistent with a potential strike against Iran, passing through Syrian and Iraqi airspace. As the aircraft approached the Iranian border, they turned around and returned to Israel, the sources said. The intrigue: U.S. officials said the Israelis knew that Iran's air defense systems would detect the sortie. According to the sources, Israel notified the U.S. in advance and described the operation as a training exercise intended for "power projection" and aimed at deterring Iran from launching attacks against Israel ahead of the elections. However, some U.S. sources said they had the impression that Israel was hoping the Iranians would fire at the aircraft, providing a justification for launching strikes against Iran. Fox News reported on Tuesday that the Israeli Air Force conducted a drill towards Iran. Driving the news: Last week, Axios reported that Netanyahu and President Trump discussed in early October the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections. Netanyahu told Trump he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program. Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir told Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine at the time that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said. Trump initially seemed to be inclined to resume attacks, but then grew hesitant and eventually decided against Netanyahu's proposal. State of play: An Israeli official said Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir will not allow any unjustified military activity that could undermine the Oct. 27 elections. What he's saying: On Wednesday Netanyahu said at a military graduation ceremony that Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei "has decided to follow in his father's footsteps" and allowed Iranian scientists to move forward with building a nuclear weapon. "He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again trying to develop its bombs of death," Netanyahu said. "Therefore, there is only one way to eliminate this threat once and for all: to overthrow the regime in Iran. And that is the directive I have given to the IDF, the Mossad and the security agencies," he added.

events.title: How Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russia crippled the world’s second-largest diesel supplier
events.summary: Ukraine's drone strikes on Russian refineries have grown to such a scale, reach and effectiveness that they have crippled the world's second-largest diesel exporter. The Ukrainians are regularly launching swarms of drones that number in the hundreds. They are also striking refineries much deeper in Russian territory. Kyiv learned to target complex refinery equipment that is harder to repair. Diesel prices have surged due to the wars in Eastern Europe and the Middle East. Ukraine launched massive drone assaults against Russia this week, hitting key oil infrastructure and signaling Kyiv intends to block the Kremlin from increasing diesel exports in defiance of President Donald Trump . More than 1,000 Ukrainian drones targeted Russia on Sunday alone in one of the largest attacks this year, according to state media reports. The strikes set ablaze an oil export terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city and President Vladimir Putin 's hometown. Kyiv has ended its brief adherence to an energy ceasefire that Trump declared between Ukraine and Russia on Oct. 11. Moscow ignored that truce from the start and Kyiv vowed to retaliate. Ukraine's drone strikes have achieved a scale, range and effectiveness that they have crippled Russia's diesel exports, said Tatiana Mitrova, an expert on the Russian oil industry at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy. Before the attacks, Russia was the second-largest diesel supplier in the world after the U.S. As a result, Trump's deal with Putin to boost Russian diesel exports is likely dead in the water, said Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler. "It seems unlikely that they'll be able to bring the volume of diesel back to the market that they are talking about without an energy ceasefire," Smith said. Kyiv's strikes on Russian refineries and related oil infrastructure almost tripled to 31 in July compared with 11 in January, according to data from open-source intelligence firm Rochan Consulting in Warsaw, Poland. The attacks slashed Russia's diesel exports by more than 75%, to 141,000 barrels per day (bpd) in September, compared with 608,000 bpd in the same period last year, according to Kpler data. In response, Moscow banned exports in July to preserve domestic supplies. The Kremlin partially resumed shipments this month to fulfill the Trump-Putin deal. Under Trump's diesel deal to relieve pressure on surging fuel prices, the Kremlin agreed to supply the global market with about 75,000 bpd in October and 124,000 bpd in November. But those export volumes are a rounding error compared with total demand, Mitrova said. The Ukrainians are regularly launching swarms of drones now that number in the hundreds, compared with dozens earlier in the war, Mitrova said. They are also striking deeper into Russian territory, she said. In July, Kyiv hit Russia's largest refinery at Omsk , deep in Siberia near the Kazakhstan border, more than 1,000 miles from Ukraine. And they have learned to target more complex refinery equipment that is harder to repair, Mitrova said. A destroyed fuel tank takes just a couple of weeks to fix, she said. But replacing a secondary refining unit, for example, requires supply chains outside Russia, the analyst said. "You cannot just order it on Alibaba," Mitrova said. "You need to make your order in advance and therefore securing this equipment quickly is not possible. You need to compensate for the risks of all the parties involved because [counterparties] are violating sanctions." "You have to wait at least for several months if the right equipment is destroyed," she said. With midterm elections less than two weeks away, Trump has blamed Ukraine for surging diesel prices that are jeopardizing Republicans' election chances. Nationally, diesel cost $6.32 per gallon on average Tuesday, nearly 75% above the same period last year, according to AAA. But the diesel market was already under pressure due to Trump's decision to go to war with Iran in late February. Tehran's attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and strikes by its Houthi militant allies on oil infrastructure of U.S. Gulf Arab allies have disrupted fuel exports from the Middle East. Diesel exports through Hormuz, for example, are down about 540,000 bpd compared with last year, Kpler's Smith said. Global diesel exports have fallen about 1 million bpd due to lost supplies from Russia and the Middle East, he said. Trump's options to reduce fuel prices are limited. The underlying problem is the shortfall of refining capacity due to damage from two wars that don't appear close to ending soon. U.S. refiners are already working at maximum capacity to fill the gap as much as possible. The International Energy Agency warned this month that diesel supplies will likely remain constrained well into 2027. "The diesel tightness is likely going to persist in the coming months and prices are going to remain elevated," Smith said.

events.title: New PowerToys utilities make everyday Windows tasks easier
events.summary: PowerToys 0.102 is here: new mouse utilities, Command Palette improvements and much more We’re back with a fresh PowerToys release! This one brings two new mouse utilities, Mouse Button Lock and CursorHide , an optional quick-access shelf for Command Palette , snip dictation in ZoomIt , and a set of new command-line tools for automating PowerToys. Color Picker and Text Extractor also move to WinUI 3, and Keyboard Manager picks up some long-requested remapping features. Get the update by checking for updates in PowerToys or by heading to the release page . Let’s dive in! 🖱️ Mouse Button Lock and CursorHide Holding a mouse button down during a long drag or selection can be tiring. With Mouse Button Lock , press and hold a button for a moment, then let go. Windows keeps treating it as held, so you can continue dragging or selecting until you click any button. This is especially useful for gaming, working in professional applications that require extensive dragging and selection, and improving accessibility for users who find it difficult to hold down a mouse button for extended periods. CursorHide is the second new mouse utility. It hides the mouse pointer while you type, after a period of inactivity, or both , and shows it again as soon as you move the mouse. PR #50271 (Thanks, @DamianEdwards !) ⚡ Command Palette gets a quick-access shelf Compact mode in 0.101 kept Command Palette out of the way until you needed results. Now your favorite commands can be one keystroke away too. Turn on the quick-access shelf in Settings > Appearance > Compact mode to show your pins below the search box while the palette is collapsed. Press Alt+1 through Alt+9 to launch them, or Alt+Shift+number to select one without running it. Drag to reorder, right-click for more actions, and optionally show recent commands and apps next to your pins. The shelf is just one part of a big Command Palette update: Settings search: Fuzzy search finds options, extensions, commands, aliases, and assigned shortcuts, then takes you straight to them. Keyboard-first Dock: Press Win+Alt+J to focus the dock and move between its items from the keyboard. Copilot key support: Choose Command Palette as the Copilot key app in Windows Settings, and press the key again to toggle the palette. Multiple clocks: Pin several dock clocks, each with its own time zone and format. Language and links: Pick an app language for Command Palette, and copy links that open a page, run a command, or jump to a specific setting. Polish: Sharper app icons, faster grid and gallery browsing, results that keep loading at the end of a list, and clearer nested menus. Massive thanks to @jiripolasek for the sustained Command Palette work across this release! ZoomIt can now capture what you say along with what you snip. Turn on Snip with dictation in the ZoomIt settings, then press Space while you drag out a snip and describe what you’re capturing. ZoomIt transcribes your speech on your device, and a single paste delivers both the screenshot and your text. Dictation uses the microphone selected under Record. ZoomIt also gets smooth zoom transitions , better audio pacing in recordings, and a fix for silent recordings on multichannel and spatial-audio devices. More of PowerToys can now be scripted from the terminal: Advanced Paste: Run built-in and custom actions without opening the UI, using files, stdin/stdout, or the clipboard. AI actions use your configured providers and policies. Light Switch: Check status, set or toggle the theme, and manage schedules, with JSON output. Settings: See which utilities are enabled, and turn them on or off even while PowerToys isn’t running. Peek: Preview multiple files and folders from the command line. PowerDisplay: JSON Lines output makes results and errors easy to consume from scripts. On your PATH: FancyZones, Image Resizer, File Locksmith, and PowerDisplay commands now work from any terminal folder. PRs: #50834 , #50459 , #50507 , and #49724 (Thanks, @daverayment !) ⌨️ Keyboard Manager adds tap-alone remaps and easier editing Keyboard Manager now supports tap-alone remaps . Tap a key by itself to trigger a different action, while the key keeps working normally in shortcuts and mouse combinations. Large remapping lists are easier to manage too, with search, modifier and app filters, and bulk deletion . The new editor also gets a searchable key picker , so you can select any key, including media keys or keys your keyboard doesn’t have, and build a full shortcut with just the mouse. Recording now only listens while the editor is in focus, and Tab moves you out of the recording field. IT admins can also deploy and export remapping profiles with DSC v3 . PRs: #49136 and #49287 (Thanks, @MasaYan24 !), #51150 , and #49427 (Thanks, @Gijsreyn !) Color Picker and Text Extractor: Both move to WinUI 3, with a new overlay, editor, and magnifier for Color Picker. Your existing shortcuts and settings carry over. FancyZones: Scroll the mouse wheel while dragging a window to switch layouts, with an optional indicator showing the selected layout’s name. Peek: Added read-only SQLite previews, file and subfolder counts with scanning progress for folders, a plain-text fallback, and Alt+Left/Alt+Right navigation between files. Screen Ruler: Measure in device-independent pixels to account for each monitor’s scaling, with improved edge detection. Environment Variables: A new Remove duplicates action cleans up PATH while keeping the original order. Quick Accent: A searchable character reference in Settings lets you browse language sets and copy characters directly. Grab and Move: Exclude specific apps so they keep their normal modifier-key behavior. Shortcut Guide: Added shortcuts for Claude Desktop and Ableton Live, and made indexing more resilient to malformed manifests. Workspaces: Now asks for confirmation before launching an unverified app configured to run as administrator. Awake: Windows can now turn off the display while the PC is locked, without ending your keep-awake session. New+: Fixed a File Explorer memory leak and improved long-path handling. Settings: Added an interactive animated welcome scene, fixed a memory leak when switching pages, and kept module on/off preferences when a utility fails to load. As always, a big thank-you to everyone who contributed — we couldn’t do this release without you!

events.title: The AI boom is good for people who write about AI. Ask Derek Thompson.
events.summary: Courtesy of Derek Thompson; BI The AI boom is swallowing the US economy. That extends to people who make a living writing, says author Derek Thompson: Stories about AI are the most lucrative thing he can produce. Thompson, who writes about a wide range of topics, says he's torn between writing stories he knows his audience wants, vs other topics he cares about. Derek Thompson writes and talks about a lot of things. But some things pay better than others: "Dimes for analysis, dollars for facts, and Benjamins for facts about artificial intelligence," he tells me. Thompson, a longtime Atlantic writer who left to launch his own Substack in 2025, has an avid following — Barack Obama reportedly reads him to stay on top of AI developments. That following also creates an inherent tension: If he only creates work he knows will have a big audience, it squeezes out other subjects he's passionate about, like the way technology affects the media we consume. Or why he thinks Americans should embrace a pro-building mindset — the subject of " Abundance, " the recent book he co-wrote with Ezra Klein. I talked to Thompson about AI — of course — along with some of his other passions, like why he thinks pro sports are a conspiracy that lets the richest people in the world turn "their already-elevated wealth into exospherically extreme wealth." You can hear our entire conversation on my Channels podcast. The following is an edited excerpt: Peter Kafka: Perhaps the only thing Americans agree on is data centers — they hate them , and don't want them built in their communities. What is the "Abundance" view on data centers? Could you argue that building them is good for the country — just like building more housing is good? Derek Thompson: I don't see data centers and houses as being equivalent. I think data centers are houses for chips. Really, they're igloos for chips because they're very, very cold houses. While I feel incredibly passionate about removing barriers to building housing where people want to live, I feel less passionate about saying we need to make sure that every AI company can site every data center wherever it wants to build it. There are costs to an economic infrastructure project that leans so heavily into data centers that other modes of construction are being starved for resources. Jason Furman , an economist at Harvard, just published a graph showing that in the last year, while data center construction's up by more than 60%, construction of hospitals is down, construction of offices is down, construction of housing is down, construction of just about everything else that you can name, including manufacturing facilities, is down because data centers are essentially eating the economy and crowding out a lot of other investment. Am I anti-data centers in the extreme? No. Do I think data centers are just like houses? Absolutely not. I think houses for people are more important to emphasize as a matter of public policy than houses for chips. Last year, you wrote this great piece about how " Everything is Television ," where you argue that it's inevitable that all media becomes video. But you've also said that you've become a video podcaster because your podcast company nudged you to do that. How much of the video push is corporate incentive, and how much is what people want? My theory is that it's corporate incentives because it's what people want. Companies have attempted pivoting to video infinity times. But other pivots to video, especially in the last few years, have essentially become the norm. Everyone's podcast goes to YouTube now, or Spotify or Netflix . That suggests to me that the instinct to pivot to video reflected a reasonable corporate interpretation of an underlying consumer reality: that, at the end of the day, what most people want to do with most of their time is sit on a comfortable couch or chair and look at moving images. There does seem to be something spookily, biologically inherent about the degree to which we want to just watch moving images. Television went from zero to 50% adoption rate in a decade. There is just something true, with a capital T, about the media success of a technology that allows us to do nothing but turn our minds into a receiver for moving images. I'm not saying that's good. I'm just saying that apparently is the situation. How has going independent changed how you work and what you make? When you go from being a salaried employee, where you make one amount of money all year, no matter what, to being self-employed, where the line goes up the harder you work, it's very hard to ignore that signal and not work harder. I feel more harried about work than I did. When that line doesn't go up, when it starts to slip, when 12 months has elapsed since a big article I wrote last year, and because 10% to 20% of subscribers are gonna drop out of the list, it sucks to see any number go down. And then I start to think, "God, I gotta work harder. I gotta get that next article to make the revenue line go back up." Are you more inclined to think, "That story about sports billionaires did well, let's do more of those," in a way you might have been insulated from at The Atlantic ? Yeah, there's no question. And again, this is not something I think is altogether good. I said one thing I've learned from a year on Substack is that it's dimes for analysis, dollars for facts, and Benjamins for facts about artificial intelligence. Recognizing that it's dimes for social analysis and Benjamins for AI analysis, there is a part of the job that pulls me toward writing more about AI than I might ... Because the market wants it. The market clearly wants it. That said, I do think artificial intelligence is not only the most important but also the most interesting story in the world. It's an economic story. It's a safety story. It's a stock story. I have this long list of essentially social essays that I want to write. Stuff like "Everything Is Television." But I know that if I only write those essays for a month, if I only write those essays for a year, the line's gonna go down. And so I'm interested in AI, and fortunately, the AI stuff sells. The AI reporting that I do creates a zone of extraordinary comfort for me to spend time writing stories that I know won't make money, but I think could be really, really broadly read as social analysis. events.title: Energy secretary leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfield
events.summary: Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaigners Miatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the giant Rosebank oilfield, sources have told the Guardian, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners. After approving the smaller Jackdaw gasfield on Wednesday, officials say the energy secretary is leaning towards refusing approval for what would be one of the biggest oilfields in the North Sea. But she could still be overruled by Andy Burnham, who may hear different representations from the chancellor, John Healey. A final decision is expected before the end of this year. In comments that will be read as a signal of her intent, Fahnbulleh told the Guardian that the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it. “One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.” In contrast, Healey told ITV he expected “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, a suggestion he is anticipating new oil revenues. Burnham would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision. Labour MPs warned on Wednesday there would be a major pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessity as part of the transition to net zero. MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent. Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet taken a final decision on Rosebank. The field would emit about seven times the carbon of Jackdaw and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe that it would do less for UK energy security, given most of the oil would be exported. A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This is speculation. As the energy secretary has said, each project will be assessed on its own merits.” On a visit to Aberdeen, Fahnbulleh said she had been satisfied that Jackdaw, which is due to begin producing gas within weeks and will add an estimated 36m tonnes of carbon emissions, would not violate the UK’s climate commitments. “As we make the transition, we are going to need gas,” she said. “At a point when we have got conflict in the Middle East that is triggering an energy crisis, energy security is vital, and homegrown energy is key.” She admitted, however, it would not help achieve the government’s main energy target of bringing down bills, saying: “This is not about bills.” The UN Environment Programme has recommended that global carbon emissions be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin. The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland , where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted. But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party. One Labour MP close to the energy secretary said she knew her credibility was “on the line” and that she was able to show she was pragmatic by approving Jackdaw but drawing the line at Rosebank. “She’s putting up a fight and I want to be supportive of Miatta – I understand what she is fighting,” they said. The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential But they said the decision would ultimately come down to Burnham. “Andy is not a climate guy – he is under pressure. If he wants to do it, he’ll do it.” Several serving ministers have said they would find Rosebank a more difficult decision to back and it would cause greater problems in their constituencies. The former minister Catherine West said climate change “is not a future threat but a present reality” and that the answer to job losses in the North Sea was not to “double down on new fossil fuel developments”. Afzal Khan, the Labour MP for Manchester Rusholme and chair of the all-party parliamentary group on climate change, said: “Approving projects on the scale of Rosebank, on top of today’s decision to approve Jackdaw, cannot be justified.” Burnham is seeking more ways to lower energy bills, telling MPs on Wednesday that ministers would consider whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills to ease cost pressures on households.

events.title: Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen | Zoe Williams
events.summary: Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen This foolish decision undermines hopes that this government will take the necessary steps the climate crisis demands W hen the news broke that the UK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield , I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately, the theme suggested by readers was what can the public actually do in the face of what feels like paralysing climate doom? There is so much going on that is hopeful: biodiversity tracking, river protection, rewilding. Shruti Suresh, from the independent watchdog Global Witness, told those in attendance that if they wanted to effect change, they should protest against Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project. The message was so well understood that it didn’t need labouring. The mood in the room when the news came in was one of audible dismay. People had just watched the minister for climate transition declare that she could see the challenges ahead and was ready for them. The Jackdaw announcement will face immediate protest and legal challenge, but it sends a very clear signal from the government: we don’t mean what we say about ending emissions. It turns out you can take all imaginable personal responsibility to arrest the climate crisis, make lifestyle adjustments that even five years ago you wouldn’t have dreamed of, miraculously summon the energy to take collective action from what is often private despair, but it will be insufficient as long as corporations – assisted by the government – are working against you, in effect with impunity. At some point, you need to get the people you elected to do what we all know – and they acknowledge – is necessary. The Jackdaw decision had been quietly parked during the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when the threat of the Greens seemed greater to Labour than it turned out to be . But while Labour successfully buried the issue during the campaign, the underlying issues surrounding Jackdaw – and Rosebank, which is yet to be decided upon – persist. Since the 2015 Paris agreement, we have been committed to try to limit temperature rises to 1.5C, and we’ve known for at least five years that means the vast majority of fossil fuels have to stay in the ground. As of 2024, there’s been scientific consensus that the target of 1.5C is “deader than a doornail” , while this week’s emissions-gap report could not be clearer: the threshold will be breached and it will cause unimaginable damage, yet with urgent emissions reduction, there is a way back from the abyss. There is no workable argument that runs: “Everyone has to leave their fossil fuels in the ground, as a matter of the utmost urgency, except for us; everyone has to prioritise the long-term survival of a livable planet over energy bills, except for us; we all need to reach carbon neutrality and worry about high-skilled jobs later, except for us.” The Jackdaw field isn’t huge, will peak in a short time and won’t on its own reduce energy bills , which are determined by global markets. So it’s tempting to shuffle it off as a side-order issue, but it matters: it destroys our moral authority as a nation and it extinguishes hope. The climate debate operates on two tracks that don’t meet. On the one hand, we talk about non-linear irreversible tipping points whose effects would be so seismic that the question of mitigation is too vast and, frankly, too painful to consider. The only bearable discussion of the collapse of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) – a system of currents within the Atlantic Ocean – is how to avoid it, and the contested matter of whether that is even possible. We talk about heat deaths across 854 European cities over the past summer, and we talk about areas in the UK of environmental deprivation, flood risks and poorly insulated housing. We also talk about food security both in the short term, with potato crops destroyed by the weather, and in the long term, with supply chains subject to the incomprehensible devastation of every country going through its own particular climate crisis simultaneously. We look at the social unrest across Europe – which is the fastest-warming continent – and ask to what extent the deprivation created by an unstable climate is being weaponised by a far right hell-bent on choking off climate action. Then we gate off all that knowledge, all that anxiety, all that will to action, and turn our attention to the UK’s immediate energy compromises. The arguments here run that since we’re going to import gas from somewhere anyway, because any transition will take time, we may as well get it at home. Even though it’s well known that household energy prices won’t be reduced , the government can use the tax take to reduce VAT. Some categories of emission are lower from UK gas than they would be from energy imported from the Gulf.

events.title: Expanding AI trade is turning safety stocks into a 'Texas hedge'
events.summary: When a hurricane looms, panic buying clears store shelves of household essentials like water, canned food, dry goods, and toilet paper. A similar dynamic is playing out in the market. Investors are bailing on higher-volatility growth stocks and running toward the shelter of perceived safety sectors like utilities and consumer staples. The key difference? They may not be so safe. As valuation multiples across capital-intensive AI infrastructure plays — such as specialized data center hosting providers CoreWeave (CRWV) and Iren Ltd (IREN) — take on water in the form of massive debt loads due to aggressive capex buildouts, investors may want to take a portion of their equity exposure into more protected water. The issue with utilities is that while it is traditionally considered a conservative sector, more recently it has become part of the AI story as the massive data center build-out is accompanied by surging power demand. This is one of the reasons that in recent years utilities outperformed staples. However, if the bloom of the AI rose helped fuel that outperformance, it would be a “Texas hedge” to buy it now on concerns that the AI trade is getting wobbly. In other words, buying so-called safety stocks might actually increase your risk. In this context, consumer staples, most easily traded with the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLP) is a better choice. Unlike AI infrastructure, hyperscalers are dependent on enterprise IT budgets and continuous capital infusions. XLP's constituents—led by market heavyweights like Walmart (WMT) , the world’s largest grocery store chain, Costco (COST) , a perennial “Holly Index” constituent, Procter & Gamble (PG) , and toilet paper and diaper maker Kimberly-Clark — generate consistent revenues. I often joke that when the market goes sideways, investors probably need more diapers and toilet paper, not less. Plainly put, consumers buy toothpaste, groceries, and cleaning supplies regardless of macro or micro economic stress. Consumer staples tend to deliver steady cash flow and XLP distributes a lot of that back to shareholders with a ~2.6% annualized dividend yield. This provides an organic return buffer during market pullbacks, contrasting sharply with high-beta data center operators that re-invest every dollar into equipment and facilities. Leveraged AI hosts trade at elevated multiples, leaving minimal room for execution errors. Consumer staples offer lower beta (read lower downside in a general equity market pullback). Options strategy: bullish call diagonal spread To capture a structural rotation into staples over a horizon extending into early 2027, a long call diagonal is capital efficient and risk-defined. Buy January 2027 $85.00 Call: (these are in-the-money) With a ~0.65–0.70 delta, these calls provides a more stock-like exposure for considerably less than purchasing the stock outright (one does sacrifice dividends versus the stock), but this also reduces the “extrinsic” premium associated with buying them - thus less decay or “theta”. Sell November $92.00 Call: Assuming these expire worthless one could further monetize short-term upside movements by repeatedly selling out-of-the-money upside calls against the longer-dated position to lower the net cost basis over time. Assuming the long calls remain in the money by expiration the calls can be exercised and one would own the underlying shares. Max Risk: Capped strictly at the initial net debit paid for the options strategy. Max Gain: Achieved if XLP trends steadily toward the 92–95 target by the nearer dated expiration, are unlimited if the nearer dated options expire worthless and no new short upside call options are sold against the longer-dated calls. events.title: Tech firms monitor city council meetings to track data center sentiment
events.summary: Data-center companies are ponying up to find out which communities will resist them the least. Startup Hamlet has parsed tens of thousands of city council meetings by scraping local governments’ video recordings, tagging comments as friendly or hostile to a potential project. CEO Sunil Rajaraman told Semafor that a large fund that finances data centers and a data-center developer are among its paying customers, looking for whiffs of a moratorium. “Where there might be more favorable political views” may well determine where future projects get built, Rajaraman said. Investors backing these projects are also obvious customers for a real-time feed into Americans’ growing antipathy toward data centers. The appetite for such data shows the lengths to which the tech industry is going to find where projects are most likely to go through, in the face of a national groundswell of anti-data center activism that has turned community sentiment into a financial risk. Other Hamlet customers include real estate developers, political action committees, and retailers, Rajaraman said. The company on Tuesday launched new rankings for where cities and counties stand on a host of hot-button issues (ranging from zoning laws to pickleball), and a portal for people to look up what their elected officials have said. (Among large local governments, Corpus Christi, Texas ranked No. 1 in speakers’ opposition to data centers.) “This is public sphere data,” Rajaraman said. “The data needs to be out there so America can make better decisions.”

events.title: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy
events.summary: Government decision is about how much oil and gas is sensible for UK to produce on the way to net zero A ndy Burnham hit the nail on the (well)head in his first fortnight as prime minister when he said : “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is, where does it come from?” It was a nod towards several awkward energy facts. First, oil and gas provided 75% of the UK’s energy in 2025, government data shows. Second, even with the rollout of domestic renewables for generating electricity, about 43% of overall energy was imported last year. Third, all credible paths to net zero emissions by 2050 involve using a lot of oil and gas on the way because we’re still in the foothills of electrification. Fewer than 2% of UK households have heat pumps, according to the lobby group Electrify Britain. While sales of EVs are accelerating, nearly 95% of vehicles on the road run on petrol and diesel. Meanwhile, hydrogen and biomethane have barely taken off as alternatives to gas for those industrial processes that require higher temperatures than electricity can achieve – tricky for a government pursuing “reindustrialisation ”. Fourth – and this one must alarm Downing Street – the global energy market has simply become less reliable. The strait of Hormuz can close overnight. The US president can threaten to ban diesel exports . Russian ships prowl the North Sea . Even the nice Norwegians, with an eye on their own energy consumers, scrapped a planned electricity cable to Scotland in 2023. It is no longer a world of always-available “just in time” supply. Thinking has shifted to “just in case” scenario-planning. And a truly scary scenario would be disruption to the 725-mile Langeled pipeline that is the primary route for gas supplies from Norway, 40% of the UK’s consumption last year. The pipeline is a security vulnerability if ever there was one (if you doubt it, watch Sky News’ recent report ). Now we have the start of an answer to Burnham’s “where should it come from?” question. The Jackdaw gasfield, 150 miles east of Aberdeen, has finally been approved to produce in time for winter. About time, too. All the arguments from pragmatism were in the field’s favour. As this column has said in the past , less North Sea gas would inevitably mean more imported liquefied natural gas, with the extra carbon emissions created by chilling the fuel to -160C for shipment and then “regasifying” it at the other end. Such cargos were 20% of UK gas imports last year, mostly from the US. It already feels absurd that the 24m UK households with a gas boiler burn any gas at all from the shale fields of Texas and Pennsylvania. Why increase the exposure if lower-polluting supplies are available off Aberdeen? More UK North Sea gas production won’t lower the price for consumers much, if at all. But that was never the argument. It was always about tax receipts, jobs, the national balance of payments, relative emissions and the security that comes with having domestic volumes piped straight into the national gas network. Jackdaw is not a gamechanger – it will be 6% of UK North Sea gas production at peak – but it’s definitely worth having while the UK is still using gas, which will be at least as long as the field’s 11-year life. The next question is whether other “tie-back” gasfields in already-explored areas, such as Tornado, west of Shetland, will follow. The line in the government’s announcement about “asking the regulator to consider urgent cases that could benefit from similar measures now” suggests so. Rosebank, also near Shetland, is a trickier political proposition because it’s mostly oil, which is more polluting, and will be producing for longer. But the arguments aren’t wholly different. The common elements are still jobs, investment, taxes and the government’s ability to impose higher environmental standards during the production stage. Meanwhile, the “it’s all exported” objection to Rosebank misses the fact that the UK oil industry operates within a European network. If the UK had more than four refineries (compared with nine at the turn of the century), a chunk of Rosebank’s output might be processed at home. As it is, some – perhaps the majority – will come back to the UK as petrol, diesel and jet fuel once it’s been refined in Rotterdam or elsewhere in north-west Europe. Take a step back and the North Sea debate is really about how much oil and gas it is sensible for the UK to produce itself on the way to net zero. On the current trajectory, only about a third of consumption will come from domestic sources on a net basis. Even offshore lobbyists reckon a boost to North Sea production would only get the ratio up to about a half, albeit the figure would obviously increase if consumption of fossil fuels can be made to fall faster. Nobody is talking about the UK becoming a net exporter again. Commitment to net zero by 2050 was intact, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted.

events.title: Microsoft and Alphabet opt out of tokenized stocks in latest blow to ambitious plan from OKK and NYSE parent firm
events.summary: A growing number of companies are pushing back against tokenized trading of their shares. Microsoft and Alphabet are the latest to complain about the practice, joining 14 other public companies that have formally objected to a plan by OKXICE, a new platform co-chaired by former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, to trade blockchain-based versions of their shares. The two tech giants joined Goldman Sachs , Caterpillar , McDonald’s, Qualcomm and Western Digital in a new batch of objections disclosed Monday. They joined nine companies—Cerebras Systems, AppLovin , Applied Digital, Rocket Lab, CoreWeave, Verizon , Applied Optoelectronics, Broadcom and UnitedHealth Group—whose objections were disclosed last week. Cuomo downplayed the wave of objections, framing the pushback as a predictable reaction to a major market shift. “We always anticipated that, because this is such a dramatic and revolutionary change, many companies would want to wait and see how it goes rather than be the first to participate,” he said in a written statement to Fortune . OKX did not respond to questions about when trading would begin or whether the objections had changed its launch plans. The objections come two weeks after Cuomo announced plans to launch OKXICE’s tokenized stock-trading platform. The venture, a partnership between crypto exchange OKX and ICE, the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, would offer round-the-clock trading in blockchain-based versions of 63 U.S.-listed stocks. The venture is seeking to use a temporary exemption granted by the Securities and Exchange Commission last month that allows qualifying platforms to offer trading in tokenized stocks without registering as national securities exchanges, provided they meet certain conditions. The veto’s limits Under these rules, trading platforms do not need a company’s permission to offer tokenized versions of its shares. Instead, they must notify the company, which then has 30 days from receiving the notice to object before the platform can proceed. “There’s not a proactive consent right. Rather, it is a reactive right to object,” said Erin Martin, a partner and co-lead of fintech and digital assets at law firm Morgan Lewis, who spent over a decade as a senior lawyer at the SEC. “If they don’t object within that 30-day notice period, the [venue] can go ahead and start to tokenize and list those securities.” Applied Optoelectronics, a technology company that makes equipment for high-speed networks, said it objected because the framework is new and its potential effects on the pricing, liquidity and volatility of its stock remain uncertain. “At this stage, we don’t see a clear benefit to AOI or our shareholders that justifies these uncertainties,” a spokesperson told Fortune . The company also said investors could mistakenly believe it backed the offering, which it neither sponsored nor endorsed. The other 15 companies declined to comment or did not respond to requests for comment. But a company’s objection only blocks trading on that platform under the SEC exemption. It does not stop other firms from offering tokenized versions of its shares overseas or through other legal arrangements. The 30-day deadline can also create practical problems. Under the SEC’s rules, platforms must send notices to a company’s main executive office, where they could get buried in other mail before reaching its legal team, Martin noted. An unanswered notice lets the platform proceed after the deadline. “It has not been contemplated in the existing SEC order,” Martin said regarding whether a company can pull its stock after the 30-day window closes. A new era of stock trading? OKXICE’s push to tokenize stocks aims to tap into a $35 billion market , offering investors round-the-clock trading without some of the delays associated with traditional stock markets. “The market never sleeps, so why should trading? Ownership shouldn’t have office hours,” Cuomo said when he first announced the venture.  But the benefits are less clear for the companies whose shares would be traded.  One concern is that the digital tokens could trade at different prices from the shares they represent on the NYSE or Nasdaq, especially when few people are buying and selling. Martin, the digital assets specialist at Morgan Lewis, notes that companies have an additional concern when it comes to 24/7 trading. Namely, she points out that they would lose the pause they normally have to announce earnings or other important news while markets are closed, which allows investors time to digest the implications. Protecting investors also presents hurdles if the software handling trades fails or the firms holding the underlying shares run into trouble, according to risk disclosures detailed in OKXICE’s public notice with the SEC. Meanwhile, Apple , Nvidia , and Amazon are among the remaining 47 companies that have not yet publicly objected to plans to trade tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE. As of Wednesday, that received notices in early October could have until early November to respond, depending on when they received them. If all 60-plus companies in OKXICE’s planned lineup object within the 30-day window, the platform would have no stocks left from that list to offer under the exemption. Ignoring those objections would mean losing the exemption, Martin said.  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
