events.title: Burnham proposes plan to cut standing charges from gas bills
events.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked ministers to develop a plan to remove standing charges from gas bills. These are fixed daily fees that cover the costs of connecting to a supply. They vary by region and households must still pay them even when energy is not being used. Industry body Energy UK said whether the proposed changes would make a difference to bills would depend on how or where the charges were reallocated on the bill. But an influential research foundation argued it would be a progressive move that would help those on low-incomes and knock £27 off a typical annual bill. During Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham said the "pragmatic decision" on giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea would allow the government to increase investment in renewables and "do more to help people with bills". He said he had asked the Chancellor John Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh "to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this house at the earliest opportunity". No details have been given on how removing standing charges would work in practice. But the suggestion has been made by research firm Nesta that they could be moved to the unit rate , external , so people pay for what they use. This would probably benefit customers who don't use much gas, but heavy users could end up paying more. For nearly two years, regulator Ofgem has run a series of consultations on standing charges, with a massive public response including vociferous opposition from low-energy users who can do nothing to cut standing charges. Ofgem is running a pilot scheme on low standing charge tariffs, but is yet to draw any firm conclusions, suggesting there are no easy answers. Higher cost of electricity standing charges Average standing charges are 54.8p a day for electricity and 29.7p a day for gas. When asked why electricity standing charges would not be scrapped as well, the PM's official spokesman said VAT had already been cut on electricity bills. Standing charges cover costs such as transporting energy to homes via pipes and wires, and the upkeep of that infrastructure. The standing charges also fund schemes to support low-income households. Many of these costs will need to be recouped somehow, but Citizens Advice has warned , external about the potential consequences of reform for vulnerable customers. Vulnerable people who don't have a high income, but have high energy usage, could be penalised. But Madeleine Gabriel, director of sustainable future at Nesta, said: "Abolishing the gas standing charge and moving those costs onto the unit rate would help those worst hit by rising energy prices." Pressure remains on the chancellor to offer more fundamental, targeted energy support this winter in his Budget next week, with energy prices forecast to rise by 16% to a four-year high in January . In addition to standing charges, Burnham said investing in renewables would also bring household bills down "substantially" by breaking the link between gas and electricity prices "in this parliament". Electricity prices in the UK are mainly set by gas prices, and this is often cited as a reason why electricity prices in the UK are higher than many other countries. events.title: OpenAI says its agents disabled their own safety monitors
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts OpenAI says its AI agents disabled their own safety monitors It is the latest example of autonomous AI models seemingly breaking containment. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic ) Two OpenAI agents disabled or weakened tools used to detect incidents of AI agents acting against human commands. The two instances happened earlier this month, with one later telling its programmer it had not stripped out its monitor. The incidents adds to mounting disease about how well AI companies are controlling their autonomous systems. OpenAI has revealed that two of its artificial intelligence agents disabled or weakened systems built to catch them misbehaving, with one later denying it had done so. The cases are the latest in a string of safety scares at the world's top AI developers involving agents, AI programs that carry out tasks without human involvement. In a report released this week, the ChatGPT maker said that during two internal coding jobs, its agents switched off or undermined tools for detecting incidents of AI models acting against human wishes. On October 3, an agent running on OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol model, which had been told not to send any messages on the workplace chat app, took that as license to switch off safety alerts meant for the company's security team while fixing a testing system. This latest incident follows an earlier instance in which an OpenAI model accessed a Medicare statistics reporting service. ( ABC News ) Three days later, a GPT-6 Astra agent stripped out its own monitor while copying code from another project, then told the human programmer it had done no such thing. The company said it had also seen several cases of agents launching software with monitoring switched off, exposing a gap in its oversight. OpenAI said it is still trying to determine whether the models were simply overzealous in following instructions or have a particular tendency to evade monitoring. Will an AI-cloned free tool spell the end of expensive software? AI data centre company cold calling about buying land, inquiry told Tech giant shares plunge 40pc after delays to Melbourne data centre Embattled AI company Firmus still wants funds for Tasmanian data centre The disclosure adds to mounting unease over how well leading labs can control increasingly autonomous systems. In July, a group of OpenAI agents broke out of their test environments and launched a cyberattack on AI firm Hugging Face, causing international alarm. Other companies have since reported similar incidents. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also accused the AI company's models of infiltrating a Medicare website with both public and private data, although no personal information was accessed in the incident. The incidents have fuelled calls in the United States and abroad for tighter oversight of AI development. But US President Donald Trump, under the advice of top AI executives like Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, has urged the industry to police itself. events.title: Macron makes surprise Saudi visit as France secures extra diesel supplies
events.summary: French president meets Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh to discuss energy, security, and infrastructure as cost-of-living protests rage at home. French President Emmanuel Macron has arrived in Riyadh on a surprise “solidarity” visit, making him the first Western leader to touch down in Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s Houthis intensified their attacks this month. Macron met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in the Saudi capital, and the two discussed regional and international developments, as well as coordinating efforts to strengthen security and stability, the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported on Wednesday. list 1 of 3 France’s Macron says protesters won’t be allowed to ‘cause chaos’ list 2 of 3 What are Italy’s new measures against violent protests? list 3 of 3 Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict? The unannounced trip comes as Saudi Arabia agreed to supply extra diesel to France “for as many months as necessary”, the Elysee Palace told the AFP news agency. The visit aims to “demonstrate France’s solidarity with the kingdom in the face of the attacks carried out by the Houthis against its territory, and to continue efforts undertaken on securing and diversifying hydrocarbon supplies”, the French presidency said earlier. The diplomatic push follows days of rioting in France, fuelled by the cost of living, especially as the US-Iran war and Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have kept energy prices high. Faced with criticism of his Gulf tour at home, Macron told reporters earlier in Doha that he was just “doing his job” in a bid to “ease tensions” over petrol prices, one of the causes of social unrest in France. “There must be no sign of febrility,” he said. “I am fulfilling my role. I am at my post.” The deal follows pledges secured earlier in Macron’s Gulf tour. The presidency said on Tuesday that the United Arab Emirates had committed to about 100,000 tonnes a month , with a further 100,000 tonnes monthly to be secured in Bahrain. Together with Saudi deliveries, France now has commitments for 295,000 tonnes a month, just more than 10 percent of its consumption, it said. Meanwhile, France is also sending military assets to Saudi Arabia , under an earlier agreement, to help protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which has come under attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God). The United Kingdom also announced on Tuesday that it would deploy fighter jets to help shield the kingdom. Both countries say their support is purely defensive. Analysts say the moves protect Saudi oil exports that matter to Europe’s energy markets and bolster the Gulf alliance as the US shows reluctance to offer direct military help. They also carry risks, analysts say, potentially drawing the two European states into the protracted Saudi-Houthi conflict.

events.title: Intel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that’s at least 5 years behind schedule
events.summary: Intel’s first Ohio fab was originally expected to begin production in 2025. Operations are now targeted for 2030 or 2031. Intel says construction and tool installation are underway at its next Arizona fab, with operations expected by the end of 2028. Reported discussions with SK Hynix could bring memory production to the Ohio site, but no deal has been confirmed. Intel has hit a milestone in the construction of its massive chip fabrication plant in New Albany, Ohio, that's running at least five years behind schedule, a delay that's coincided with soaring demand for advanced chips. On Wednesday, Intel announced that crews have installed the first major structural truss in Ohio, which means the next part of the construction has finally begun. "This represents another significant step toward expanded U.S. leading-edge semiconductor capacity," Intel Foundry head Naga Chandrasekaran wrote in a post on the company's website on Wednesday. Intel still needs customers to make the investment pay off. In September, reports surfaced that the world's leading maker of high-bandwidth memory, SK Hynix , could team up with Intel in Ohio to lease some foundry space to make memory chips at the new site. Neither company would confirm any plans. When Intel first announced the Ohio factory in 2022, it was expected to start delivering chips in 2025. Intel pushed back that timeline, now aiming to finish construction in 2030. A second Ohio fab is also planned for completion in 2031 at the site, just northeast of Columbus. The delay reflects a broader recalibration of Intel's foundry ambitions under CEO Lip-Bu Tan. The Ohio factory is only one piece of Intel's ambitious build-out to start making chips for outside customers that began under former CEO Pat Gelsinger. When Tan took the helm in 2025, his turnaround strategy was more cautious, choosing to wait for customer demand before forging ahead with ambitious chip fab plans. Still, by late 2025, Intel was in high-volume production at its Arizona chip fab , producing its most advanced 18A chips. On Wednesday, Chandrasekaran also announced that operations at its next fab in Arizona are expected to begin by the end of 2028. But Intel has yet to land a major external customer for those 18A chips coming out of Arizona. Instead, Intel is using them to make its own processors for devices. Once a dominant force in the chip manufacturing landscape, Intel hit major delays with its 7- and 10-nanometer nodes, triggering the stock's worst year ever in 2024. Customers have been reluctant to commit again since. Now, Intel's window of opportunity may have arrived alongside record demand for AI, as leading chip manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. can't make chips fast enough. Even for the biggest chipmakers like Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices , Apple and Broadcom , "competition is extremely fierce," to get space on TSMC's factory lines, according to Mizuho Securities analyst Jordan Klein. Intel could offer customers an alternative source for chip production, according to TechInsights analyst Dan Hutcheson. "People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC's arm and keep them honest on pricing," Hutcheson said. "All the big ones have been testing there." events.title: What the GOP activist who confronted El-Sayed really got wrong
events.summary: David’s view If Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan’s Senate race next month, the Saturday clip of him admonishing a GOP activist about freedom of religion will achieve legendary status in his party. “It’s you who need to understand the Constitution, not me,” El-Sayed told Thomas Teepell during an appearance in the small Michigan city of Caro. The candidate accepted Teepell’s challenge to “disavow the Muslim Brotherhood,” then denounced the “dual loyalty” smear it seemed like the activist wanted to make. If El-Sayed wins, I’d expect Republicans to study that clip, too. That’s because the lesson conservatives can take isn’t that the topic of El-Sayed’s religion is too hot to touch. Teepell struggled to follow up because he couldn’t handle the moment. From President Donald Trump on down, Republicans are very comfortable contending that Muslim immigration threatens America and that the liberal crusade for diversity is national suicide. They love running against El-Sayed, even in the 49 states where he’s not on the ballot. And they don’t hold their tongues anymore for fear of political backlash. “What excites him is this prospect of wielding the power of a country he hates,” Vice President JD Vance told Michigan Republicans about El-Sayed this month. “He wants to litigate ancient grievances with your tax dollars, and he wants to use the grievances of faraway lands to punish you.” This isn’t a swerve away from the GOP’s midterm message. It is the message: Foreigners are undermining America from within, and Democrats won’t stop them. (Never mind that El-Sayed was born in Rochester Hills.) Teepell was very much in line with the Trump-era Republican rhetorical strategy to demonize the “other.” Where he went wrong was, in part, failing to go toe to toe with one of the most skillful extemporaneous talkers in Democratic politics. He was also working against a new reality: The Trump administration’s border closure and shutdown of most asylum claims has made “immigration” less critical to most voters. Casting El-Sayed as the enemy simply wasn’t as easy as he might have hoped. But the bigger context is more favorable to MAGA conservatives: With no Democrat running on a return to pre-Trump border policies, they see that topics once considered forbidden or offensive by media gatekeepers can win elections. The El-Sayed-Teepell moment happened as Paris was gripped by riots; Trump, his White House, and supportive media outlets warned that Democrats would bring the same migration-driven chaos across the Atlantic. Those media gates of the past might not even be standing anymore. They were sturdy in 2008, when Republicans campaigned more cautiously around questions of race and immigration. El-Sayed has indulged comparisons to Barack Obama, whose 2008 campaign convinced the young Muslim that he could one day run for office. In his 2020 memoir, El-Sayed wrote that after he graduated from the University of Michigan, he brushed off the idea (floated by Bill Clinton, his commencement speaker) that he might have a future in politics. Of course not: His name was Abdulrahman Muhammad El-Sayed. But one year later, “someone whose father had immigrated from eastern Africa — someone who was marked by a funny name and dark skin,” won Michigan by 16 points. The idea that something had changed, and that attacking Islam or a foreign name didn’t work anymore, ran through El-Sayed’s 2018 campaign. At one stop, he was buttonholed by Laura Loomer, then a semi-cancelled independent muckraker, who asked how he could “reconcile your own personal practice of Islamic law with your Marxist, socialist political platform.” Loomer was fairly easy for that campaign to brush off. She’s now one of the most influential conservative activists in America, with a direct line to the president. Republicans in the Bush years, who briefly hoped to build a lasting multiracial coalition, were hesitant to attack Obama over his pastor, or to elevate rumors that he was a Muslim. ( “No, ma’am.“ ) On the right, it’s widely believed now that this was a loser’s strategy. That’s why Teepell’s biggest error, in the eyes of the right, was simply lacking a clapback. If Republicans lose big next month, there’ll be a brawl to assign blame — which consultants blew it, which ads wasted money, which issues didn’t work. The party’s margins with non-white voters and first generation Americans, which improved in 2024, will get a harder look. But I wouldn’t expect them to ditch tactics like the El-Sayed confrontation, tactics that the new media environment is built for. Notable In Slow Boring, Matthew Yglesias wrote about the edgy conservative debate over “the Indian question,” and whether Republican rhetoric about immigrants was hurting them. “You either need to be willing to bite the bullet and say you’re eager to keep good people out or else you need to redefine good behavior as bad.”

events.title: Microsoft’s Nadella is back in business
events.summary: The Satya Nadella I interviewed last week for Future Proof at Microsoft’s headquarters in Redmond, Wash., was a very different version of the CEO I saw there in 2023, who wanted to make Google “dance.” Back then, generative AI was the exciting (and scary) new thing, and without Microsoft’s investment in compute, OpenAI wouldn’t have been able to build ChatGPT, and the industry’s trajectory might have been very different. We’re now four years on from the launch of ChatGPT and, outside of software development, AI’s impact on the world has been incremental, not exponential. And Microsoft is less about making competitors dance than it is about getting down to the nitty-gritty of making AI work predictably and reliably — Nadella has gone back to being the CEO of a company that is building a sturdy dance floor. “We, as an industry, have to wake up to this,” Nadella said. “It’s not about the shiny object and FOMO.” Wall Street is happy with the strategy. Microsoft’s stock is up 27% over the past six months and it’s valued at close to $4 trillion. But will it outpace the frontier labs and Nvidia in the long run? Nadella calls the frontier labs “magical businesses,” but points to Microsoft’s remarkable 51-year history. “I look at them and say, hey, this is not an industry where your initial success means anything,” he said. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: T.J. Holmes and Amy Robach are married — and their exes are engaged. Here's a complete timeline of their relationship.
events.summary: TJ Holmes and Amy Robach are married. Taylor Hill/FilmMagic/Getty Images Former "GMA3" co-anchors Amy Robach and T.J. Holmes are married. The two first sparked controversy when they were spotted cuddling while still legally married. Nearly four years later, the two are now legally wed, and their exes are engaged. As one of the internet's favorite sayings goes: Never let your spouse stop you from finding your soulmate. "GMA3: What You Need to Know" co-anchors T.J. Holmes and Amy Robach sparked controversy in November 2022 after their relationship became public when photos of them cuddling were published by The Daily Mail. The relationship between the two journalists — who were legally married to other people at the time — subsequently made national headlines.  Holmes married attorney Marilee Fiebig, 49, in 2010, the same year Robach married actor Andrew Shue, 59. After the news broke, both Holmes, 49, and Robach, 53, said they were either separated or in the midst of divorce proceedings when they were photographed together. "To be clear, we were outed as being in a relationship, but everyone else thought we were being outed as adulterers — being outed as cheating on our spouses — and it wasn't the case," Holmes said on a December 2023 episode of their podcast, " Amy & T.J. " In October 2025, nearly three years after the first headlines about their relationship, Holmes and Robach announced on their podcast that they had gotten engaged. One year after their engagement, Robach and Holmes married on September 19, 2026, in Holmes' home state of Arkansas, according to public marriage records. People reported the news on October 13. In a happy twist, Shue and Fiebig are also in a relationship and have been together since December 2023. They announced their engagement just over a week after Robach and Holmes' marriage became public. Here's a timeline of the scandal that rocked "GMA3" and led to both Holmes and Robach exiting the morning show. Holmes and Robach did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Keyaira Boone, Esme Mazzeo, and Libby Torres contributed to a prior version of this article. November 30, 2022: The Daily Mail published photos of Robach and Holmes. Amy Robach and T.J. Holmes at the 2022 ABC Disney Upfront in May 2022 in New York City. Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images Robach and Holmes began cohosting "GMA3: What You Need to Know" in 2020, although they had worked together at ABC since Holmes' hiring in 2014. In November 2022, The Daily Mail posted images of them together in a series of intimate situations, including having drinks in a New York bar and traveling to a cottage in the Shawangunk Mountains of upstate New York. The two were pictured laughing together, holding hands, and casually touching one another. Shortly after, Entertainment Weekly reported that Holmes shuttered his X and Instagram accounts, and Robach deactivated her Instagram profile. December 2022: Shue deleted pictures of Robach on his Instagram profile. Amy Robach and Andrew Shue attended The Breast Cancer Research Foundation in New York City in 2015. Gilbert Carrasquillo/FilmMagic Shue's account was wiped of pictures of his wife the day after The Daily Mail published their photos of Robach and Holmes, E! News reported. December 2022: An interview with Robach and Reese Witherspoon from earlier in the year resurfaced, hinting at similarities between "GMA3" and "The Morning Show." Reese Witherspoon and Amy Robach also spoke on-camera in 2015. Lou Rocco/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images An October 2022 interview between Robach and Witherspoon resurfaced on Twitter, reminding viewers that the host had once possibly hinted at drama occurring behind-the-scenes of "GMA3." Witherspoon, who was promoting her Apple TV+ drama "The Morning Show," asked Robach and her co-hosts whether the fictional workplace drama "hit home a little bit." "We can give you a few more plot lines," Robach replied, as her colleagues laughed. Witherspoon jumped on the opportunity to take the show's stories to the next level.  "Email me," she told Robach. December 2022: "GMA3" staffers said Robach and Holmes did not start dating until they were separated from their spouses. Amy Robach and T.J. Holmes ran the New York Marathon together this year. Bryan Bedder/New York Road Runners via Getty Images People reported that Holmes and Robach were both effectively single when they began dating, citing sources.  "This was two consenting adults who were each separated. They both broke up with their spouses in August within weeks of each other," a source said. "The relationship didn't start until after that," they added. Meanwhile, the two anchors continued filming. On December 2, they even joked about what "a great week" they were having in a sarcastic tone, according to Page Six . December 5, 2022: Robach and Holmes were pulled off the air. Amy Robach and T.J. Holmes host the show in and out of the studio. Lou Rocco/ABC via Getty Images Robach and Holmes were placed on hiatus from "GMA3" amid the scandal. The New York Times reported ABC News' then-president, Kim Godwin, called the news frenzy surrounding their relationship an "internal and external distraction" on a morning editorial call. It came amid claims from staffers that Holmes had engaged in relationships with other colleagues at ABC during his time there, while married. He has not publicly commented on the accusations. December 28, 2022: Holmes filed for divorce. Holmes has begun the process of ending his marriage to Fiebig. Johnny Nunez/WireImage Holmes filed for divorce from Fiebig in New York. They were married for nearly 13 years and share one daughter, Sabine. On the same day the news broke, Holmes and Robach were photographed making out in Miami. She confirmed that the divorce between Fiebig and Holmes was progressing. "To that end, T.J.'s lawyer and I have been working together to move their divorce forward privately, expeditiously, and as amicably as possible," Lehman continued. Lehman criticized Holmes' public actions. "Notwithstanding, we continue to be disappointed by T.J.'s lack of discretion, respect, and sensitivity toward Marilee and the party's daughter," she added. The divorce was ultimately settled in October 2023, People reported. January 27, 2023: Holmes and Robach exited "GMA3" permanently. TJ Holmes and Amy Robach running in New York City in 2021. events.title: Meta and Tesla bulls get confidence boost after SpaceX earnings
events.summary: Meta and Tesla are set to report Wednesday after the bell. Both names are seeing bullish options flow. Tesla is expected to see a larger-than-usual move. A big rally in SpaceX after earnings is giving hope to Meta and Tesla bulls ahead of their reports due Wednesday afternoon. Options trading in both stocks leaned bullish after the open Wednesday, with Meta options looking particularly one-sided as traders bought more calls than puts and more put trades likely initiated by sellers than buyers. More than 30,000 calls traded at or above the ask, suggesting they were bought, versus under 17,000 puts, Cboe LiveVol data shows. Meta options have generally been bullish since the stock's March low, when the put/call ratio of open contracts plunged to 0.5, meaning two calls open for every one put contract, and that hasn't budged much since, Barchart data show. Almost $22 million of trades were done with a bullish intent on Wednesday, compared to $7.5 million looking for downside. Market-makers are pricing a 6.5% swing for Meta after earnings, a little under the 9% average the past four quarters. The most popular contract to buy on Wednesday was the 800 strike call expiring Friday that costs $1.40 and needs Meta to rally 14% into the weekend, SpotGamma data shows. In Tesla, the flows also lean bullish, but with less conviction. The put/call ratio of open contracts is 0.75, compared to Meta's 0.5, though more calls did trade Wednesday morning than puts. Of the 520,000 contracts traded in Tesla, 315,000 were calls, as traders bought 88,000 calls and 65,000 puts, according to Cboe LiveVol data. There was also notable call-selling, with 83,000 call contracts likely sold and seven of the top 10 trades by dollar-amount call sales. Still, traders spent more money buying calls than they did puts, with call-buying premiums amounting to over $200 million, compared to $84 million in puts, according to SpotGamma's analysis. Market-makers are pricing a 5.5% swing in Tesla after its report, above the four-quarter median of 3.5%. That said, Tesla's last report caused a 14% selloff in the stock that makes the average move in that period 5.5%. The most-heavily traded contracts by volume Wednesday were the 385 and 400-strike calls expiring Friday, with buyers favoring the cheaper 400-strike call and sellers leaning into the 385-strikes, SpotGamms data show.

events.title: Every Kennedy family tragedy that has fueled rumors of a 'Kennedy curse'
events.summary: Joseph P. and Rose Kennedy surrounded by their children at a family gathering at their home in Palm Beach, Florida. CORBIS/Corbis/Getty Images After Robert and John F. Kennedy were assassinated, a rumor formed that the family could be cursed. Their history has been marred with tragedy, from four plane crashes to a deadly skiing accident. In 1969, Ted Kennedy publicly referenced the curse when apologizing for fleeing a fatal car crash. Members of the Kennedy family have reached the highest positions in public office, becoming senators, congressmen, and even the president. Now, the next generation of Kennedys is carrying that legacy forward. Still, the family has also endured profound losses across generations. Most recently, Kyle Kennedy, the granddaughter of Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy, died at 42 in September. The family has also dealt with numerous tragedies , from illness and assassinations to fatal accidents and addiction. The family’s history of loss has fueled the long-running notion of a “Kennedy curse.” Here are the many tragedies that have affected the Kennedy family. Kennedy patriarch Joe Kennedy Sr. had high expectations of his children. Some conspiracists have suggested he was to blame for what would befall his family. Joe Kennedy Sr. with his sons John and Joseph Jr. in 1937. Corbis/Getty Images Joe Kennedy Sr. rose from reasonably humble beginnings to become an ambassador to Britain, and he made millions working as a bank president, selling liquor, and owning a Hollywood studio, The Atlantic reported. Conspiracists have maintained that the Kennedy patriarch committed crimes like bootlegging to make the fortune that eventually supported future Kennedy endeavors. The New Yorker reported these crimes were often mentioned "in the same breath" as the tragedies that struck the Kennedys, "assuming that there is a dark pattern in the way things happen." The first Kennedy to feel the brunt of his ambition was his daughter, Rosemary, born in 1918. Kathleen, Rose, and Rosemary Kennedy in formal gowns and carrying bouquets at Buckingham Palace in 1938. Corbis/Getty Images She had seizures and tantrums and was intellectually disabled, though her parents worked hard to keep that a secret from society.  To avoid the suspicion that anything was different about Rosemary, she was presented alongside her sister Kathleen at Buckingham Palace with other eligible debutantes, Marie Claire reported. "To present Rosemary, an intellectually disabled adult, to the monarchy at Buckingham Palace during the debutante season was more than a bold act," Kate Clifford Larson, the author of " Rosemary: The Hidden Kennedy Daughter ," said, Marie Claire reported. "A debutante with intellectual disabilities would have stirred long-held prejudices about passing along 'defective' traits to the next generation," she said. "Joe and Rose were determined to keep the family secret, making sure that Rosemary was treated just like all the other eligible young women presented at court that year." In 1941, Joe Kennedy Sr. organized for his daughter, then 23, to have a lobotomy, with disastrous consequences. Eunice and Rosemary Kennedy pictured aboard the S. S. Manhattan in New York in 1938. Bettmann/Getty Images At the time, the media said the operation was "easier than curing a toothache," NPR reported, and was frequently used to "treat" people with mental illnesses. However, the lobotomy only made Rosemary's condition worse. For months afterward, she was unable to walk or talk, and she was put into an institution and cut off from her family for the next two decades. Rosemary lived at a mental health facility until her death in 2005. The next tragedy struck the eldest son, Joseph P. Kennedy Jr. Joseph P. Kennedy Jr. at Harvard University in 1938. Bettmann/Getty Images Joe Jr. had been groomed for political office his whole life. When he was born, his grandfather, who was then the mayor of Boston, had told the press he would become president one day, according to the National Park Service . Joe Jr. was successful both as an athlete and a student, Vanity Fair reported. When he graduated from high school, he was awarded a trophy for the best student in both "scholarship and sportsmanship," according to Vanity Fair. Joe Jr. left before his senior year at Harvard Law to volunteer as a Navy flyer in World War II. He died during a failed secret bombing campaign. Joe Kennedy Jr. smiles at the camera in 1944. Bettmann/Getty Images According to the National Park Service, Joe Jr. volunteered for the mission, which involved flying explosives over enemy territory, detonating them, and parachuting to safety. However, the explosives were accidentally set off early, killing both pilots on board the aircraft.  "His worldly success was so assured and inevitable that his death seems to have cut into the natural order of things," his brother John wrote in a family memorial. In 1948, another plane crash rocked the family when Kathleen "Kick" Kennedy died in a plane crash in France. John F. Kennedy and Kathleen Kennedy at Palm Beach, Florida, in 1934. Corbis/Getty Images She had been a headstrong child, and her decisions in her love life caused a rift in the family — her mother, Rose, disapproved of Kathleen's soon-to-be marriage to a Protestant man, The Atlantic reported. Months after their wedding in 1944, her husband was killed in battle, and she began an affair with Earl Peter Wentworth Fitzwilliam, a married man.  Before the couple traveled to Paris to seek her father's blessing, People reported that their 10-seat plane encountered turbulence and crashed into the mountains between Paris and Cannes. Both Kick and Peter, who was piloting the plane, were killed on impact. She was 28 years old. Only her father, Joe Sr., attended her funeral, according to The Atlantic. After Joe Jr.'s death, Joe Sr. turned his focus to John F. Kennedy, who told a friend, "Now the burden falls on me." John F. Kennedy and his father Joe P. Kennedy poses for photographers onboard the SS Queen Mary in 1938. Bettmann/Getty Images Joe Sr. helped him begin his political life, using his contacts to call in favors and spending tens of thousands of dollars on his campaign, The Atlantic reported. He reportedly said, "We're going to sell Jack like soap flakes," per PBS . In 1960, John F. Kennedy became president of the US, and his family became forever regarded as American royalty.  President John F. Kennedy was assassinated while riding in a motorcade in downtown Dallas. President John F. Kennedy and his wife Jackie in a motorcade minutes before he was killed in 1963. Bettmann/Getty Images He was fatally shot on November 22, 1963. President Kennedy was 46 years old. events.title: A plan to ensure energy is affordable for all | Letters
events.summary: A plan to ensure energy is affordable for all Dr Alex Chapman calls for a government-funded price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas, in response to an article by Nils Pratley Nils Pratley thinks that the secretary of state, Miatta Fahnbulleh, should “keep things simple” and develop a targeted social tariff to protect vulnerable households from surging energy bills ( The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff, 14 October ). Unfortunately, there is nothing simple about such a scheme. Pratley’s proposal would mean creating a new benefits system inside our privatised energy industry. If the interminable debates about our current benefits system were not enough to put him off, we can look to the failing social care system to see where it might lead. Andy Burnham has made it his life’s mission to dismantle this lottery that can strip pensioners of their savings and the family home. Just as he now plans a universal public provision of adult social care, we at the New Economics Foundation have such a plan for energy. Every household should be able to afford the energy essentials: enough warmth to survive a winter; enough electricity to switch on the lights and run a fridge. We should recognise this as a universal right rather than waste time tinkering with a targeting system that arbitrarily separates the “worthy” from the “unworthy” (the “rough justice” of the Resolution Foundation’s proposal , which penalises households based on the income of the highest earner, is a case in point). The long-term design of a universal offer can be debated. But as another energy crisis bears down on us, we should keep it simple: have the Treasury fund a true price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas. This would be a policy from which everyone wins (especially if electrically heated homes are allowed to transfer across their gas allowance). In the longer term, one way to help pay for this could be to charge households with very high energy consumption more. But there are other ways. The Australian “ solar sharer ” scheme gives every household three hours of free electricity in the middle of the day, bringing hope that renewables could soon give true energy security. Dr Alex Chapman Head of economic and environmental policy, New Economics Foundation Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

events.title: ‘You’re no longer an influencer … you’re a cofounder’: MrBeast’s business resembles a Fortune 500 holding company, investor Steven Bartlett says
events.summary: Nearly 15 years ago, Jimmy Donaldson uploaded his first video under the moniker MrBeast—a three-minute Minecraft walkthrough. The YouTuber, who made his debut at just 13 years old, has since garnered 522 million subscribers on the platform and grown his net worth to an estimated $2.6 billion thanks to not just his competition-style videos, but also a multimillion-dollar chocolate brand, fast-food burger chain, an Amazon deal, and production company MrBeast LLC. Donaldson’s astronomical rise to success has become a blueprint for the future of the creator economy, according to Steven Bartlett, an investor and host of The Diary of a CEO podcast. Speaking with Fortune Daily host Ellie Austin, Bartlett explained that Donaldson has transformed his business from monetizing YouTube videos to effectively being a massive conglomerate overseeing a swath of subsidiaries. It’s part of a larger evolution of online celebrities becoming entrepreneurs in their own right. “I’m an investor in Jimmy’s company, and when you look at how that company is built, it resembles a Fortune 500 holding company,” Bartlett said. “This is, for me, the last era that we’re heading towards within this creator economy, where you’re no longer an influencer, you’re no longer an equity partner, a creative director. You are an owner or cofounder.” Beast Industries , the North Carolina–based company under which Donaldson manages his ventures, was founded in 2012 and now has more than 1,000 employees, according to PitchBook, and is valued at $5 billion. In the past few years, Beast Industries has begun to resemble a more traditional corporation, installing former Shutterfly CEO Jeffrey Housenbold as president and chief operating officer in May 2024, before promoting him to chief executive in September of that year. Donaldson remains the majority owner and creative head of Beast Industries. Other creators have followed similar paths of using YouTube as a launching point to becoming a larger corporate entity. Tech YouTuber Linus Sebastian became the founder and CEO of Linus Media Group , the company behind several technology-oriented YouTube channels. In 2022, merchandise like plushies and hoodies generated nearly one-third of the company’s revenue. Brothers Logan and Jake Paul similarly took the leap from vloggers to launching brands like hydration drink Prime and personal care brand W , respectively. The pipeline from influencer to entrepreneur didn’t exist when Bartlett was first building his own businesses, including Social Chain, an influencer and social media marketing agency, in 2014. “In my early career, I was building a business where we were booking hundreds and sometimes thousands of influencers—[what] we used to call them back then—per month,” he said. “And the deals were that the industry used to look at creators like me as kind of billboards where you pay them to post something.” That was the first era of the creator economy, Bartlett explained. The second era began when influencers began becoming “creating directors” of brands as part of a deal, which evolved into a third era of creators being given equity in a preexisting company, in addition to some creative influence. Today, creators are transitioning to becoming business cofounders, according to Bartlett, marking the fourth era of the creator economy. Donaldson, however, is among the few YouTubers entering the most recent maturation of creators-turned-entrepreneurs because of the maintenance of multiple different corporate entities. The MrBeast founder appears to be interested in expanding his reach even beyond retail and entertainment. In February, Beast Industries acquired fintech app Step , a money-management tool built for young people. “I think the fifth era is when—and we’re starting to see this with people like MrBeast—is when actually their companies—the creator—engages in M&A and acts more like a Fortune 500 company,” Bartlett said. “It has a C-suite that often comes from publicly listed companies. They just bought a bank.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Before the ambulance arrives: How AI is helping the NHS rethink patient care
events.summary: When someone in the UK dials 999 for an ambulance, their focus is understandably on when help will arrive. Less visible is the planning, training, analysis and coordination that happen long before a paramedic reaches the patient. “We all think about the ambulance when it’s on scene, but there’s so much that happens before that goes on before an ambulance crew even arrives with a patient,” says James Goulding, chief clinical information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service (YAS) NHS Trust. YAS is one of 200 plus trusts, or organizational units, of the UK’s National Health Service. That preparation includes planning services, recruiting and training staff, analyzing population health data and understanding the experiences of patients who do not speak English fluently. “So much goes into making sure that when that paramedic arrives in front of a patient, that we’ve done all of this work to make it really easy for them to make good decisions for patients,” Goulding says. James Goulding, chief clinical information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service. Photo by Joanne Crawford for Microsoft. Following an earlier trial involving 30,000 employees, NHS England announced plans in June 2026 to make Microsoft Copilot available to as many as 505,000 clinicians and support staff. Participants in the trial reported saving an average of 43 minutes per working day — which adds up to about five weeks of time per person a year. Dr. Alec Price-Forbes, national chief clinical information officer for NHS England, says that the NHS is still in many ways an analog system. “It’s critically important that we use the opportunity that we have in front of us to truly reimagine the NHS,” he says, “to reduce cognitive load and administrative burden for healthcare professionals, make sure they get a better experience and then are in the position to give the best quality care.” AI and digital tools such as Microsoft Copilot can help sustain the NHS by reducing administrative burden, releasing clinical capacity and enabling more productive, connected and person-centered models of care. Helping NHS teams manage information Tom Smith sees that work from several angles. As an area operations manager for Yorkshire Ambulance Service, he oversees operational managers and frontline teams, plans staffing and specialist resources, and responds personally to significant incidents as a tactical commander. The service received about 1.25 million calls to its 999 number in the 2025-26 fiscal year. “It’s everything and anything,” he says. “No day is the same.” Smith also has to read and produce many reports. Microsoft Copilot does not make decisions for him, he says. Instead, it organizes information into a format he can review and interrogate using his operational expertise. “What it does is just give me all the information in a helpful format, which is easy to understand,” Smith says. “It does a lot of my admin tasks for me that would previously have been really time consuming. Then I can just review what it’s done.” Tom Smith, area operations manager for Yorkshire Ambulance Service. Photo by Esme Mai for Microsoft. For Smith, who is dyslexic, that support extends beyond saving time. Writing an email can take longer when he begins to overthink the wording or spelling, he says. The ability to structure a draft, summarize a long report and ask follow-up questions helps “level the playing field” for him. His experience comes as NHS England expands access to generative AI tools across the health service in England. The NHS has put clear, strict safeguards around its use of Microsoft Copilot: it is only for administrative tasks, not clinical work, says Price-Forbes. The NHS is supporting its digital transformation with standards for clinical safety, information governance, cybersecurity, interoperability and real-world evaluation, with transparency and human oversight considered essential to maintaining the confidence of staff and the public. Like healthcare systems in many countries, the NHS serves an aging population, and many patients have multiple chronic illnesses. Price-Forbes says, “It means that we’ve got the opportunity to redesign because we just cannot continue with the old analog model of healthcare delivery. And this is a challenge across the globe. So we now need to redesign care around people and technology, digital and data, and AI is going to be the only way to create those new service models of care.” “Artificial intelligence can transform the NHS — improving care, giving time back to staff and delivering greater value — but only if we turn ambition into trusted action at scale,” he says. “Proven tools, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, must move rapidly beyond isolated pilots and into everyday workflows wherever evidence shows they improve outcomes, productivity or staff experience.” “Done well, AI will not replace the human heart of the NHS; it will protect it — strengthening decisions, restoring time for care and helping create a safer, more personal and sustainable health service. The world has changed. We’ve got to create a digital front door for the NHS.” Dr. Alec Price-Forbes, national chief clinical information officer for NHS England. Photo by Joanne Crawford for Microsoft. He says that this transformation goes beyond technology; it requires that work be redesigned so that AI can help clinicians amplify their expertise while relieving them of unnecessary burdens. This will free “clinicians to focus on judgment, validation and human connection.” He also says that trust is essential for success. “Patients and staff must know when AI is being used, how it shapes decisions and where human oversight applies, with unambiguous accountability for consequential choices,” he says. The challenge now is to use digital capability to redesign pathways, improve flow, support clinical decision-making and release capacity back into care, Price-Forbes says. That means moving at pace, but with discipline. Copilot “gives us that ability to join dots that we wouldn’t see ourselves without a laborious several hours’ worth of trawling through data reports and trying to look at common themes.” Samantha Robinson, chief digital information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service. Photo by Joanne Crawford for Microsoft. Samantha Robinson, chief digital information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, is responsible for helping information move between frontline teams, local operations and the wider NHS. Copilot “gives us that ability to join dots that we wouldn’t see ourselves without a laborious several hours’ worth of trawling through data reports and trying to look at common themes,” she says. The NHS’s information flows in all directions, Robinson says. She may need to turn operational information from across the ambulance service into a briefing for senior NHS leaders. At other times, she must translate national guidance into clear, practical instructions for different teams.

events.title: America’s national debt plan is ‘clearly not in order,’ says Ken Griffin. He believes part of the problem is Europeans who ‘don’t want to go to work’
events.summary: Citadel CEO Ken Griffin is one of many people growing increasingly concerned about America’s $40 trillion national debt burden, and the budget deficits that add to it year after year. But Griffin has an alternative perspective to some of his peers: This isn’t an issue that can be solved in Washington, D.C., alone, he says. The feathers of debt hawks have been ruffled further over the past few days following the Treasury’s confirmation that it ran a $2 trillion deficit for fiscal year 2026. More than half of that deficit came from interest rate payments to service the debt. Economists have a range of ideas on how to improve the U.S. fiscal picture. Some call for policies supporting economic growth to better balance government borrowing versus income. Others say spending needs to be cut to shave budget deficits down as a portion of GDP. Griffin suggests the matter also requires impetus from U.S. allies—namely, them needing to grow their own economies. Speaking at the Citadel Securities Future of Global Markets event in New York yesterday, Griffin said: “Our fiscal house is clearly not in order.” When asked where he would begin, the Citadel CEO said, “We really need to play the productivity card as hard as we can.” He added: “In order of what priorities need to be, grow the damn economy.” But the U.S.’s allies also need to be growing, Griffin added. “You actually want the Europeans to grow their economy,” he explained. “The tariff war with Europe’s a fiasco because at this moment we should use all of our political capital: ‘Europe—you want us to pay for your defense? Guess what? You’re going to go back to work.’ “In France, there are strict limitations on how many hours you can work a week, strict limitations. It’s ridiculous. Like the French want the Americans to provide the defense for Europe, and they don’t want to go to work. This just doesn’t work for the American people.” France does indeed have labor laws to ensure workers don’t work for more than 48 hours a week, or 44 hours per week on average over a period of 12 consecutive weeks. A break of at least 20 minutes is also legally mandated for every six hours of work, to be taken within or immediately after that period. The French nation is also famous for a cultural—but not legal—break that many workers take in July or August. Les grandes vacances refers to the phenomenon of workers taking a month out of their five weeks of annual leave to escape busy city hubs and enjoy the countryside. Workers in service industries and essential services often continue working. However, Griffin’s suggestion that more hours worked will equal more economic growth is perhaps oversimplified. A working-hours study from Charlie Giattino, Esteban Ortiz-Ospina, and Max Roser for Our World in Data showed that in 2023, Norway’s GDP per capita was close to $99,000 for annual hours worked of 1,412. The U.S., by contrast, has GDP per capita of a little under $73,000 for an average of 1,789 hours worked per employee every year. Griffin’s comments perhaps refer to the debate over defense spending among the G7 countries, a point which President Trump has forcefully made since returning to the White House. The U.S. spends approximately 3.1% to 3.4% of its GDP on defense, with the Pentagon awarded more than $1 trillion in funding earlier this year. France’s military budget, per Politico , will be increased to €63.4 billion ($71 billion) for 2027, and tends to be roughly 2% of its GDP. Further measures Of course, the U.S. fiscal picture can’t be improved on the actions of allies alone. And Griffin has plenty of other ideas for what to look at next: “We need to make sure that data centers are built in America. But we need more oars in the water; we need more focus on nuclear fusion … We need more focus on robotics. We need more focus on the technologies that will unleash productivity for the next 20 years. Like, that should be the singular focus of our administration from an economic policy perspective. “Grow our economy and push our allies to engage in meaningful reforms that grow their economies. The entire Western world is in the same boat together … We’re not going to get out of these waters by torturing each other. We’re going to get out of these waters by making the pie bigger for all of us.” Improving education is also key to unlocking growth, Griffin said, as well as getting immigration policy right: “Every single brilliant person around the world. I want them to live in America.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: How AI divided New York's democratic socialists
events.summary: The News The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America is divided over whether the AI industry is a destructive capitalist force that could kill everyone, or merely an overhyped capitalist hustle. The rift within the largest chapter of the left-wing organization centers on whether the New York DSA should acknowledge the possibility that AI could lead to mass automation and to systems that escape human control — the kind of warnings that gained traction after recent AI-powered hacks. Some tech leaders and Democratic politicians — including America’s leading socialist, Sen. Bernie Sanders — have warned that without guardrails, there’s a chance AI could lead to human extinction. At the chapter’s convention on Nov. 14, members are expected to consider a resolution proposed in September by two graduate students and local DSA members: They warn that industry “negligence” creates “the potential for loss of control of AI agents to cause catastrophic harm.” But the group’s established Tech Action Working Group is not persuaded. Some in the self-described “ techno-skeptical ” committee that steers the chapter’s technology policy see things differently, arguing that dire warnings of doom are an attempt to inflate company valuations, and AI is already doing enough damage. Members of the group’s leadership proposed to amend that measure by removing clauses on automation, loss of control, and catastrophic risk: “ AI alarmism and AI hype are the same story ,” the group posted to Instagram in September. The resolution also calls for “the democratization and socialization of AI ,” but the amendment deletes that phrase. Know More The socialist organization is now mired in procedural infighting. Alexei Gannon and Zachary Jones, who wrote the original resolution, accused the TAWG of presenting its leaders’ views as the group’s official position, even though the group never formally voted on where it stands on AI risk. The TAWG, Gannon and Jones wrote in a Substack post, hasn’t held a membership meeting since March. “To equate worrying about catastrophic risk with buying a Silicon Valley narrative is to lump hundreds of DSA comrades… and 60% of the American public into the same bucket as Sam Altman and Elon Musk,” they wrote. Gannon and Jones declined to comment; the New York City DSA chapter and the Tech Action Working Group didn’t respond to requests for comment. The DSA is also grappling with how to use the technology itself: The local chapter’s tech working group voted in January to ban using generative AI text, images, and video for “any DSA purpose.” The national DSA’s tech committee this month adopted a policy that “ neither endorses nor prohibits ” AI coding tools for its own software. J.D.’s view The discourse in the DSA in many ways mirrors the broader debate confronting the American left over AI, as Democrats look to stake out a position on the issue ahead of the 2028 presidential election. How the DSA and other left-wing factions speak to voters about AI risk could shape what regulation looks like if Democrats retake Congress in the midterms, and which candidates win over the party’s AI-skeptic vote. I got a glimpse of how progressives are positioning on the issue at the People’s AI Assembly on Monday, organized by the AI Now Institute and More Perfect Union. The event centered on the impacts of data centers, surveillance, and the concentration of power in a handful of companies. Sanders-esque warnings about AI threatening humanity weren’t a focal point, suggesting the DSA camp that’s more focused on mitigating present harms is setting the terms of the conversation, at least in New York. “Even as we reckon with these larger societal questions, there are still rules that we can implement and hold these kinds of companies to account for,” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a DSA member, told the crowd. Room for Disagreement It was clear at the People’s AI Assembly that broad swaths of the left remain united on a number of AI-related fronts, including data centers, the concentration of corporate power, and the broader need for regulation and oversight. Brian Romero, a DSA member and incoming state assemblymember who has worked with the chapter’s tech working group in the past, framed the debate as a complex, fast-moving issue that factions across the political spectrum are having. “It’s not unlike any other policy issue,” he said. “There’s going to be differences of opinion on the left.” As another attendee at the People’s Assembly told me: “It wouldn’t be the DSA if there wasn’t debate.” Notable Sanders is facing pushback from some on the left over his doomerist AI rhetoric, WIRED reported. “Some of us are looking at Bernie and saying, what happened? ” one NYC DSA member said. The broader DSA has no “ consistent line on what elected socialists should advocate for regarding AI,” Zhao Levi, a DSA member, wrote in Cosmonaut in September, proposing a national working group to draft one for the 2027 national convention.

events.title: Meta tops Big Tech lobbying as AI labs talk antitrust
events.summary: The Scoop Both OpenAI and Anthropic lobbied lawmakers on the ability of AI companies to share information with one another without running afoul of antitrust rules in the third quarter of this year, according to federal lobbying disclosures reviewed by Semafor. Anthropic’s lobbying form lists the Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act, a bill that would allow labs to coordinate with each other on security risks, as a point of focus for the company on Capitol Hill. The legislation could make it into law as part of must-pass defense policy legislation, Semafor previously reported . OpenAI’s lobbying form is less specific, listing “AI-security collaboration and information-sharing, including proposed antitrust protections” as topics discussed in Washington. Lobbying forms don’t say whether companies are arguing for or against the proposals discussed in meetings. The antitrust lobbying is of interest given the talks around a coordinated AI development “slowdown” pitched by AI leaders last month. The companies regularly lobby Washington lawmakers on proposed AI regulatory bills, as well as legislation on export controls and data centers. OpenAI’s head of global affairs, Chris Lehane, has argued that an antitrust exemption specifically for model pacing would not be necessary. But Trump administration officials criticized AI leaders for calling for such a carve-out, saying they were capable of deciding to slow down among themselves without the government’s blessing. Know More Meta spent $5.9 million lobbying Washington lawmakers in the third quarter of 2026 — the most of any big tech firm during that period — as the AI race grew more competitive and high-profile hacks put pressure on the AI safety debate in Washington, according to Senate lobbying filings. Meta often is the biggest lobbying spender among its Big Tech and AI counterparts, but OpenAI and Anthropic have been spending more and more each quarter, nearly doubling and tripling their spends in the first half of the year, respectively, as they navigate Washington’s discussions about containing their technology. Google, Amazon, and Apple lagged behind Meta in spending but beat AI and chip companies, though Nvidia also posted its highest-ever quarter at $2.2 million as the chipmaker stays dominant and influential in the Trump administration. All three companies have built up massive lobbying portfolios on a range of tech policy topics including kids’ online safety, immigration, taxes, education, and energy policy.

events.title: SpaceX stock jumps 10% after earnings beat and Musk hints at Tesla tie-up
events.summary: SpaceX stock popped after reporting strong revenue growth and beating estimates. The company pinned the results on its growing AI business, and recurring revenue from its satellite business. Billionaire owner Elon Musk also floated a potential merger with his electric vehicle firm Tesla. SpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX- Tesla merger. The space company, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in the biggest initial public offering ever in June, reported third-quarter revenue on Tuesday of $14.6 billion, up 161% from the previous year, and beating LSEG consensus estimates of $12.72 billion. Meanwhile, its operating income came in at $2.8 billion, with net income of $4.4 billion, after reporting a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period a year earlier. On an earnings call, Musk said he's considering a combination with Tesla — which would mark the largest merger in history — and that the boards of both companies have created specific committees to discuss a consolidation. "I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said on the call. Tesla is set to report third-quarter earnings after the closing bell on Wednesday. SpaceX forecasts first-quarter 2027 revenue between $33 billion and $37 billion, beating the average analyst estimate of $22.2 billion, according to LSEG. "We delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business," SpaceX's chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said in the earnings release. Johnsen pinned the strong results on recurring revenue from its satellite internet business, Starlink , and significant expansion of its Super Intelligence [SI] infrastructure. The company has dived into artificial intelligence this year, which it's now calling SI. The segment is its largest business unit, with revenue soaring ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year. Commentary on computing during the earnings call supported "continued pricing power and shorter payback periods" for AI cloud providers, Truist Securities analysts said in a Tuesday note. "Despite market concerns relating to financing for AI cloud providers this past week, we believe SpaceX's third-quarter 2026 represents the first data point during the earnings season to support the bull case for AI cloud providers," they added. They explained that demand appears "insatiable," with SpaceX noting that it could rent out its capacity several times over. The analysts said Coreweave and Nebius are set to benefit and capture demand as "pricing power will more than offset higher rates." The shares of neoclouds Nebius and Coreweave traded marginally lower, while Iren and Applied Digital climbed in early trading on Wednesday. — CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report. Correction: Bret Johnsen is chief financial officer at SpaceX. An earlier version misspelled his name. events.title: AT&T's CEO throws shade at Musk's Starlink mobile ambitions
events.summary: "I wouldn't over-rotate on what I would call one carrier of low band spectrum," John Stankey said Wednesday, referring to Elon Musk's Starlink. Win McNamee/Getty Images (Musk); Lluis Gene/AFP via Getty Images (Stankey) AT&T CEO is brushing off concerns that satellite-based internet could threaten his business. "I think LEO constellations are fantastic for delivering bandwidth to rural areas," he said. When it comes to where lots of people live, he said fiber-connected performance can't be beat. Elon Musk wants SpaceX to become a major US mobile carrier. AT&T CEO John Stankey says: not so fast. AT&T has an advantage from years of investment in dense urban and suburban areas, he said on AT&T's third-quarter earnings call, a day after Musk and SpaceX chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell reported more than 22 million monthly Starlink Mobile users . "Our competitors cannot and will not match our operating proficiency, network performance , or exceptional converged value proposition," Stankey said. Stankey sees a use case for satellite-based internet to soften the edges of fiber-connected and 5G networks, especially in places where it's too expensive to build out the physical infrastructure, he said. "I think LEO constellations are fantastic for delivering bandwidth to rural areas," he said, using the acronym for low-Earth orbit satellite arrays. Shotwell said Tuesday that Starlink recently got FCC approval to launch 15,000 V2 satellites. She also noted a recent agreement to acquire a portfolio of low-band transmission spectrum, or wireless frequency licenses, which better penetrate buildings to reach indoor devices. Stankey was unimpressed. "How you perform indoors, of course, is extremely important, and we shouldn't think about those as being nominal loads," he said. "They're significant loads, even with robust Wi-Fi networks that are out there." This is especially critical in crowded environments like stadiums and hospitals, where he said AT&T has been focused on beefing up signal support. "I wouldn't over-rotate on what I would call one carrier of low band spectrum," he said, referring to Starlink. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: This Startup Is All In on Recursive Self-Improvement. Its Latest Model Is Scary Good
events.summary: For the past few days I’ve been testing an impressive open-weight AI coding model called Flint. It suggests that fully recursive self-improvement , or RSI—an exciting and controversial approach that uses AI to build AI—is getting closer. Flint is the first offering from Recursive, a company that aims to use RSI to advance both AI itself and other areas of science using AI . “Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI,” Recursive CEO and cofounder Richard Socher told me. Socher says his company used its recursive AI system, dubbed the Eureka Machine, to automate most elements of the model’s development. This enabled a company with a handful of researchers to build a world-class model in just a few months, he says. Socher told me that the Eureka Machine devised a number of innovations, including a new way of training the base model, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon chips. Recursive shared benchmark scores that suggest Flint outperforms other models of similar size and architecture on coding tasks. AI is already widely used to help build, test, and improve AI thanks to its amazing coding skills. This can speed up the process of refining a model and testing new ideas without the need for as much input from humans. It is also possible to create a loop through which AI decides what improvements to make and then begins another round of improvement. For the moment this technique is limited, but if AI can contribute to every aspect of model development, then the process could theoretically continue indefinitely. Some experts worry that letting AI improve itself in this manner could ultimately lead to disaster . These doomsayers claim that AI capable of improving indefinitely could escape human control and might decide that humans are an impediment to its goals. Those concerns gained wider notice this September when a researcher quit Anthropic and warned that advances in AI, including recursive self-improvement, could lead to human extinction within a few years—a concern then echoed by a number of other experts. The idea of RSI has become so controversial that several bills in Congress propose to ban it. Recursive sees these fears as more sci-fi than reality and believes legislation to prevent RSI is an unnecessary impediment to progress. Socher says Flint was built using a system incapable of escaping human control. He says the goal is for the Eureka Machine itself to achieve full recursive self-improvement, but this would still be overseen by humans who could stop the process if it goes awry. “We hope that this shows people that indeed we have all the steps in place” to build such a system, he says. Recursive has raised $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation from Google Ventures, Greycroft, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Socher was previously the chief scientist at Salesforce, and his cofounders include Jeff Clune, a professor at the University of British Columbia who researches ways of building AI systems capable of learning indefinitely. I must say I am impressed with Flint. I tested it on a Mac with 48 GB of RAM—a healthy amount but only enough to run a modest-size AI model like Flint, which has 40 billion parameters. The biggest models out there have several trillions of parameters, and they can only run on racks of industrial servers. I used Flint to build a bunch of programs and found it to be both fast and very capable. In my experience, models of this size can be annoyingly error-prone or slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed my coding requests every time. I used it to create a command line to-do list, then tried having it build a program that scours the web for interesting research related to recursive self-improvement. I also had Flint whip up a simple website that explains how RSI works. You can see that here . It’s unclear how much progress other US labs have made chasing recursive self-improvement, but some published work suggests fully recursive systems are already feasible. A team from Microsoft, Carnegie Mellon University, and the University of Virginia recently published work, for instance, showing how an AI coding agent can recursively improve itself by modifying the software harness that turns reasoning into useful action and its own model’s weights. Perhaps there are risks to full RSI if you are close to building a godlike intelligence, but for the time being it seems like a very promising way to improve your own AI models. This is something I’ve dabbled with in previous editions of AI Lab . Indeed, Socher says the approach used to build Flint could make cutting-edge AI more accessible. “It's the only way this very small team can produce a model that's actually better than any other model in its class,” he told me. “This will hopefully show people that [recursive self-improvement] is actually quite nice and will benefit a lot of people.” This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter .

events.title: Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs
events.summary: Civil servant Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by working multiple full-time public sector jobs Published 21 October 2026, 13:08 BST The civil servant accused of fraudulently earning more than £284,000 by juggling multiple public-sector jobs admitted making mistakes but said ''I do not believe there was criminal intent". Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court, Kashim Chowdhury told the jury he had made mistakes because he was ''overwhelmed and stressed'' and had felt ''terror and panic'' at the thought of losing his livelihood. He told the jury he had been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2015 and that it had been triggered in 2021. The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain. The prosecution alleges Chowdhury failed to reveal to his employers that he had other full-time employment. But Chowdhury told the jury some of his managers knew he had other jobs. He told the court that staff and managers at the Department for Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra), the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, East London NHS Trust and the Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) all knew he had jobs elsewhere. At the height of the alleged deceit, Chowdhury held five full-time jobs on full-time salaries within the public sector. In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days. Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023. Chowdhury said the jobs were a "lifeline" during a time his mother's health had declined. Asked by defence barrister Pieter Briegel what extent stress in his life was due to the number of jobs, he replied: "The jobs at the time were my lifeline at the time, that was what I survived on at that particular moment. "And they gave me a link to the outside, they were the only thing I had to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time," he told the court. The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity". A succession of Chowdhury's line managers have told the jury that he performed poorly in his roles. Abigail Mounde, who was Chowdhury's line manager at the Department for Business and Trade previously told the court: ''Any basic tasks I asked him to do he either did late or not to the standard I would have expected." Chowdhury was asked whether he accepted the criticism of his performance, including the allegation he failed to deliver work on time. He replied: "I reject them all." The prosecution also alleges Chowdhury used sick notes from his doctor as part of the cover-up. But the prosecution said while he was telling some employers he was sick and unfit to work because of "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" he was not giving sick notes to other employers. The prosecution said this ''underlines the dishonesty involved in the whole affair". His line manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, arranged a video call in May 2023, to support him returning to work after a period of absence. In previous evidence she told the court she was surprised when he logged on wearing white make-up because his name led her to expect to see an Asian man with darker skin. She told the court that as the call went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck." Prosecuting barrister Lucy Organ told the court: ''This almost laughable incident demonstrates quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit.'' events.title: The oil market's 2027 relief hopes are fading fast
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Traders are betting that oil prices will remain elevated for longer than they anticipated just weeks ago, threatening to prolong the inflationary pressures that businesses and consumers have weathered for months. Why it matters: Oil inventories have helped cushion the blow from disrupted Middle Eastern supplies, but much of that buffer has been depleted since the war began. The possibility of sustained price pressures into next year throws into doubt the logic that central banks traditionally rely upon to look through energy price shifts — that they represent a one-time shift in relative prices, not an ongoing inflationary process. That leaves the global economy more vulnerable to another energy price surge, with potentially more lasting consequences for growth, inflation and interest rates than energy shocks of yore. By the numbers: Oil futures for delivery in 2027 — contracts to buy or sell crude next year — have climbed to their highest levels since the Iran war began. Prices for January 2027 are up 17% since early September, to more than $97 a barrel. Markets still anticipate some relief next year, but considerably less than they expected just weeks ago. It's a reversal from late summer, when hopes of easing tensions with Iran and a recovery in Middle Eastern oil supplies briefly pushed futures lower. June futures have jumped 18%, to $88 a barrel, while December futures are up 13%, to about $81. State of play: Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf, including shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, surpassed prewar levels in the week ending Oct. 18, according to the Wall Street Journal . But the costly workarounds enabling that recovery have their limits. Those include ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait of Hormuz, where security risks have deterred some vessels. "You're coming up against limitations on actually how much volume you can move out of the Middle East, even with these processes," Christopher Haines, global head of oil at Energy Aspects, tells Axios. Restoring confidence among shipping companies and insurers that vessels won't be attacked will be "exceptionally hard," Haines adds. Zoom in: Economist Robin Brooks argues that oil prices reflect higher shipping costs and fears of further attacks more than actual shortages. Using earlier monthly data, he estimates that Persian Gulf crude exports had recovered to 91% of prewar levels, with a "temporary fear factor" adding at least $20 a barrel. What to watch: The Trump administration is seeking to ease fuel prices ahead of the midterms, most recently by allowing more Russian diesel onto the market. But relief may be minimal: Ukrainian attacks have damaged Russian refineries, while sanctions complicate repairs, limiting additional exports, Haines says. The bottom line: "The market narrative has shifted from "transitory" to "new normal" right before our eyes," Bob Elliot, chief investment officer at Unlimited Funds, wrote Wednesday morning .
