events.title: Shoppers turn to Amazon for fresh produce and seafood, helping it take market share from supermarkets
events.summary: Amazon's expanded fresh food delivery is helping it win market share from more traditional retailers. : Deb Cohn-Orbach/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Amazon's sales of fresh groceries like seafood and produce are growing fast, new data show. The retail giant is also gaining market share against more traditional retailers, Nielsen IQ found. The data shows momentum for Amazon in a business it's spent years trying to break into. Amazon is gaining ground in grocery thanks to items like fresh shrimp and berries. Roughly a year after expanding same-day fresh grocery delivery to thousands of cities and towns in the US, Amazon's perishable grocery sales are booming — and taking market share from traditional retailers, according to data from market research firm Nielsen IQ. Sales of groceries such as seafood, dairy, and produce on Amazon increased severalfold between June and August, per Nielsen IQ's data. Amazon also posted market share gains in the food category for the year through late August as traditional grocery stores lost it, Nielsen found. Amazon gained market share in food sales, both overall and online, as rivals such as grocery stores lost it. Nielsen IQ "Shoppers are increasingly embracing Amazon for categories that historically represented one of the largest barriers to online grocery adoption," Nielsen wrote in its report. Amazon has spent years trying to break into grocery, though it hasn't hit a home run in the category as it did with books or cloud computing. The company acquired Whole Foods, opened and shuttered another brick-and-mortar grocery chain , and created a selection of private-label groceries, among other steps. The Nielsen IQ data suggest that Amazon's latest push — toward delivering fresh groceries quickly across much of the US — is yielding some results in the competitive grocery space. Many of the shoppers buying fresh foods on Amazon come from households with incomes over $100,000 and tend to be older, according to Nielsen IQ. They also tend to be frequent Amazon users, placing more orders and spending more money on the platform than an average user. That means fresh groceries, one of the most frequent purchases for US households, are "a potentially important lever for increasing shopper frequency and overall spend" on Amazon, the report reads. To keep the momentum going, Amazon will need to take on formidable rivals. One is Walmart, which already uses its stores and its own army of gig workers to deliver groceries same-day . Amazon is considering opening about 1,000 same-day fulfillment centers around the US by 2031, Business Insider reported in September. That move would create the same sort of advantage that Walmart has by placing more fulfillment centers close to more customers, one analyst said. events.title: Martha Stewart says people need to get it through their ‘thick skulls’ that there’s ‘no such thing as balance’—even at 85 she starts work at 7 a.m.
events.summary: Martha Stewart ’s career has spanned Wall Street, television sets, the modeling studio, and even federal prison. Through it all, the lifestyle mogul has built a business empire worth an estimated $400 million today. But achieving that kind of success has come at a cost: Stewart believes the idea of perfectly balancing work and life is a myth. “There is no such thing as balance—just get that through your thick skulls,” Stewart said earlier this month in conversation with Vivian Tu, who runs the social media account Your Rich BFF . “You can’t balance it. It doesn’t balance.” Major life events, including marriage and divorce, inevitably throw things off course, Stewart said. And while she acknowledged that some people may occasionally manage to strike a balance, she isn’t convinced it’s the norm. “This thing about balance, I don’t know who thought about that—but it just doesn’t work,” she said. “Maybe infrequently—and I’m jealous of those people—but they’re also boring.” Even at 85, Stewart shows little sign of slowing down . She wakes up at 4 a.m., reads the entire New York Times, and heads to Pilates or a session with her personal trainer. By 7 a.m., Stewart is at work on projects ranging from her lifestyle brand to an AI startup —and expects her staff to be working, too. Stewart staged a career comeback by embracing change: ‘I have choices’ For Stewart , success also means seeking out excitement and embracing the unexpected. She brushed off the idea of her career being described in major “pivots”—in fact, she said she “hate[s] the word pivot.” Instead, she prefers to think of her journey as a series of metamorphoses, an idea inspired by author Franz Kafka. “Why be bored?” Stewart said. “If you even feel a moment of boredom or you can’t get up for some reason—because you don’t want to face the day—that is not good.” Stewart said if something no longer excites her, she always finds something new to pursue rather than resign herself to boredom.  “When I get up in the morning, I have choices,” Stewart said. “I can do whatever right now; I can do anything I want to do every day, but I like being able to look forward to what’s going to happen in the day, and the surprises are also good.” Her affinity for freedom may come as no surprise considering Stewart knows what it’s like to have it restricted: She served five months in federal prison for crimes related to an investigation into a stock sale. But since being released in 2005, she has notably staged a major comeback in rebuilding her public profile and expanding her brands. From TIAA’s CEO to Barack Obama, leaders agree with Stewart that work-life balance isn’t always possible While work-life balance remains a top priority for many aspiring young professionals , Stewart isn’t alone in arguing that the ideal is often impossible to achieve. TIAA president and CEO Thasunda Brown Duckett made a similar case on Fortune’s Titans and Disruptors of Industry podcast earlier this year. “Work-life balance is a lie. It never reconciles … So get rid of that,” Duckett told Fortune editor-in-chief Alyson Shontell. For Duckett, that realization came during her time working at JPMorgan Chase , where she had climbed the corporate ladder to CEO of Chase Consumer Banking. Long workdays and commutes left her struggling to make time for her family, leaving her feeling as though she was falling short in every part of her life. “I was feeling like I was failing my husband, I was failing my children, I was failing my mom, my dad, my brothers, everyone,” she said. “I was just not winning, and I needed a win.” The answer, Duckett said, was to stop trying to make sure every part of her life fit neatly into balance. Instead, she learned to accept that some periods would inevitably demand more of her attention at work, while others would allow her to focus more on family. Former President Barack Obama has offered a similar perspective , arguing that excellence often requires periods of intense focus at the expense of other priorities. “If you want to be excellent at anything—sports, music, business, politics—there’s going to be times of your life when you’re out of balance, where you’re just working and you’re single-minded,” Obama admitted last year on The Pivot Podcast . This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Colorado Marijuana Regulators Failed to Protect Consumers From Potential Contamination, Audit Finds
events.summary: Cannabis samples in the process of testing at Kaycha Labs in Denver Stephen Swofford/The Denver Gazette The agency charged with regulating Colorado’s first-in-the-nation legal recreational marijuana market potentially put consumers at risk of using contaminated products, a new state audit found. The report pointed to inconsistent oversight by the Marijuana Enforcement Division and loose state rules around testing marijuana products or contaminants. As a result, it found, nearly 75% of marijuana processed for eventual sale from 2023 through 2025 evaded testing for pesticides. The audit, released Monday , identified a host of issues, including regulators’ failure to meet regular inspection schedules or to conduct sufficient random checks at dispensaries for contaminated products. It also found that delayed agency warnings to the public allowed potentially contaminated products to remain on shelves for months, sometimes years. The audit’s conclusions echo several findings of an investigation this year by The Denver Gazette and ProPublica into the Marijuana Enforcement Division’s lapses in policing contaminants entering the legal marketplace.   In one case highlighted by the newsrooms, it took 15 months for a manufacturer to discontinue production of a marijuana sleep aid pill despite consumers warning regulators that the product was harming their livers. The pills had herbal extracts that researchers say can cause liver damage. Auditors said they did not identify evidence of “widespread health and safety issues” but did find that deficient regulations still left consumers vulnerable. The audit found that unsafe products had remained on the market for as long as three years before the Marijuana Enforcement Division issued a public warning. The auditor’s review of the agency’s health and safety advisories found that, on average, from 2023 through 2025, contaminated products that were the subject of an advisory remained on shelves for more than seven months. That’s the same number of months the news organizations found contaminated products stayed on shelves before warnings were issued. The audit also found that it took the agency three and a half months, on average, in 2025 to issue an advisory once it launched an investigation into potential contamination. Even after investigators determined an advisory was needed, it still took the agency a month on average to issue one.  “These issues limit MED’s ability to meet its core objective to identify product safety risks and to help ensure that licensed marijuana businesses meet product safety requirements,” the audit stated. “As a result, there is an increased risk that marijuana products sold in Colorado may have contaminants or that the potency listed on the labels is inaccurate.” Colorado allows marijuana businesses to test far less frequently than required by state guidelines if they can show consistent compliance with testing rules. The reduced testing program results “in a significant portion of the marijuana product being sold in Colorado not undergoing testing to ensure it is safe,” the audit stated. Manufacturers also can rely on other testing exemptions, such as for certain marijuana-derived skin and body products, but there is “limited MED oversight” of how manufacturers determine they qualify for an exemption. Auditors reported that a survey of MED investigators found that more than half said there are or may be widespread marijuana product safety issues in Colorado’s regulated market.  In a statement released Monday night, the Marijuana Enforcement Division emphasized that state auditors found no evidence “to support claims of widespread health and safety issues” with marijuana products for sale in Colorado, but the agency agreed the audit identified areas for improvement. It said that among other things, it would be assessing exemptions to tests currently allowed under state laws and regulations. The state auditor’s review “allows us to take a critical look at how we can continue to carry out our work, consistent with our commitment to integrity, safety, and continuous operational improvement,” Dominique Mendiola, senior director of the MED, said in a statement. The auditor’s report highlighted a criticism her agency has repeatedly sidestepped: the absence of independent collection of samples for safety testing. The Denver Gazette and ProPublica found that more than half of states with regulated marijuana markets rely on private labs or an independent third party to collect samples. Colorado marijuana businesses are free to collect their own samples submitted for testing. The enforcement division’s own investigators told auditors that, as a result, Colorado relies largely on an honor code to ensure the safety of marijuana sold in the state’s dispensaries. Auditors said that allowing businesses to select their own samples “increases the risk that businesses do not pick samples that are representative of the overall quality of their marijuana product.”  MED regulators at the start of the year said they planned to pursue an overhaul that would have required private lab personnel to collect samples, but they abandoned that effort after manufacturers said it would increase their costs. On Monday, Kyle Lambert, the enforcement division’s deputy senior director, told legislators that the agency opted against an overhaul this year, chiefly because he said it would be a geographic challenge to do away with self-sampling for rural businesses.  “It was decided now wasn’t the right time to propose that as a policy change,” Lambert said, adding that the agency still might revisit the issue. State Sen. Byron Pelton, a Republican from Sterling, pushed back, saying it was a loophole he thinks the agency should consider closing. “If I’m a shady character, I know which products I’m going to go sampling and which ones I’m not,” he said. “That’s a pretty gray area to me.” The audit also questioned the agency’s reliance on businesses voluntarily recalling contaminated marijuana products, saying that “some of these recalls did not succeed at stopping the businesses from selling potentially unsafe product.” Just last month, The Denver Gazette and ProPublica reported that a Colorado manufacturer voluntarily flagged 49 of its popular marijuana vapes for recall, nearly six weeks after a third-party lab notified the company and regulators that it detected methylene chloride, a chemical the Environmental Protection Agency has sought to ban for most uses because it can cause cancer. The MED issued a health and safety advisory a day after the publications first reported the manufacturer had warned dispensaries to stop selling the vapes, which consumers had been purchasing for over a year. The post Colorado Marijuana Regulators Failed to Protect Consumers From Potential Contamination, Audit Finds appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley are dominating the AI stock boom. Here's their edge
events.summary: Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan captured nearly 80% of top five bank equity trading revenues so far this year, generating a combined $52 billion. Growth was driven by "insatiable" hedge fund borrowing for leveraged bets on AI hardware and Asian semiconductor supply chains. The Big Three’s massive balance sheets allow them to absorb possible losses and handle risks that force smaller rivals to cede share. Relaxed rules around leverage helped to unlock bank balance sheets to meet record demand, though bodies including the International Monetary Fund cautioned against rising leverage. Fueled by the global boom in artificial intelligence stocks, relaxed capital rules and greater lending to hedge funds, big Wall Street banks have already had a banner year for equities trading — even with one quarter left to go. The five biggest investment banks have generated about $67 billion in equities revenue through Sept. 30, according to company filings. That is $7 billion more than what the group made during all of 2025, which itself was a record haul. But it's Wall Street's Big Three that have captured the largest slice of what is shaping up to be the industry's most lucrative arena: Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley have made a combined $52 billion in stock trading revenue so far this year, nearly 80% of the total. "When it comes to the AI mega trade, the Big Three consider each other their main competitors, and that's pretty much it," Mike Mayo , Wells Fargo banking analyst, told CNBC. "They've been best positioned to take advantage of this market." Wall Street banks are experiencing an epic run of blockbuster profits as the total value of the stock market balloons and trading activity from institutional and retail investors rises across stocks, exchange-traded funds and derivatives. Helping drive this activity are the loans that the banks, through their prime brokerages, are extending to hedge funds so that they can amplify their bets. Prime brokerage — the business of providing hedge funds with margin loans, securities lending and other trading services — has become a key battleground and source of growth. The Big Three's prime brokers are central to the larger equities story because they serve the largest funds across markets and products. Demand for leverage to make bets on AI hardware, hyperscalers and chip suppliers has reached new heights, bank executives said last week. At Goldman Sachs, equities financing activities jumped 96% in the third quarter to a record $3.37 billion. JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley don't break out that figure, but said they saw a similar dynamic. "I like your 'insatiable demand for capital' point. That feels about right," JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said on the bank's third-quarter conference call, responding to analyst questions about financing demands. "In this moment where AI is such an overwhelming theme ... there is capital being tapped through all kinds of different mechanisms," Barnum said. That demand has helped transform equity desks at the Big Three from cyclical, transactional businesses into more durable, high-margin lending engines, Wall Street executives say. The performance gap between Wall Street's giants and rivals including Bank of America and Citigroup highlights a widening divide in capital markets. "For clients, the value isn't just a price on one trade, it's coverage and continuity," Rachid Alaoui, JPMorgan global head of equities, told CNBC in an interview. "You want a dealer that can give you the full suite across products, and you want that service to travel with you across regions. That matters in stressed markets and periods of volatility." Executing multibillion-dollar bets, like leveraged swaps on volatile AI stocks or sector ETFs, can require an enormous balance sheet. The biggest banks can absorb potential $100 million losses without threatening their quarters, according to trading executives. Smaller or more niche banks can't underwrite single-trade risks of that magnitude, forcing them to decline the business or cede share. U.S. prime brokers have also benefited from the retreat of European banks including Credit Suisse from the equities business, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Herman Chan . "Prime is one of the ultimate scale businesses," Chan said. "If you have a strong equities franchise, the hedge funds will want to transact with you because you have a bigger pool of trading opportunities with counterparties." While U.S. markets were swept up in software and cloud computing giants this year, trading executives say the fastest-growing frontier for equities was in Asia. Institutional investors poured into South Korea and Taiwan, targeting the "picks and shovels" of the AI supply chain: the memory chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers supporting data center construction, Alaoui said. For the Big Three, with their footprints across Tokyo; Hong Kong; Seoul, South Korea; and Mumbai, India; the Asia trade was a goldmine.

events.title: Apple’s iPhone Duo launches with scarce stock, no walk-in sales across much of Asia
events.summary: Production of the iPhone Duo is hobbled by complex mechanisms that take time to source and put together. SAN FRANCISCO – Apple said on Oct 21 it will have “limited” number of its folding iPhone Duo phone available for walk-in customers when the device launches on Oct 23, after initial online orders sold out in minutes and pushed delivery times for some customers to January. Apple announced its first folding phone in September , with analysts expecting it to quickly come to dominate a niche segment where rivals such as Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies have sold premium offerings for years. But the iPhone Duo is also a more complex product than standard candy-bar iPhones, with a tight-fitting hinge that analysts believe may take time for Apple to learn to manufacture in high volumes. “On Friday morning, our teams look forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores to experience iPhone Duo and the incredible iPhone line-up for themselves,” Apple said in a statement. “Apple Stores will have limited iPhone Duos available for walk-in customers, and we’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers’ hands as quickly as possible,” it added. The availability of walk-in units will vary by country, Apple said. Online order pickup and limited walk-in purchases will be available in the United States, Australia, Canada, Mexico and much of Britain and Europe. But other regions will only have iPhone Duo units available for customers who already bought them online. Those include mainland China, France, Hong Kong, India, Japan, Malaysia, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates, Apple said. On the China-governed island of Macau, the iPhone Duo will be available for walk-in customers only, with limited inventory, Apple said. REUTERS

events.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
events.summary: Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild. Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin. The flaws at issue are present in PHP , the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal , Magento , Joomla and WordPress . Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server. Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure. OpenAI , which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.” Censys , a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP. Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog]. “These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.” The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure. The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12 , 8.4.27 , 8.3.36 , and 8.2.35 . According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework. “A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.” The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif , another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws. This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps. Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

events.title: Content creator who labelled beauty salon a ‘scam’ on Instagram ordered to pay $15k for defamation
events.summary: The judge found that while Mok Wai Kwan had misgivings about the salon’s practices, she had not proved it was unethical. A Singapore content creator called a beauty salon a “scam” on Instagram and was ordered to pay $15,000 for defamation after the court found her claims were not proved. District Judge Sim Mei Ling said Mok Wai Kwan had real concerns, but she did not prove the salon had designed to cheat customers, and she did not genuinely believe her own posts. The salon won general damages, but not extra compensation or an injunction, because it failed to prove the posts caused lost sales and there was no sign she would repeat the allegations. SINGAPORE – A content creator who labelled a beauty salon a “scam” on Instagram after she was unhappy with its prepaid treatment packages has been ordered to pay the business $15,000 in damages for defamation. District Judge Sim Mei Ling found that while the customer had genuine misgivings about the salon’s practices, she had not proved that it was an unethical business designed to cheat or defraud customers. In a written judgment released on Oct 15, the judge also found that the woman did not genuinely believe what she had stated in her Instagram posts, which she had pinned to her profile under the title “SCAM !!”. However, the judge declined to award the salon additional damages for alleged lost sales, or to grant an injunction to prevent the woman from repeating the allegations. The court heard that Mok Wai Kwan – who goes by the handle @vivianmok_ on Instagram – was a customer of Beauti Instinct at Far East Shopping Centre from 2020 to early 2025. She bought a six-session “Silk Peel” facial package for $488 through the beauty salon’s website in January 2020. At her first consultation, salon director Cheang Norita told her that her skin was too sensitive for the treatment and that she needed other treatments, the court heard. Mok said she felt pressured into signing up for a membership. She eventually bought a trial membership costing $1,000, which gave her 1,000 treatment credits and access to treatments at discounted rates. In November 2020, she bought a Gold membership for $5,000, which entitled her to 6,340 treatment credits. She later bought promotional treatment packages costing thousands of dollars. Mok’s unhappiness stemmed partly from occasions when she said she had gone to the salon expecting a treatment but instead spent time discussing packages or buying products. On one occasion in December 2022, she received a treatment costing $757 when she had only 537 credits remaining in her membership. She had to pay an additional $220. The salon charged Mok the full price for the treatment and not the discounted member’s rate because her remaining credits were insufficient to pay for the session in full. Cheang acknowledged in court that she had not told Mok the treatment’s cost before carrying it out. On this issue, the judge said: “It is good business practice for a business to be upfront and transparent about pricing, so that customers can make an informed choice about whether to proceed. This would also minimise any subsequent dispute.” Another source of frustration arose in November 2023 when Mok was told that some of her remaining treatment credits could not be used without doing the “Silk Peel” treatment, but she was down to her last credit for that s ervice. On Feb 13, 2025, after a further disagreement over her remaining Silk Peel credits, Mok decided to stop patronising the salon and give up her unused credits. By then, she had received treatment at the salon on 26 occasions over about five years. Mok then posted a series of Instagram stories recounting her experiences. The posts described the salon as “HELL” and said it should be reported to the Consumers Association of Singapore. The posts also alleged that she had been trapped by an “unethical business model”. She later pinned the stories to her Instagram profile as a highlight under the title “SCAM !!”. Two months later, on April 11, 2025, she changed the title to “BEWARE!!”. The highlight was subsequently removed around July that year. The salon sued her for defamation, arguing that the posts portrayed it as a business that cheated customers, engaged in fraudulent operations and used deceptive practices. Mok argued that her posts merely described the salon’s unethical business practices and were justified by her experiences. She also relied on the defence of fair comment. The judge drew a distinction between the stories themselves and the additional “SCAM !!” title. Viewers who saw the stories directly would understand them to mean that the salon employed unethical business practices or had an unethical business model, the judge found. Those who viewed them through the highlight while it was titled “SCAM !!” would also understand Mok to be accusing the salon of being a business designed to cheat or defraud customers.

events.title: Putin tells Witkoff he is ready to resume direct peace talks, Russia releases U.S. detainee
events.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin told White House envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday that he "agrees in principle" resuming trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. to end the war, the Kremlin said. Why it matters: The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after President Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. For now, it seems the only concession Putin agreed to is to negotiate. Driving the news: During a three-hour meeting in St. Petersburg, Witkoff presented Putin with an updated proposal to end the war in Ukraine . Trump envoy Jared Kushner joined virtually. Before the meeting, Russia released U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, 74, who had spent more than four years in captivity after being seized by Russian troops in eastern Ukraine in April 2022. Putin announced his release at the top of the meeting with Witkoff. "He is at Pulkovo Airport," Putin told Witkoff in front of the cameras. Witkoff in response thanked Putin and called him "a humanitarian." Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) expressed outrage at Witkoff's comment. "WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of 'humanitarian'. What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say," Tillis wrote on X. Cornyn wrote : "No. Putin is stone cold killer." "Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no 'swap' necessary for this release," Trump wrote on Truth Social. State of play: Witkoff arrived in Russia after a day of talks in Oslo , Norway, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland and representatives from France, the U.K., Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO. Zelensky said Tuesday that the next step should be a trilateral meeting between him, Putin and Trump — a format Russia has so far rejected. The discussions in Oslo focused on developing a unified proposal for a "framework agreement" to end the war. What he's saying: "I believe the talks [in Oslo] were productive, and I would like to say that there is progress, and I will update you on this. I hope that we have truly laid the groundwork for a successful end to hostilities in this Ukrainian-Russian conflict," Witkoff told Putin. Witkoff asked Putin to "consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States, where we could discuss the next steps toward achieving a settlement." Witkoff said the talks could include representatives of technical groups of specialists who could discuss these issues in detail. "We have brought several documents outlining approaches to achieving a peaceful settlement in the Ukrainian-Russian conflict. I would ask you, Mr. President, to review these documents a little later," Witkoff said. The other side: After the meeting, Putin's foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, told Russian reporters that Putin agreed to hold trilateral talks between negotiation teams. "Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations on the main topic around the 10th of November," he said, adding that the talks could take place in Abu Dhabi. Ushakov claimed Putin was ready to resume the trilateral talks several weeks ago, but the Ukrainian strikes on Russia on the day of the parliamentary elections led to their cancelation. Putin's adviser said Witkoff briefed Putin on the discussions in Oslo. "The Oslo talks didn't contain much that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis," Ushakov said. The intrigue : Putin also told Witkoff he wants to discuss the possibility of Russia mediating between the U.S. and Iran. "You know that we have a special, trusting relationship with Iran, with our partners in Iran, our friends, built over decades, and if there's anything we can do to resolve this crisis, we'll be happy to do so. You're also well aware of our proposals in this area," Putin said. What's next: Putin told Witkoff he wants to discuss a possible meeting with Trump in China in mid-November.

events.title: EBay to lay off 9% of workforce in its second round of job cuts this year
events.summary: EBay will cut about 1,000 jobs as the online marketplace works to focus its operations on its "top strategic priorities." This is the second round of layoffs this year, following job cuts of about 800 in February. EBay recently acquired clothing resale platform Depop from Etsy for $1.4 billion in cash. EBay will lay off about 9% of its workforce in a move to streamline its operations and focus on its fastest-growing areas, a company spokesperson confirmed to CNBC. The layoffs will affect approximately 1,000 employees. "As we work to capture the significant opportunity ahead, this step was taken to ensure we continue to operate from a position of strength by aligning our teams and resources with our top strategic priorities," the spokesperson said in a statement. The company also said it will continue to hire in "priority areas aligned with our strategy." As of the end of 2025, eBay had roughly 12,300 employees. Reuters first reported the news, citing a memo to staff from CEO Jamie Iannone that read in part, "Our strategy is working." "Continuing to capture the significant opportunity ahead requires us to make thoughtful choices about where we focus and invest," Iannone said in the memo, seen by Reuters. This is the second round of layoffs for the online marketplace this year, following a 6% workforce reduction that affected about 800 employees, in February. The company has been steadily shrinking its headcount over recent years at the same time it's ramping up spending on artificial intelligence. EBay also acquired the used clothing resale platform Depop — a brand with a strong customer base of Gen Z and millennial users — from Etsy earlier this year. The $1.4 billion deal was finalized in July . — CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed to this report.

events.title: A $50 sports bet costs a young investor hundreds later. Here's how
events.summary: Studies show people are using savings or potential funds for investing to gamble, especially younger generations. The hidden cost of this gambling habit is compounding, one of the most powerful forces in investing that most people never learn. The first working years are an investor's most valuable to begin compounding returns. Those are the very years betting apps compete for the hardest. Football season is here. It's a great time for some financial wisdom. On any given fall Sunday, a 25-year-old can watch the early game from her couch and put $50 on a parlay from her phone before kickoff. While exciting entertainment in the short term, it comes at a potentially large long-term cost that is still underappreciated by many: compounded returns. According to a survey of 1,000 U.S. retail investors that Betterment published in August, 52% of Gen Z investors this past year took money they had set aside for investing and put it toward sports betting instead. About a quarter said they now treat betting as part of their long-term financial strategy. Yet data from the Bank of America Institute shows just how that is going, with bettors getting back less than 75 cents on average for every dollar they sent in this year, and Gen Z, the best gambling performers of any generation, still getting back only about 80 cents in July. It's easy to understand the appeal, since a winning bet can look like a shortcut when rent is high and a first home feels out of reach. Plenty of people bet for fun, and betting out of an entertainment budget is a personal choice. The trouble comes when the money is taken from savings or money set aside to invest. A recent National Bureau of Economic Research study found that in states that legalized sports betting, household savings fell, as bets that lose money on average crowded out investments that grow, and the hit was biggest for households that could least afford it. Most young bettors don't realize that the $50 they lose on an app is the smallest part of the cost, because that $50 never gets the chance to compound, and invested at 7% a year from age 25, it would be worth about $750 at 65. Every bet made with investment money takes from her future, and that cost never shows up on the app. That hidden cost is compounding, probably the most important idea in investing, and the one most people never learn. Compounding simply means your investment returns get reinvested and start earning returns of their own, and over time compounding is the force that turns small, regular sums into real wealth. In our new book, "Investment Wisdom for Our Friends and Loved Ones," my co-author, Jenny Harrington , provided a simple example. A house worth $100,000 increases in value over a year by 10%, to $110,000. Then that house value, now at $110,000, rises another 10% to $121,000. That means that second year adds $11,000 rather than $10,000 because the gain was earned on a bigger base. Over decades, those returns on past returns become the largest source of growth in a portfolio, which is why the 25 women co-authors for this book, who spent their careers in finance, kept coming back to compounding as key. Let's go back to our young sports fan. Say she bets $50 every week, or about $2,600 a year. If she put that money into a low-cost stock index fund earning 7% a year, she would have roughly $519,000 by age 65 on contributions of about $104,000. In her last year alone, the account would have grown by around $34,000 on its own. If she did as well as the average Gen Z sports bettor instead, she would lose roughly $500 a year and have nothing working for her at 65. This brings us to the second most important part of compounding, which is that starting early matters even more than the amount. If she invested $50 a week for only ten years and then stopped, she would still have about $273,000 at 65, more than a friend who started at 35 and invested every week for 30 years, ending with about $246,000 despite putting in three times as much. The first years of a working life are an investor's most valuable, and they are the years the betting apps compete for the hardest. Skipping the betting apps, or at least thoughtfully budgeting for them as entertainment, is only part of it, because money left sitting in savings accounts also misses out on compounding. Spending most of my career in bond and money markets, one learns how large that gap is. Since 1900, U.S. Treasury bills, the closest thing to cash in the bank, have returned about 3.4% a year, compared with about 9.8% for U.S. stocks, according to the UBS Global Investment Returns Yearbook . After inflation, that works out to be about 0.5% a year for bills and 6.6% for stocks.

events.title: The architect of Trump Accounts wants the program expanded to every American under 40
events.summary: Brad Gerstner, founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, wants Trump Accounts expanded to Americans under 40. Bloomberg/Getty Images Investor Brad Gerstner wants Trump Accounts expanded to every US citizen under 40. The plan would create early IRAs that employers and donors could fund. Gerstner, regarded as the architect of Trump Accounts, said the change would require new legislation. Brad Gerstner , the investor and architect of Trump Accounts, is pushing to expand the investment accounts beyond children and make them available to every US citizen under 40. In an interview with CNBC on Wednesday, Gerstner said the change would require new legislation rather than a regulatory rule change. Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts created under President Donald Trump’s tax-and-spending law. Right now, they are available to Americans under 18, while children born between 2025 and 2028 are eligible for a $1,000 federal seed contribution. When account holders turn 18, the accounts become traditional individual retirement accounts, or IRAs. "Every year, 3.7 million kids age up into IRAs," Gerstner said. "Why not pull forward 20 years of IRAs? We can create all of those today, everybody under 40." Gerstner's idea would create the accounts for adults under 40 without necessarily requiring the government to make an upfront deposit. Instead, he said, it would give employers, philanthropists and companies a ready-made vehicle through which to contribute. That structure could allow companies or private citizens to contribute to accounts, he said, creating a "vessel" for the funding. On Monday, Elon Musk said he planned to give one share of SpaceX stock to every American child through Trump Accounts. Giving a share to the roughly 72 million children in the US would be worth around $11.5 billion, based on SpaceX's share price in Wednesday trading. Other major donors, including Michael and Susan Dell, Ray Dalio, and SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell, have also backed the initiative. Gerstner pointed out there has already been innovation in the investment field, mentioning the federal Saver's Match, created under the bipartisan SECURE 2.0 law, which is scheduled to begin in 2027. The program will provide a federal match of up to $1,000 a year for eligible low- and middle-income workers who contribute to qualifying retirement accounts. In comments to the New York Post , Gerstner said he was working on the legislation to make Trump Accounts available to anyone under 40, potentially within months. The proposal could also make account funding permanent. The proposal's prospects in Congress, including its cost and whether lawmakers would support new matching funds, remain unclear. events.title: Jensen Huang’s Vision for Europe Runs on Plug-In Data Centers
events.summary: Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics , AI agents, and modular data centers , with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all. “To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.” The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face —doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch. Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said. The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out. Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs. Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said. On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data. He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher. In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair. events.title: Booking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scams
events.summary: European Commission calls accommodation website’s approach to fraudulent listings and phishing scams as ‘absolutely substandard’ EU regulators have opened an investigation into Booking.com, alleging that the accommodation website has not done enough to protect consumers from fake listings and scams. The European Commission , which regulates the world’s biggest tech companies operating in the EU, said Booking.com may have breached the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) with its “absolutely substandard” approach to tackling fraudulent listings and phishing scams, where criminals impersonate a third party to trick people to hand over money. A commission official said Booking.com should be carrying out risk assessments and acting to prevent fraud as required under the DSA. “We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” said the official. “Although they take measures, they could go much further and they could have much more solid systems to prevent fraud.” EU officials will also investigate whether Booking.com has breached advertising transparency rules, by potentially not making clear to users that some accommodation providers had paid to make their business more visible on the website. Under the EU’s DSA, which aims to protect people from harmful and illegal internet content, a company could be fined 6% of its worldwide annual turnover. The commission said that opening the investigation did not prejudge the outcome. Booking.com, which is headquartered in Amsterdam and claims to have 28m accommodation listings, said it was engaging constructively with the commission. “Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com,” a company spokesperson said. “We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to ‌combat cybercrime and online fraud, and protect travellers and partners.” The investigation comes after researchers at the UK consumer group Which? exposed security lapses at Booking.com when they used the site to set up – and accept payment for – a fake offer to stay at 10 Downing Street. EU officials are investigating similar scams, with less high-profile addresses, where consumers thought they had booked a stay, only to find on arrival at a property that it had been fraudulently listed on Booking.com. Officials are also assessing a second category of scams, dubbed “reservation hijacks” where scammers use hacked data to impersonate an accommodation provider. Criminals send WhatsApp messages and have even used Booking.com’s own platform to request payments from Booking.com’s customers, supposedly to secure a stay. Cases seen by Guardian Money in 2025 involved the theft of several hundred pounds. EU officials will examine whether the company has sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused. The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment The Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said it had received 200 reports of scams costing people €65,000 that involved Booking.com in 2025, up from 89 reports worth €25,000 the previous year. These cases were “just the tip of the iceberg”, it said, as many victims would not report to its fraud helpdesk. Booking.com told the BBC in 2024 it had seen a 500 to 900% increase in scams in the previous 18 months, driven by generative AI tools that enable fraudsters to create very realistic-looking fake emails and internet booking links. Agustín Reyna, director general of the pan-European consumer group BEUC, said: “It is positive to see the European Commission investigating Booking.com for failing to meet EU digital rules. This is a systemic problem.” Henna Virkkunen, the commission’s lead official on tech policy, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.”

events.title: New prize launches for books co-written with AI
events.summary: After months of controversy over the possible use of AI by winners of prestigious awards, the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA is rewarding fiction written with the help of LLMs A prize for AI-written books has launched this week. The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA invites submissions of manuscripts co-written with AI tools, with the winner promised publication. Entrants are asked to submit an unpublished manuscript of between 10,000 and 50,000 words, along with information about which AI model and prompt were used to generate the text. All major language models are allowed, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA. Entrants can be based anywhere, but entries must be submitted in French. The Prix Pascal is named after Blaise Pascal, a French polymath who helped invent one of the first mechanical calculators and also wrote theological texts, including Pensées, which Pope Francis praised for its “philosophical depth and literary charm”. While the terms and conditions ask for a work of fiction, the prize also states that submitted texts should help solve an ethical, social or ecological problem threatening humanity. The prize was founded by Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentré, all of whom are technology entrepreneurs. Rodriguez is a founding partner at the mergers and acquisitions advisory firm Avolta, and is described as a “leading figure in the European crypto and blockchain industry” on the company’s website. Serviant is a digital media entrepreneur and former chair of the LGBTQ+ magazine Têtu. Meanwhile, Mentré is a former civil servant with a PhD in philosophy who teaches at Harvard and the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne. Mentré also co-founded Electis, an online voting platform. The Prix Pascal is launching after months of controversy over the possible use of AI by finalists and winners for a number of literary prizes this year, including the Commonwealth short story prize , the Caine prize and the Prix Goncourt , France’s most prestigious literary prize. Applications for the Prix Pascal opened on Tuesday, with entrants invited to submit via the prize’s website , and are set to close at the end of November. A shortlist of 10 will be drawn up before the winner is announced in early December. The jury will be made up of a panel of five or six writers, critics, journalists, philosophers and publishers, to be announced early November.

events.title: 6 things I wish I knew before setting foot on a cruise ship that all first-timers should keep in mind
events.summary: The reporter's first cruise was a seven-day voyage aboard Royal Caribbean's Wonder of the Seas. Joey Hadden/Business Insider If I could take my first cruise again, I'd pick up a case of water on my way to the port. I'd pack a bar of laundry soap. And I'd leave my formal dress at home. The closest thing I'd seen to a cruise ship was the Staten Island ferry. That changed in April 2022, when I left my home in NYC to take my first cruise . I flew to Fort Lauderdale, Florida, for a seven-night voyage on one of the largest cruise ships in the world, Royal Caribbean's Wonder of the Seas . We sailed to Roatán, Honduras ; Cozumel and Costa Maya, Mexico; and Royal Caribbean's private island in the Bahamas. I had a good time, but some things would've made my trip easier, cheaper, and more comfortable. Here's what I think all first-time cruisers should know before setting sail. Some cruise ship cabins, like those at the front of the ship, can be rockier than others. The reporter's room was at the front of the ship. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Before booking, I should have researched how a cabin's location can affect how much motion you feel while the ship is moving. My ocean-view cabin was at the front of the ship, and I felt more movement than I expected. As a first-time cruiser, I found it uncomfortably rocky. Shaky nights made it tough to sleep. Several seasoned cruisers on the voyage told me that the front of the ship was one of the worst places to feel motion. Higher decks in the middle of the ship felt calmer and more stable. If you are as prone to motion sickness as I am, I suggest choosing a room in the middle of the ship. The restaurants included in the cruise rate had a variety of high-quality dishes, so splurging on specialty restaurants wasn't necessary. Joey Hadden/Business Insider One of the most distinctive things about cruising is that most meals, snacks, and drinks are included in the cruise rate. However, on Wonder of the Seas and many other mega-ships, more than a dozen restaurants with specialty offerings, such as sushi, are not included and incur additional charges, either as a one-time fee or per dish. I paid $40 to $60 for each specialty meal.  I reserved all specialty restaurants before my trip, but I found myself wishing I hadn't booked so many once I realized the included restaurants offered a wide range of delicious food. There were multiple buffets, and the main dining room served a three-course meal with changing menu items each night. These included options that satisfied every craving. One of the best meals I had was in the main dining room. Since I booked so many specialty restaurants, I didn't have time to try all the buffets or eat in the main dining room more than once. If I had known they'd be so satisfying, I would've saved money and eaten more of the included meals instead. Formal nights weren't enforced, so don't waste luggage space on nice outfits if you don't want to participate. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I have an aversion to dressing up, but I knew my cruise included formal nights , so I brought one nice dress. After the first formal night, however, I learned that the dress code wasn't strictly enforced. I noticed people wore a variety of outfits, from suits and evening gowns to T-shirts and track pants. I was happy to relax my look on the other two formal nights, but the dress felt like a waste of the limited space in my carry-on suitcase . If I had known it wasn't necessary, I would've left it at home and brought multiple other articles in its place. Though it was a Caribbean cruise, I got chilly on the top decks, so bring some warm clothing. Joey Hadden/Business Insider My favorite times to be on the top decks of the ship were early in the morning and late at night, when there weren't as many crowds. These were also the coldest, windiest parts of the day. Instead of my shiny, poofy, formal dress, I should've brought another pair of pants and another sweater to keep me warm. Since I didn't, I ended up wearing the same pants and sweater nearly every morning and evening. Laundry on board can be expensive, so consider bringing a bar of laundry soap to save money. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Since I brought only a  carry-on luggage , I hoped to get some laundry done on board, but then I saw the pricing sheet . Living in New York City, most of the apartments I've rented haven't had in-unit laundry, so I'm used to paying to have my clothes washed. But rather than pricing by weight, as local New York laundromats do, Royal Caribbean charged for each article of clothing. Each shirt was $4, and a dress cost $9. Most surprisingly, washing just one pair of underwear would have cost $2. I thought this would add up fast, so I didn't do any laundry on my trip. In hindsight, I should have brought a bar of laundry soap to hand-wash a few things.  I would've brought my own case of water if I knew it was allowed. Joey Hadden/Business Insider To ensure I stayed hydrated throughout my trip, I opted for the water bottle package while booking trip extras like restaurant reservations and excursions. For $16, Royal Caribbean delivered a case of 24 water bottles to my cabin. It seemed expensive for a pack of water, but I thought this was just part of the price of cruising. When I was boarding the ship, though, I noticed people carrying their own cases of water. That's when I realized Royal Caribbean allows guests to bring their own nonalcoholic beverages. If I had known this, I would've brought my own water and saved a few bucks. If I had known these details before my cruise, I could have had a better time while saving some money. Hopefully, my findings will help other first-time cruisers. The author poses at a port in front of the world's largest cruise ship Joey Hadden/Business Insider While I enjoyed parts of my cruise, some of this knowledge could've made my trip much more comfortable. On my next cruise, I'll remember what I learned about cabin locations, formal nights, and cool, windy mornings sailing in the Caribbean Sea. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The political ad wars are still being fought over the airwaves even as digital gains share
events.summary: Broadcast TV is set to capture 48% of political ad spending, or $5.6 billion, ahead of the midterm election, according to AdImpact. Industry leaders and experts disagree about whether broadcast's success is due to a well-designed strategy or simply muscle memory stemming from decades of placing ads on local television. Publicly traded broadcasting companies, including Nexstar, Gray Media, Sinclair and E.W. Scripps, are set to win big as a result. The companies have already recorded high political advertising revenue in the most recently reported fiscal quarter. While advertising dollars increasingly shift toward streaming and digital platforms , the political ad war is still being fought over the free airwaves. Broadcast television companies are set to capture the greatest portion of political ad spend ahead of the midterm elections , according to advertising intelligence company AdImpact. The 2025-26 election cycle is forecast to be the most expensive on record , with a predicted $11.6 billion in total spending. That's higher than the $11.2 billion spent on advertising during the 2024 presidential election cycle and the $8.9 billion spent during the 2022 midterms. An estimated $5.6 billion of advertising spend ahead of the midterms, or 48%, is expected to go to broadcast companies, AdImpact found. "It's still a local game," said StoneX Equity Research Analyst Daniel Kurnos in an interview. "Yes, there are national elections, but you have to win counties. And if you have to win counties, you have to reach voters in these counties." Broadcast audiences — those tuning into NBC, ABC, CBS, Fox or their local affiliate stations — are generally more politically active, Kurnos said: "You cater to the demos that vote. You cater to the votes that matter." That makes political advertising one of the last bastions of broadcast's dominance. While broadcasters are expected to capture roughly half of political advertising spending this cycle, they account for just 7.7% of the more than $470 billion in general advertising spend forecast for this year in the United States, according to Magna data published by S&P Global in July. Terry Nelson, a founding partner of Plus Communications and the national political director for former President George W. Bush's 2004 reelection campaign, told CNBC that broadcast spots allow political strategists to reach large numbers of voters "as efficiently as we can from a cost perspective." Though cord-cutting has reshaped the TV landscape as customers drop cable, broadcast remains free and broadly accessible. Broadcast, which transmits local news, sports, classic game shows like "Wheel of Fortune" and national networks, captured more hours of television use than cable in July, according to Nielsen's most recent monthly streaming report, The Gauge . The category accounted for 19.5% of television use, while cable captured 18.7%. Streaming led television use by far, at 49%. Broadcast is still particularly good at delivering high viewership during live sports games, Nelson noted. "If you think about an NFL audience, for example, you're still going to deliver big audiences amongst large segments of the population," he said. "So no matter how you dice that demographic, whether it's men, women, or old people, young people, or whatever the case might be, the NFL game is still going to deliver large segments of all of those audiences." Brad Seitter, CEO of TVB, a trade organization representing the local broadcast industry, boiled down broadcast's strength during election cycles to "trust, reach and because it works." Seitter told CNBC in a statement that television's perceived reliability is of utmost importance for political campaigns. "Gaining the trust of a voter equals a vote for your candidate or issue," Seitter said. He also said that he believes broadcast does a better job of promoting political candidates and issues than some digital channels. "You may see a political ad on social media, but you don't trust the content of the ad because users are conditioned to not trust what they hear or see on social media," Seitter said. "Conversely, viewers trust their local broadcast TV news, so when they view a political ad, they are more likely to believe the content of the ad on a platform they know has long-standing rules, regulations and trust." Strategic prowess or muscle memory? Seitter said that political campaigns continue to place advertisements on traditional TV because there is clear evidence that they are influential on voting behavior. "Nothing moves the needle in polling like running an ad on broadcast TV," Seitter said. According to a study conducted by TVB, 42% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans said broadcast or cable television was the most important form of advertising media in influencing how they cast their vote.

events.title: 16 outfits Taylor Swift has worn this year, ranked from worst to best
events.summary: Taylor Swift at the Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles on October 17. Gilbert Flores/Variety/Getty Images Taylor Swift has been busy attending awards shows, sporting events, and more this year. Her signature style has been on display at every occasion. Swift's best looks have been simple and elegant. Her worst was too corporate. Taylor Swift is back . No, she hasn't announced her 13th studio album or another massive world tour . She's simply stepped back into the spotlight after a few quiet months away. Since March, the music icon has been photographed at awards shows, walking around New York City, and sitting in suites at Arrowhead Stadium — in support of her husband, Travis Kelce , of course. Naturally, she's worn statement outfits for each occasion. Designer jackets, expensive jewelry, and luxury handbags remain her signatures. Some of her recent looks are the epitome of her effortless street style , while others haven't made much sense. Here's how we'd rank what she's worn this year, from worst to best. Taylor Swift brought back peplum tops in May, but she probably shouldn't have. Taylor Swift in New York City on May 14. Aeon/Getty Images She was photographed in New York City wearing a $1,190 white button-up blouse from Stella McCartney, $1,350 The Row trousers, sandals from the same brand, and a black leather belt. The bottom half of the outfit was chic, but her top looked too formal, making the outfit feel corporate. It couldn't be saved by Swift's $4,500 Fendi bag or her Cartier Santos Demoiselle watch . The outfit she wore to a Chiefs game in September wasn't memorable. Taylor Swift at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri, on September 20. David Eulitt/Getty Images Swift was spotted on September 20 standing in a suite at Arrowhead Stadium with her mom and mother-in-law. She kept her outfit simple that day: denim bottoms, a black leather belt, and a $40 Chiefs tank top from Wear by Erin Andrews. There was nothing really wrong with the outfit; the musician looked cute and comfortable. Still, it was so simple that most fans probably won't remember it next season. The same could be said for the checkered dress she wore a few days earlier. Taylor Swift at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri, on September 14. David Eulitt/Getty Images At another Chiefs game, Swift wore a $295 checkered dress from Guest in Residence. It was a sweet, festive choice for the occasion, especially when paired with her signature red lipstick. At the same time, though, the pattern made the dress resemble a picnic tablecloth, which wasn't ideal. One tweak could have saved Swift's 2026 MTV Video Music Awards look. Taylor Swift attends the MTV Video Music Awards in September 2026. John Shearer/WireImage/Rich Polk/Billboard via Getty Images She arrived on the blue carpet wearing a couture gown from Tamara Ralph. It had a halter neckline, a black velvet bodice with a mesh back, and a sparkling silver skirt that wrapped around her hips and reached the floor. From the front, Swift looked powerful and stylish. Unfortunately, the thick, lace-up feature on the back of the dress made it look less elegant. She chose elevated basics for an NBA playoff game, though they weren't super memorable. Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce at a 2026 Knicks and Cavaliers game. Tim Phillis/AP Swift and Kelce were sitting courtside when the Knicks played the Cavaliers in the NBA Eastern Conference Finals. Both wore denim outfits for the game, though Swift's look was undoubtedly flashier. She paired $790 Stella McCartney jeans with a black denim jacket and a chain-embellished tank top from the designer. Swift also sported a Dior purse, Stella McCartney sandals, and an assortment of gold jewelry — including her massive engagement ring . The outfit was fun, but also simple and a little forgettable. Swift was ready for fall when she made a surprise appearance on "Saturday Night Live" in October. Dakota Johnson and Taylor Swift at "Saturday Night Live" on October 3. NBC/Will Heath/Getty Images She took the stage alongside her friend, Dakota Johnson , wearing a $595 Simkhai brown plaid minidress. Swift also wore a $1,500 Yves Saint Laurent chain belt, a gold Cartier bracelet, Burberry boots, and hoop earrings. The outfit didn't make for her flashiest fashion moment, but it was cute and understated. She embraced her girl-next-door vibe for a New York City outing in June. Taylor Swift in New York City on June 15. Aeon/Getty Images Photographers captured Swift wearing a $295 Guest in Residence polo top, light-wash denim jeans, Gucci sandals, a matching leather belt, and an assortment of gold jewelry. She also carried the large Chloé Penelope bag. It was one of Swift's most cohesive looks so far this year. The musician accepted 7 iHeartRadio awards in a green corseted minidress. Taylor Swift at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards. Phillip Faraone/Getty Images Wiederhoeft designed the ensemble, which was sleeveless and decorated with silver sparkles. Swift wore it with $36,000 Dena Kemp earrings and Jimmy Choo sandals. The assortment of rings and bracelets she wore also retailed for $36,000. Swift looked pretty, and her outfit was solid. It wasn't her best look of the year, but it was far from her worst. Swift's street style reemerged in April, and it was strong from the start. Taylor Swift in New York City on April 27. Aeon/Getty Images On one New York City outing, Swift paired a blue-and-white striped Staud dress with $1,195 Christian Louboutin sandals and a yellow mini Lady Dior bag. The outfit was fun and perfect for summer. The mix of diamond and opal jewelry she wore with it only added to the look. Her date-night style this year has been feminine and flowing. Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce in New York City on May 15. DAMEBK/Bauer-Griffin/Getty Images Just look at the floral Doen dress she wore for a night out with Kelce in May. The off-the-shoulder design had puffed sleeves, a semi-sheer skirt, and a ruffled neckline. The dress was cute on its own, but it looked even better with Swift's choice of accessories: $920 Aquazzura sandals, gold jewelry, and a small raffia bag. Swift proved that you can't go wrong with a classic black-and-white outfit. Taylor Swift in New York City on May 12. DAMEBK/Bauer-Griffin/Getty Images On a different night in New York City, Swift was photographed wearing a white Retrofête minidress. The simple garment had a high neckline, long sleeves, and a short pleated skirt. On its own, the dress might not have stood out on Swift. However, she accessorized to perfection. She contrasted the garment with a slouchy black Dior purse, Gucci slingback heels, and a ponytail. Even as a wedding guest, Swift sparkled. Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce in New York City on May 16. XNY/Star Max/Getty Images Swift and Kelce attended a wedding in New York City in May and were photographed outside the event. While Kelce sported a black Essentials suit with subtle pinstripes,

events.title: I spent $100 on dinner for 2 at LongHorn Steakhouse. I now understand why the chain is so successful.
events.summary: LongHorn Steakhouse is outpacing many other casual-dining chains. After visiting for the first time, I can see why. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I recently visited LongHorn Steakhouse as the chain reports positive sales growth this year. Many casual-dining chains are struggling, but LongHorn is performing surprisingly well. I thought the food was high quality and a great value for the cost. LongHorn Steakhouse is having a moment. While many casual-dining chains continue to struggle, LongHorn has posted some of the strongest sales growth in Darden Restaurants' portfolio. In the fiscal first quarter, which ended August 30, LongHorn same-store sales rose 6.2% from a year earlier, outpacing sister chain Olive Garden , whose same-store sales rose 1.1%. LongHorn's overall sales across all locations increased by nearly 11% to $861 million, making it Darden's fastest-growing major chain that quarter. During the company's earnings call, CFO Raj Vennam said LongHorn's first-quarter sales growth reflected both stronger sales at existing restaurants and the expansion of its footprint. LongHorn grew from 595 to 624 restaurants over the past year. LongHorn's success is not a recent comeback, but rather a steady rise to the top. In the preceding quarter, which ended May 31, LongHorn's same-store sales rose 9.5%, while total sales increased nearly 22% to more than $1 billion. Darden credited a record-breaking Mother's Day weekend and strong lamb-chop sales for the results. The chain has now posted positive same-store sales for 22 consecutive quarters, and its sales at existing restaurants have climbed 17% over the past three years. Still, it's a tough time for casual dining. Applebee's same-store sales fell 1.8% year-over-year in its most recent quarter, while Cracker Barrel's sales at existing locations fell 2.1% and its total revenue declined 2.2%. In an environment where chain restaurants are constantly competing for customers, I wanted to find out what about the Texas-inspired steakhouse chain was drawing people in. I visited LongHorn for the first time and was surprised by the quality of the food, generous portions, and overall value for the price. I tried LongHorn Steakhouse for the first time to see what the hype was about. Erin McDowell/Business Insider LongHorn Steakhouse has quietly become one of casual dining’s biggest success stories, and recently outpaced its sister brand, Olive Garden, in same-store sales growth. I’d never been before, so I brought a friend along to our nearest location in Queens, New York, to see whether the food, atmosphere, and value lived up to the hype. The restaurant felt much warmer and more polished than I expected. Erin McDowell/Business Insider I expected a fairly standard chain-restaurant experience, but the entryway felt inviting right away. The stone accents, dark wood, and low lighting gave it a cozy, classic steakhouse atmosphere. It was casual, but it did not feel cheap. I could see why it would potentially work for both casual weeknight dinners and slightly more special celebrations. Despite visiting on a Friday night during the dinner rush, we were seated quickly in a booth at the busy shopping center location. The dining room was busy, but it still felt comfortable and relaxed. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The restaurant had plenty of tables, yet it did not feel overly crowded or chaotic. The warm lighting made the large dining room feel more intimate. It was definitely family-friendly, but couples and groups of friends were also dining there. About halfway through our meal, one of the tables next to us broke into a rendition of "Happy Birthday" for a guest. I also thought the vibe was much more polished than a typical casual chain. It was more on par with chains like Red Lobster than slightly more casual ones like Chili's or Applebee's. The menu had a surprisingly broad selection beyond just steak and sides. Erin McDowell/Business Insider LongHorn’s menu is centered on steak, but there were plenty of chicken, seafood, salad, burger, and sandwich options, too. Even though I went in wanting to understand the chain’s steakhouse appeal, there were enough tempting appetizers and sides that narrowing down our order was harder than I expected. My friend and I started off with a round of cocktails. Erin McDowell/Business Insider A steakhouse dinner calls for a drink, and the classic "Perfect" margarita ($11.49) was a refreshing — and surprisingly inexpensive — way to start the meal. It was ice-cold and citrusy, served in a generously sized glass with an extra shaker on the side. My friend ordered the Texas tea ($10.99), LongHorn's version of a Long Island iced tea, which she said was sweet and not too strong. We were both impressed by the price and serving size of our drinks — they were on par with what we'd spend at a dive bar in Brooklyn, but with much better service and flavor. The complimentary bread was a nice start to the meal. Erin McDowell/Business Insider The bread arrived warm with a side of butter before our appetizers hit the table. It had a slightly sweet, honey-wheat flavor and a tender texture. It was simple, and probably could have had a better crust — but it was free.
