events.title: France’s diesel deal with Gulf states will not make fuel 'cheap overnight’ for European country
events.summary: France's deal to buy diesel from Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Bahrain will not make the fuel “cheap overnight” for the European country although it will also not make it more expensive, according to experts. The three Gulf states are to sell France the equivalent of 10 per cent of its usual diesel consumption in the coming weeks, French government sources said on Tuesday during President Emmanuel Macron's regional tour . The aim is to reduce European energy prices, which have drawn protests and public anger in France and elsewhere. The deal “will not make French diesel cheap overnight, but it can stop it [from] becoming scarcer and even more expensive”, said Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer at Zaye Capital Markets. “The bigger value is psychological: France is no longer buying in a panic,” Mr Aslam added. “Gulf supply gives refiners, distributors and traders confidence that physical barrels are coming, which can compress the scarcity premium before it fully reaches the pump.” European diesel has reached about $200 a barrel amid the war in Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. That compares with about $80 at the start of 2026, with refined products rallying much harder than crude prices this year. Temporary easing of supply While the deal can temporarily ease France’s diesel supply shortage, it is unlikely to drive a sustained decline in fuel prices, according to Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial. “The additional diesel arriving in France would ease competition among importers for limited supplies. This could reduce the scarcity premium that buyers pay for immediately available fuel, particularly if inventories are low,” he added. France previously obtained guarantees from Saudi Arabia to sell the country 95,000 tonnes of diesel in both October and November, totalling 190,000 tonnes. The UAE and Bahrain are in the coming weeks expected to separately sell 100,000 tonnes of diesel to France for an unknown duration. The duration of the supply agreements matter – if UAE and Bahrain shipments continue for several months, they could have a longer-lasting effect on supply security and prices, Mr Valecha said. “If they are temporary or cargoes are delayed, the relief could be short-lived. The wider diesel shortage is a significant driver. The diesel supply squeeze remains severe. The International Energy Agency has warned that shortages could persist well into 2027.” On October 2, G7 leaders pledged to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release , prioritising diesel supplies. About 96 million barrels of the 400 million pledged in March have yet to be released. The IEA expects higher refinery output to return the diesel market to a seasonal surplus by early next year but said the recovery would be insufficient to replenish inventories depleted during the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. European commercial gasoil inventories fell to a 25-year low in July, while US diesel stocks reached a 14-year seasonal low by September. Combined gasoil exports from Russia and the Middle East dropped by more than 60 per cent, equivalent to 1.3 million barrels per day. With Mr Macron’s current Gulf visit, the focus would remain on making fuel more affordable at the petrol station rather than just securing France’s fuel supply security, Mr Valecha said. “Analysts estimate that a large release of diesel reserves could lower wholesale prices by $20 to $30 per barrel, or about €0.10 to €0.15 per litre, at the pump, with prices possibly dropping within a few days,” he added. Market signal The latest deal’s importance “lies in the signal it gives to market”, Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer, said. “Despite the recent escalations, oil products find their way out of the Middle East. One should look beyond this specific deal. More supplies from the Middle East ease oil products tightness globally, irrespective if the buyers of single cargoes are in Europe or elsewhere, as this is a global market,” he said. There is indication that oil product exports from the Middle East are picking up and that refineries in Asia are putting more oil products on the market, he added. However, according to Mr Valecha, diesel exports are not expected to pick up any time soon from the Middle East in a way that could bring down costs significantly. “This is because oil product markets are expected to remain tight through mid-2027, even if current war-related disruptions ease. The reason for this being [that] global supply is constrained by an unusually large upswing in refinery maintenance,” he said. Even when Middle East diesel exports rise again, the price effect will lag the headline, agreed Mr Aslam. “The constraint is not only production – it is secure shipping, insurance, tanker availability and the ability to move refined products reliably into Europe,” he said. “The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain are showing why dependable Gulf suppliers matter: sustained cargoes, rather than one-off emergency shipments, are what would truly pull diesel prices down.” What next? Europe could diversify imports to reduce reliance on a single source, with potential deals with the US or Asian suppliers helping to ease the current crunch, according to Mr Valecha. “Fuel tax cuts and price subsidies may also offer immediate relief, but they are costly and risk sustaining demand when supplies are tight,” he said. While there have been suggestions that consumers curb demand by shifting to electric vehicles or car pooling, Europe cannot solve a diesel shortage by simply asking consumers to drive less, said Mr Aslam. “Diesel is the bloodstream of its freight, construction, farming and industry. France and its neighbours need a three-part response: co-ordinated reserve releases, guaranteed supply contracts with reliable producers, and a faster shift of freight toward rail and electrified alternatives,” he said. “The mistake would be treating this as a temporary oil price spike. It is a refining and logistics security problem.”

events.title: I didn't realize how much I needed a happy moment until I saw 18,000 hockey fans cheering for a stranger
events.summary: The author went to see the Flyers play. Courtesy of the author I was at a Flyers game when an 84-year-old woman appeared on the Jumbotron and stole the show. The crowd cheered for her and booed the mascot, Gritty, whenever the camera switched away. Watching thousands of strangers celebrate her brought me to tears during a difficult time. Since our  kids left for college , my husband and I have been to many Philadelphia Flyers games. The most recent, against the Colorado Avalanche, felt magical, and it wasn't just the high of a second consecutive win after a nine-game losing streak. There was an older woman, way up in the upper section, who, in a purely joyful moment, stole the show and captured the hearts of all 18,353 of us in attendance. I'm calling her Good Luck Granny. People were being shown on the Jumbotron During the third period, the Flyers were up 3-1, and the crowd was electric. Could they make it two wins in a row? During TV time-outs, cameras stationed throughout the arena pan to fans — parents holding ear-muffed babies aloft, kids jumping up and down, waving "My 1st Flyers game!!" signs — or to our beloved mascot, Gritty , in his Chaos Corner, doing what Gritty does. I love seeing the reactions of people who make it on the jumbotron, and, yes, I may have, on occasion, attempted to wave at a camera pointed in our direction. Being at the game means losing myself and any worries I might have for a few hours in something everyone can agree on. With less than 10 minutes left in the third period, the camera found a grey-haired, bespectacled woman, straight out of central casting, in a royal blue hoodie. She was chair dancing, arms up in the air, her bright orange Flyers microfiber towel ready for waving. The arena exploded into a unanimous uproar for this stranger. The camera panned to Gritty, and everyone booed. Then they went back to the woman , and we watched her moment of recognition in real time along with the guy seated next to her who'd been pointing her out to the cameraman. She lit up and began pointing at herself, as she mouthed, "Oh, that's me!" This was met with uproarious cheers. I swallowed the sudden lump in my throat and fought back tears as we continued to scream for her. Everyone was excited for her Everyone wanted more, and the camera operators obliged, cycling half a dozen times between Gritty, who played along with the boos and disappointment, and Good Luck Granny, who elicited raucous cheering, much to her and everyone's delight. I'm not sure why it made me so emotional, but the feeling remains. After the game, fans followed and cheered her all the way out of the building, taking photos along the way. Fans went crazy for her in the comment section, too. Under a video posted by Sports Radio 94WIP Reporter, Dave Uram, @anfieldcards wrote, "I sat right next to her and her daughter, she was crying after being on the screen. It meant so much to her. She's 84 years old but was screaming and cheering all game." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dave Uram (@daveuram) That woman was the distraction I needed Maybe it's because 2026 has been filled with what feels like an endlessly worrisome, increasingly overwhelming news cycle, along with some personally painful moments. When my mother died in January, a few months shy of her 82nd birthday, I hadn't seen or spoken to her in 17 years. Not surprisingly, this has brought up some complicated feelings. Turning 59 this summer brought up a lot of thoughts, too (because I am a professional overthinker), about my own mortality and what the state of the world might be for my grandchildren. For those three hours, though, being enveloped by the energy of strangers who come together for a shared, emotionally vested experience, the games have been a salve and a healing distraction. I also believe that now more than ever, we're all craving joyful, feel-good moments like cheering for an unsuspecting elderly woman in a crowded hockey arena. So, thank you, beautiful stranger, our Good Luck Granny, for your infectious good vibes and an experience that will not soon be forgotten. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: US stocks nudge higher as SpaceX, Tesla and Nvidia climb
events.summary: The U.S. stock market is drifting higher following strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One Financial and other big companies NEW YORK -- The U.S. stock market is ticking higher Wednesday as strong profit reports from SpaceX , Capital One Financial and other big companies help offset updates from Netflix and AT & T that investors found disappointing. The S & P 500 rose 0.2% and is on track for a third straight modest gain . The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 47 points, or 0.1%, as of 10 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.7% higher. SpaceX helped lead the way and climbed 11.2% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Elon Musk, who runs the company that makes money from artificial-intelligence technology, rockets and other businesses, also said that SpaceX took a step to consider a possible merger with Tesla, his electric-vehicle company. Tesla, which will report its latest quarterly results late Wednesday, climbed 3.8% and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S & P 500. Other stocks rallying on profit reports that topped analysts’ expectations included Capital One Financial, which rose 4%, and Winnebago Industries, which climbed 6.5%. Expectations are high for profit growth during the summer, and companies will need to meet them to justify the big runs their stock prices have made toward records despite worries about high inflation , higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street. Winnebago was able to report a more resilient profit than analysts expected even as high fuel prices and frustration among U.S. shoppers restrain interest in recreational vehicles, for example. CEO Michael Happe said its more expensive towable RVs are a tougher sell, but customers are interested in its “more accessible” offerings. It helped offset a drop for Netflix, which fell 2.7% even though the streaming service reported a stronger profit than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix’s momentum may be slowing. The company’s forecast for revenue growth in the final three months of the year fell short of analysts’ expectations. AT & T fell 4.4% even though it likewise delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for growth this year in an underlying measure of earnings before income taxes and some other things that fell short of some analysts’ expectations. Among AI stocks, which have been at the center of the market’s action in recent weeks, the movements remained unsettled. After leading the rest of the market for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry have become shaky on worries that the build out of data centers may slow because of how much more expensive it’s become to borrow money. Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony DOJ official clashes with judge in DC golf course case after Trump attacks her 2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly volatile. On Tuesday, it careened between a loss of 6% and a gain of 5%, for example. On Wednesday, it fell 1.4% after erasing an early gain of nearly 4%. Other AI-linked stocks were more solid, though. Nvidia's gain of 1.8% was the strongest force lifting the S & P 500. Besides SpaceX’s profit report showing strength for AI spending, another encouraging signal for the industry came from Super Micro Computer, which sells AI servers and services. It said it expects to report stronger revenue for the summer than it had earlier forecast because of “increased demand for AI platforms,” and its stock rallied 12%. Another potential boost for the AI industry came from an easing of Treasury yields in the bond market, which helps dictate how expensive loans are for the U.S. government, companies and regular Americans . The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.09% from 5.12% late Tuesday, though it remains far above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation higher. Oil prices remained unsteady on Wednesday following big swings this month on uncertainty about when the energy industry can return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude slipped 0.6% to $108.14 after crossing above $111 earlier in the morning. It’s been yo-yoing between $97 and $112 in October. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.3% for one of the world’s biggest moves as AI stocks regained strength. events.title: We left our house in a city for a rural cabin. Parts of the monthlong experience were great, but I wouldn't do it again.
events.summary: Leaving city life for a rural cabin meant confronting a lot of my fears. Kate Irwin I spent most of my adult life in cities before moving to a rural cabin for my husband's job. It was hard to adjust, and I had to confront many of my phobias before moving back home. Although I wouldn't choose to live in a cabin again, I'm grateful for what the experience taught me. At the end of the summer, I packed my bags and two cats and got on a plane by myself, leaving our spacious home in Portland, Oregon, for a two-bedroom cabin in the remote woods of upstate New York. I was planning to live there temporarily so I could spend some time with my husband, who had rented the place while he was working on a movie in the area. He had moved to the area a few weeks earlier to start work, and he would stay there until mid-November when the project wrapped. His options for where to stay were limited: a room at a Best Western , or a quaint cottage with a wood-burning stove and brick flooring on a historic acreage with farm animals. If I hadn't planned to come, he might have just chosen the hotel room, but he wanted a pet-friendly option with a little more space. I saw staying in the cabin as a chance to slow down a bit after feeling work-related burnout — but I was nervous, too. The cabin showed me what I took for granted at home The cabin was a far cry from our house in Portland. Kate Irwin Immediately, there were some things I genuinely loved about rural living . One of my favorite parts was the privacy. The cabin sat next to a creek and a grove of trees on a massive acreage at the foot of a mountain. It was part farm, part forest. I rarely saw other people most days, and got plenty of work done. While at the cabin, I started working on the second draft of my novel while planning for my next full-time role. However, it was also tough to adjust to rustic life. For most of my adult life, I'd lived in cities, including Los Angeles, New York, Atlanta, and Portland. Back home in Portland, I'd gotten used to our walkable neighborhood with incredible coffee shops just steps away, plus a slew of local wine bars, restaurants, and other small businesses easily accessible by bike. Although there were a few charming spots in the general area, the surrounding town beyond the acreage was pretty lackluster, and we were living in a grocery-store desert . I was surprised by how little there really was to do, considering we were only about a two-hour drive from New York City. Then there was the cottage itself. After living in a house with a dishwasher and an espresso machine, I had to get used to sputtering hot-water taps and Keurig coffee. Still, none of these inconveniences was the end of the world, especially since I'd only be living here for one month. The biggest challenge, though, was confronting my obsessive-compulsive disorder . Living near so many insects forced me to face my OCD Our property had plenty of animals and insects. Kate Irwin Rustic cabin living meant that there were bugs everywhere , pretty much all the time. Moths, stinkbugs, crane flies the size of my palm, spiders, grasshoppers, and even crickets managed to sneak their way inside. Outside, I'd get swarmed by mosquitoes and gnats. One night, I counted over two dozen sizable bugs that had somehow snuck into our cabin. Sometimes the bugs made me feel trapped because I couldn't fully escape them, no matter where I was. This might be an annoying inconvenience for people used to suburban life or climates with fewer bugs, but for me — someone with OCD — it felt like a test from the universe. Although every person with OCD can and will have completely different fears, obsessions, and compulsions, many of mine center on fears of germs, disease, or contamination. For me, a fear of hurting myself or my pets due to something in the environment — for instance, ticks with Lyme disease — can trigger compulsive handwashing, body-checking, and a general sense of anxiety throughout the day. When these compulsions come into play, I often become less productive, more distracted, and late for everything. The presence of so many bugs, plus corners layered with dust and cobwebs, triggered my fears of contamination and heightened my anxiety. Early on, I was even afraid of walking on the grass outside, since upstate New York has many more reported cases of Lyme disease than in Oregon, my home base. I was also concerned that my spouse, while working on location in the woods or other areas, might bring ticks home on his clothes, transmit them to me, or fall ill from a bite. Being exposed to my fears eventually helped them fade I'm glad I had the chance to confront my fears head-on. Kate Irwin Despite all of this, about a week in, I started to settle into cabin life a bit. My fears were there, but nothing bad happened. The bugs didn't go away, but they didn't get us sick. The cats were happy. At one point, I walked across the grass to go see the goats on the property, and I didn't get any ticks. It might sound silly, but for me, this was a bit of a breakthrough. I love animals, nature, and traveling the world, but the intense, intrusive thoughts that OCD brings can make it difficult to enjoy a new adventure without a constant baseline feeling of anxiety. The best part about living in this rural landscape was being able to see and get close to so many animals. On the property, there were free-range chickens and geese, plus wild turkeys, foxes, deer, and tons of blue jays. And there was this squad of hilarious goats, sheep, and a cow. With time, I was able to enjoy the experience. Spending a month in upstate New York isn't something I'd do again, and after a month at the cottage, I was excited to return to our spacious house and walkable neighborhood. But I'm grateful for the experience that allowed me to try out a new lifestyle, challenge my OCD , and come out stronger. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Foursquare co-founder says equity holders saw no returns from the company’s acquisition
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Last month, advertising company Infillion acquired location-data platform Foursquare, a once popular social network, at an undisclosed value. Now, in a new blog post , Foursquare co-founder and former CEO Dennis Crowley said that investors didn’t see any returns from the sale. Crowley referenced a post by an angel investor , inferred that neither preferred nor common stockholders got any value out of the deal, and said he was disappointed by the outcome. “I was heartbroken by this ending. So many people put so much time and energy and passion and love into building Foursquare — the company, the products, the brand, the culture. If you were part of it (or even close to it), you know exactly what I’m talking about. To our ~1600 former employees over 17 years, I am sorry the Foursquare story ended in such a way that makes it seem like our collective efforts were worth … nothing?” he said in the post. Crowley said that the company did well after it started focusing on enterprise business and had consecutive years with over $100 million in revenue. In 2019, the company raised capital from a private equity firm and in 2021 brought in the banker who led the raise as CEO. Crowley blamed the final outcome on that transition, saying that the management of the company wasn’t able to preserve or create new value. Foursquare, which had raised over $411 million in funding according to PitchBook data, eventually shut down its app in 2024 . Several people reacted to Crowley’s post and said that Foursquare was very useful to them in discovering new places in their cities and also gave ideas for new apps . events.title: AI promises productivity, but for managers, it’s mostly a headache for now
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Companies are giving employees AI tools to make them more productive, but the tools appear to be creating new problems for their managers. More than half of senior leaders say they find it harder to evaluate employees’ work after adopting AI, according to a Nielsen survey of 1,700 directors and senior managers across seven countries, commissioned by work-management company Monday.com. The reason is that much of employees’ output now arrives polished in the manager’s inbox, making it hard to tell how much came from the employee and how much from AI. As a result, nearly half of managers say they spend more time reviewing and guiding their teams’ output than they used to. That’s not to say managers are unhappy about AI. Quite the opposite, in fact: 94% of the managers polled said they were excited to improve work using AI, and many are confident they know where to use it to get the most value. Michal Miller Levi, head of market research and customer insights at Monday.com, compared the enthusiasm to the early days of the internet in the 2000s, saying people see a similar kind of “magic” to AI. But the problem, she told TechCrunch, is simply that AI is developing faster than companies can adapt. “AI works very well for [managers] individually, but they also have a different role as managers. They need to drive the organization as well … Their struggle is [due to] the fact that AI is just moving faster than the organizational processes,” Levi said. Managers are also reconsidering how they judge their teams: 78% of respondents said they have changed how they evaluate employees after adopting AI, placing greater weight on how well staff can create prompts, decide which tasks to delegate to AI, and experiment with new ways of working. But how fairly can employees be judged when managers can’t easily tell how much of their work was produced by AI? And what if the managers themselves are increasingly relying on AI to make those judgments? The survey found that 46% of managers use AI to help inform their decisions, and 39% of leaders are using AI to draft performance reviews. That practice runs the risk of introducing even more bias than usual into the review process, given that LLMs are, at their core, prediction machines and tend to repeat human patterns found in their training data. Research from the Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research earlier this year found that “in the absence of clear objective standards and when individuals are rated independently,” LLMs tend to rate performance similarly to humans. And a research paper in early 2025 found that AI models can be biased against black male candidates, and “demonstrate significant biases, varying in terms of the directions and magnitudes across different social groups.” When I asked Levi whether using AI to weigh in on people’s performance could introduce outside bias into the process, she said companies have yet to work out how to handle such issues. AI is also changing what a manager’s day looks like. Someone has to decide which tasks to hand over to AI agents, check what they produce, and step in when something goes wrong. The report suggests that this supervision could amount to a new layer of “invisible labor.” The software itself is becoming harder to manage. Fifty-seven percent of managers say their organizations now have more tools in circulation than before, and about 51% said their tools had grown more interdependent and clustered since adopting AI. Only 29% described their AI infrastructure as fully optimized and centralized. Levi said businesses had expected AI to help shrink their software stacks. Instead, they’re dealing with more apps, integrations, and shadow AI usage as employees adopt tools outside their companies’ approved systems. “Managers completed 2025 with the feeling that they will consolidate tools, actually, that they’ll reduce the number of software. But what happened is that the number of tools that they’re using increased,” Levi said. “More than 50% are saying that they’re using more tools now than they did last year, and it’s not stopping.” This need for control seems to be growing urgent as companies deploy AI agents that can act on their own. The survey found that 58% of managers expect to oversee more AI agents than human employees within the next year, and 46% worry about losing control over those agents’ actions. There’s also quite a bit of fear over being held responsible for decisions made by AI (35% of respondents said so), as LLMs are still largely unpredictable. “They don’t want their agents to be fully autonomous,” Levi said, explaining that managers want people to be involved and consulted by AI when it comes to crucial tasks and decisions.

events.title: Investors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising
events.summary: Nebius' chief revenue officer told CNBC that AI computing prices are continuing to rise and are running ahead of its expectations. The comments come as investors scrutinize the debt, borrowing costs and economics of companies building AI infrastructure. BERLIN — Nebius is seeing AI computing prices rise more than expected, a top executive told CNBC on Wednesday, offering a bullish view as neocloud firms' business model comes under increasing scrutiny . Investors have grown wary after CoreWeave , one of the biggest neocloud players, saw the spread on its five-year credit default swaps hit levels generally viewed as signs of distress. The yields on CoreWeave's bonds also climbed. The CoreWeave developments and questions around the amount of debt being used to fund the data center buildout have weighed heavily on other neoclouds like Iren and Nebius, whose stocks have dropped sharply over the last month. Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer at Nebius, said his company wasn't in CoreWeave's position because "we're not carrying the kind of debt that they are." He also said that if the AI infrastructure company brought its 2027 capacity online, it would sell out. There could be "the same type of dynamic" in 2028, supporting a positive longer-term demand outlook, he said, as companies race to secure access to computing power. When asked whether he sees the price per megawatt continuing to rise ahead of expectations, Boroditsky replied: "Yeah." Nebius is among a new wave of Neocloud companies that are investing billions to buy up Nvidia 's graphics processing units, build data centers and rent that capacity. Nebius ran an auction for computing capacity on Tuesday, which showed continued price rises, the revenue chief said. "We're seeing continued upward mobility in terms of the kind of price per megawatt," he told CNBC. Price per megawatt, a key measure among new cloud companies, shows how much a company can charge customers for a certain amount of computing capacity. Chase Lochmiller, CEO of Crusoe, an Nvidia-backed AI company that is building data centers, was also bullish on pricing, saying the company was seeing rising prices for GPUs, including older Nvidia chips. "We're seeing higher pricing today for A100s than we saw in 2020 or 2021. We're seeing higher pricing for H100s than what we saw when they were first deployed in 2023," Lochmiller said. "There's tremendous demand and a lot of it is because the underlying model capabilities have gotten so much more advanced that people are just creating so much more value out of the compute infrastructure." The comments come amid an investor debate over how quickly Nvidia's GPUs lose their economic value as more powerful chips enter the market. The ability to continue renting out older chips at attractive prices is crucial to AI infrastructure companies that need to recover their investments and generate profits, while spending billions on GPUs. Lochmiller's comments suggest that, at least for Crusoe, older generations of Nvidia chips are commanding higher rental prices than when they were first deployed, potentially strengthening the economics of its AI cloud business. Nebius stock rose on Wednesday after SpaceX reported revenue at its AI business jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion. SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said pricing is "currently tracking slightly above the high end of the $30 to $50 per watt range," underscoring the pricing power for those renting out compute capacity. Cloud providers CoreWeave, Iren , and Applied Digital also rose in premarket trading on Wednesday following Johnsen's comments. "I'm thrilled by SpaceX's results. It's confirming what we already know, which is that it's a very dynamic market and that supply continues to fall far behind demand," Boroditsky said.

events.title: Telehealth Giant Hims Wants to Test Every Dude for Low Testosterone
events.summary: Talk of testosterone deficiency is hard to escape these days, with podcasters and politicians obsessing over how to avoid a “low T” lifestyle. As the hormone’s cultural salience deepens, demand is growing. In a timely move, telehealth giant Hims just launched a testosterone replacement therapy service for cisgender men. The direct-to-consumer juggernaut will offer two types of injectable treatments, as well as an oral pill option that can be sent to patients after they take an at-home capillary blood test. Peter Stahl, a urologist and a senior vice president of men’s health at Hims, wants to “cast as wide a net, and get as many people tested, as possible.” Hims, which started out selling erectile dysfunction medications, has expanded into women’s health and grown from a startup to a publicly traded company serving 2.9 million customers since it launched in 2017. Offering testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, is both a new phase for the health platform and a doubling down on men’s health care. “When we first started, we didn't have the capabilities to take care of a complex condition like testosterone deficiency,” Stahl says. “We've finally grown up.” The company will compete with a wide array of online clinics offering testosterone therapy, many of which have cropped up in the past few years using turnkey telehealth services to launch quickly. Many of these services market the medication as a lifestyle enhancer or anti-aging solution. Stahl sees testosterone deficiency as a medical condition that’s “really underdiagnosed” and “really misunderstood.” Testosterone became a controlled substance following the 1990 Anabolic Steroids Control Act, and for decades, taking it has carried an association with muscle-obsessed gym rats. “That created a lot of stigma,” he says. Older research also showed that testosterone therapy came with cardiovascular risks, though more recent findings suggest those concerns were overestimated. Testosterone levels have become a MAGA fixation. This fall, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth announced a mandatory testosterone deficiency screening for most male troops in the US armed services. Texas Republicans have been hurling the phrase “low T” as a masculinity-questioning insult in a hotly contested Senate midterm race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico. A survey of 2,000 American men this summer commissioned by Hims indicates that they are increasingly willing to talk to one another about testosterone treatment, but the stigma persists around taking medication to address low levels. Because testosterone is a controlled substance, it can’t be dispensed like many other treatments popular with digital clinics. Unlike GLP-1s and estrogen-based hormone replacement therapy , which are now often prescribed by clinicians after patients simply fill out a quick questionnaire , TRT requires "synchronous" care. That means any would-be users have to have a video chat with a clinician before getting a prescription, and for ongoing monitoring. “It's important to remember that testosterone therapy can cause infertility, and you don't give it to someone trying to conceive,” says urologist Mohit Khera, the director of Baylor College of Medicine’s Laboratory for Andrology Research at McNair Medical Institute. Khera sees telehealth TRT services as promising ways to expand access to the medication, “as long as it’s monitored appropriately.” While laboratory testing can show whether testosterone levels are below thresholds set by groups like the American Urological Association to indicate potential issues, diagnoses aren’t made based on bloodwork alone. Instead, clinicians assess labs along with patients’ symptoms and medical history. Common symptoms of hypogonadism (the technical term for the diagnosis) include sexual dysfunction and muscle loss. Stahl calls it a “powerful biomarker” for understanding someone’s health. “Quite frankly, it’s underutilized,” he says, noting that men with low testosterone have a 35 percent increased risk in overall mortality. The test doesn’t require a standard blood draw. Instead, Hims will send patients a Tasso blood collection device, a round single-use wearable that sticks to the upper arm and punctures the skin with microneedles to collect a small sample. (It may sound suspiciously like Theranos , but Tasso devices have a solid track record .) From there, the patient sends the collection off to a lab that will conduct an analysis of a broad selection of 21 different biomarkers to assess health, including triglycerides and thyroid hormones as well as testosterone. Based on the results, a patient might be prescribed a compounded injectable testosterone, a commercially available injectable testosterone, an oral pill—or something else entirely, if their testosterone levels are not low. Stahl sees hormone testing as a way to persuade otherwise-reticent men to go see a doctor.

events.title: Heat pump tech is 170 years old — Pascal thinks it’s time for an update
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When the experimental results came back, they puzzled Adam Slavney and Jinyoung Seo. They had been testing a new class of materials for more efficient refrigerators, air conditioners, and heat pumps, a mission that the cooling appliance industry has been on for eons. The measurements for the materials that the team was testing shouldn’t have been different, but they were. “Why are these things different? What did we change?” Slavney told TechCrunch. “We had an inkling of it within three-ish months, but we didn’t have definitive proof for a year or two.” That proof is now underpinning Slavney’s startup, Pascal , where he’s co-founder and CEO and Seo is co-founder and CTO. The company recently raised $8.5 million in a follow-on to its seed round, co-led by Sazze Partners and LB Investment with participation from KDB Silicon Valley, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. A refrigerator or heat pump using Pascal’s material promises to be around 20% more efficient than existing models, he said. (Both heat pumps and refrigerators use the same basic technology.) The startup has signed a contract with a multinational beverage company for a pilot of the technology. “This whole funding round came together originally because we got a customer contract earlier than we were expecting to,” Slavney said. Pascal is on track to deliver its first prototype early next year, and it hopes to follow that with a batch of more polished refrigerators in 2028. Scientists have been searching for better refrigerants for almost as long as refrigerators have existed. More recently, they’ve been looking for compounds that don’t harm the atmosphere in one way or another. They exist, but they also need to be at least as effective as existing refrigerants. “We’ve been playing whack-a-mole with refrigerants for 35 years, 40 years,” Slavney said. Older gaseous refrigerants like Freon ate a hole in the ozone layer, while newer ones like R-134a are still extremely potent greenhouse gases. “It’s just a never-ending treadmill,” he said. One alternative that has attracted researchers’ attention is a class of materials known as solid-state refrigerants. Because they’re solid, they can’t escape to the atmosphere, eliminating the climate and ozone concerns that haunt modern refrigerants. Solid-state refrigerants promise to make refrigerators and heat pumps more efficient. They work similarly to traditional refrigerants, giving off heat when squeezed and absorbing it when that pressure is released. Before his serendipitous discovery, Slavney and his colleagues at Harvard University had been researching the materials. “We wanted to do some high-pressure measurements, and the instrument that we were using required us to use gas. So we used the gas and then we swapped to a different gas and we were like, why are these different?” Slavney said. After numerous additional experiments, the team realized they had discovered another path toward solid-state refrigeration. Rather than squeeze a solid block of material, Pascal’s heat pumps compress a gas — carbon dioxide — into a cartridge that contains a sponge-like material, which Slavney said is proprietary. As the carbon dioxide works its way into the porous material, the gas molecules inside the pores start bouncing off the walls. Those collisions transfer energy to the material, warming it up. A heat exchanger then exhausts some of that heat. Run it in reverse and the material absorbs energy from the heat exchanger and transfers it to the carbon dioxide molecules. In a Pascal refrigerator, two cartridges are running at any given time. One is absorbing heat from the inside of the refrigerator, transferring it to the carbon dioxide, while the other takes the heat from the carbon dioxide and transfers it to the outside air. Eventually, the cartridges become too hot and too cold, so the flow gets reversed. “The material is very robust,” Slavney said. “We’ve cycled it up to 300,000 times. It’s the equivalent of a year or so in operation.” The entire system moves heat more effectively than other solid-state refrigerants, which means that Pascal doesn’t have to operate at high pressures like other solid-state refrigerants might demand. “We’re using conventional systems to do it,” Slavney said. “That means we believe we can make it cheap, and that means we can make it widespread.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor.

events.title: I thought loneliness came from having too few friends. For me, it came from having too many.
events.summary: Focusing on a smaller circle of friends made me feel less lonely. Carrie Berk Despite having a lot of friends in college , I felt like I was surrounded by strangers. After a careful analysis, I discovered meaningful connections fulfilled me more than casual ones. I stopped spreading myself too thin and have since focused my time on a smaller circle of friends. My 21st birthday party was packed with a dozen faces I half-knew. They all smiled as I blew out the candles and made a wish, yet I felt as if I were surrounded by strangers. As I looked out into the crowd, I realized that most of my friendships were surface-level, rather than genuine connections. We talked about upcoming school assignments, trending TV shows, and our favorite restaurants , but I wanted more. What was supposed to be a celebration turned into a rude awakening: Did these people even know me at all? I've always been someone with many hobbies, which meant making friends across all walks of life. Although I'm lucky to have so many people in my corner, there came a point where it felt like I was collecting friendships like tokens rather than forming meaningful relationships. The realization set in: I had tons of friends, but somehow, I was lonely. I needed to learn how to distinguish casual friendships from meaningful ones I realized friendships with a strong emotional connection were the most fulfilling. Carrie Berk Even years after graduating from college, I couldn't shake the feeling that I'd been collecting the wrong type of friendships. I realized many of my relationships had been rooted in transactions or shared activities, which may explain why I was still feeling lonely. Upon reflection, I noticed that the most genuine friendships I had involved some emotional depth and connection. I only have two of these in my life — one who lives close by, and another who is across the country. Regardless of where they are, the empathy goes both ways — I share in their joys and sit with them through their struggles, and they do the same for me. We're not just shoulders for each other to cry on, but supportive pillars who help each other walk through life. These were the friendships that fulfilled me most, and I needed to make more room in my life for them. I used to be scared of sharing my feelings with friends, but I realized that it was the only way to strengthen my relationships. Carrie Berk In order to do this, I needed to figure out what was holding me back. I came to the conclusion that, when it comes to friends, I'd kept many people at a distance, afraid that opening up would make me seem like "too much" or leave me hurt again. I'd also been spreading myself too thin, trying to maintain too many relationships instead of investing in the ones that mattered most. For example, I felt like I rushed through dinners to mentally check a box that I was keeping up the relationship. Not only was that a waste of time, but it led to major emotional burnout . Now, I focus on a handful of friends with whom I can build a deeper bond. Even though I only have time to see a select few people, I make sure the few hours we spend together are packed with thoughtful, not superficial, conversations. Recently, I spent some time with a work colleague outside the office, and we discussed how fitness helped us during difficult points in our lives. We connected on something beyond our jobs, and for the first time in a long time, I felt less lonely. Once I stopped chasing a bigger circle and was more vulnerable, I felt less alone Investing more time and energy into my close friendships has been so rewarding. Carrie Berk At first, it was difficult to let go of my larger circle. There's nothing wrong with casual friendships , but they couldn't give me the depth I was craving. Instead, the friends I need are the ones who will hold me up at my worst and cheer me on at my best without expecting anything in return — and I never think twice about doing the same for them. These connections take more time and care to develop, but are well worth the wait. Once I started watering the friendships I truly valued, I noticed our moments together aren't rushed, and our connection is stronger now because of the care we put into each conversation. This year, I'm thinking about having a birthday dinner with two or three close friends rather than a larger celebration. Ironically, when I began filtering superficial relationships out of my life, I felt less lonely — and that's all I could have ever wished for. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Double blow to Healey as inflation rises to 3.5% and monthly deficit hits £24bn
events.summary: Consumer prices rise by more than expected while government’s debt interest payments surge to record high for September Inflation surged to 3.5% last month while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn, in a double dose of bad news for John Healey before next week’s budget. The Office for National Statistics said annual inflation rose from 3.1% in August , overshooting City forecasts of a rise in the consumer prices index (CPI) to 3.4%, as a result of the surging cost of fuel. Oil and gas prices have soared since the end of February, when the US and Israel launched their war on Iran , throttling the flow of fuel through the strait of Hormuz. Rising inflation has also contributed to higher government borrowing costs – the key factor behind the deterioration in the public finances since the spring statement in March. Official figures showed the government paid £10.9bn in debt interest last month: the highest September figure since records began, and only the eighth time the monthly number has been above £10bn. Payments on some government bonds rise in line with inflation. The ONS said higher inflation had added £4bn to debt interest costs in September alone. Total government debt is estimated to have hit £3tn for the first time – although as a share of the size of the economy it has fallen to 94%, from 95% a year ago. In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £97.8bn, the ONS said – £4.4bn lower than last year, but still £6bn higher than the independent Office for Budget Responsibility had expected. The twin pieces of bad news underline the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure. The ONS said a rise in the cost of motor fuels was the single largest factor pushing up inflation in September. The average price of petrol rose by 8.2p a litre from August compared with a fall of 0.2p in the same period last year. Diesel, which is often refined in the Middle East, rose by 10.7p a litre last month compared with a fall of 0.4p a litre in September 2025. Air fares, which are heavily affected by the price of fuel, dropped in September by much less than usual after the traditional summer peak. In better news for the chancellor, the cost of clothing fell slightly and food prices growth remained steady at 1.3% as competition among supermarkets offset increases in transport costs. Rising prices make it even more likely that the Bank of England will raise interest rates from their current 3.7% level when its monetary policy committee (MPC) meets next month. Rate setters are concerned that inflation will jump above 4% next year as the price of a wider range of goods increases in response to higher oil and gas prices. September’s reading commits the chancellor to raising most working-age welfare benefit payments from next April by more than expected. For instance, the 3.5% rise will uprate weekly child benefit by 95p, to £28 for the first child. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning It also means a bigger than forecast inflation-linked rise in business rates in England. The tax firm Ryan said this could raise more than £1bn in extra receipts for the Treasury and would be paid mostly by organisations in the hospitality, leisure, education, health, transport and utility sectors. September’s CPI reading came in lower than the 3.9% wage growth figure for the three months to July , meaning that the state pension will almost certainly rise by the latter figure under the formula that dictates the triple lock. Healey blamed the inflation rise on the war in the Gulf. “We know that price rises from conflicts in the Middle East and Europe are hitting Britain and countries worldwide,” he said, adding that his budget would “drive for growth in every postcode” to improve living standards. Charlotte O’Leary, an economist at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said the run of three months of rising annual inflation was likely to continue through the winter, even if there was some resolution to the conflict in the Middle East. “Higher fuel and transport costs will likely push up food prices, and January’s large price cap increase will land as household energy demand peaks. Given this, inflation could reach 4%, double the Bank of England’s target, by early 2027,” she said. Martin Beck, the chief economist at the consultancy WPI, said the higher than expected inflation rate meant it was almost inevitable that the MPC would raise interest rates when it met on 5 November, but he cautioned against persistent rises in the cost of borrowing. “Raising interest rates cannot produce more oil or gas, and further tightening risks weakening an already fragile economy,” he said.

events.title: French borrowing costs hit 24-year high as civil unrest and budget fears spook markets
events.summary: Yield on 10-year government bonds passes 5% amid failure to pass budget and fallout from violent street protests France’s borrowing costs have climbed above 5% for the first time in 24 years as political concerns and the government’s failure to agree a much-delayed budget spook the financial markets. With some civic buildings still smouldering from recent riots, a fresh bout of selling pushed up the yield – or interest rate – on bonds issued by the second largest economy in the eurozone. The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor ( Oat ) , issued by the French Treasury – rose more than 8 basis points to 5% in morning trading, before easing to 4.99%. The French government has yet to pass its budget for next year, while the country has been rocked by increasingly violent street protests in recent weeks. Protests that began in September with students calling for extra funds to deal with mould- and rat-infested schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes evolved into wider demonstrations about the rising cost of living. Initially calm protests have often been met with aggressive police tactics , sparking riots in many towns and cities. Stores such as Louis Vuitton have been hit by looting, while protesters set fire to the town hall in Limoges. No single party has had overall control of parliament since the French president, Emmanuel Macron, called a snap election in 2024 . The parliamentary gridlock has blocked his plans to increase the pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to reduce or redirect state spending. France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP. Forecasts for the deficit and debt show both increasing in the current financial year without remedial action. International lenders have become increasingly reticent about lending to Paris, accusing the government of becoming “fiscally incontinent”. Some have withdrawn from lending to France, notably Japanese fund managers, and those that remain have demanded a higher price for their loans, especially longer-period loans. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Matthew Ryan, the head of market strategy at the currency trading and payments platform Ebury, said French woes were also dragging down the value of the euro against other major currencies. “The euro continues to lag most major currencies as the political risk premium in France looks unlikely to fade any time soon,” he said. “It remains unclear whether the 2027 budget will clear parliament, and even if it does, it seems set to be so riddled with concessions to both the left and the right that the deficit problem is left insufficiently addressed.”

events.title: "I am giving you money!" Nvidia's CEO wants every country to build its own AI
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is crisscrossing Europe with a multibillion-dollar checkbook and a grand ambition: Make his company the indispensable backbone of the global AI economy. Why it matters: As fears of an AI bubble rattle Wall Street, Huang is working to spread the boom beyond the U.S. and China — courting governments, bankrolling startups and cultivating massive new markets for Nvidia's chips. The big picture: The godfather of AI is trying to single-handedly build a new market for Nvidia chips, betting that governments and institutions around the world will want their own, highly customized data centers running open models. If it works, it could shore up demand for Nvidia chips just as another big group of customers — neoclouds — appear financially shaky. Driving the news: Part showman, part salesman, Huang has spent the past week preaching the gospel of AI across Europe ahead of a keynote Wednesday at Nvidia's flagship conference in Berlin. In France, Huang announced investments in four startups and joked, whisky glass in hand , that he's "the biggest VC in Europe." President Emmanuel Macron welcomed him to Paris, while France's economy minister compared the AI revolution to the Gold Rush. In Britain, Huang channeled Oprah Winfrey while announcing stakes in five startups. "I am giving you money! And I am giving you money! And I am giving you money!" he shouted from the stage of a converted London church. In Sweden, Huang unveiled a supercomputer backed by the country's industrial elite, likening Nvidia's technology to a "time machine" capable of compressing years of scientific research into days. In Germany, Huang challenged Chancellor Friedrich Merz to loosen Europe's regulatory instincts. "There's nothing to regulate if the industry doesn't thrive," he warned Monday. "Give Germany a chance. Give this industry a chance." Zoom in: At the heart of Huang's global strategy is "sovereign AI" — the idea that every nation should build and control its own AI infrastructure, data and models, rather than depend on U.S. or Chinese tech giants. In addition to roughly $10 billion in investments in Europe, Nvidia is helping build national AI ecosystems across Saudi Arabia, South Korea, India, Malaysia and Africa. For Huang, the prize is a vast new class of customers, including entire countries that see AI infrastructure as an economic and national security imperative. Between the lines: Huang's global offensive comes at a precarious moment for the AI industry, with Wall Street increasingly questioning whether the technology's enormous promise can justify its astronomical costs. Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave and other "neocloud" providers have plunged, fueling fears that the companies borrowing billions to buy Nvidia's chips may struggle to pay their debts. Investors are also scrutinizing a circular flow of money in which Nvidia helps finance the very companies buying its products, raising questions about how much demand is self-sustaining. What to watch: Huang has emerged as the AI industry's chief cheerleader during periods of market turmoil, countering predictions of a bubble with assurances that demand is still accelerating. His Berlin keynote offers another chance to calm investors by arguing that the next wave of AI spending will come from governments treating the technology as a national necessity, not a speculative bet. The bottom line: Countries racing to secure their independence in the AI age may find themselves more reliant than ever on one American company.

events.title: UK cinemas report ‘bonkers’ demand for documentary You Can See Everything
events.summary: Tickets for film about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes said to be selling out after $15m opening weekend in the US It is the film everyone seems to be talking about, spawning memes and fuelling feverish online debate about its subject, the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Now, a month before Nathan Fielder’s documentary You Can See Everything reaches UK cinemas, tickets for screenings are already selling out after its remarkable $15m (£11.3m) opening weekend in the US. Clare Binns, the creative director of Picturehouse Cinemas, said the excitement was reminiscent of the response to Greta Gerwig’s Barbie, which became a global box-office phenomenon in 2023. “People are hungry in a way that we haven’t really seen since then,” she said. “And for it to be a three-hour documentary, it’s bonkers.” Tickets for the film, which opens in the UK on 20 November, went on sale at Picturehouse Central in London before its US opening, Binns said, and demand has prompted the chain to add extra screenings. At the Ritzy in Brixton, the first screen had almost sold out, leading the cinema to sell tickets for a showing at a second. “It’s fantastic, it proves again that there’s a different kind of audience coming to the cinema,” Binns said. “They came to see Backrooms, they came to see Obsession, they came to see NAZA . “There’s a real appetite for smart films that talk to an audience differently than the studios have talked to them before. With this documentary, you’ve got a story that has been mined to some extent with the Dropout and podcasts. But I think the fact that Nathan Fielder spent a month with Elizabeth Holmes is a huge draw. He’s a smart guy, and audiences want something they can relate to.” Cineworld has also reported strong demand. Stuart Crane, its international vice-president of content, said “the speed and scale of demand has been remarkable”. Initial screenings at Cineworld Leicester Square sold out after tickets went on sale at about 40 cinemas on Sunday. The chain has since added more screenings at Leicester Square and expanded bookings to a further 35 cinemas nationwide. Vue has reported similar excitement. Dean Cross, its senior screen content manager, said it was “seeing incredible buzz both within the industry and amongst cinemagoers”, and it was “particularly encouraging to see a documentary capturing the attention of younger audiences”. Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday The momentum for You Can See Everything has been building since it was unveiled at a secret screening at the Telluride film festival in Colorado in September, where audiences were required to surrender their phones. A teaser trailer released the same day quickly went viral, with Holmes herself joining the online conversation, responding to tweets about the film and its trailer. Co-directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the film has won widespread critical acclaim. The Guardian described it as “a modern masterpiece of deceit”, praising its unsettling exploration of Holmes and the blurred boundaries between documentary and performance. Its US opening was the biggest for a documentary in more than 20 years, with more than 2,000 screenings selling out at 855 cinemas. More than 70% of its opening-weekend audience was under 35. “People want to enjoy films in a cinema with other people,” Binns said. “The younger demographic want shared experiences. They want to talk about it with their friends, and you can’t do that when you’re sitting on your own watching a TV. “Cinema has been ruled out so many times. Covid, the rise of streamers. Everybody is aware cinema has to change, it has to offer customers something different. But never rule us out.”

events.title: House prices across capitals post steepest quarterly decline ever: Domain
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts House values drop in all capital cities for first time in 15 years, Domain says Australia's most valuable homes are falling the most in value. ( ABC News: Charlie Mclean ) House prices have fallen across every capital city for the first time in 15 years, Domain reports. Data shows Australia's most expensive homes have recorded the biggest drops this year, while lower-value homes have remained largely stable. Experts say rising interest rates and lower market confidence are driving the downturn. House prices have fallen 4.7 per cent, the steepest quarterly drop on record, according to new data from Domain. Prices dropped in every capital city in the September quarter, the first time in 15 years and only the second time on record. The real estate platform's data showed the sharpest decline was in Perth, where prices dropped 7.4 per cent. Combined capital city house prices fell to $1,226,566. Domain said markets that started the year in very different positions "are now moving in the same direction". Houses and units dropped in price for a second consecutive month. ( ABC News: Steve Keen ) Australia's biggest property markets, Sydney and Melbourne, recorded their largest quarterly house price drop in four years, falling 4.7 per cent and 3.3 per cent, respectively. Unit prices also fell 3.5 per cent, marking the second consecutive quarter both property types declined. It marked a clear shift in the housing cycle, according to Nicola Powell, Domain's chief residential economist. Nicola Powell says conditions have shifted to be more favourable for buyers. ( Supplied ) "What began as weakness concentrated in some cities has broadened considerably," Dr Powell said. "The balance of power has shifted towards buyers. "Homes are taking longer to sell, there is greater scope to negotiate, and sellers are having to be more realistic about price expectations." The cumulative impact of rising rates, lower affordability, and cost-of-living pressures has reduced demand, according to Gerard Burg of data firm Cotality. "It's been a demand-led downturn," Mr Burg said. Gerard Burg says the fall in prices has been driven by lower demand. ( ABC News: Darryl Torpy ) Australia's most valuable homes falling the most While all major markets across the country have joined the downturn, prices have not been dropping equally within cities. Australia's most valuable homes are dropping the most, while lower value homes were relatively stable in three months to September, according to property data firm Cotality. One place in Australia abolished stamp duty and boosted economic activity Tribunal quashes council's over-55s caravan park plans Queensland's plan for 1 million new homes leaves some feeling squeezed out The world is procrastinating about financial reform, but a reckoning is near In Sydney, the most valuable quartile of homes dropped more than twice as much as the least valuable quartile. Nationwide, lower-value homes have seen a much slower price drop, Cotality said. Prices grew in Darwin's lowest value quartile. The sharper downturn in more expensive properties reflects fewer buyers and higher borrowing costs, according to property economist Cameron Kusher. "They've typically seen larger increases in values over recent years and when you see that market slowdown, there's overall fewer buyers for those properties," he said. Cameron Kusher says fewer buyers and higher interest rates are pushing down the prices of more expensive properties. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) However, he said the ultra-top end of the market had remained largely stable. Mr Burg agreed, saying lower-priced homes remained affordable to more buyers. "The median house really appears kind of out of reach of the median income household across much of the country," he said. Prices were falling before federal budget The federal budget was a factor, but not the only factor, in house price falls, according to Mr Kusher. House prices peaked last year and had already begun to drop before the changes to investment taxes in May's federal budget, Mr Kusher and Mr Burg both noted. Mr Burg said prices were already falling in many capital cities, and three consecutive interest rate hikes had dampened market confidence. The real estate industry says new laws targeting agents underquoting a house price are well-intentioned but poorly designed. Auction activity, a common gauge of market confidence, has roughly halved from last year, with 1,423 auctions across capital cities last week, according to Cotality. "Confidence has really evaporated.

events.title: E-scooter hospitalisations more than triple since 2019
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts E-scooter and e-bike hospitalisations on the rise in Australia, report finds Topic: Transport Accidents and Incidents The report found boys aged between 12 and 15 had the largest increase in hospitalisations due to e-scooter falls. ( ABC News: Marcus Stinson ) A report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) has found e-scooter hospitalisations have more than tripled since 2019. There were 4,089 hospitalisations involving e-scooter in the 2024-25 compared to 1,291 in 2019-20. Two-thirds of those hospitalised in 2024-25 were male with largest increase in young boys aged between 12 and 15. Teenage boys riding e-scooters drove a sharp rise in hospitalisations over the last five years, according to a report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW). The number of boys aged 12 to 15 hospitalised following e-scooter falls saw a 15-fold increase between 2019/20 and 2024/25. Boys in that cohort were four times more likely than girls to end up in hospital because of an e-scooter fall. It also found hospitalisation rates increased for e-bike riders, but these data were harder to capture because of how these injuries were classified. The report found e-scooter-related deaths increased over the last decade from seven in 2014/15 to 20 in 2024/25; however, the proportion of deaths was stable. New codes introduced in July this year will help better differentiate between e-mobility devices such as e-scooters and e-bikes, the report said. AIHW spokesperson Jacqueline Rek said the improved data will help better understand the risks surrounding e-mobility devices. "Meaning these findings should not be interpreted as precise counts of injuries involving e-scooters or e-bikes alone," Ms Rek said. E-bikes and e-scooters are now mainstream, with almost 1 million privately owned by Queenslanders, according to University of Queensland research. When Barnaby Joyce was deputy prime minister and transport minister in 2021, his assistant minister Kevin Hogan made a quiet, but hugely significant change to the Road Vehicle Standards Act. Richard J Buning, who worked on the research, said improving safety was crucial given the growth. "Every single year over the last five years, the growth in e-mobility device purchases has risen by 30 per cent," he said. Dr Buning said unsafe devices such as over-powered e-bikes were among his chief concerns. Last year, the federal government introduced stronger e-bike import standards similar to those in the European Union (EU), limiting access to unsafe devices. "It's these unsafe, uncompliant, illegal devices that are creating much of the problems of people riding really fast on high-powered devices," Dr Buning said. "But the safe, compliant devices, they don't provide more power than just a normal typical average fit person can provide." Dr Buning highlighted Queensland as one jurisdiction in the country leading e-mobility device regulation. People riding e-bikes in the state must be 16 or older and hold a valid driver's licence, including a learner licence. Children aged between 12 and 17 (where 16- and 17-year-olds do not hold a driver's licence) will only be able to ride an e-bike or e-scooter with parental supervision. New laws for e-mobility devices in effect from today: what you need to know Laws for e-bike and e-scooter riders come into effect from July 1: we've unpacked the changes for you Dr Buning disagreed with licensing e-bikes but praised the state's e-bike assurance scheme, which followed EU regulations. It will mean from March 2027, all e-bikes in the state must have a compliance label to ride in public. "So stopping those things from being sold and making sure that the public knows if they buy one of these devices that are uncompliant, they cannot legally ride it on the road," he said. Dr Buning also suggested more targeted initiatives to better educate those who are riding unsafely, which was mostly younger people. "Because the vast majority of people that use e-bikes are actually much older, 70 per cent of e-mobility device users are over the age of 40. "That highly visible behaviour may be obscuring public perception of an overall quite inclusive and sustainable transport mode." events.title: How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written
events.summary: Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another editor from the project has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots. And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working? Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles? Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity. A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else. But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option. Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search? Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to. The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?” I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe. A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”
