events.title: GIC, Temasek rebut allegations of pressuring MSCI to downgrade Indonesia
events.summary: This was not the first time MSCI has warned that it would downgrade Indonesia. It previously warned in January that it could downgrade the country from emerging to frontier market. GIC and Temasek denied claims they pressured MSCI to downgrade Indonesia. GIC said it invests based on “company- and asset-level fundamentals”, while Temasek said the claims are “patently untrue”. MSCI is reviewing whether to reclassify Indonesia from an emerging market to standalone status. It says its decisions use “transparent and rules-based methodologies” and will decide by June 30, 2027. The warning has shaken Indonesian stocks, with the Jakarta Composite Index falling more than 14% before recovering 5%. IDX is tightening rules on concentrated share ownership to avoid exclusion from MSCI benchmarks. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC and investment company Temasek have rejected allegations that they or their staff pressured index provider MSCI to consider downgrading Indonesia’s stock market classification. This follows accusations on Oct 20 by former Indonesian trade minister Muhammad Lutfi that the two investors coerced MSCI to consider downgrading Indonesia. The former minister claimed that a downgrade could trigger market panic and create opportunities to acquire Indonesian equities at lower prices. A GIC spokesperson told The Straits Times: “Our investment decisions are not driven by index classifications or top-down views of a market, and instead by company- and asset-level fundamentals. “We have been invested in Indonesia for over 30 years across asset classes and will continue to invest where we find good, bottom-up, risk-adjusted opportunities.” Fock Wai Hoong, head of Asia-Pacific excluding China and India at Temasek Global Investments, said the allegations have “no basis and are patently untrue”. “No one from Temasek – neither the institution nor the individuals working for the institution – has ever reached out to MSCI in order to influence any decisions they have ever made around any exchange across the region. “Maybe I’ll leave it at that,” he said. Fock was responding to the media during the launch of the e-Conomy SEA 2026 report at Google’s office in Mapletree Business City on Oct 21. Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) president director Jeffrey Hendrik defended the independence of MSCI on Oct 20 following the allegations. “We have always believed, and continue to believe, that global index providers are independent,” he told reporters at the IDX building in Jakarta. MSCI, meanwhile, told ST that its index decisions follow transparent and rules-based methodologies. It is accepting market feedback until April 30, 2027, and will announce its decision by June 30. “MSCI will continue to monitor developments in the Indonesian market and engage with market participants and authorities,” it said, adding that it does not disclose investor feedback during an open consultation period. The controversy comes after a record two-day market sell-off following MSCI’s warning on Oct 15 of the possible removal of Indonesia from its global indexes. Among its concerns were shareholding opacity, insider trading and regulatory enforcement. Every year, MSCI reviews all global markets and determines whether they should be classified as developed, emerging, frontier or standalone, based on economic development, market size, liquidity and accessibility. The index provider has launched a consultation on whether to reclassify Indonesia from an emerging market to standalone status, a move which can be a big blow for the country as its stocks would be excluded from indexes used by investors. Any reclassification could have significant implications for Indonesian equities, including investment flows from funds that track MSCI indexes , which are widely used as benchmarks for tracking different global markets. The index provider’s move indicates that the concerns extend beyond market size or liquidity and relate to more fundamental issues involving the integrity and credibility of trading mechanisms, said Eastspring Investments, an asset management business of Prudential. Other standalone markets include Argentina, Lebanon and Zimbabwe. The Jakarta Composite Index fell more than 14% from Oct 16 to 19 following MSCI’s warning. However, the index recovered 5% on Oct 20, after IDX said the night before that it would expel companies with highly concentrated share ownership from its flagship index in its latest attempt to avoid ejection from MSCI’s global emerging markets benchmark. The announcement followed a virtual meeting between the exchange and MSCI officials. Such companies, which make up almost a fifth of the index’s combined market value, include Dian Swastatika Sentosa and Barito Renewables Energy – two of the biggest companies in the index by market value. The exchange did not say when the expulsions would take effect.

events.title: Europe Wants Data Centers. Its Climate Goals Are Getting in the Way
events.summary: Earlier this year, the German government laid out an ambitious plan : By 2030, it would double the scale of the country’s data center fleet, and quadruple the amount of compute available for running artificial intelligence models. The idea was to minimize Germany’s dependence on the United States for access to AI—a point of concern across Europe —and boost its faltering economy. However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy. As part of its broader climate commitments, the previous German administration voted through the Energy Efficiency Act in 2023. Among other things, it required all new data centers to recycle a portion of the waste heat generated by their computer equipment, ideally into nearby municipal heating systems. It seemed like a no-brainer, says Patrick Graichen, who served as a senior official at Germany’s Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy at the time, before resigning over cronyism allegations. “We need clean heat, and data centers are a source of clean heat,” Graichen tells WIRED. In June, a month before the rules were due to finally take effect, the German federal government walked them back . Data center firms had complained that the requirements made it almost impossible to build in the country; the German Data Center Association characterized an early version of the bill as a “ data center prevention act .” Under an amended bill, which will be put to the German parliament for ratification imminently, data center operators would no longer be obligated to reuse waste heat, only to scope out the possibility. Graichen and others have accused the German government of sacrificing climate targets for a chance to ride the AI wave. But countries across Europe find themselves pulled between these same two poles, under simultaneous pressure to cash in on rapid growth in the energy-intensive AI sector—and limit dependence on the US—and to protect the climate. The German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy did not respond to a request for comment. Among data center developers, the chief objection to the original Energy Efficiency Act was the chance it could land them in an impossible bind, obligated to reuse waste heat even when there was no available offtake—whether a municipal heating system or an industry, like greenhouse agriculture. “Some of the things they had to comply with were outside of their control,” says Barbara Smitten, associate director for critical systems at consulting firm Cundall. “It felt that [the burden] was all on the data center.” In the last 18 months, multiple data center proposals have fallen through in Germany: Stack Infrastructure canceled a $3 billion facility in Hesse, and state-owned Komm.ONE withdrew from a project in Baden-Württemberg. Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act. Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says. When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.” Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change. The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten. But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns.

events.title: US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors
events.summary: Can Iran's rail network offset expanding US sanctions? As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade. The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran , this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult. On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast. Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) . The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey. Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it. Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives. The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year. Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices? Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan. The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies. Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days. In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days. For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz . But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences. A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability. It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days. The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran. Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay. Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries. Rail works best for critical inputs Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade. "A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW. Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport. That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line. US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran? Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges. For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit. Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging. If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived. "Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said.

events.title: What’s brewing behind South Korea’s Mega Coffee deal rush?
events.summary: Mega MGC Coffee, South Korea’s largest coffee chain with 4,500 outlets, now harbours an appetite for a larger share of the retail landscape. Mega Coffee is using its strong cash flow and franchise network to chase bigger retail deals, moving beyond coffee into supermarkets and drinks. It lost the Homeplus Express bid to Harim Group, but is now shortlisted for Haitai HTB, a deal worth about 300 billion won, with enough cash likely available. Mega is also growing fast at home and abroad, while possible bids for Burger King and Tim Hortons remain uncertain because of weak fit and different business models. SEOUL – In South Korea’s food and beverage deal market these days, the most persistent bidder sells cheap coffee . Mega MGC Coffee, the country’s largest coffee chain with 4,500 bright-yellow storefronts, no longer seems content merely selling Americanos. It now harbours an appetite for a larger share of the retail landscape. “With a nationwide franchise logistics network and strong cash generation, Mega Coffee has emerged as a key strategic investor in F&B deals,” one industry official said. The hunt began in the spring with Homeplus Express, the supermarket unit carved out of embattled retailer Homeplus. MGC Global, Mega Coffee’s operator, made it to the main bidding round, but Harim Group, the parent of NS Shopping, ultimately won the deal in May. The coffee chain’s goal, industry officials say, was to become an everyday retail platform by adding supermarket retail to its cafes and to the food supply business of Boratr, a Kosdaq-listed sister company. MGC Global Chairman Kim Dae-young founded Boratr in 2000, built his fortune on it and used it to buy Mega Coffee in 2021. Homeplus Express’ stores, logistics and familiar name would have let Boratr sell its meals and fresh food directly to consumers, and its global sourcing network could have filled the shelves with imported goods. The chain might also have carried Mega-branded ready-to-drink beverages and private-label food. Undeterred, MGC Global has since turned its attention to Haitai HTB, the beverage unit LG Household & Health Care is selling, though it is keeping separate its Coca-Cola bottler. MGC Global and private equity firm Godo Partners have made the shortlist for a deal LG H&H hopes will fetch about 300 billion won (S$289.5 million), with a main bid looming but no date yet disclosed. Should it prevail, MGC Global is expected to draw on Haitai’s plants and logistics network to produce cup coffee and bottled drinks. Funding is unlikely to be the obstacle. Parent company Wooyoon, which holds 82.3% of MGC Global, had 195.1 billion won in cash and short-term financial instruments at the end of 2025. Boratr held another 150 billion won in cash and liquid financial assets in the first half. Together, the two Kim-controlled firms can tap at least 350 billion won, and analysts say acquisition financing could stretch that far enough for a sizeable deal. Meanwhile, Mega pursues growth with equal vigour. It opened its 4,500th outlet in October and has expanded abroad with stores in Mongolia and Cambodia. Japan is under review, and a US store is reportedly on the way. MGC Global’s revenue jumped 30.4% on-year to 646.9 billion won in 2025, with operating profit of 111.4 billion won. MGC Global has also lately surfaced as a potential suitor for BKR, the South Korean operator of Burger King and Tim Hortons, after sale advisers Deutsche Bank Securities and Lazard Korea floated the business to the coffee chain, according to investment banking sources. Affinity Equity Partners, which owns BKR, is even mulling a carve-out of Tim Hortons, which would spare Mega a clash with its core business, the sources added. For now, synergy between Mega and Burger King remains an open question, except for the likely prospect of Mega coffee at the burger chain. Sceptics argue that coffee shops and burger chains differ in operations and customer demand, and that most Burger King Korea stores are company-run, unlike Mega’s franchise model. “The Haitai HTB outcome, and the money it requires, will decide whether Mega joins the Burger King race,” another industry observer noted. events.title: Data centre gas plant could be mothballed after two years, court told
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Court hears gas power plant for Moss Vale data centre could be mothballed An artist's impression of one of three data centres planned for the Moss Vale site. ( Supplied: Cloud Carrier ) Nakar Property is appealing in court to build a $23 million gas power plant and battery storage system in the Southern Highlands. Its lawyers say the gas plant will be eventually replaced with cheaper energy supplied via the grid. Cross-examination of expert witnesses will continue for the hearing's third day on Thursday. A gas-fired power station proposed for the NSW Southern Highlands could be mothballed once the grid can meet the energy demands of an onsite data centre, a court has heard. The NSW Land and Environment Court is considering an appeal by developers Nakar Property, after Wingecarribee Shire Council refused its development application for a 16-megawatt power station and battery energy storage system in Moss Vale. The station is one of three planned to power a data centre campus on site proposed by Sydney company Cloud Carrier. Barrister James Smith, acting for Nakar Property, told the court the power plant was needed to provide constant power for customers using the centre. "[Cloud Carrier's] investment in computers is circa a $1 billion; the fundamental requirement is firm supply," Mr Smith said. "It's akin to enrolling your child in school without any teachers; Cloud Carrier can't sell any product unless there is firm supply." The proposed gas-fired power plant would be used to run Cloud Carrier's data centre campus. ( ABC Illawarra: Penny Burfitt ) The second day of hearings before Commissioner Nicola Targett came after the court travelled to Moss Vale to inspect the site of the $23 million project on Tuesday. In his opening submissions, Mr Smith said developers would stop using gas power as soon as a reliable supply of energy from the grid could be secured. "The cost savings per year via connecting to the grid is approximately $14 million per year," he said. "There is clear financial incentive to use the grid when that power becomes available. The issue is there is not sufficient supply." Referencing expert reports, Mr Smith said the power plant was projected to emit less greenhouse emissions than if it were powered by the grid until approximately 2029. Addressing Commissioner Targett, barrister Michael Staunton, for Wingecarribee Shire Council, said that power supplied by the grid had been touted as a "panacea" to the project, but not investigated thoroughly. "All of that work and investigation should have been done, and you'll find when you get to the documents, it hasn't been," Mr Staunton said. After an adjournment, Wingecarribee Shire Council tendered draft conditions of consent in the middle of the hearing. These included a new requirement that canopy trees be planted across approximately 40 per cent of the development site. Expert air-quality, electrical and engineering consultants appeared as witnesses for cross-examination about reports they had prepared for the project. Mr Staunton argued during cross-examination that the project would not have the secure power needed to fill the full capacity of servers in the proposed data centre for two years, when an upgrade of a nearby power substation operated by Endeavour Energy would be completed. "You've got no firm supply for two years," Mr Staunton said. "That time could be spent negotiating with Endeavour Energy while you wait for the permanent connection." The matter will return to court on Thursday for a third day of hearings. events.title: Singapore to update restructuring and insolvency framework to better serve economy, businesses
events.summary: Law Minister Edwin Tong speaking at the Singapore Insolvency Conference on Oct 21. The IRDA will be amended to make judicial management a clear rescue process. Applicants must show how it can save a business and why it is better than liquidation. Cross-class cramdown rules will be made easier to use. Voting thresholds will be refined, and shareholders may be bound in some cases, with safeguards to protect fairness. Singapore will adopt two more UNCITRAL model laws on group insolvency and insolvency-related judgments. This will improve cross-border cooperation and support its role as a restructuring hub. SINGAPORE – Forty years after judicial management was introduced in Singapore, the process has not always fulfilled its purpose of rescuing beleaguered but viable businesses and preserving their value. “Too often, it has become a precursor to liquidation, adding time and costs without necessarily achieving meaningful rehabilitation,” said Minister for Law Edwin Tong on Oct 21. “This is unacceptable,” he added, giving the keynote address at the Singapore Insolvency Conference organised by the Insolvency Practitioners Association of Singapore. His ministry will amend the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution Act 2018 (IRDA) to make it clear that judicial management is a rehabilitative process, with the first reading of the Bill in Parliament slated for later in 2026 or early 2027. In May, the Ministry of Law broadly accepted reform recommendations made in 2025 by the Committee to Enhance Singapore’s Corporate Restructuring and Insolvency Regime, after a public consultation. Tong stressed that premature liquidation can destroy value and that financial distress does not necessarily mean a business is no longer viable. “The company may well have a very sound underlying business and good assets, but an unsustainable debt burden or temporary liquidity difficulties. And in such a situation, premature liquidation or prolonged administration can destroy them,” said Tong, who is also Second Minister for Home Affairs. “In a mature economy like Singapore’s, business cycles, ups and downs will be inevitable. They will be recurring, and industries will go through periods of growth and decline. We need a stronger restructuring framework to allow businesses to recover and to absorb the shocks of that ebb and flow.” Under judicial management, control of a financially distressed company is temporarily placed under an independent, court-appointed judicial manager with the aim of keeping the company afloat, or to work out a debt restructuring plan. The company is protected against lawsuits by creditors during this period. The business typically shifts to liquidation and winding up if the creditors reject the proposed rescue plan by the judicial manager. As part of the amendments to the IRDA, applicants for judicial management must be able to explain how the process is expected to rehabilitate the company or its business, and the tangible benefits compared with winding up the company. A company, its directors or a creditor can apply to the court for a judicial management order. Should judicial management fail to rehabilitate the company and it proceeds to liquidation, the circumstances leading to this must be explained. The judicial manager will also typically not be allowed to transition into the company’s liquidator role. “Not every rescue will succeed, even when there were good prospects at the outset for a successful restructuring,” Tong said. “But it is really about making sure that the judicial management is pursued for the right reasons, with clear objectives and, importantly, in this case, accountability for the outcomes that are sought.” The second recommendation is to make cross-class cramdown to be more accessible and user-friendly. Cross-class cramdown allows the court to approve a restructuring plan even if there are dissenting classes of voting creditors. Such plans are typically structured to ensure a better overall outcome for stakeholders compared with other alternatives. In a cross-class cramdown in Singapore , a restructuring plan must be approved by at least one group of creditors who would be worse off or whose rights would be affected by the plan and who would receive some payment if the company were wound up. At least a majority in number and 75% in value of the creditors across the classes must vote to support the plan. At the conference, Tong noted that the cross-class cramdown mechanism has seen limited use since its introduction in 2017. In its report, the committee noted that the “overall numerosity and value cramdown conditions jointly constitute a high threshold, which deters the putting together of a plan that involves a cross-class cramdown”. Tong said voting thresholds will be refined under the reform, and cross-class cramdowns will be extended to shareholders in appropriate circumstances.

events.title: Polymarket removes contract allowing wagers on fate of Cornell students accused of sexual assault
events.summary: Polymarket has removed a contract from its prediction market platform that allowed users to wager on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting or exploiting a Cornell student in 2024 will be charged with a felony sex crime Polymarket has removed a contract from its prediction market platform that allowed users to wager on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting or exploiting a Cornell student in 2024 will be charged with a felony sex crime. The market was made available on Sept. 30 and was slated to close on Jan. 31. It had more than $450,000 in volume before it was taken off Polymarket's international platform. The company's U.S. exchange is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which bans trading related to “activity that is unlawful under Federal or State law.” “Our primary goal at Polymarket is to bring objective, data-driven insight to the most important questions of our time,” a Polymarket spokesperson said Tuesday. “This market addressed whether the government would take action — a process that deserves scrutiny, particularly in a case of such serious concern. That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market.” Front Office Sports was the first to report on the contract. Some outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has an endorsement deal with Polymarket, and he recently appeared in a star-studded commercial that also included cameos by Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Sue Bird and several celebrities. Messages were left by the AP on Tuesday with representatives for James, Jeter, Manning and Bird. Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour. Messages were left by the AP seeking comment from each organization. A spokesman for Spike Lee, who also appeared in the Polymarket commercial with James, said the director had no comment. Messages also were left with representatives for actors Craig Robinson, John Leguizamo and Alexandra Daddario — who were also part of the commercial with James. A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren’t involved. Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony DOJ official clashes with judge in DC golf course case after Trump attacks her Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Online critics characterized the Polymarket contract as degrading and questioned why celebrity ambassadors would associate themselves with the company. An online petition launched by UltraViolet, a women-led national advocacy organization, singled out James, Manning, Daddario and model Emily Ratajkowski while calling on other famous endorsers to cut ties with the company. A message was left seeking comment from a representative for Ratajkowski, who also appears in the celebrity-filled commercial with James. Prediction markets provide an opportunity to trade on the result of future events. Sports account for a major portion of the volume generated by the array of typically yes-or-no question, depending on the platform. When a U.S. Army sergeant was indicted earlier this year over bets on the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, he was trading on Polymarket’s international platform. The Associated Press reported in April that 50 brand new accounts on Polymarket’s international platform placed substantial bets on a U.S.-Iran ceasefire in the hours, even minutes, before President Donald Trump announced a ceasefire on social media, raising concerns of insider trading. Polymarket had an active market on its international platform on Tuesday that allowed customers to trade on whether Cornell president Michael Kotlikoff will be out by Oct. 31. events.title: A 2027 turning point? Goldman, Citi see stabilising signs in China’s housing market
events.summary: Encouraging holiday sales and shrinking supply point to recovery for country’s property sector, according to Goldman Sachs and Citi As China’s housing market downturn enters its fifth year, global investment banks including Goldman Sachs and Citi say they expect the sector to pivot as soon as 2027, with expectations fuelled by signs of shrinking supply and robust sales over the National Day holiday in early October. Citi holds a positive view on the sector and saw 2027 as a pivotal year for home price recovery in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. Home prices in China hit their lowest point in June 2024, according to Citi. Shanghai became the first city to post positive year-on-year growth in secondary home prices in September, with prices rising 0.8 per cent, according to the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday. “While we need further confirmation before declaring a sustained recovery, the evidence increasingly points to stabilising and potentially rising home prices in top cities, with most tier-two cities likely to lag,” said Griffin Chan, an analyst at Citi Research, in a report on Tuesday.

events.title: Lao Huo Tang’s parent firm given 4 more weeks to clear CPF arrears
events.summary: Soup Empire Holdings owes about $18,900 for May, June and July CPF contributions. SINGAPORE – Restaurant chain Lao Huo Tang’s parent company, Soup Empire Holdings, has been given four weeks to pay its remaining Central Provident Fund (CPF) arrears. A State Court heard that the company has paid off about $5,300 so far and has about $18,900 in outstanding CPF contributions for May, June and July. During an Oct 21 hearing, the company was given a four-week adjournment until the next hearing on Nov 11 to clear its CPF arrears. Soup Empire operates a portfolio of restaurant brands, including Eng’s Wantan Noodle and Kenny Rogers. This comes after two other companies linked to the Lao Huo Tang restaurant chain cleared their CPF arrears, with charges against them disposed of after the matters were compounded, a court heard on Oct 6.

events.title: UK approves long-awaited Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
events.summary: Britain on Wednesday approved the Jackdaw North Sea ​gasfield , ending years ​of legal and political wrangling that had ⁠pitted the Labour government's climate commitments against its push ⁠to bolster energy security. Energy Minister Miatta ​Fahnbulleh said the project will start to supply gas to British homes and businesses from as ⁠early as the end of this month. At the same time, she said a new Energy Wealth Fund would be established by the government with a £2 billion downpayment to reinvest oil and ⁠gas revenue into the climate transition. Ms Fahnbulleh said Jackdaw was expected to increase ​domestic gas ⁠production by about 6 per cent at ‌its peak and support the country's gas supply over its lifespan of up to ​11 years, boosting energy security and protecting hundreds of jobs. “At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help,” said Prime Minister Andy Burnham. “Even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.” Adura, the joint venture between energy giants Shell and Norway's Equinor that operates the project, has said Jackdaw will produce gas equivalent to up to 40,000 barrels of oil a day at peak output. Environmental groups could mount a fresh legal challenge to the approval. The issue ​has become a rallying point for climate activists, who say approving new fossil fuel projects undermines Labour's green pledges and ignores warnings from a summer of record-breaking heat across Europe. The fate of Jackdaw had been in ​limbo for years and has forced Mr Burnham to take sides in a battle over the future of the North Sea while risking alienating voters. The relatively small gas project has become a symbol of a bitter political fight over Britain’s energy transition. Approving Jackdaw risked a backlash from some on the left of the Labour Party and the Greens. Rejecting drilling in the field would have fuelled criticism from Reform UK, the Conservatives and the oil industry that climate policies are costing Britain jobs and investment. The previous Conservative government approved the project ‌in 2022, but climate activists challenged ⁠the decision in court alongside approval for ​the Rosebank oil and gasfield. A 2025 ruling barred operators from ​extracting oil ‌or gas until they received fresh government consent that takes into account emissions from the burning ⁠of the fields' hydrocarbons. The decision has taken on added significance for Mr Burnham since ⁠he took office in July. In its 2024 general election manifesto, the Labour Party pledged to block new drilling in the North Sea, but officials say decisions on Jackdaw and Rosebank – the largest undeveloped oil and gas reservoir in British waters – fall outside that commitment because they involve licences approved years ago under the previous government. “Jackdaw has been made into this big issue because it’s become a symbol of the wider North Sea debate,” said Jess Ralston, head of energy at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, an independent non-profit. “But even if the government approves it and Rosebank, the North Sea debate isn’t going to get any less flammable.” Even once drilling gets under way, few believe the UK could ever compete again with major oil and gas regions. Its stretch of the North Sea is 90 per cent depleted for commercial resources, according to consultant Wood Mackenzie. The international companies that pioneered drilling there 60 years ago have retreated.

events.title: Scaling CPO Testing Beyond A Single Die
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Fiber alignment is the main bottleneck to optical engine testing, which would be alleviated significantly by multi-site probe cards. Optical connectors must be optimized for the best optical properties yet be mechanically robust to withstand assembly and use. Simultaneous loopback on both optical and electrical sides could simplify testing. Experts At The Table : The industry is forging a path from single-site to multi-site testing while system architectures and connector types continue to evolve. Semiconductor Engineering sat down with Matt Griffin, senior product manager for optoelectronics test at Teradyne ; Ira Leventhal, vice president of research and venture at Advantest America ; Dave Armstrong, fellow at ISE Labs, a subsidiary of ASE Group ; and Kazuo Yamaguchi, silicon photonics researcher and engineer at Keysight Technologies . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one, click here . Fig. 1: (L-R): Teradyne’s Griffin; Keysight’s Yamaguchi; ISE Labs’ Armstrong; Advantest’s Leventhal. SE: Is it true that you can only test one die at a time today? Armstrong: I would hope some insertions will go away over time, but right now there are more things being added than being subtracted. It’s a hard one. In terms of testing one die, that depends on the die. If an 8 kW GPU is your main ASIC, and you have multiple connectors around multiple sides of the part from a tester resource standpoint, and the amount of power a tester can deliver and take out of the part, it’s pretty challenging to get beyond one die. But if you look down the NPO-versus-CPO path, NPO is typically a single connector device. You’re going to have to be able to go to multi-site to scale that to high volume. Insertions two and three are the fertile ground for multi-site. Those are longer more complex test insertions. PIC wafer testing tends to be single-site today. From my experience, there is some hope on the horizon to bring it up a little bit higher with some capabilities in the probe card area, notably from Technoprobe. Griffin: I agree with Dave. Most production solutions today are single-site, and when you talk about the optical engine, the main bottleneck is fiber alignment. Many companies are working on multi-site solutions, and I hope they succeed and take off because that only helps the whole industry ramp faster. But we’ve got a little bit longer to go there. SE: For these alignment ports, can you repeatedly test at that site? Griffin: Ideally, you’re able to repeatedly test almost infinitely because you should never be contacting the device with the optical probe or the fiber array unit (FAU). When you’re bringing up a new test solution, you do sometimes crash FAUs on first systems. In reality, the bigger concern is contamination on the FAU, so cleaning is needed. On the connector side, at the module level or for optical engines with receptacles attached, the optical connector lifecycle is where we need more effort, because the device-side connector is designed to be attached once and, hopefully, never disconnected. And every new connector generation changes both the connector recipe and the automation recipe. Leventhal: In a sense, this is nothing new. For instance, with BGAs, if you socket at the device too many times, then you start worrying about damaging the balls on the BGA. It’s a similar problem and the industry will gravitate toward connector designs that are more robust. Matt made a really important point about how your test side connector needs to be some sort of a hardened connector that doesn’t wear out easily after 20 to 50 insertions. It needs to last for tens of thousands or 100,000 insertions. So you’ve got to go to a hardened metal, and then you’ve got a hardened metal going against the receptacle on the device, which is not going to be that hardened metal. If you’re not careful, you could damage that connector sooner than the spec lifetime. So as the industry evolves to the winning connector designs, robustness on the device side is going to be a really important part of that. SE: What are the challenges with making simultaneous electrical and optical connections? Armstrong: It’s just a question of time. Yamaguchi: Beyond DC and optical probing, the harder part of simultaneous electrical and optical connection is characterizing electro-optic devices in RF. Modulator and photodetector performance is ultimately validated through S-parameters, so you need optical and high-frequency RF contact at the same time. Probe cards can only fit a limited number of RF lines, and their bandwidth is also limited, while today’s devices are characterized beyond 200 GHz. At wafer and die insertions, simultaneous connection is really an RF probing challenge. Leventhal: Warpage is going to create additional challenges on top of just trying to solve the problem in an ideal case. You need to be able to align in multiple axes. And the BGA has a crazy amount of pins that you have to make reliable contact with, so that problem is getting more challenging. Adding to that is being able to do the right level of alignment, either coming from the top or coming from the side. It’s significantly challenging. I agree with Dave, it’s a question of time in multiple senses. Each insertion takes time, although there are ways of minimizing that by integrating certain operations together. But also, it’s going to take time for all of this to mature to the point that it’s going to be easier to test at scale. Griffin: At its core, there’s an optical and an electrical interface to the device at every insertion, and sometimes those interfaces are on the top side of the device, sometimes the bottom side, and sometimes both. And then when you talk about module level, they’re on two to four sides of the package across some number of optical engines. So if you look at optical alignment on its own, it’s not that big of a challenge. But when you start combining it with all the different, I’ll say, flavors of architecture that we’re seeing, and trying to design a scalable test system that can handle as many of those flavors as possible for your customers, that’s really where some of the fun challenges are. Armstrong: I also chair the IPSR test roadmap for photonics, and in our latest report we highlight a test methodology for AC testing. AC testing, bit error rate testing, will be one of the bigger time sinks. If we had good DFT, we could just do loopback on the optical side and loopback on the electrical side at the same time. And technically, there’s no reason you couldn’t combine those two tests. But today, most people are saying, “Okay, I’ll do loopback on one side or the other side, and a bit error rate test of some nature on the other side, so that becomes a very expensive setup that doubles the effective test time. Photonic integrated circuit (PIC) performance is increasingly bounded by fabrication realities such as sidewall angle, critical-dimension bias, thickness variation, and line-edge roughness, which idealized, as-drawn FDTD simulations fail to capture. Here, we show a Fab Technology Co-Optimization (FTCO) workflow that connects GDS layout import, three-dimensional process simulation, GPU-accelerated FDTD, design of experiments (DOE), with AI-based surrogate modeling. We show that when manufacturing variations are included in the modeling that the simulation results align well with experimentally reported results. A directional-coupler DOE with 25 unique combinations of 4 different process variations requiring a 65-million-cell 3D FDTD model and completes in under 10 hours on a single NVIDIA A100-equipped workstation is showcased. The generated digital twin provides intuitive and real-time access to the process-to-performance relationship for non-simulation experts: A game-changer in the industry. Achieving the requisite target yield as early as possible during silicon ramp is a lead indicator of product success. Delays in reaching yield entitlement can impact time-to-market, increase manufacturing costs, and reduce overall product competitiveness—particularly at advanced nodes where complexity and cost continue to rise. As a result, incorporating a solution that can rapidly identify and resolve systematic yield limiters has become essential to enabling efficient ramp to high-volume production. Such a solution requires analytics-driven volume diagnostic and failure analysis capabilities to reverse engineer test failures captured on automatic test equipment (ATE). These capabilities identify the precise failing location within the chip, rank failure candidates based on yield impact, and provide the highest-priority candidates to the failure analysis lab for final root-cause confirmation. Corrective action can then be performed on either the design or the silicon process to correct and improve the yield of your chip and ultimately enable you to go to high volume production and into the market ahead of the competition. events.title: UN projections say world is losing ground in fight to curb climate change
events.summary: Humanity is losing more ground in its fight against climate change WASHINGTON -- Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says. If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday's update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That's about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year's projections by the same science team. “This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas. “In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report. The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries' climate fighting plans. He wasn't part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound. The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year's projection. Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact . The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees. The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.” Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen. “The report's message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn't part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.” Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world," said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. “An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous.

events.title: What a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would mean
events.summary: Elon Musk believes a merger between Tesla and SpaceX is a good idea, he said on Tuesday, publicly backing an idea that would create ​one ​of the most valuable companies in the ​world, worth about $3.5 trillion. While electric-vehicle maker Tesla and rocket company ⁠SpaceX were once seen as largely separate businesses, the lines between them have blurred as ⁠Mr Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing , satellite communications and computing infrastructure, ​including data centres on Earth and potentially in orbit. Here's what a potential merger could mean: Why merge the companies? A merger would create a ⁠single company at the centre of Mr Musk's long-term vision: an integrated technology and manufacturing empire spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications, and transportation on Earth and beyond. “I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained ⁠from co-operating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation (of orbital data centres), connectivity,” Mr Musk said on Tuesday. Bringing ​the companies ⁠together could also simplify decision-making. Many of Mr Musk's projects ‌already cut across multiple companies, requiring approvals from separate boards and shareholders. A combined company would give management more freedom to deploy capital, engineering ​talent and infrastructure where it sees the greatest opportunity. Mr Musk has long argued that he needs greater influence over Tesla to pursue its AI and robotics strategy. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and holds voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate his influence. What does it mean for investors? Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX's rapidly growing Starlink broadband operation, launch services business and future space ventures. SpaceX investors would gain ownership of Tesla's vehicle, energy storage, autonomous driving and robotics businesses. A merged company could also become one of the world's most valuable corporations, with a market value of about $3.5 trillion, combining leadership positions in cars, robotics, satellite communications, launch services, energy storage and AI infrastructure. Supporters would likely argue that the combined company could allocate capital more efficiently across businesses that are increasingly interdependent. Critics, however, argue that investors would be assuming exposure to a much broader range of technical, regulatory and execution risks, some of which have little connection to one another. Where could SpaceX and Tesla work together? Starlink satellites could provide communications links for Tesla's robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of Optimus humanoid robots. Tesla's battery and energy-storage products could help support SpaceX's growing power needs, including future ​data-centre projects. Mr Musk has already announced one major Tesla-SpaceX collaboration, Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project aimed at producing ‌the advanced chips needed for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and ⁠Optimus robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-centre ambitions. Mr Musk ​hopes it can start volume production by late 2028. Tesla's expertise in large-scale factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialise Starship production, ​while SpaceX technologies ‌have already appeared in Tesla products, most notably the planned use of rocket-derived components in the next-generation Roadster. A merged company could also co-ordinate efforts to secure strategic ⁠supply chains, leveraging Tesla's scale in batteries, semiconductors and manufacturing equipment alongside SpaceX's demand for specialised metals, electronics, propulsion components and satellite ⁠hardware. What are the key risks? The biggest challenges may be geopolitics and regulation. SpaceX is a major contractor for the US military, intelligence agencies and Nasa. Tesla, meanwhile, remains deeply tied to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in vehicle production and sales. That combination could invite heightened scrutiny from US regulators and national-security officials as well as from Beijing. The merger would also face shareholder and governance hurdles. Investors ​would need to be persuaded that combining two already complex businesses creates more value than keeping them separate. Questions about conflicts of interest, voting control and capital allocation would inevitably follow. Then there is execution risk. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centres, mobile communications and orbital infrastructure are all expensive, technically challenging bets. Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not reduce those risks. It would simply place them under one roof.

events.title: Plans for commercial helium production on Yorke Peninsula
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Commercial helium production planned for the Yorke Peninsula Neil McDonald (left) during a proof-of-concept exercise with extracted helium. ( ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly ) Gold Hydrogen has announced plans for commercial helium production at its Yorke Peninsula site. It will be the first time helium is produced in Australia since 2023. The plant is expected to be up and running within 18 months. Australia's only commercial helium production is expected to begin on the Yorke Peninsula within 18 months, aiming to address a global shortage of the rare and vital gas. Three months after it first extracted the gas at its Ramsay 1 site just outside Port Vincent, Gold Hydrogen has announced plans to turn the project commercial. It would be the first helium production in Australia in three years. While additional testing and approvals are required before a commercial plant can begin, managing director Neil McDonald said he was feeling positive. "Based on the robust numbers, not of just having the world's best helium purities ever reported, but all our geology and all the economics, we're very confident." The drilling process involves an almost 900-metre-deep hole in the ground. ( ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly ) As part of commercialisation, a modular helium plant "the size of two tennis courts" will be constructed on the company's 75,000-square-kilometre Yorke Peninsula tenement, creating additional jobs. "As we progress with working out the feasibility ... we'll be able to then isolate what type of specialty jobs and ongoing normal jobs would be available," Mr McDonald said. "But it will be reasonably significant for the size of York Peninsula." Helium has not been produced in Australia since Santos's Darwin LNG plant exhausted its supply in 2023 , and at the time there was little concern about supply constraints. But a global shortage has developed after about a third of the world's helium supply was taken out by Iranian missile strikes on Qatar's Ras Laffan gas plant in March. Mr McDonald said he believed there was enough helium at the Yorke Peninsula site for "tens of years" of domestic and international supply. Gold Hydrogen's Ramsay 1 site, just outside Port Vincent, has produced helium gas. ( ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly ) There is an estimated 41 billion cubic feet (BCF) of the gas in total at just one of the company's seven permits. "To give that context, the world consumes approximately 5BCF of helium per year," Mr McDonald said. Mr McDonald said local and international markets were interested. "Our initial plan is to scale up and make sure that we can supply initially the domestic market and get as much supply into the domestic market as we can," he said. "But like all commodities ... quite often Australia produces a lot more than they can ever consume." events.title: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
events.summary: Published 21 October 2026, 05:13 BST Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together . Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes." The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed. With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever. Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together. "In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group. The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said. Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects. Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations. The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers. Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year. Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car? But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions. Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors. He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said. But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added. "There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said. SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%. Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine. In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said. Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models . Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus. Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3 Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said. "The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added. The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights. The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January. The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year. The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider. A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said. "The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said. However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said. The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month. "I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said. The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

events.title: Samsung, SK Hynix upgrading China plants to make more advanced chips: Sources
events.summary: Both companies are now required to seek US licences annually if they want to install US-made equipment such as etching machines in China. Samsung and SK Hynix are upgrading China plants to make more advanced NAND chips. They want to meet AI demand and compete with China’s YMTC, but US export controls make the work difficult. Samsung’s Xian site may switch to 286-layer V9 NAND, with output targets of 5,000 wafers a month in December 2026 and 40,000 by December 2027. Samsung says the plan follows US rules and does not add capacity. SK Hynix aims to make 240-layer-plus NAND at Dalian and may seek approval for 300-plus-layer research. YMTC has grown fast, reaching 38.5% of China’s NAND market in the second quarter, while Samsung and SK Hynix have lost share. SEOUL/BEIJING/NEW YORK – Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are upgrading their China factories to produce more advanced memory chips, four people familiar with the plans said, aiming to fend off competition from a fast-growing Chinese rival and meet huge AI demand. How much to invest in their Chinese operations has become a tricky question for the South Korean semiconductor giants ever since the US began imposing export controls on some chip-making equipment in 2022 amid an effort to slow China’s technological progress. The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security also said in 2025 it did not intend to grant licences to upgrade technology and expand capacity at the foreign chipmakers’ factories in China. The regulatory headaches have limited their ability to refit their factories and contributed to loss of market share to Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC). Executives at the South Korean chipmakers have publicly warned that geopolitical tensions are undermining their Chinese operations. Samsung and SK Hynix confirmed in statements to Reuters that upgrades were underway and were being done in close consultation with Washington, but did not disclose details of production plans that are being reported here for the first time. Reuters could not, however, determine to what extent US authorities have granted export licences for equipment that Samsung and SK Hynix need for their planned upgrades. According to the sources, the two companies are working to manufacture flash NAND memory chips with more than 200 layers at their Chinese plants, which would bring them in line with what is being produced in South Korea. NAND, a type of memory chip that retains data without power, is widely used in smartphones, PCs and solid-state drives for AI data centres. More layers per chip means more storage density and lower costs. Samsung sets signs on 286-layer chips Samsung’s plant in Xian in north-western China, which accounts for about 40% of the company’s global NAND output, currently makes chips that have about 200 layers, according to two of the people. As part of a project known internally as “Monami” – from the French for “my friend” – Samsung is converting the facility to make 286-layer V9 NAND chips, aiming for monthly output of 5,000 wafers in December 2026 and then a jump to 40,000 wafers by December 2027, one of the people said. Samsung said its upgrade was in compliance with US export regulations, adding: “The upgrade is aimed at meeting growing demand from global customers, including those in the US. The company is not expanding production capacity or constructing new manufacturing facilities.” SK Hynix is looking to switch to producing NAND products with 240 layers or more at its Dalian facilities in north-eastern China, three people familiar with the matter said. It currently makes products with 192 layers there, one person said. SK Hynix acquired the Dalian site when it bought Intel’s NAND operations in 2021 and it remains the sole NAND chip manufacturing site for that business, which is now named Solidigm and is preparing for a US initial public offering. One of the sources said the company is authorised to make chips with up to 240 layers at Dalian and may seek permission from Washington to conduct research and development on 300-plus-layer chips there that would help it lay the groundwork for potential production in the US. The company is in discussions with the Trump administration over plans to build a new NAND factory in the United States. The US government’s Bureau of Industry and Security did not directly address Reuters questions on the status of approvals for the South Korean chipmakers. It referred Reuters to its 2025 statement that the bureau intended to grant licence applications for them to operate their existing factories in China, but not expand capacity or upgrade technology. As Samsung and SK Hynix have wrestled with the question of how much to invest in their Chinese plants, YMTC has made great strides. It commanded 38.5% of China’s NAND market in the second quarter, up from 28% for all of 2025 and overtaking Samsung, according to research firm Omdia.

events.title: Singapore sets aside $45m to help advanced manufacturing SMEs use AI solutions
events.summary: Minister of State for Energy, Trade and Industry Gan Siow Huang speaks at the Industrial Transformation Asia-Pacific event on Oct 21. Singapore has set aside more than $45 million over three years to help advanced manufacturing SMEs use AI. The Catalytic AI Solutions initiative will offer ready-to-deploy tools for design, scheduling and predictive maintenance. Enterprise Singapore will co-fund adoption of AI solutions for eligible SMEs, and is working to extend the initiative to the logistics and wholesale trade sectors. SINGAPORE – More than $45 million has been set aside over the next three years to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the advanced manufacturing industry deploy artificial intelligence solutions. This is one of the initiatives under Singapore’s national AI strategy that were announced by Minister of State for Energy, Trade and Industry Gan Siow Huang on Oct 21. Gan said the Catalytic AI Solutions initiative will make the technology more accessible to SMEs, and support them in overcoming common barriers when adopting AI. “We want AI to be accessible not just to large manufacturers, but also to our SMEs,” she said at the Industrial Transformation Asia-Pacific (ITAP) event at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre. “Through this initiative, manufacturers can access ready-to-deploy AI solutions to improve productivity, optimise efficiency and strengthen their competitiveness,” she added. Under the initiative, Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) will work with trade associations and chambers and qualified vendors to offer a suite of solutions to SMEs, with some firms having already confirmed their interest. The solutions will enable tasks such as the optimisation of product and component design, and the enhancement of production scheduling and predictive maintenance. EnterpriseSG’s assistant managing director for manufacturing Wong Zeng Yi said: “AI is creating new possibilities for manufacturers to improve productivity, quality and responsiveness, while opening new revenue opportunities through faster innovation. “We want to help more manufacturers embed AI into their core operations, so they can realise these gains at scale.” Eligible SMEs will have their adoption of AI solutions co-funded by EnterpriseSG, which plans to extend the initiative to the logistics and wholesale trade sectors. Another initiative announced at ITAP was a manufacturing jobs portal developed by the Singapore Manufacturing Federation. Gan encouraged prospective employers and job seekers to sign up for the Manufacturing and Talent Connection Hub, which is expected to be operational later in 2026 . The manufacturing industry accounts for around 20% of Singapore’s gross domestic product, and employs about 12% of its workforce. Industrial transformation has never been more important, Gan said, as manufacturers are operating in a more complex environment, with tight labour markets, intensifying competition for investments, and supply chains that are being reshaped by geopolitics. Companies must also become more sustainable while remaining competitive, she added. Gan said: “Advanced technologies such as robotics, digital twins and AI can help our manufacturers raise productivity, strengthen competitiveness, and bring about skilled roles for our workforce. “If we move decisively, Singapore can strengthen our position as a critical global node for advanced manufacturing, where companies develop new technologies and engineering capabilities, deploy them at scale, and contribute to global manufacturing.” A set of national AI missions, namely in advanced manufacturing, connectivity, finance and healthcare, was announced by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong earlier at Budget 2026. This came alongside the creation of a National AI Council, chaired by PM Wong, to help Singapore harness AI as a strategic advantage. The advanced manufacturing mission aims to reimagine the industry to grow its output and productivity. This involves advancing product and process innovation, anchoring best-in-class factories in Singapore, and building a base of industrial AI companies that develop AI solutions locally and export them to the rest of the world. Gan said the AI Centre of Excellence for Manufacturing, jointly established by A*STAR and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry in September 2024 , has been an important enabler of this mission. Companies including drinks producer Coca-Cola and tech manufacturer Philips had signed on to collaborate with the centre at its launch. In all, Gan said the centre has collaborated with 30 manufacturers in sectors including aerospace, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and energy, ranging from local firm Sunningdale Tech to the multinational Rockwell Automation. It has also completed 23 projects that deployed AI solutions to companies.
