events.title: How might Andy Burnham tackle Thames Water debacle?
events.summary: A look at some of the options after PM is urged to consider radical alternatives to deal with stricken company Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company. Here are some ideas the prime minister is being urged to consider. Burnham must introduce emergency legislation immediately to protect the supply of water for the public, said Richard Murphy, tax accountant and the brains behind Corbynomics. A new state-owned company, with a management team in waiting and all the necessary steps ready to take over the existing company’s systems, has to be put in place now. “A prime minister who cannot deliver water to maybe a quarter of the UK’s population would not be someone to be trusted with anything else. Andy Burnham has no choice but to address this matter, now,” said Murphy. The 1971 nationalisation of the Rolls-Royce aeronautical engineering company, to protect the national interest after it collapsed into receivership, could be used as a blue print. A similar national emergency exists now to protect the supply of water, Murphy said. Murphy said that, in essence, Thames Water was financially insolvent, with real doubt about whether it could survive into 2027. It was failing in its regulatory obligations, including to maintain clean water supplies and keep rivers and beaches clean. Use Emergency legislation should ensure that the nationalisation is of the assets and undertakings of Thames Water, and not of the company itself. All financial liabilities of Thames Water would be left for the old company to settle. The government should not acquire them. The new company needed to be structured within days, said Murphy. “There is no time to wait.” Public control – probably via the courts Burnham must be prepared to go to court to take Thames Water back into public control, said Ewan McGaughey, professor of law at King’s College London. Moody’s has estimated a one-off cost of £14.5bn in 2019 to bring water into public ownership. But privatisation, said McGaughey, would cost up to £22bn extra for bill payers from 2025 to 2030, or £176 a household a year, in returns on capital to shareholders and banks, as set by Ofwat’s price review. McGaughey believes that this year public ownership of failed water companies will cost closer to £0, using the special administration procedure within the 1991 Water Industry Act. The higher the repair bills, the less that creditors or shareholders deserve under UK law, international law and our investment treaties, he said. He advises Burnham to prepare to go to court – creditors will probably sue – but they have no reasonable prospect of success. McGaughey says privatised water and the regulators have failed so badly that England pays among the highest bills in Europe, while nearly every river is illegally polluted, taps run dry and a trillion litres of water is leaked each year. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters The government should bring our accounting practice up to international and European standards, by separating public corporation borrowing from the national debt, so that the borrowing of a publicly owned company does not contribute to national debt. Continuing the theme of using the special administrative powers of the 1991 legislation, Cat Hobbs of We Own It wants Thames Water’s licence taken away immediately. Hobbs has written to the government and water regulator, Ofwat, calling for bill rises to be blocked and for Thames Water to be brought into public hands. “It is absurd that Thames Water is now asking its creditors for a further £2.4bn to stay afloat – this saga has dragged out since July 2024 when the company was first in breach of its licence conditions,” said Hobbs. Under the 1991 act, companies can have their licences removed if they are insolvent or if they fail to fulfil their statutory duties to provide water, protect the environment and properly manage wastewater. Hobbs told Burnham his government should be using this power and facing down threats from the water industry and the prospect of a legal challenge from special administration under the 1991 act. Public ownership of water would deliver savings of £3bn to £5bn a year over time from cheaper financing costs – no shareholder dividends, less expensive debt. Taking water into public ownership would reduce the cost of living burden as well as freeing up money for infrastructure. The government should make it possible for new publicly owned water companies to borrow to invest on their own account – rather than adding to the national debt – as is standard practice elsewhere in Europe. Hobbs pointed out that when Network Rail’s debt of £31bn was transferred to the public sector, bond yields fell from 3% a year to 2.2% a year.

events.title: ‘I can charge my car for £6’: could new rules cut costs for EV drivers?
events.summary: Owners in England with no driveway can now slash their costs by installing a cross-pavement gully – but it’s a postcode lottery W hen Alison Williams bought her electric Volkswagen ID.3 two years ago, she thought she was making the right choice for the environment, having already upgraded her end-of-terrace London home with insulation and solar panels. However, charging the car has proved more costly than she hoped, as she is not able to install the cross-pavement gully – a narrow electric vehicle cable channel embedded in the pavement – that she would need to charge at home. That will remain the case despite a change in the law. From Wednesday, drivers in England who do not have off-street parking will no longer need to get planning permission to put in a pavement gully outside their home. The gullies sit flush within the pavement and allow an EV charging cable to reach a parked vehicle without creating a trip hazard. By charging in front of their house via an energy supply in their home, rather than using a public charger, drivers can slash the cost by up to 90% . But some of the 9.3 million households without off-street parking will be left frustrated as more than 20 local authorities will still not allow the installation of gullies after the law changes. Williams’s council is Ealing, which does not allow them for cost and safety reasons. She charges her car at a public charger, at much greater cost than if she could do it at home. “It’s really frustrating,” Williams says. “When we decided to buy an electric car … the reason we wanted to buy one was for the environmental impact. “You either have to have enough money to have a house with a driveway, or you have to be able to afford the additional cost of charging at a public charger.” Motorists are not allowed to string EV charging cables across the pavement from their home to the road, but many councils allow cross-pavement charging if you use a gully. To use one, a charging cable is run from the home through the gully and then plugged into the car. This previously meant getting planning permission from the local authority. Removing that step will save drivers between £300 and £500. However, anyone who lives in a conservation area will still have to apply. Caroline Pidgeon, a Liberal Democrat peer, campaigned for the change in the law. She says one in three households in England do not have a driveway. Approval for the gullies has taken up to 15 months in some areas, she says. “Simpler rules will make it easier for people to switch to an electric car,” she adds. The government has given £25m in funding to councils in England for pavement gullies for people with on-street parking, but the money is being distributed in different ways, depending on the local authority. How much you pay for installation varies widely around the country. If you want to apply for a gully to be installed, you should check with your council to see whether it allows them and, if it does, it should direct you on how to apply. Kerbo Charge, a company that installs gullies, operates a postcode checker you can use to see whether you can get one in your area and sign up for an alert if that changes. Ben Whitaker of Kerbo Charge says the average fee for the work is about £1,200 (including VAT) without a grant. “Some [councils] are using it [the funding] to provide half-price channels to early adopters, others are making it totally free while funds last – but, after that, residents will have to pay full price,” he says. “For example, Surrey is £499 for the channel and installation, South Gloucestershire is £250,” he adds. “Sadly, there is quite a variety of approaches and prices.” To illustrate the difference in prices between local authorities, Redbridge council in London says the grant will cover up to £1,200 of installation costs. But applicants must pay £815 in fees and for a bond, as well as any additional installation costs. On top of the cost of installing the gullies, some councils charge an additional annual fee for maintenance. For example, Redbridge charges an “ongoing annual licence fee” of £185. Enfield, also in London, charges £107 a year . Shayne Rees of Gul-e, a company that has installed 400 gullies, says it takes between one and two hours to put the unit in place. “It’s a really heavy-duty steel channel that can take a truck driving over it, and once we put it in the ground, that will be there for decades and decades without any maintenance,” he adds. It emerged in May that more than 20 local authorities appear to be holding out against having the gullies installed, among them Kent, Leicester and Worcestershire. Most of the holdouts are in London, including Waltham Forest and Hackney. The reasons given often concern safety and maintenance, and because of issues over who will be liable if there is an injury.

events.title: Childcare chain collapses amid wave of closures
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Childcare chain's collapse into administration highlights private credit risks A former national children's commissioner says a lot of private providers are divesting childcare centres or pulling out of the sector altogether. Childcare chain Shared Beginnings has hit financial strife, becoming the latest early education provider to run into trouble amid a wave of closures in the sector. The childcare service, owned by private lender Finexia Financial Group, operates centres in Queensland, Victoria and the ACT. Finexia wrote to staff, informing them the centres had been operating "at a loss". The collapse highlights the risks of the private credit sector, with Finexia taking on ownership of the centres in the 2025 financial year after the previous owner, Genius Education, defaulted on substantial loans owed to Finexia. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has recently said it was closely scrutinising private lending , which has typically been a much more lightly regulated sector than the banking industry, and was concerned "the first significant cracks" were appearing. The impact on childcare places and jobs at Shared Beginnings remains unclear as the administrators continue to operate the centres. The firm said the decision came after exhausting all other options. Neil Sheather says all options to save Shared Beginnings have been exhausted. ( Supplied: Linkedin ) Finexia managing director Neil Sheather said placing Shared Beginnings into administration was not taken lightly, but was necessary. "Ultimately, the administrators are in control of Shared Beginnings." In a letter to staff, Mr Sheather said the administration would affect all seven of its centres, including Sinnamon Park and Kenmore in Queensland, Reservoir, Mont Albert and Beaumaris in Victoria, and Bonython and Conder in the ACT. All Shared Beginnings centres remain open under the control of administrators. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) In a separate letter to parents, Mr Sheather assured families that all centres remained open, and care would continue as normal. Bill Karageozis and Nick Keramos of DVT McLeods have been appointed administrators to find suitable buyers. Minister for Early Childhood Education Jessica Walsh said she acknowledged the news from Shared Beginnings would "cause disruption and uncertainty for families and educators". "Since coming to government, we've seen 1,200 new centres, 52,000 more educators and 57,000 more children in early learning." A September report by the Early Learning and Care Council Australia has found the rate of early childhood education and care (ECEC) service closures has continued to increase. The report said 152 long daycare services had closed since 2024, with a further 276 services (both long day care and preschool/kindergarten) identified as at risk of closing in the next 12 months. Anne Hollonds AO says the childcare sector is undergoing a significant adjustment. ( Supplied: Australian Human Rights Commission ) Former national children's commissioner Anne Hollonds AO said the childcare sector was undergoing a significant adjustment, driven by increased regulatory costs and a number of prominent crises. For-profit centres dominate the long daycare sector. Most of the growth in recent years has been in private for-profit providers, with a recent report from the Mitchell Institute finding they made up 74 per cent of long daycare places. Ms Hollonds said the sector would be better if it were shared 50-50 between non-profit and for-profit organisations. "We really need to focus on the safety and well-being of children as the priority," she said, adding that she had no problem with for-profit providers as long as their operation was up to scratch. A recent report finds for-profit centres drive substantial instability in the long day care sector. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) The Mitchell Institute also found substantial instability or "churn" in the long daycare sector was driven by for-profit centres. "Since 2013, about one-third [32 per cent] of long day care services open in 2025 had changed approved provider," the report said. "The rate is higher in for-profit centres where 40 per cent have changed provider, compared to 11 per cent of all other centres." events.title: Fortescue senior executive sacked after sexual harassment probe
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Executive at Andrew Forrest's Fortescue Metals sacked after sexual harassment, bullying probe A senior Fortescue executive has been sacked for alleged ( Supplied: Fortescue Metals Group ) A senior executive at Andrew Forrest's Fortescue Metals Group has been sacked following an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment and bullying at the iron ore miner. The executive, who was not named by Fortescue in its short statement about the matter, "breached Fortescue’s policies, as well as our values", it said. Fortescue had engaged law firm MinterEllison to examine a series of allegations about the employee's conduct. "Sexual harassment, bullying, and other behaviour that makes people feel unsafe has no place at Fortescue," the company said. Mining magnate Dr Andrew Forrest is the founder of Fortescue. ( ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates ) It said it would provide "ongoing support" to those who took part in the investigation. In August, Reuters reported Fortescue had allowed the executive to continue working at the firm while the MinterEllison investigation was underway. The company's energy chief Gus Pichot said at the time the company was "quite confident we are following the proper process" in allowing it. It comes after a group of female Fortescue employees launched a class action in the Federal Court against the company in June, alleging rape, sexual assault and stalking at remote FMG mine sites in WA's Pilbara. The allegations included drink spiking, promotions offered in exchange for sexual favours and a widespread culture of sexual harassment and denigration. Andrew 'Twiggy' Forrest warns Fortescue staff after sexual harassment class action In an email sent to all staff, Mr Forrest said: "Anyone who thinks this behaviour has a place at Fortescue is in the wrong company." The sacking comes despite a 2023 deal with WorkSafe WA in which Fortescue agreed to spend $1.4 million on addressing inappropriate workplace behaviour after allegedly failing to supply documents about dozens of sexual harassment allegations to the work safety regulator. FMG is not the first mining company to face claims of unsafe work practices and a toxic culture. Hundreds of women have come forward in the two years since BHP and Rio Tinto were taken to federal court over similar allegations . A 2022 report into the sexual harassment of women in the mining industry by a parliamentary committee found nearly three quarters of women in mining had experienced sexual harassment at work in the past five years, and that it was generally accepted in workplaces. The scathing report found mining companies failed to recognise the problem or act on it, and while the government accepted its recommendations, not all have been enacted. Some of these included changes to equal opportunities laws, which the WA government yesterday announced it would introduce , four years on from the landmark report. events.title: McDonald's bid for Phillip Island restaurant knocked back by council
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bass Coast Shire Council rejects proposal for McDonald's on Phillip Island Topic: Regional Development and Planning Plans had been submitted for a proposed McDonald's restaurant in Cowes, on Phillip Island. ( Supplied: Bass Coast Shire Council ) Bass Coast Shire Council has rejected a bid by McDonald's to open a restaurant on Phillip Island. The application drew an angry response from members of the Phillip Island community. McDonald's can appeal the decision to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. An application by McDonald's to build a restaurant in the Victorian tourist hotspot of Phillip Island has been rejected after councillors voted to refuse it a planning permit. The fast-food giant lodged its application earlier this year with the Bass Coast Shire Council to build a new restaurant in Cowes , which has a population of 6,593. But councillors unanimously voted to reject the application, saying it was inconsistent with the local planning scheme. The public gallery was full at Bass Coast Shire Council's meeting. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Island ward councillor Tim O'Brien said the proposal failed the community "on so many levels". "Where is the community benefit?" Mr O'Brien said. "This will be muscling its way into a part of a market it had no part in building." The plan to build a McDonald's on Phillip Island has angered some community members. ( Supplied: Say No To McDonald's Cowes group ) Councillor Mat Morgan, who is a Greens candidate at the upcoming Victorian election, said the application "should obviously be rejected" because of inappropriate residential development. "There are a thousand ethical and moral reasons to throw this in the bin," he said. The proposal raised the ire of thousands of residents , with more than 5,800 people signing a petition rejecting the proposal, citing traffic concerns and the threat to small businesses in town. The no vote came after a recommendation by council officers to grant McDonald's a planning permit, which they found "acceptable" after assessing it against the planning scheme. Councillor Jan Thompson told the meeting that the decision would likely be overturned on appeal to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT), but voted to reject the application anyway. The council received 1,543 objections and 32 submissions relating to the McDonald's application. The proposed site is home to a petrol station and a vacant plot of land. Cowes is the main township on Phillip Island. ( Supplied: Bass Coast Shire Council ) Cowes resident and business owner, Trevor Ware, said the community's concerns were heard by the council in rejecting the proposal. "We didn't need this, and I think the community has done very well to fight it," he said. Trevor Ware says the community has been heard. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "There's still a big track ahead and [McDonald's] are going to push very hard. We just can't let it just ride through. "The way it's been approached and the area that they put it in so close to the school, everything was just so wrong." Island residents celebrate after Bass Coast Shire council's rejection of the planning permit. ( ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery ) Cowes resident Megan Ryan said the decision made her emotional. "If McDonald's haven't got the message, we don't want them here," she said. "My dad lives at Melaleuca [aged care] right next door to here. He's lived here, he's served here, and the last thing I want my dad to hear in the middle of the night is, 'Do you want fries with that?' because there's a 24-hour McDonald's sitting right there." "The proposed restaurant represents a significant investment into Phillip Island and will mean more than 100 new local jobs, as well as more support for local community groups in the area. "We remain committed to working collaboratively with Council, being a good neighbour and making a positive contribution to the Cowes and broader Phillip Island community." events.title: World must cut emissions by 18% in four years ‘to find our way back’, UN says
events.summary: Action needed to avoid disastrous overshoot of climate targets, according to organisation’s environment body The world needs to cut carbon emissions by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin. Although the “window has closed” on holding temperature rises to 1.5C , in line with scientific advice, limiting the “overshoot” of that target is still possible, according to the UN Environment Programme (Unep). But countries are failing to translate their long-term targets on reducing emissions into short-term actions, a report on the “emissions gap” between climate goals and policies has found. Global carbon output appears to have stalled: the emission levels in 2025 were broadly similar to those of the previous year. But Unep analysts were wary of calling it a peak or plateau, given the vast uncertainties of geopolitics and an increased reliance on fossil fuels, despite strong growth in renewable energy . Cutting greenhouse gases by 18% by 2030, and by 45% by 2035, would yield a good chance of limiting temperature rises to 1.7C above preindustrial levels. This would still allow events such as the record heatwaves of the last few months to become frequent and common, but could help prevent them from getting drastically worse. Governments were warned for years that time was running out, said Inger Andersen, the executive director of Unep. “[We used to say] there’s still an opportunity if we make this herculean effort [to stay within the 1.5C limit],” she said. “It’s now clear the herculean effort was not made. We procrastinated, and now we are saying this window has closed.” Nevertheless, she urged countries to keep the 1.5C goal – the centrepiece of the Paris climate agreement. “We can make the overshoot as brief and as short as possible. It’s not time to throw in the towel and give up. This is about how to find our way back, as shortly and quickly as possible.” Under Donald Trump, the US – the world’s second biggest emitter, after China – has withdrawn from the Paris climate agreement and is threatening to reverse its longstanding trend of falling greenhouse gas emissions. Bill Hare, the chief executive of the Climate Analytics thinktank, said: “All governments have a job to do, but in particular it is time for major fossil fuel producers such as the US and Saudi Arabia, which produce 20-25% of fossil fuels globally, to stop playing politics and face the scientific reality. Right now they are looking at the fire, denying it exists and pouring more petrol on it, while their own citizens increasingly face searing heat, wildfires and other impacts.” Other countries appear to have been affected by US intransigence – pledges made last year on greenhouse gases were noticeably weak, according to UNEP analysis. At the Cop30 climate summit in Brazil last November , governments were supposed to make fresh commitments under the Paris agreement to cut emissions. But the commitments made were nowhere near strong enough. Even if all of those updated pledges were fulfilled, temperatures would still rise to 2.6C above preindustrial levels, according to Unep’s projections, endangering life across swathes of the globe. Policy has also not kept up with pledges: on current policies around the world, temperatures would rise to 2.8C. Every five years of greenhouse gas emissions at current levels pushes up forecasts of global heating by 0.1C. Scientists also fear that the greater the margin by which we exceed 1.5C, the greater the likelihood of triggering tipping points in the climate system . Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, said: “The tragedy is that we have the solutions within our grasp. Solar and wind power are growing far faster than anyone expected, yet governments are still failing to move away from fossil fuels quickly enough. The technology is racing ahead while political leadership is dragging its feet.” The shortfall in countries’ commitments is supposed to be corrected under a Paris agreement mechanism called the “global stocktake”, an assessment of emissions targets next scheduled for 2028. But that has also been thrown into doubt: this week, the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change failed to set a timetable to publish its latest report before the global stocktake, which would prevent governments from assessing their progress against the latest science. Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and one of the world’s leading climate scientists, said rows over the timing of IPCC reports must not be allowed to stall government action. “If all current national commitments are implemented, global emissions are projected to reach approximately 50 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually by 2035, when they should be below 35 gigatonnes. The science is already clear.

events.title: AI data centre company cold calling about buying land, inquiry told
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts AI data centre company cold calling rural residents about buying Tasmanian land, inquiry told Vica Bayley said locals were told the interested buyers wanted agricultural land close to the north-west transmission line. ( Facebook: TasNetworks ) Locals in a north-west Tasmanian rural area have been telephoned and asked about selling land to a data centre developer, the Greens say. Firmus, which has plans for three data centres in Tasmania, has previously said it was not behind the proposal. The Tasmanian government says the proponent has not yet confirmed a final site. Consultants for an AI data centre company have been cold-calling residents in north-west Tasmania, wanting to buy their land, the Greens say. At a state parliamentary energy committee hearing today, Greens MP Vica Bayley asked the acting coordinator-general whether an AI data centre was proposed for Nook. "We've been contacted this week by locals in Nook, near Sheffield," Mr Bayley said. "They've been contacted by a Sydney consultancy firm wanting to purchase, my understanding is, agricultural land adjacent to the substation there, recently upgraded because it's part of the north-west transmission line, and allegedly for a large data centre." Mr Bayley questioned the appropriateness of locals finding out about the proposal from a "Sydney consultancy firm". ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) Acting Coordinator-General Dennis Hendriks said there was "probably not a lot I can say about that". "We are aware that there is a proposal in the north-west that is moving forward," he told the committee. "It's at an early stage of development; we've made some introductions to the planning authority." Proposals for six new data centres were revealed in Tasmanian parliament last month, though the government did not disclose the names of the proponents. Mr Hendriks confirmed the proposal referred to by Mr Bayley was project B — a 200–300 megawatt data centre in the feasibility stage in the north-west. Mr Bayley questioned the appropriateness of locals finding out about the proposal from a "Sydney consultancy firm". Mr Hendricks said the office only had a "very limited amount of information" about the project. He took a question on notice about identifying the proponent to the committee. Government says no final site confirmed Mr Bayley asked Minister for Business, Resources and Industry Felix Ellis if agricultural land should be used for AI data centres. "There's a statutory planning process and environmental regulation and legislation," Mr Ellis replied. The Greens said north-west residents have been told about a potential AI data centre development for Nook, which is near Sheffield (pictured). ( Wikimedia Commons: CucombreLibre ) A government spokesperson said it would continue engaging with the proponent. "This proposal was included in information previously tabled in parliament," they said. "We understand it remains under consideration by the proponent, and no final site has been confirmed. AI data centre company Firmus Technologies has previously said it was not behind any of the six confidential new proposals. Firmus has three data centre projects underway in Tasmania — one under construction in Launceston, another approved for construction at Long Reach in the Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone, and another waiting for approval at Wesley Vale, in the state's north-west. 'Going to cause huge tension with their neighbours' Wade Rockliff, a farmer in Sheffield, has heard rumblings of consultants asking to buy farmland in the area for AI data centres. "I think they're offering way more than the land's worth," he said. "The people that they're asking, it's probably life changing for them. "Some of them are probably generational families in the community and it's going to cause huge tension with their neighbours because if they build some monstrosity — they're talking bigger than the one that's going in at Bell Bay, so it's a massive data centre — everyone's properties around it are going to devalue." Mr Rockliff does not believe "data centres are going to employ that many locals once they've been built". "And when you look at the ethos of a data centre, it's about replacing jobs.

events.summary: Supermarkets and gas stations in Naples are facing shortages due to weeklong protests by truck drivers against high gasoline costs MILAN -- Some supermarket shelves and gas station pumps were empty in the southern city of Naples on Tuesday due to a weeklong protest by truck drivers against the high cost of diesel driven up by the Iran war. Protesters blocked the loading and unloading of fresh food and other goods at supermarket distribution warehouses near Naples on Monday, Sky TG24 reported. The truckers are adding their voices to demonstrations that have spread across Europe as the war disrupts economies. One supermarket in the city posted a note on empty shelves apologizing that “some products may be temporarily unavailable or available in a reduced range" due to the truckers' strike. Shortages of fresh pasta, packaged cheeses and meats as well as produce have been reported in Sicily, partly due to stockpiling by shoppers. Partially empty supermarket shelves were also reported in the southern regions of Calabria and Puglia. events.title: Veggie Thursdays and vegan surprises! How Ghent became a plant-based paradise
events.summary: In 2014, 13% of the population of this Belgian city described themselves as flexitarian. This year, 83% did. Here is how everyone was convinced to eat their greens – and love them S ixty bowls of slime-green soup sit waiting for the children to arrive. Pupils rush in from their morning lessons, grab the bowls by the handles and start slurping. No complaints, no refusals. (OK, maybe a few “bleurgh” faces.) Chicory soup dispatched, they get stuck into the main course: falafel, Mediterranean vegetable tagine and couscous. Some ask for seconds; most grab a piece of fruit for dessert and run out to play. This is a typical Thursday lunchtime in BS De Stadspoort primary school in Ghent, Belgium. Similar meat-free menus are being eaten in other schools and nurseries across the city, plus community centres, care homes and assisted living facilities, not to mention many work canteens and restaurants. Thursday in Ghent is officially “Veggie Day” , with residents encouraged to eschew any meat or fish. So how did a city get its children – and everyone else – to eat their greens? It didn’t happen overnight. “The success story of Ghent is one where we had an amazing grassroots movement, with people asking for more climate action. But the magic happened when politicians actually listened and implemented policy to introduce the Thursday Veggie Day in 2009,” says Vanessa Debruyne, the head of communications for the nonprofit organisation ProVeg Belgium , who is showing me around town. “It got the ball rolling, companies and restaurants joined, the population got used to it, and more entrepreneurs made the move to plant-based. We’ve been unstoppable ever since! Ghent is the best town in Belgium for plant-based food.” Veggie day was just the start, agrees Hafsa El-Bazioui, the Green deputy mayor of Ghent, who has cycled over to join us (the city centre has been largely car-free since 2017). “A few years ago, we changed to prioritise plant-based protein,” she says. In 2021, the Flemish government launched the Green Deal Protein Shift – a commitment to switch the ratio of animal to plant proteins consumed from 60:40 to 40:60 by 2030. Ghent has already reached the target. As well as vegetarian Thursdays and vegetarian options every day, school caterers have turned traditional meat dishes such as burgers, sausages and meatballs into hybrids, cutting out at least half the beef or pork and replacing them with, say, lentils. Stews might combine meat with chickpeas or beans. An incredible amount of effort is put in to making each dish taste good: they are screened by a “taste panel” made up of dietitians, chefs, childcare professionals and people with sensitivities to flavour, bitterness, texture and mouthfeel. Recipes are constantly modified and improved after feedback from children, parents and school staff. As a result, children get to eat the food they know and like, but the dishes are healthier and better for the planet – Ghent has reduced the carbon footprint of its school meals by 38% since 2018. Although she is a vegan herself, El-Bazioui believes reducing meat consumption across the board is the most effective and achievable policy, rather than trying to convince people to cut it out altogether. “When you approach a lot of people, the impact is more than if you focus on a small group of vegans,” she says. “That’s my philosophy in food, in politics, in life.” This stealth approach is echoed all over the city. I pop in to the Viernulvier art centre , AKA De Vooruit, for a chat with Tom De Vleesschauwer, its kitchen coordinator – De Vooruit is as popular for its large art deco cafe as for its programme of theatre, dance, film and music. “A few years ago, we made oat milk the default: if you don’t ask for cow’s milk, you get oat,” says De Vleesschauwer. “About 90% of customers now have oat milk. If we had a sign saying you can choose, it would only be 10-20%.” There have been other changes in De Vooruit’s cafe, too. The soup is now always vegan; the dish of the day is vegetarian; the staff and performers are served a daily “ Ottolenghi -style vegetarian buffet” instead of cheese and charcuterie. And, as in the school canteens, the few meat dishes on the menu – today just spaghetti bolognese and meatballs in tomato sauce – have been hybridised. “We cut down the meat by 70% and increased the carrots, cutting them to the same size – 30% still gives the flavour and the idea of meat, and carrots give sweetness,” says De Vleesschauwer. “People say plant-based is niche, but we have a very wide audience.” There are plenty of fully vegan businesses in the city, too, such as Madam Bakster , where I drink coffee with homemade hazelnut milk and devour rich, chewy chocolate-chip cookies fresh from the oven. Laura Verhulst, the founder, sees her cafe as more, not less, inclusive. “I wanted to make desserts that everyone could enjoy: vegan, allergen-free, non-refined sugar,” she says.

events.title: Last drinks for Boag's as final Tasmanian beers roll off production line
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Final Tasmanian-brewed Boag's beers come off production line as brewer exits home state Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry The last Tasmanian-brewed Boag's beers were packaged up in the Launceston factory today. Parent company Lion announced the closure of the 145-year-old brewery in June, with the brand now to be fully produced on the mainland. Decommissioning the brewery is expected to take a year, with the Tasmanian government interested in buying the large CBD site. The last Tasmanian-brewed Boag's beers were bottled in Launceston this morning, marking an end to 145 years of local production. In the past century and a half, Boag's has cemented itself as a state icon and often run ads about being brewed with clean Tasmanian water. The final bottles exited the assembly line this afternoon, ahead of the brewery shutting its doors for the final time on November 6, taking with it 42 local jobs. Boag's will cease their Tasmanian operations in Launceston in November after 145 years of local operation. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) While the bottle production finished today, the final brewing day was in September. Brewer Adrian Hinds, who has been a Boag's employee for 22 years, said it was an emotional day. "To be honest, I'm holding it together; it's quite emotional," he said. "Today was the last drop of Boag's put into containers; tanks are empty, everything's on a carton or pallet ready to go out to the public. "Everyone was on the packaging line watching the bottles go through the labeller; it just shows what it means to the staff here. Brewer Adrian Hinds has been a Boag's employee for over two decades. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) Mr Hinds said for the last mashing, "everyone came up, got a sample of grain, put it in the mash tuns, so everyone had that final little touch on the last brew of draught that we did". "After everyone left the brew house and I was in there by myself, I just sat there for a while and just listened to all the sounds, the pumps going and then sugar going in and then smelling the hops going in. "To be here for the last fill, it's sad. I didn't think it would ever happen; it's a shame it's happening, but you can't control it. The Boag's Brewery site sits on the banks of the North Esk river in central Launceston. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) Tasmania to start importing Boag's from mainland Boag's has existed in Launceston longer than electricity. Originally called the Esk Brewery, Scottish migrant James Boag and his son James Boag II began the operation in 1881. Bottling machines in the brewery's early years. ( Supplied: State Library and Archives Tasmania ) In 2008, Lion Australia, owned by Japanese beer giant Kirin, snapped up the brand for $325 million. But in June, Lion announced an end to local brewing operations in Launceston , citing inflation and long-term declines in beer sales. Brewing of the Boag's brand will continue on the mainland in New South Wales, Queensland and Victoria. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Most of Boag's brewing had already been moved interstate the previous year, leaving the Launceston operation running at one-fifth of its capacity. The Boag's brand will continue to live on, being brewed in Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland. Tasmania will now become an importer of its beverage icon. Boag's tour guide Phil Crowden has been taking visitors from around the world into the Boag's Brewery's inner sanctum for 17 years. He said the skills of the local brewers were "unparalleled", but he had faith the mainland-brewed Boag's would still hit the spot for rusted-on fans. James Boag beers can be found in every northern Tasmanian pub, bar and bottleshop. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) "The technology's got so good at the moment," he said. "I mean, breweries are making beers for other breweries around the world, and you can actually emulate the water from any particular place in the world." An online petition was launched in a bid to try and stop the closure of the brewery. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Tasmanian water has long been lauded as the essential ingredient in Boag's, something the brand has heavily promoted in its advertising. Mr Crowden said the exact mineral count of Tasmanian water would be replicated at the other breweries to get as close to the taste as possible. A spokesperson for Lion said the company were considering whether the equipment from the Launceston site may be deployed to its other sites. Decommissioning of the brewing equipment will begin after the November closure date and is estimated to take an additional 12 months. Boag's is easily the bestseller at Launceston mainstay The Gunners Arms.

events.title: Singapore’s DayOne said to weigh options for US IPO after data centre rout
events.summary: DayOne was initially considering raising as much as US$5 billion from the listing as soon as the fourth quarter. DayOne Data Centers is weighing a delay or smaller US IPO after a data centre market rout, with plans still under review and no final decision made. The Singapore-based firm may cut fundraising to US$2.5 billion-US$3 billion, down from an earlier target of up to US$5 billion and a US$20 billion valuation. Investor caution is rising across data centre and AI-linked listings, after failed or delayed IPOs at Firmus Grid, AirTrunk and others, while DayOne keeps talking to investors. DayOne Data Centers is weighing options for its US initial public offering , including a potential delay or size cut, as volatility around data centres increases, according to people familiar with the matter. While Singapore-based DayOne has been waiting for the right window to launch the IPO, it has also been considering the possibility of pushing back the share sale until the market recovers, the people said. Other options include going ahead with a smaller listing that may raise US$2.5 billion (S$3.2 billion) to US$3 billion, roughly half of what it had originally aimed for, the people said. DayOne, whose backers include Coatue and Hillhouse, is continuing to engage with potential investors and still wants to move forward as soon as the market allows, the people said. The company was initially considering raising as much as US$5 billion from the listing as soon as the fourth quarter, people familiar with the matter said previously. It had been eyeing a valuation of about US$20 billion, the people have said. Deliberations are ongoing and DayOne has not made any final decisions, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. The company could still opt to move ahead with the offering in the coming weeks, according to the people. While data centres have drawn global investor demand amid a boom in sectors related to artificial intelligence, a more negative sentiment has started to have ripple effects on IPOs. DayOne has been raising billions of dollars in private funding rounds as it seeks capital to build out its pipeline. Australian data centre company Firmus Grid pulled its roughly US$5 billion IPO when investors balked at the valuation it sought, while AirTrunk, which also operates data centres, delayed a planned real estate investment trust IPO in Singapore to 2027. South Korean digital infrastructure company Elice plunged 32% in its Seoul trading debut on Oct 20. Coreweave’s shares have more than halved since their May peak, and Nscale is facing pushback over its target IPO valuation, Bloomberg News reported. On Oct 21, shares of Australian data center operator Nextdc plummeted after it cut earnings guidance. Some investors are hoping that the recent market volatility will pass after the US midterm elections on Nov 3. They are also looking ahead to the performance of Anthropic PBC’s upcoming listing as an important gauge of sentiment toward the AI sector. DayOne filed for a US IPO earlier in October. The offering is being led by Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase & Co., Bank of America and Citigroup IFR reported on Oct 19 that DayOne was gathering more investor feedback before launching the share sale. DayOne is running or developing data centres in Singapore, Malaysia , Indonesia, Thailand, Hong Kong, Japan, Finland and Spain. Other backers include GDS Holdings, the SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

events.title: An AI slowdown could be exactly what businesses need
events.summary: The artificial intelligence industry has spent years feathering the accelerator of frontier model development in a fierce contest to dominate the technology . Now, it is considering something that until recently seemed almost unthinkable: slamming on the brakes. The prospects of the frontier labs are closely linked to the fortunes of the US stock market, and they buttress vast spending on infrastructure. But for businesses still working out how to harness AI’s illusive productivity gains, a slowdown is not a bad thing. It will give them time to close the yawning gap between AI’s accelerating capabilities and their productive use of them. Still, calls to pace the frontier grow louder. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei made the case in an essay in which he said capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to understand, align and control them. His proposal was to deliberately slow the improvement enough to give safety research and independent evaluation time to catch up. Is it practical? There remains considerable disagreement over whether this is practical, desirable or possible. But that’s beside the point for businesses, since most of them are nowhere close to exhausting the AI capabilities they already possess. According to the Stanford 2026 AI Index, 88 per cent of organisations surveyed reported using AI in at least one business function last year. But breadth of adoption is not the same thing as depth. The research shows that the use of AI agents remained in the single digits across almost every business function. Relatively few have fundamentally redesigned how work gets done around it. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis found that generative AI accounted for only 5.7 per cent of total working hours by August last year. This tells us that companies already have powerful AI, and are simply failing to make the most of it. They don’t need another massive leap in model capability to claim the productivity gains that are already on the table. A METR randomised study found that experienced open-source developers working on highly familiar repositories actually took 19 per cent longer when allowed to use early-2025 AI tools. The reason is that the bottleneck is increasingly organisational. Companies have to connect models to proprietary data. They have to integrate AI into existing systems. And they need to redesign workflows rather than simply insert a chatbot into them. They also need appropriate governance, security and human oversight, while employees have to learn how to delegate effectively to AI. Managers, meanwhile, need to rethink roles, performance measures and decision rights. Those changes happen at a comparatively glacial pace when compared with the speed at which AI labs have been pushing the frontier. More capabilities OpenAI's enterprise research finds that the heaviest AI adopters use substantially more capabilities across more tasks than the median employee. These intensive users report much larger productivity benefits. Seventy-five per cent of surveyed workers also reported being able to perform tasks using AI that they previously could not do. So the AI productivity frontier inside most companies sits far behind the technological one. This is not unusual. General-purpose technologies typically arrive before organisations learn how to exploit them. Electricity existed before factories were redesigned around distributed electric motors, and computers came along long before companies reorganised processes around digital information. AI is likely to follow the same pattern, which only strengthens the case for hitting the brakes. That will not stall the AI economy , which is so crucial to public equity markets, because it will give companies the badly needed time to extract value from the marvellous capabilities already at their fingertips. That means moving beyond experimentation towards workflow redesign. Moving from individual productivity tools towards end-to-end processes. Connecting AI to enterprise data and systems. Using agents where they genuinely add value. Building governance that allows experimentation without unacceptable risk. And, perhaps most importantly, developing the organisational capabilities required to use AI well. Executives should continue watching the frontier, of course. Better models will create new opportunities, and a substantial slowdown is far from guaranteed. But they should not confuse a slower technological frontier with a slower business opportunity. Even if frontier development paused dramatically tomorrow, companies would still have an enormous backlog of economically valuable opportunities across customer service, software development, finance , procurement, marketing and many other functions. So just because the frontier slows, it doesn’t mean the business opportunity does. The AI race, at least for enterprise users, needs to shift from simply building better AI to building better businesses around it.

events.title: Asian stocks climb as strong earnings buoy Wall Street
events.summary: Overnight, stocks on Wall Street were mildly positive, pushing the S&P 500 0.3% higher as oil prices and Treasury yields eased. SINGAPORE – Asian stocks rose and bonds stabilised at the start of trading on Oct 21 following Wall Street’s gain as early indications from the corporate earnings season pointed to strong profits for global companies and bolstered investor confidence. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was up 1.5%, led by a 4% gain for Korean shares, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 climbed 1.3%. S&P 500 e-mini futures rose 0.3%. Stocks in the region have steadied since a wrenching selloff last week but have traded in a tight range since then. With 13% of S&P 500 companies reporting, 86% have beaten earnings estimates, according to LSEG data. “Global equities were mixed, with solid earnings supporting US markets while ongoing concerns around the AI trade and elevated oil and borrowing costs weighed more heavily elsewhere,” Westpac analysts wrote in a note. “Oil prices fell on unconfirmed reports of renewed peace negotiations, before largely retracing the move after the reports were denied.” However, French stocks fell as fears remained around the government’s plans to curb recent unrest . French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would reinforce police with a “massive” deployment of troops to quell protests planned for Oct 24 . The yield on the French 10-year OAT was up 2.7 basis points at 4.94%, nudging the yield differential compared to the German 10-year bund 0.3 basis point higher to 153.1 basis points. Brent crude was 1.1% higher at US$110.03 a barrel as trading resumed in Asia, extending gains after touching a five-month high during a volatile session on Oct 20 as traders weighed a meeting between the Iranian president and Pakistan’s army chief, a key US-Iran mediator, against continued Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. US envoy Steve Witkoff is due to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin later in the day after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway, as US President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war. The yen was 0.1% weaker against the dollar at 158.33 yen after government data released on Oct 21 showed Japan’s exports in September rose 16.7% from a year earlier, missing estimates. Strong demand for semiconductors and AI-related products offset weakness in other sectors. A Reuters poll found a majority of economists believe the Bank of Japan will refrain from hiking interest rates on Oct 30 before voting for a 25-basis-point increase in December, followed by quarterly hikes. Economists polled also believe the Federal Reserve will skip a hike at its next meeting on Oct 28 before raising rates in December. Fed funds futures are pricing an implied 83% probability of a hold later in October, little changed from a day earlier, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was up 1 basis point at 5.123%. In emerging markets, traders are awaiting a decision from Indonesia’s central bank , which is battling to halt the rupiah’s slide following a market rout from an MSCI warning that it may exclude the country’s stocks from its major benchmarks. Bitcoin was up 0.3% at US$82,988.76, while ether was 0.2% higher at US$2,452.59. REUTERS

events.title: A battle for control of Tata Group, India’s biggest business empire
events.summary: A battle for control of the Tata Group, India’s biggest business empire Tata Sons chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran was re-elected after he earlier said he would seek a new five-year term. The Tata Group is in a power struggle over who controls India’s biggest business empire: the founding trusts, professional managers, or the government. Noel Tata and the trusts want Tata Sons to stay private, while chair Natarajan Chandrasekaran and some board members now back a stock market listing. The dispute matters because Tata is central to Indian life, and a listing could weaken family control, raise capital, and reshape corporate power in India. MUMBAI, India – Who actually controls India’s biggest company? A bitter power struggle over the Tata Group, a 158-year-old conglomerate with more than one million employees worldwide and US$180 billion (S$230 billion) in annual revenue, has become a test of who calls the shots in Indian capitalism: owners, professional managers or the government.

events.title: Tech giant shares plunge 40pc after delays to Melbourne data centre
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NextDC value on ASX smashed by delays to West Footscray data centre The value of NextDC, which operates a data centre in West Footscray, has plummeted. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) The value of a multi-billion-dollar tech giant has plummeted amid ongoing delays to its data centre plans in Melbourne's inner west. The community backlash has forced NextDC to drastically cut its earnings and revenue forecasts. NextDC, which has 17 operational data centres in Australia, has another nine centres in the development or planning stages. Community opposition to one of Melbourne's largest hyperscale data centres has smashed the value of one of Australia's biggest companies. A neighbourhood dispute over power poles has forced multi-billion-dollar tech giant NextDC to cut its net earnings and revenue forecasts by tens of millions of dollars, with a planned expansion hit with power supply and government approval delays. The company, among Australia's largest 100 listed companies, notified the stock exchange this morning that its net revenue for the current financial year would be slashed by a third — now $475 million to $500 million — down from $615 million to $640 million. The company's operating profitability was also revised down to $245 million to $265 million, from $385 million to $410 million. Following this morning's announcement, NextDC's stock plummeted by 40 per cent. NextDC attributed the revised estimates to delays to electricity network upgrades by energy supplier Jemena, required to increase power supply to its M3 data centre in West Footscray. The West Footscray data centre, located just 15 metres from homes, has long been the subject of community opposition due to concerns over diesel and noise pollution . Located only 10 kilometres west of Melbourne's CBD, this data centre spans 41,000 square metres. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The installation of towering power poles to accommodate the facility's vast electricity use became another flashpoint earlier this year. In September, Jemena was forced to halt the installation of 15-metre-high power poles in Yarraville after being met with resistance from residents, several of whom blocked crews by leaving their cars and bins out. The power poles can carry up to 66,000 volts of electricity, approximately 160 times the voltage of previous power poles. Local councils and residents argued that they had not been adequately consulted over the upgrades. The installation of power poles in Yarraville was met with fierce resistance from residents. ( ABC News ) Company 'exploring all avenues' to accommodate facility's power needs In its announcement to the ASX on Wednesday morning, NextDC said the delays meant the next grid supply for West Footscray was now not expected until mid-2027, deferring "the delivery and billing of contracted capacity". "Jemena has advised NextDC that it has suspended parts of the network works required for the next increase in grid supply to M3 Melbourne," NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie said. "We have taken the affected M3 contracts out of FY27 guidance until we can reliably estimate their contribution." In a call with investors this morning, NextDC's group chief development officer Simon Cooper said the company was "exploring all avenues", including finding alternative locations for the power poles, or placing electrical cables underground. "Undergrounding does take time and there's not an immediate option that we can work on now. But it is something that we are absolutely considering," Mr Cooper said. Independent senator David Pocock today used a National Press Club address to propose a "modest" 5 per cent levy on data centres operating in Australia from next year. Senator Pocock accused the federal government of being "starstruck" by US artificial intelligence companies, and being "blind" to community sentiment regarding artificial intelligence. He said the levy would generate more than $500 million by the end of 2030. "In the context of a forecast $200-billion investment and little to no corporate tax paid by foreign data centre companies in this country, it's really not much," Mr Pocock said. events.title: Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity
events.summary: Voters in Alberta have overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with four-fifths of votes counted showing 75% support for staying EDMONTON, Alberta -- Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in the country, referendum results showed Tuesday, delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for national unity as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats rally Canadians around their country. With more than 1.9 million votes counted and results reported from 90% of voting areas and locations, 75% of voters supported remaining in Canada , while 25% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta. The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada . “It’s a great result for Canada that Albertans have chosen unity,” Carney told reporters Tuesday before a Cabinet meeting in Ottawa. Carney said the roughly one-quarter of voters who backed beginning the separation process did not necessarily want independence, suggesting only a smaller “hard core” favored leaving Canada. Some voters said they wanted to send Ottawa a message rather than separate. Alberta separatist organizer David Parker acknowledged the scale of the defeat. “Independence feels far away and we should not pretend this was not a defeat,” he wrote on social media. In a televised address Tuesday night, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the result and pledged not to hold another referendum on separation while she remains in office. “Yesterday, Albertans voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining a province of Canada,” Smith said. “The voter turnout was historic and a powerful testimony of the passion Albertans feel for our country and our province.” Smith said Alberta would continue pressing Ottawa for greater provincial autonomy, but disputes would be settled within Canada’s political and legal institutions rather than through separation. Carney said he spoke with Smith on Tuesday morning about the results and greater federal-provincial cooperation, including immigration. “Don’t mess with Canada. President Trump is watching this,” Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters. Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves , is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada's federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but hasn't traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. Despite the overwhelming rejection, separatist leaders vowed to continue pressing for independence. Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said. Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. Airman killed rappelling from Alamodome's ceiling in Salute to Armed Forces ceremony DOJ official clashes with judge in DC golf course case after Trump attacks her Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say At a separatist referendum night gathering at an Edmonton restaurant, the crowd fell quiet as results rolled in. “We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project. “We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.” Rath said before the vote that he would be thrilled with 30% support. He also said he wanted Smith ousted as UCP leader and believed the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party. Ian Brodie, a University of Calgary political scientist and former chief of staff to Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper, dismissed Rath and fellow separatist organizer Mitch Sylvestre as “nobodies,” saying they failed to gain traction even in a district that elected a separatist to Alberta’s legislature in 1982. “Even on a very soft question — whether to hold a referendum on separation — they couldn’t gain real traction," Brodie said. Edmonton voter Shawn Campbell said he voted to begin the separation process even though he doesn’t want Alberta to leave Canada. “It sends a message to Ottawa that Albertans are not happy,” he said. Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a “referendum on a referendum” rather than healthcare. With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united. Instead we’re fighting among ourselves.

events.title: The Secret Terms of Trump’s Venezuelan Oil Deal
events.summary: Alejandro Betancourt, a 46-year-old Venezuelan energy baron, is the key figure in a historic oil deal with the Trump administration. Venezuelan opposition leaders and U.S. congressional Democrats have criticized the agreement because Betancourt has been the target of investigations of alleged corruption. Antonio Heredia/El Mundo In late August, President Donald Trump announced what he called the “biggest oil deal in world history.” Since then, the full text of the accord — which grants the U.S. sweeping access to Venezuela’s oil reserves — has been one of the most sought-after secrets in Washington, D.C.  ProPublica has reviewed a copy of the 18-page strategic partnership agreement signed for the United States by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The document reveals carefully constructed terms that favor U.S. interests at every turn and cements the power of a small group of people handpicked by the Trump administration to govern and profit from the deal. The role of the Venezuelan government and the potential benefits to its people are largely absent from the text. One of the most criticized aspects of Trump’s announcement has been his choice of a partner: Alejandro Betancourt, a globe-trotting Venezuelan oligarch who has faced money-laundering investigations in three countries.  The Trump administration is taking a 35% stake in Betancourt’s firm, North American Blue Energy Partners, by acquiring shares in a Barbados-registered parent company. The deal document provides little information about the owners and investors behind the parent company, who could receive enormous wealth from the arrangement.  The agreement also safeguards Betancourt’s position as chief executive of NABEP and says the U.S. government will work with the parent company to appoint a powerful seven-member board to govern the venture for an initial 15-year term. Those aspects of the deal, according to people with knowledge of how it came together, were designed to prevent future U.S. and Venezuelan leaders from dismantling the enterprise.  Orlando Alvarado, a name not disclosed by the Trump administration as a party to the accord, signed the agreement on behalf of the parent company, alongside Betancourt, Hegseth and Rubio. Alvarado has held senior roles in multiple Betancourt businesses, including as chief financial officer of an energy firm that became embroiled in scandals a decade ago. According to the Miami Herald , federal prosecutors identified Alvarado as an unindicted co-conspirator in a scheme to embezzle money from Venezuela’s national oil company. NABEP spokesperson Terry Wade said that “neither Mr. Betancourt nor Mr. Alvarado has ever been charged with any crime in any country, and any claims against them are baseless.”  Do You Know More About This Topic? events.title: When AI models refuse to fight hackers
events.summary: In the race to fend off AI-enabled cyber threats , security teams are confronting a new problem: The AI models they rely on to investigate attacks can suddenly refuse to help. Why it matters: While AI giants race to build AI tools that can respond quickly to hacking or other malicious online threats, strict guardrails on their most powerful models lock out defenders mid-investigation, leaving them scrambling for alternatives at critical moments. What's happening: OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, said it was compromised over the weekend, allowing attackers to obtain API keys belonging to some customers, including keys for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google services. OpenCode said the breach was "related to a large scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users." OpenCode co-creator Dax Raad said attackers had been targeting its systems continuously for 48 hours, forcing the company to keep its own AI agents running around the clock to respond. OpenAI , Google and Anthropic have said they worked with affected customers to revoke exposed API keys and address unauthorized usage charges. Zoom in: Raad said on X that frontier AI models initially helped investigate the breach but then "started refusing." The models' safety restrictions reportedly began blocking requests as the investigation turned to potentially malicious code, even though OpenCode was trying to defend its own systems. OpenCode then gained access to OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted cybersecurity defenders access to models with fewer restrictions. "We definitely need to be more proactive and we've made so many improvements over the last few days," Raad wrote on X Monday. The big picture: The incident underscored a dilemma facing cybersecurity teams trying to figure out when to use powerful proprietary AI models, which come with built-in restrictions, or open-weight alternatives that offer greater control over how they're deployed. When Hugging Face discovered suspicious activity on its systems that it later linked to OpenAI's own agents, its security team turned to a Chinese open-weight model to help investigate after encountering restrictions on frontier models. Yes, but: AI companies maintain that they need to gate access to their most powerful models to ensure that malicious actors can't abuse their cyber capabilities. Between the lines: Cybersecurity teams will have to figure out how to balance the need for faster AI-powered defenses with restrictions designed to keep those same capabilities out of attackers' hands, Chris Jones, chief technology officer at Nightwing, told Axios. "We're all going to have to figure out how that race gets modulated over time," Jones said. "That's a big piece here." Go deeper : Anthropic and OpenAI are now cybersecurity's kingmakers

events.title: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes following call with Rubio
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners following recent Russian attacks that he said occurred without enough notice to Ukraine KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles following recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice , leaving civilians vulnerable. For at least a week , the Ukrainian leader has said that his country has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. Such intelligence, he said, saves lives by allowing the public to be alerted and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles. Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio . “We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I’m speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming,” Zelenskyy said on a visit to Norway. “So we are thankful to American side now that it works.” Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio acknowledged mutual frustration between the U.S. and Ukraine over intelligence sharing and weapons supplies but emphatically denied that the Trump administration has made any changes to previous policy on either issue. In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelenskyy sought more American and European help. Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff , who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war . Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with the Ukrainian president in Norway's capital. Gahr Støre said Witkoff planned to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders, exchange ideas from the Oslo meeting and share proposals from European and American colleagues. “Today was a good day for peace,” Stubb said. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow is willing to listen to new U.S. proposals about Ukraine but doesn’t expect any “miracle” from Washington. At the White House, President Donald Trump stepped up the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again . “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.” If that doesn’t happen, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing.” The conversation with Rubio came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes “some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us.” Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russian ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine. The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX’s satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations . Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia , a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow’s full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February. Zelenskyy said he had “a substantive conversation” with Rubio. “I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position,” Zelenskyy said on social media. events.title: Netflix posts higher Q3 profit but revenue growth worries pull shares lower
events.summary: Netflix, which announced layoff plans last week, posted a third-quarter profit above Wall Street’s expectations Netflix, which announced layoff plans last week, posted a third-quarter profit above Wall Street's expectations, but investors sent shares down after the streaming company lowered its ad sales guidance, prompting worries about slowing revenue growth. Netflix said Tuesday it earned $3.66 billion, or 87 cents per share, for the July-September period. That's up 44% from $2.55 billion, or 59 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 12% to $12.87 billion from $11.51 billion. Analysts surveyed by FactSet predicted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $12.87 billion. “With Netflix under pressure to find alternative lines of revenue beyond subscriptions, it’s concerning that the company lowered its estimate for its ad business,” said Emarketer senior analyst Ross Benes. “Revamping content strategy is not enough to fix this challenge but it is a worthwhile start. Guidance is not as aggressive as investors have grown accustomed to.” Last week, the Los Gatos, California-based company announced that it plans to lay off about 6% of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions, as the company makes wider “organizational changes.” At the end of 2025, per regulatory filings, Netflix had about 16,000 full-time employees worldwide. The most recent layoff announcement marks the biggest round of cuts that the company has rolled out in years. Netflix also announced last week that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. Bajaria was with Netflix for nearly a decade. Rice will lead Netflix’s global content organization, overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film, live events and more across all regions. He takes over the post on Oct. 26. While Netflix has benefited from membership sign-ups and price increases, the company is dealing with intense competition in the streaming sector from companies such as Amazon’s Prime Video and Disney+. There's also Skydance , after Paramount’s $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery put HBO Max and Paramount+ under the same roof. Netflix walked away from its offer to buy Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming business in February. The company is also competing for people's attention with YouTube and TikTok, where short videos are extremely popular.
