events.title: US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect
events.summary: Billionaires like Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Sundar Pichai and Elon Musk, pictured here at President Donald Trump's 2025 inauguration, have seen their wealth soar thanks to the stock market boom and beneficial tax changes. Chip Somodevilla/Pool Photo via AP The buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections may be affordability , but growing anger over inequality is behind the sentiment. A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans – including 4 in 10 Republicans – believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this. This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs. I’m an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices – including taxation and public spending – enabled this 40-year rise in inequality. Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%. Inequality by the numbers Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow . The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999. These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data. But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026. Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories. Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall . The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom. How taxes play a role Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive , often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats. The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – including international studies – doesn’t back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth. Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940 . While many voters cite affordability as a top concern, concerns over inequality have increasingly been part of this debate. AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from. Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership , allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash , usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares. By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%. The new drivers of inequality Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed. One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs. The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil. Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%. This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “ A Brief History of Equality ,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.” Markus Schneide

events.title: A scuff on your bag, a dent in your mug – and suddenly it feels like time for a new one
events.summary: Would this bother you? 500px/Getty Images Imagine you have a bag you really like. It felt like “the one” when you bought it. Over time, it starts to look worn. There are some scuffs on it. Nothing is actually wrong with the bag, and it still works exactly as it should. Yet, once you notice those imperfections, you start thinking about buying a new one to replace it. Consumers do this all the time. They replace phones that still work , furniture with a scratch and sweaters with a small snag. Often, what has changed is how people see these items. We are marketing researchers who study why people buy, use and get rid of stuff. This obsession with perfection began when one of us, Aprajita Gautam , moved from India to the U.S. in 2019. She was struck by how different the culture of buying and owning things was in the two countries. In our peer-reviewed research paper , published in August 2026 in the Journal of Consumer Research, we identified one reason for this pattern: Some people care much more than others about having flawless things. We call this penchant a desire for perfect products. Not the same as perfectionism We began by interviewing 17 people in Austin, Texas, in 2023. They included real estate agents, entrepreneurs, stay-at-home mothers and people employed by an nonprofit that promotes reuse. We asked them about their possessions and what made things seem perfect or imperfect. We then surveyed about 540 more people, some online and some in a university research lab. The results suggested that people who strongly preferred flawless items had more elaborate ideas about what their ideal product was and were sensitive to even small deviations from those ideas. Their standards also kept rising. Seeing something better than what they owned could raise the bar further for them. Next, we developed questions to assess how much people care about having flawless possessions. We used people’s answers to determine how strongly they desired perfect products. We also found that this tendency is related to but distinct from perfectionism . While perfectionists hold themselves to high or even impossible standards, people who want perfect stuff hold what they buy and own to lofty standards. You might easily shrug off a bad day at the office but be far less forgiving of a scratch on your new coffee table. For people who feel they have to own perfect products, even a small imperfection can overshadow everything else they like about something they own. Finally, we conducted 12 experiments where we recruited participants – University of Texas at Austin students and online workers participating in crowdsourcing marketplaces – to test the behavioral effects of the desire for perfect possessions. It can affect how you shop In our first online experiment, we asked 402 consumers across the country to imagine booking a hotel in California’s Napa Valley using filters like those on travel websites, such as star rating, Wi-Fi or a spa. Consumers who desired perfect products used more filters and set higher cutoffs, narrowing their search to hotels that came closer to meeting their standards. Newness itself also had value for them. In another online experiment with 301 consumers, those who cared most about owning flawless possessions were quicker to upgrade to the latest iPhone, even when it offered little real improvement over the previous one. This urge can be costly. It can mean paying extra for something new when the old one works fine, or spending more time searching for a product that meets every standard that may not actually matter. If you can live with imperfections, you can buy some of your stuff used. Moment/Getty Images Makes people less open to repairs This preference also affects what people do with the stuff they already own. In our next online experiment, we asked 1,004 U.S. participants to chose between two options: an insulated coffee mug and an insulated water bottle. When told that the product they chose had a small dent on the bottom, those who were most bothered by flaws in their possessions were more likely to swap it for the other option. We found a similar pattern with repairs . In an online experiment with 601 consumers, we found that those who want to own perfect products were less interested in fixing a broken keyboard when the replacement key wouldn’t match the color of the other keys. This highlights a problem with repairs that isn’t usually part of discussions about sustainable consumption : Fixing something can restore its function without necessarily making it look as good as new. A factor for donations Consumers with exacting standards for their things also applied their high standards to items they were getting rid of. In an experiment we conducted in a university behavioral lab, we asked 339 students to help with a “Clean Out Your Closet” drive. They examined pieces of clothing that others had discarded and sorted them into two bins: one to donate and one to recycle. Those who strongly preferred flawless items were less likely to donate imperfect but still usable clothing. This attitude can shorten a product’s useful life. That finding has implications for sustainability . Much of the academic research about sustainable consumption focuses on what people buy. But another way to consume less is to keep products in use longer. That becomes harder if small imperfections make otherwise useful products seem less valuable. Learning to value imperfection Our research suggests that how someone responds to flaws in their possessions can vary depending on what those flaws mean to them. We were inspired in part by the Japanese concept of wabi-sabi , which finds beauty and value in imperfection and change. In our final online experiment, 1,203 consumers learned about hoodies with subtle variations in color and pattern. When those variations were described as making each hoodie unique, consumers who love having perfect products responded less negatively to them. A mark on a well-used object can be seen as a flaw, but it can also become part of its history. And replacing products because of minor imperfections can lead consumers to waste their money. None of this means consumers should keep everything forever. Mugs break and clothing and shoes get worn out. Sometimes people simply want something new. But consider that bag again. Its scuffs could mean it is no longer the perfect bag you originally bought. Or they could mean you’ve carried it hundreds of times because you like it. The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

events.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
events.summary: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it's suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that's required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. Selon vous, quel secteur gagnerait le plus à retrouver cette clarté avant que la pression ne décide à sa place ? AI is making it possible to discover new materials much faster. But how quickly can we test them under real working conditions? A promising discovery still has to prove itself in manufacturing, installation, and years of everyday use. I wonder if our ability to validate these discoveries will keep up with the speed of AI. 🔹 Discovery speed in a lab usually depends on how quickly one result changes the next decision so the compute helps only as far as that loop is clean. Simulation is one thing. How do the lab teams handle prioritizing the candidate batches? How can a common man from Nigeria meet with you? A year's worth of gathering research, done in just a couple of hours with Microsoft Discovery. That's an incredible head start for Saint-Gobain's scientists. More time to test new ideas for making cement with fewer emissions. Spot on, Satya Nadella! Integrating advanced technology and AI-driven platforms to accelerate the development of sustainable, low-carbon materials is critical for heavy industries. In industrial governance and asset management, addressing the heavy carbon footprint of sectors like construction requires transitioning from reactive emission controls to systemic material science innovation. Leveraging digital discovery tools to optimize the lifecycle and efficiency of critical materials bridges the gap between ambitious climate targets and practical, large-scale execution. From an industrial strategy perspective, what key scaling framework do you find most effective to ensure that AI-accelerated material innovations move swiftly from laboratory discovery to widespread deployment in heavy infrastructure? This is a great example of the concrete, mutually beneficial partnership between our two companies, of which we are very proud: Saint-Gobain’s solutions and scientific expertise can also contribute to the development of more efficient, resilient and lower-carbon data centers. events.title: A concrete vision: Saint-Gobain and Microsoft Discovery build for the future
events.summary: PARIS — Saint-Gobain’s business is construction materials. It got its start in 1665, when King Louis XIV charged the company with making the mirrors for his lavish new palace in Versailles. And he needed a lot of mirrors. The idea was to break the monopoly that glass-making power Venice had at the time, cutting costs and improving efficiency. These days, Saint-Gobain has 161,000 employees in 81 countries making construction materials — glass is still important, but there’s also gypsum for plaster board, insulation and concrete admixtures and cement additives. These last elements — products for cement and concrete — represent one of the company’s most important product groups, and like glass in 1665, one of the most challenging. Cement production uses a lot of energy, and accounts for around 7% of annual CO2 emissions globally. Saint-Gobain is looking for chemical elements that could reduce those carbon emissions and improve the strength of cement. “It would have taken our researchers a year to create the knowledge base. Using AI, it took us a couple of hours.” Mojdeh Rastgoo-Lemaitre, a digital acceleration program manager at Saint-Gobain, said that using Microsoft Discovery saved months of time for researchers working to improve an additive for cement. Photo by Chris Welsch for Microsoft. So, when the company’s researchers collaborated with engineers from Microsoft earlier this year in using Microsoft Discovery , a new AI-powered agentic platform for scientists and engineers, to find solutions, the results stunned them. “We actually gathered 62,000 patents and 44,000 abstracts,” says Mojdeh Rastgoo-Lemaitre, a digital acceleration program manager overseeing the project to find lower-carbon, less expensive options. “Without using this technology, it would have taken our researchers a year to create the knowledge base. Using AI, it took us a couple of hours.” With a broad smile, she says Microsoft Discovery helped the team to narrow the data, analyze some novel possibilities in the chemistry involved and come up with several hypotheses about new ingredients for cement additives worth testing in about six weeks. A breakthrough in how research is done “So, yes, the researchers are very happy with Discovery,” Rastgoo-Lemaitre says. “It’s a great tool to help them have new ideas, and to go faster.” Saint-Gobain was one of Microsoft’s first clients to use Discovery in private release in March of this year, and teams from both companies worked on fine-tuning the platform. The team from Microsoft was from a new operating business called the Microsoft Frontier Company, which places Microsoft engineers inside companies like Saint-Gobain to deliver solutions using AI applications and tools like Microsoft Discovery. Discovery lets scientists orchestrate AI agents to search literature, connect information, generate hypotheses, design experiments and run analyses. “The construction industry, from production to running, is 40% of the world’s carbon footprint,” Ursula Soritsch-Renier, chief digital and information officer at Saint-Gobain says. “We’re not going to stop constructing, but we can make change, and who is better placed to do that than us?” She says Saint-Gobain is embracing technology as a means to cut waste, reduce energy use and be more efficient. The efforts to decarbonize the making of cement is just one illustration, she says. “You don’t just push technology for the sake of technology. You need to always understand the ‘why’ and the ‘what for’.” Ursula Soritsch-Reiner, chief digital and information officer, at Saint-Gobain’s headquarters in Paris. Photo by Chris Welsch for Microsoft. Technology that creates real-world impact For example, Saint-Gobain has changed the way it delivers plaster board to construction sites. Before, it came in a standard size, and workers cut the board to fit the rooms being built. But the leftovers just went to the dump. “We have now a cut-to-order system,” Soritsch-Renier says. “So, we get the building information model, we optimize the cuts, then nothing goes to the landfill.” She says the new system improved time-to-installation by 30%. “In construction, time is money,” she says. “And the environment wins because in the end it is less raw material and less energy. And that’s thanks to the digital tools we’re using.” Microsoft has been a key partner, Soritsch-Renier says, and the framework agreement the two companies signed in July will benefit both companies by accelerating the search for sustainable construction materials and processes. “You don’t just push technology for the sake of technology,” she says. “You need to always understand the ‘why’ and the ‘what for.’ And with that understanding you develop and you evolve and you push things forward with new tools, like with the research platform.” Saint-Gobain’s efforts to embrace cutting-edge technology took another step at the beginning of September, when it appointed Annica Hagen to a newly created role as the company’s first chief artificial intelligence officer. She will work with Soritsch-Renier to define how AI can support the Saint-Gobain Group’s strategic plan. “It’s important not to talk about AI as a means to an end,” Hagen says. “It’s an enablement to get where we want to go. My main task is to enable growth — and how can we use AI to enable that? Now is the time to shape the future.” Annica Hagen is the new (and first) chief artificial intelligence officer at Saint-Gobain. Photo by Chris Welsch for Microsoft. An exciting time to be an applied scientist Rastgoo-Lemaitre says the teams at Saint-Gobain’s Innovation Hub Europe in the Parisian suburb of Aubervilliers were already thinking about other projects where they could apply Discovery, but that research and development on the cement additives would continue. Saint-Gobain already has a cement-additive called EnviroAdd that reduces the need for clinker in cement by about 20%. Clinker is the ingredient in cement that binds, and it’s made by super-heating limestone, which is where the production of CO2 is most significant. By searching across domains outside of the construction industry, Rastgoo-Lemaitre says, the scientists using Discovery were able to find some molecules they otherwise would not have considered. The idea is to create a new chemical additive that could further reduce the need for clinker in cement while making it stronger. “They are right now testing those molecules for the behaviors and chemistry they are looking for,” she says. If the potential bears up under scrutiny, the next steps would be passing the potential solution to the development team, which would test the additive in physical conditions. A new era of discovery at Saint-Gobain “Every day that I’m using AI today, I think, if I had only had this my life would have been so much easier, and I could have done so much more.” Silvia Mariani is the managing director of the Saint-Gobain Innovation Hub Europe in Aubervilliers, France.

events.title: Advancing digital sovereignty with greater control and choice
events.summary: Oct 20, 2026 | Douglas Phillips - President and Chief Technology Officer, Microsoft Specialized Clouds Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require. This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate. Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work. A continuum of control, built around the workload Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model. Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. Organizations can apply the level of control appropriate to each workload while maintaining a consistent approach to governance and operations across their digital estate. Sovereign Public Cloud adds capabilities for workloads that require greater control and transparency while continuing to benefit from the scale and innovation of Azure. Sovereign Private Cloud extends cloud capabilities into customer-operated environments, including connected and disconnected operations. The Sovereign Partner Ecosystem broadens the continuum through independently operated environments, specialized partners, locally relevant expertise and technologies that support customers’ sovereignty requirements. These are not isolated destinations. Customers can combine public cloud, private cloud and partner capabilities across their digital estate, applying different levels of control to different workloads as their operating needs evolve. Making control more visible in Sovereign Public Cloud For many workloads, the public cloud provides a combination of scale, innovation, integrated security and compliance. Organizations can benefit from these capabilities while applying additional sovereignty controls for residency, confidentiality, operator access, policy and continuity. Our work in Sovereign Public Cloud makes these controls easier to understand, apply and demonstrate. Sovereign Control Panel , entering public preview at Microsoft Ignite, brings these signals together in a unified Azure portal experience. It helps organizations understand their sovereignty posture, apply and manage controls, identify gaps and risks and take action to address them. It also supports business continuity readiness by helping customers understand workload dependencies and assess portability across operating environments when required. This visibility complements controls across the operator-access lifecycle. Just-in-time Access and Customer Lockbox give customers additional control over access to their environments. For customers in the European Union (EU) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), we are rolling out Data Guardian , which adds European-resident oversight by a trusted EU partner for qualifying Microsoft engineer remote access to in-scope production systems. Production Touch Ledger , also launched with phased rollout in the EU and EFTA, creates tamper-evident records of that access and the actions performed. Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM) already gives customers dedicated, single-tenant protection and control over the encryption keys used by supported Azure services. Last year, we committed to extending that control beyond Microsoft infrastructure. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, allowing customers to keep the root encryption key in hardware they own and operate on-premises or through a trusted third party. This gives organizations another option for workloads that require physical control of key hardware outside Microsoft infrastructure. Azure confidential computing helps protect supported data while it is processed in a hardware-based and attested trusted execution environment. We are also increasing transparency into the technologies that underpin that trust. Azure Confidential Clean Rooms , now in limited preview, applies confidential computing to approved multiparty collaboration, allowing participants to analyze shared sensitive data while limiting broader exposure of the underlying information. Together, these capabilities provide additional technical and operational controls that can support a broader digital sovereignty strategy aligned to an organization’s legal, policy, security, resilience and business requirements. Designing for resilience and operational independence For some workloads, digital sovereignty also means maintaining critical operations as connectivity, geopolitical and operating conditions change. Resilience must be designed from the start so essential workloads can continue operating through disruption. To help customers prepare for these scenarios, we are publishing new sovereign business continuity guidance and architecture patterns . These resources help organizations translate resilience requirements into architectures they can plan, implement and test before they are needed. For many workloads, the scale and geographic reach of the public cloud provide a strong foundation for resilience across locations and operating conditions.

events.title: The AI boom doesn’t answer to the Fed
events.summary: Liz’s view One rule of investing is “don’t fight the Fed.” Playing the contrarian to the Federal Reserve’s plans to stimulate or dampen the economy only ends badly. But Big Tech is not run by rule-followers. AI giants have been almost willfully indifferent to the rising cost of money. Rates go higher, and they borrow more. It’s a problem for the Federal Reserve, which is trying to tamp down inflation that, as Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee told us last week , is “jumping out of its lane” — spreading from AI-linked sectors into unrelated parts of the economy. The Fed’s main lever, at least so far, isn’t working. Mark Zuckerberg and Dario Amodei aren’t giddy consumers whose spending cools when borrowing gets expensive. They see themselves as great men of history, securing super intelligence for the West and ushering in an age of intergalactic abundance. They also believe customer spending on AI has only just begun, and so the coming revenue can justify their investments. That kind of existential drive can’t be discouraged by an extra 75 basis points of bond interest. Both the AI companies and the Fed are desperate for goodwill and credibility. If mortgages cost 15% and hyperscalers are still spending like there’s no tomorrow, people are going to be very mad at both of them. Notable Speaking at the IMF annual meeting in Bangkok last week, Warsh recognized that AI investment was creating a “shock” on prices, but reiterated his conviction that the technology would bring wealth and productivity in future.

events.title: Qatar is ramping up liquefied natural gas exports as prices surge
events.summary: There are more signs that Qatar is ramping up liquefied natural gas exports as prices surge and inventories dwindle ahead of the Northern Hemisphere winter. One tanker is now sailing toward Poland through the Red Sea, according to Bloomberg, and at least 20 more shipments have passed through the Strait of Hormuz to other destinations since early September. The gas could help halt the surge in consumer prices and slow the decline of Qatar’s $200 billion economy, which the IMF expects to contract by 15.6% this year. It’s unclear how the LNG is getting out: Qatar’s prime minister said last month that buyers had negotiated passage with Iran for the few cargoes that made it through during the first six months of the war. But Doha also seems to have adopted the “Hormuz shuttle” strategy Gulf crude exporters are using. Tracing the journey of Al Rayyan, one of Qatar’s oldest LNG tankers, Bloomberg tracked the vessel transferring its cargo to another ship in the Gulf of Oman before returning to Ras Laffan to reload. LNG ship-to-ship transfers are more complex than oil transfers, requiring cryogenic hoses to handle gas chilled to minus 162 C (minus 260 F). The effort is paying off, however: QatarEnergy restored LNG exports in September to about a third of prewar levels, Bloomberg reported. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Airlines shun reopened Riyadh airport after last week’s attacks
events.summary: Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport officially reopened on Sunday, but most scheduled flights have been canceled so far this week. Saudi authorities require airlines to get prior permission for every flight , according to a NOTAM issued over the weekend, while US and European regulators are warning carriers about the kingdom’s airspace. Lufthansa has suspended flights until Nov. 18, Cathay Pacific until the end of January, and Delta has pushed back the launch of its Atlanta route to March 2027. Attacks on Riyadh’s airport damaged six aircraft with a combined insured value of about $375 million, The Wall Street Journal reported, prompting Saudi carriers to evacuate aircraft worth up to $4 billion from the city. Many travelers are now driving to Bahrain, Qatar, and the UAE to catch commercial flights, while the wealthy are paying a premium of more than 50% compared to prewar rates to fly private out of al-Qassim airport, an almost four hour drive north of Riyadh, according to the Financial Times. — Ed Clowes

events.title: Trump isn't out to hurt Ukraine, Rubio tells Zelensky
events.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in a phone call Tuesday that President Trump hasn't issued any kind of order to harm Ukraine. Why it matters: The call was an effort to prevent the crisis between the U.S. and Ukraine from escalating further — and to push back on Ukrainian accusations that Trump is trying to coerce Zelensky into making concessions to Russia. The 45-minute call took place several hours ahead of a new round of peace talks with White House envoy Steve Witkoff aimed at reaching a unified position with European allies on an updated peace proposal to present to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Driving the news: The crisis broke out 10 days ago when Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia at the same time his envoys were in negotiations with Ukrainian officials in Miami. Zelensky on Monday lobbied a bipartisan group of senators to press the Trump administration to remove what he says are restrictions on intelligence sharing and weapons supplies. Behind the scenes: Rubio told reporters on Tuesday that he clarified to Zelensky that the Pentagon hasn't changed anything when it comes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine, weapons sales or restrictions on the use of the Starshield satellite system. "No change was ordered. It is not true that we restricted it," Rubio said. Rubio acknowledged to Zelensky that there could be a delay in sending Patriot interceptors that have already been paid for by NATO countries. But the reason, he said, is that the U.S. needs to make sure it has enough to protect its own military bases around the world. "Nothing is being deliberately denied. We balance between our obligations to partners and our own needs," he said. "There hasn't been a deliberate political directive to harm Ukraine." Rubio also asserted that the several cases in which Ukraine didn't get advance warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks were a result of technical failures, not a U.S. order. What he's saying: "No doubt there are tensions," he said. "That is why we had the call. The president is frustrated. The president is responding to the insinuation that he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine, which is not fair and not true." Rubio said Trump is "angry and frustrated" about the lack of progress in peace talks between Russia and Ukraine after two years of efforts. The other side: Zelensky wrote on X after the call that he is "grateful" for Rubio's "readiness to help and his clear position." He said Ukraine needs ballistic missile interceptors and early warnings to protect Ukrainian citizens and stressed that "the situation with Starlink and Starshield needs to be restored." State of play: Witkoff arrived in Oslo on Tuesday for talks with Zelensky and European leaders. The talks there are expected to include Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, President of Finland Alexander Stubb, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO. Following Oslo, Witkoff plans to travel to Russia to meet with Putin and present ideas developed in consultation with Ukrainian and European leaders.

Text of this article October 20, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Apple announces new American Manufacturing Program partners for iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro From U.S. titanium to advanced camera technology, American suppliers are producing key components in the latest iPhone lineup CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced new and expanded partnerships with American companies that are supplying critical materials and components for iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro. Through its American Manufacturing Program (AMP), Apple is partnering with Perryman Company, a Pennsylvania-based titanium producer, to supply titanium for Apple products, including iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics, headquartered in Delaware, to produce technology for the new variable aperture in the iPhone 18 Pro camera system — the most advanced Apple has ever made. Apple works with suppliers in all 50 states and supports more than 450,000 American jobs. Last year, the company deepened that commitment by launching AMP, aimed at bringing even more advanced manufacturing and critical component production to the United States as part of Apple’s $600 billion, four-year commitment to U.S. manufacturing and innovation. “We’re thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America,” said Sabih Khan, Apple’s chief operating officer. “American ingenuity is vital to all our products, from the titanium crafted for iPhone Duo to breakthrough camera innovations in iPhone 18 Pro. We’re proud to work with Perryman and Qnity Electronics to continue expanding our American Manufacturing Program and support U.S. jobs.” The grade 5 titanium enclosure on iPhone Duo is exceptionally strong, providing amazing durability to the first foldable iPhone. Apple will commit up to $100 million over the next three years with Perryman, a family-owned business and a global leader in manufacturing specialty titanium products. At its site in Houston, Pennsylvania, Perryman melts, forges, and rolls titanium with a minimum of 80 percent recycled content for iPhone Duo. Apple is also expanding its partnership with Qnity Electronics to build key camera technology for iPhone 18 Pro in the U.S. Qnity, which joined the American Manufacturing Program in March, will produce advanced films essential to the new variable aperture camera system on iPhone 18 Pro. Variable aperture is at the heart of the new 48MP Fusion Main camera, which enables incredible light and depth control. It’s powered by on-device intelligence that automatically lets in more light for darker settings and helps get sharper detail in brighter ones. Nearly 100 components in iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro — from wireless chips to the silicon that powers key functions across the devices — are produced by American companies and drawn from suppliers in more than a dozen states. That footprint continues to grow, empowering partners across the country to bring new capabilities online: Broadcom is expanding and modernizing its Fort Collins, Colorado, facility under a $1.5 billion capital investment announced in July, producing advanced radio frequency components for a wide range of Apple products. The multiyear agreement will produce more than 15 billion U.S.-made chips. Corning , an Apple partner since the original iPhone in 2007, produces specialty glass for Apple in Harrodsburg, Kentucky, including Ceramic Shield. By the end of 2026, all of the cover glass for iPhone — including iPhone Duo — and Apple Watch sold worldwide will be produced at this facility. Coherent continues building on its multiyear agreement with Apple, supplying new vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser technology from its Sherman, Texas, facility. This technology enables Face ID and other key features across iPhone and iPad, including the redesigned, even more useful Dynamic Island on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. TSMC ’s Arizona fab continues to scale its production of advanced chips used across a range of Apple products, including iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch — producing more than 100 million chips for Apple in 2026. Construction on the north campus is progressing as Apple’s partnership with TSMC in Arizona grows. Amkor Technology broke ground on its first high-volume packaging and test facility in Peoria, Arizona, in September 2025, and began shell construction earlier this year. Phases 1 and 2 of the project are expected to support a workforce of more than 3,500 local hires. Apple will be one of the facility’s first customers, marking another step toward expanding the scope of U.S. advanced manufacturing.

events.title: South Africa fears end of US trade deal amid growing rift
events.summary: South Africa’s president said the country must prepare for a future where it loses preferential trade access to the US because of the growing rift between the nations. Relations have deteriorated since US President Donald Trump cut aid to Africa, expelled Pretoria’s ambassador, and falsely accused South Africa of carrying out a genocide against its white population. Though South Africa’s president has tried to mend ties, he nevertheless warned the continent’s largest economy could be removed from the US’ duty-free trade program when the deal is renegotiated in 2028. In response, Pretoria is looking to boost trade with China and India , though a flood of cheap imports from the former has angered domestic producers . — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.summary: The US banned Chinese AI firm DeepSeek from most government systems and asked agencies to remove all technology built with it, as competition for AI supremacy between the superpowers heats up. events.title: French debt costs spiral as political and fiscal crises grow
events.summary: French government bonds again sold off on growing concern that cascading political and fiscal crises would hammer the EU’s second-biggest economy and potentially ripple across the bloc. Spreads between French 10-year debt and the German equivalent — Europe’s benchmark — widened to their highest since 2012 , reflecting the risk premium markets are demanding following a weekend in which parts of France were enveloped in violent protest ; the country also faces a huge debt burden and the prospect of a far-right leader taking the presidency. Morningstar analysts noted the demonstrations would make it harder to bridge France’s budgetary shortfall, while Commerzbank warned that “this is not just idiosyncratic French selling, but [reflects] concerns about a global debt crisis.” — Prashant Rao

events.title: For investors, the Iran war redefined energy security
events.summary: Nearly eight months of war in Iran have produced one of the most severe energy shocks in decades, exposing a sharp divide between the countries that absorbed it with surprising ease and those forced into painful tradeoffs. Resilience, it turns out, comes less from any single technology or policy than from systems-level thinking, long-term investment, and deliberate planning. The countries that coped best were not always those with the most energy resources. They were the ones that had built flexibility, redundancy, and alternative pathways into their energy systems. China drew on strategic reserves, alternative pipeline imports, and fuel switching. The US benefited from record domestic oil and gas production, regional storage and solar to improve summer grid stability, and secure North American supply chains. Highly electrified countries such as Norway relied on hydropower, heat pumps, EVs, and infrastructure located far from the conflict zone. Emerging markets fared worse. Bangladesh and Pakistan imposed electricity restrictions and other demand-reduction measures. Wealthier economies across Europe and Asia largely avoided shortages only by paying sharply higher prices for LNG and other fuels. The dividing line ran not between producers and consumers, but between countries with options and countries without them. Three lessons stand out for governments and investors: Domestic electrons are safer electrons. The principle is straightforward: The shorter and more secure the energy chain, the fewer vulnerabilities a country carries into a crisis. Energy that is produced, generated, or stored at home is often more reliable than energy that must travel through vulnerable supply chains and geopolitical chokepoints. Few countries can achieve outright energy independence, but all of them can reduce their exposure to single points of failure. Solar and storage have scaled quickly in recent years on cost and technical readiness alone. Some producers will expand oil and gas output as demand shifts away from the Middle East to places with safer access to global trade routes. The Iran war is also unlocking public and private money for nuclear and geothermal energy. Nuclear deserves renewed attention as both an energy and national security asset, since reactors provide reliable electricity largely insulated from short-term geopolitical shocks. Small modular reactors could go further, supplying dependable power close to military installations, advanced manufacturing facilities, and AI data centers. Meanwhile, breakthroughs in deep drilling and new enhanced geothermal systems could vastly expand access to around-the-clock power beyond “traditional geothermal regions.” Electrification is now as much a security strategy as a climate strategy. Every domestically produced electron reduces exposure to disruptions in global fuel markets. That shifts the burden onto the grid. The challenge is no longer simply generating enough power. It is building the systems required to deliver that power where and when it is needed. The US electric grid is one of the largest on Earth, and it is aging rapidly. Some 70% of transmission lines are more than 25 years old, and the average large power transformer has been in service for nearly four decades. Demand for transformers has surged, yet the US has only one domestic producer of the specialized electrical steel needed for transformer cores. In 2025, 80% of power transformer supply and 50% of the distribution supply parts came from abroad. The American workforce is thinning too. The power sector will need more than 500,000 additional workers by 2030, just as hundreds of thousands of existing energy sector employees retire. Permitting compounds the problem: Major US infrastructure projects can take four to five years to secure approvals, delaying as much as $1.5 trillion in investment. As energy supply struggles to keep pace with demand, those delays have drawn political attention and, finally, action, including significant legislation passed at the state level and a new bipartisan permitting reform bill proposed in the Senate. The countries that cope best with the next crisis will not necessarily be those that build the most infrastructure. They will be the ones that make the best use of what they already have. Not every energy security challenge can wait a decade for a new power plant, transmission corridor, or major industrial project. In the US, with its aging grid infrastructure and rapidly growing power demand, that constraint bites. But many of the answers already exist: Long-duration batteries can store electricity during periods of surplus and release it when shortages emerge. Grid-enhancing technologies can raise transmission capacity, ease congestion, and improve the efficiency of existing assets. Smart-grid software and demand-management tools can shift consumption away from periods of peak stress without new steel in the ground. Every crisis is said to carry opportunity. The lesson from 2026 is that the most successful energy systems of the next decade will not merely generate more power. They will store it better, move it more efficiently, and protect it more successfully.

events.title: Oil prices hit five-month high as Houthi escalation worsens supply and inflation fears
events.summary: Oil prices hit a five-month high on Tuesday after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen continued attacking Saudi Arabia, further stoking concerns over supply and higher inflation that could prompt interest rate increases. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was trading 1.52 per cent higher at $111.30 per barrel at 2.27pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 2.30 per cent to $100.80 a barrel. Crude prices were last at these levels in mid-May. On Friday, Brent hit $110 for the first time since May, while WTI topped $100 for the first time in a month. The Houthis claimed responsibility for renewed strikes on ⁠Saudi energy, airport and military targets ⁠on Monday, escalating tension in the region and bringing down stock markets in the Gulf. The rebels claimed to have carried out six attacks on the kingdom, which included strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, a military airbase near Abha International Airport, a naval task-force camp and a Saudi radar in Bir Askar. With the US-Iran conflict continuing, crude supplies from the Middle East remain choked, prompting moves to ensure adequate supplies globally. The International Energy Agency last week said it had agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel to the market amid a surge in diesel prices. Gulf oil producers, meanwhile, have pushed tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashed prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around the Strait of Hormuz buckles under congestion and persistent attacks . The fighting has kept energy prices elevated, nudging inflation upwards and, in turn, raising the probability of another interest rate increase by the US Federal Reserve, which is scheduled to meet next week. Analysts are now expecting a second straight raise as Fed officials seek to tame inflation. "Brent crude hovering near five-month highs following geopolitical tensions in the Middle East has reignited fears of sticky inflation," analysts at US energy company Duncan Oil said. "Surging energy costs have led investors to believe the Fed will keep interest rates higher for longer to tame inflation." Ship movements in the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war made up a fifth of the world's energy exports, remain under pressure. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday that Washington was willing to allow oil tankers placed under sanctions to begin a process to legitimately ship crude. Analytics firm Kpler said easing sanctions on the shadow fleet would have little effect on record freight rates. It estimated that, as of Monday, only 24 of the nearly 160 vessels under sanctions from the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control could return to mainstream trade after taking into account their age and ownership restrictions. Wholesale diesel, meanwhile, already surpassed $200 per gallon in Singapore and hit roughly $220 in Europe and the US, the Paris-based IEA said last week.

events.title: Tesla’s Roadster represents a feat, and a defeat
events.summary: Andy’s view The new Tesla Roadster is science fiction: It can zoom into the air, perform barrel rolls, and then plop down softly using cold-gas rocket thrusters. Unveiled last week at a rocket facility in Texas, the Roadster is a triumph of engineering — an exquisite toy for the super-rich, if it ever reaches production (the disclaimers on the advance orders suggest CEO Elon Musk himself has doubts). Yet, paradoxically, it also represents a defeat: The Roadster isn’t a vehicle that will turn the tables on China, outcompeting the likes of BYD in the consumer market. Instead, it represents the future in another way, one in which China owns global mass manufacturing not just in cars but everything else — machine tools, pharmaceuticals, ships. As low-priced Chinese exports swamp global markets, politicians from Washington to Brussels to Berlin diagnose the problem largely as one of Chinese overproduction, and are putting up trade barriers to protect their domestic industries. The EU and China, for example, recently agreed to set quotas with tariffs for Chinese hybrid cars, and are considering similar restrictions on other industrial categories. But this misses the broader challenge. China’s surging shipments are much more than just surplus production, the difference between what comes out of Chinese factories and what can be sold domestically in a sagging economy. They are a deliberate strategy, clearly stated in the country’s five-year industrial plans and, ultimately, represent China’s quest for national power. The implication for Western industry leaders is existential: They can either climb the technological ladder into increasingly rarefied niches — like Tesla, with its Roadster — or risk being destroyed by Chinese rivals, as is currently happening to Volkswagen in China, still its largest single market. In fact, influential Chinese strategists don’t recognize the concept of overproduction at all. Lu Feng, a professor at Peking University’s School of Government, sees a showdown on the way between China’s “industrial socialism” and the US’ “financial capitalism” — and he warns that caving to foreign pressure to curb “overproduction” would be “ tying our own hands .” In this way of thinking, since China’s desire for power is limitless, there can be no question of producing too much. Kyle Chan, a researcher specializing in China’s industrial policies at the Brookings Institution, labels Lu’s brand of economic nationalism, “industrial maximalism.” Perhaps, then, we should call the Roadster a prime example of its opposite: “industrial minimalism.” Among leading global automakers, Tesla had the best chance of owning the future of mobility. Indeed, its Shanghai gigafactory, built in 2019, and the local supply chains it developed were a catalyst for the entire Chinese EV industry. But Musk is now clear-eyed about the competition he helped spawn. Without trade barriers, he warned in 2024, China would “pretty much demolish most other car companies in the world.” Musk is now betting Tesla’s future on becoming a robot maker. But he’ll run into the same issues in that sector, too. The challenge from China is systemic, not industry specific. The country’s industrial machine is set up to commoditize products through overwhelming economies of scale, to bring down prices, and conquer global markets — regardless of financial return. This is not about profit maximization. It’s about power maximization. Writing in The Guardian, the tech reporter Chang Che, who recently visited 11 Chinese robot makers across five cities, sees a future where the US leverages its advanced research capabilities to try to build the ultimate robotic machine — one that can “mow your lawn, walk your dog, and babysit your children” — while China cranks out functioning robots for each of those tasks at a fraction of the price . Already, China accounts for 60% of all the world’s new factory robots. It also has the capacity to supply 100% of global demand for EVs. Michael Dunne, the author of the forthcoming , told The Wall Street Journal that what remains for Western carmakers “ is to move up or get pushed out. ” The Tesla Roadster is, quite literally, aiming for the skies. Other carmakers will have to make a similar vertical ascent, or bite the dust. Notable Zeroing in on the term “ scenario innovation ,” a recent Sinocities article explained China’s state-sponsored process of opening up real spaces, like roads and factories, so that companies can test new technologies in real-world settings.

events.title: European Leaders Turn to NVIDIA Vera CPUs to Build Local Infrastructure
events.summary: Nebius and Nscale are among global technology partners looking to NVIDIA Vera CPUs to build the next wave of infrastructure. Their momentum reflects rapid advancements in agentic computing. Agents do more than generate answers: they retrieve information, run software tools, execute code and evaluate results. Each step depends on fast CPU processing. Vera accelerates that work, helping agents respond faster and enabling data centers to make better use of computing capacity. Vera is designed to sustain that speed even when running thousands of tasks simultaneously, helping organizations expand services without trading responsiveness for scale. Building Europe’s Computing Capacity AI cloud providers Nebius , Nscale and Verda are building with Vera to support the growing computing needs of businesses and developers. High-performance, energy-efficient CPUs help these providers scale the data processing and software execution behind services, alongside the GPUs running models. The broader sovereign AI ecosystem also includes Aleria , a sovereign AI infrastructure and platform provider, supporting demand for infrastructure that keeps data and operations under customers’ control. Server manufacturers Bull , Dell Technologies , HPE , Lenovo and Supermicro are building Vera-based systems, giving customers more deployment options for their high-performance computing and AI data centers. Vera can power standalone CPU servers or work alongside NVIDIA GPUs in accelerated systems, supporting different workloads and deployment needs. Data processing companies ClickHouse , Cloudera , Duck Labs , Elastic , Polars , Redpanda , SAP and Starburst observed strong results on Vera for analytical, extract-transform-and-load and semantic search workloads in early testing. Vera’s per-core performance, LPDDR5X memory bandwidth and NVIDIA Scalable Coherency Fabric help achieve performance gains across the board. Software and developer-platform companies Atlassian, Inherent and Nous Research are adopting Vera for environments where AI agents work alongside developers and researchers. Atlassian is looking to Vera to accelerate the data processing that builds semantic search indexes for its AI-powered products; Inherent has tested Vera and is looking to adopt it for environments where AI agents work alongside engineers on novel scientific research; and Nous Research uses Vera to authenticate agent identities and validate every action before it executes, keeping deployments secure as agent fleets grow. Baseten-Blaxel , Daytona, E2B, Modal, Prime Intellect and Vercel provide cloud-based sandboxes, which serve as computers for AI agents, and are building on Vera to power the infrastructure agents depend on to execute code, run tools and test results. Every agent needs a secure, isolated sandbox that can be provisioned instantly, and because sandboxes spin up millions of times a day, the speed of each individual startup cycle compounds at scale. Vera’s fast per-core performance and high-bandwidth memory make it well suited to this pattern, giving sandbox providers the throughput not only to spin up sandboxes but to run agentic workloads at maximum scale without interruption. events.title: Europe to see 'biggest-ever' increase in air fares next year, Ryanair chief says
events.summary: Ryanair Holdings chief executive Michael O’Leary has forecast a record increase in European air fares next year as the Middle East war continues to push up oil prices , forcing airlines to pass on their fuel costs to consumers. Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20 per cent next year, Mr O’Leary told a news conference in Brussels on Tuesday. As a result, airline margins will be squeezed because even the jump in fuel surcharges won’t make up for the higher oil bill, he said. “You’re going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say in history, in Europe in the next 12 months,” Mr O’Leary said. “The question is, will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don’t think it will be.” The comments by the head of Europe’s largest budget carrier add to the more pessimistic outlook for the aviation industry, which has been forced to contend with a dramatic rise in costs even as travellers continue to splurge on air tickets. Mr O’Leary said most European airlines, including his own, lack significant hedging next year to protect against higher oil prices. In addition, there’s less capacity in the market as some airlines struggle, while higher taxes are further dimming the picture for the industry. “We’re 85 per cent unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said. Ryanair's shares dropped as much as 2.1 per cent, bringing the decline to 25 per cent for the year. At that rate, that would be the worst annual stock return since 2018. The chief executive used his news conference to dish out against regulation in markets such as France and Belgium, where Ryanair will reduce its footprint in response to higher taxes. He repeated that the European aviation industry will continue to consolidate as weaker players struggle to survive in a high-cost environment. Air Baltic and Spain’s Volotea are the latest European carriers to undergo restructuring as higher costs take their toll. Last week, Deutsche Lufthansa won the race against Air France-KLM to acquire a stake in Portugal’s state-owned TAP. Meanwhile, US private equity firm Apollo Global Management is laying out the framework to take over EasyJet. Airlines across the world have suffered from soaring jet fuel costs since the Iran war began in late February. Ryanair’s most recent earnings in July showed the conflict hit its profit and caused later bookings amid concern about jet-fuel supply availability. Mr O’Leary said separately that he aims to receive the first delivery of the carrier’s Boeing Max 10 aircraft in January, with about 16 more expected up to April.

Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze. In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama ’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves. events.title: 'Gulf security is our security', says former UK defence secretary
events.summary: Britain should do more to help its allies in the Gulf, including considering strikes on the Houthis , because Washington's priorities have changed and its partners must now stand together, former UK defence secretary Sir Michael Fallon has told The National . The US , he said, is “shifting its priorities to homeland defence, to the Indo-Pacific. And therefore, it means that in terms of Washington, perhaps Europe and the Middle East count for less than they used to”. That shift is structural, not a passing mood. “We've also seen a change in the United States,” Sir Michael said, recalling a country that “helped us win two world wars in Europe”. With the Gulf and Europe pushed down Washington's list of priorities, the burden falls on the allies. “I think we should be doing more,” he said. “These are our partners and friends, and we should be helping more.” For Britain, that means being ready to act against the Houthis . “That means, if necessary, we should be prepared to consider strikes as we did two years ago” he said, alongside the US and other European nations, as in the joint US-UK air campaign against Houthi targets that began in January 2024. Sir Michael, who served as the defence secretary from 2014 to 2017 under prime ministers David Cameron and Theresa May, was speaking in Dubai on the sidelines of the inaugural Middle East chapter of Signum Global Advisors, chaired by Charles Myers and launched by Raha Moradi, where he took part in a closed-door, onstage discussion. Sir Michael was careful with his words about the White House. Asked whether US President Donald Trump was an unreliable, unpredictable partner for the Gulf and Europe, he pointed to Moscow instead. “The most unreliable person clearly is President [Vladimir] Putin.” It is, to borrow the Irish, a mé féin foreign policy in Washington: me, myself and I. For America's allies, the old guarantees are no longer a given. However, he was clear that the ground had moved. “You have an unpredictable element now,” he said. “Policy shifts suddenly.” 'Gulf security is our security' “Gulf security is our security,” Sir Michael said. “It's our economic security. It's our energy security.” The trade and energy flowing through the region, he said, fed straight into the British economy and inflation, “and in the end, affects interest rates back in the UK”. “So we have a huge interest, as well as friendships and historical ties,” he said. The pressure on those ties is rising. Since July, the Houthis have been in direct conflict with Saudi Arabia , declaring a naval blockade of the kingdom and attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, while threatening to close the Bab Al Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. The Strait of Hormuz has already been disrupted by the US-Israel war with Iran. Britain has stepped up, but only so far. In April, the RAF deployed its Rapid Sentry air-defence system to Kuwait. Last month, in the first substantial foreign policy decision of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government, London agreed to a Saudi request for an RAF Voyager tanker to keep the kingdom's Typhoon jets in the air for longer. Ministers described it as a strictly defensive, “time-limited commitment”. “Well, we've responded to Kuwait's call for assistance,” Sir Michael said. “The Saudis asked us for help.” The most obvious step, he said, is to make sure the Houthis cannot disrupt the Bab Al Mandeb strait in the way Hormuz has been disrupted, which means tackling Houthi strikes “at source”. Asked whether strikes would be a big step for Mr Burnham, he said: “It would be, and clearly, they've considered it.” Labour has been reluctant before. In February, under Keir Starmer, the government initially refused to let the US use British bases, including Diego Garcia, for strikes on Iran, before reversing course. Sir Michael said the government had now “reversed that decision and said they can use Diego Garcia, but I think we should be doing more than that”. Gulf states, he said, are “with us, by the way, in the long-term battle against international terrorism ”, as they were in the international coalition against ISIS. Europe's turn to do more The same logic applies in Europe, where, Sir Michael said, the continent had been too slow to carry its share of the pressure on Moscow. He called Washington's diesel deal with Russia a misstep. This month, the US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027, and on Friday, Mr Trump signed an executive order pausing new Russia sanctions passed by Congress. “I'm afraid it's a miscalculation,” Sir Michael said. The volumes are too small to bring down diesel prices in the US and the deal is unlikely to move a ceasefire any further forward, he said. Mr Putin, he argued, would read it as weakness. “He's given up nothing in return,” he said. Russia has kept up its attacks on Ukraine 's civilian infrastructure, he added, and “he hasn't come to change any of his negotiating position about the future of Ukraine”. Asked whether it undermines sanctions as a weapon globally, he said it does. “You're either all in on sanctions or you're not.” Mr Trump, he conceded, has a point: “Where Trump is right, that our sanctions haven't been fully applied.” Europe has been far too slow to cut its dependence on Russian oil and gas, to police the shadow fleet and to use sanctioned Russian assets to help Ukraine, Sir Michael said. “Europe keeps passing new packages of sanctions, which rather casts doubt on the previous packages.” The EU adopted its 22nd package on October 12, the largest single round of listings yet at 1,569 individuals and entities. Brussels is already drafting a 23rd. Yet EU countries still bought €817 million ($917 million) of Russian pipeline gas and €615 million of Russian LNG in September. Pressure on Kyiv The stakes are highest in Ukraine . “I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Bloomberg this week. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war” against Russia “could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks.” A capitulation would not only encourage Mr Putin, Sir Michael said. It would put Russia's near neighbours “in the firing line, whether it's Moldova, the rest of Georgia, even the Baltic states, even though they're part of Nato ”. Moscow regards those countries as its “near abroad”, he said, “and they will be much more exposed. But it will also send a signal right round the world to other countries that want to extend their borders”. “China, of course, has ambitions to bring Taiwan formally back inside China, to extend its influence across the South China Sea.” The idea that might makes right, Sir Michael warned, “is very dangerous for the international community”. events.title: Europe has few alternatives to counter China other than costly protectionism
events.summary: The Scene Pascal Lamy negotiated China’s accession to the WTO in 2001 on behalf of the EU. A decade later, in a speech in Shanghai, Europe’s former trade commissioner lauded what he called a “win-win” outcome. But like a growing number of current and former European leaders, he’s grown alarmed as China’s trade surplus with the EU has ballooned. Lamy, now with the Jacques Delors Institute, was one of the authors of a recent policy paper that called for restrictions on Chinese exports using a quota system — an idea that the EU has now embraced. Q&A Andy Browne: Is the EU-China trade war now off? Pascal Lamy: I interpret the recent deal on hybrid cars’ export restraints as a first step in the right direction. I think the European side will consider this as a down payment. In my view, we need further steps to seriously address this rocketing Chinese trade surplus with Europe. So is this a tactical concession by China or a strategic shift? Both interpretations are possible. But from the EU side, this will not be seen as sufficient. Is the car deal a model for other sectors? Yes, indeed, although voluntary export restraints raise a series of technical issues. It’s certainly easier for hybrid cars than it is for chemicals or pharmaceuticals. And, of course, when you look at the numbers you need quite a lot more given the [EU’s] €350 billion annual trade deficit with China. You once called China’s WTO accession a “win-win.” Recently, you said that “China is killing open global trade.” What changed? I changed my mind because China changed. None of us predicted the speed of economic growth in China. A lot of people now say ‘you made a mistake by not forecasting that China would become an enormous elephant.’ My usual answer is: Who said that at the time? Give me some evidence that we had a choice between those who said ‘be careful’ and those who said ‘that’s a great idea.’ [Former Chinese Premier] Zhu Rongji thought that the Chinese miracle was a clever mix of Chinese characteristics and good old Western liberal capitalist market recipes. This is not the view of Xi Jinping. He believes that the incredible economic success of the past 20 years is due to the fact that China is led by the Chinese Communist Party. Also, the state-owned sector is larger today than it was in 2010. What’s changed, too, is that China no longer plays the game of comparative advantage, which is the ideological basis of the World Trade Organization. If you are better — cost and quality wise — than I am at everything, where’s the comparative advantage? Isn’t a big part of the problem that China now out-competes Europe? I’m not saying that all of China’s comparative advantage is, let’s say, WTO illegitimate. There is their education system, their engineers, their planning system, and the size of their market. But there’s another part which is not in line with an open rules-based trading system. By the way, what’s also changed is that a lot of markets that were open to China — the US, Turkey, Japan — have taken protectionist measures. China’s exports are now going to Europe, the only large and deep market that is still wide open. Germany and France have proposed a “kill switch” that could shut China out of European markets completely. Is that a good idea? I disagree with that formula. It’s like the US using Section 301 to determine whether a trade partner is playing fair or not. The Jacques Delors Institute has proposed a WTO compatible quota system with in-quota tariffs and out-of-quota tariffs. That’s a big difference — it’s predictable, rules-based, with benchmarks and numbers, and everyone understands clearly how the system works. There is no unilateral determination except for the size of the quota. China also has a ‘kill switch’ — rare earths. Can Europe really afford to risk a trade war? China’s rare earth dominance is time-limited. The US, EU, and Japan have started working on alternatives. If you over-use market dominance, markets adjust, and there’s a big price incentive to innovate. Tariffs raise prices. Are European consumers ready to pay a premium? Some prices will be higher, yes. Protection is costly. But what’s the alternative? You have to choose between that and industry closures, social problems, and the growth of extremism on the right and left of European politics. Can China be persuaded to compromise? I’ve been trying to convince my Chinese friends that they should care about this. We have to convince them that if the people who will govern Europe are the products of industrial and social shocks that China is creating, they will be much tougher with China than we, traditional center left or center right, are.
